chapters.title: Notice
paragraphs: Anyone caught trying to find a motive in this story will be prosecuted. Anyone caught trying to find a moral in it will be banished. Anyone caught trying to find a plot in it will be shot.
BY ORDER OF THE AUTHOR, PER G. G., CHIEF OF ORDNANCE.

chapters.title: Explanatory
paragraphs: This book uses a number of dialects, namely: the Missouri negro dialect; the roughest form of backwoods Southwestern speech; the ordinary “Pike County” dialect; and four lightly altered versions of that last one. The differences were not worked out carelessly or by guessing. They were done with great care, and with the steady help of a close, firsthand knowledge of each of these ways of talking.
I give this explanation because, without it, many readers would assume that all these characters were trying to talk the same way and failing at it.
THE AUTHOR.

chapters.title: Chapter I — Civilizing Huck
paragraphs: You won’t know about me unless you’ve read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn’t matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote that book, and mostly he told the truth. He stretched a few things, but mostly it was true. That’s nothing special. I never met anybody who didn’t lie once in a while, except Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly (Tom’s Aunt Polly, that is), and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all in that book, which is mostly a true one, with a few stretchers in it, like I said before.

Now, here’s how that book ends. Tom and I found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars each, all in gold. It was an awful lot of money, all piled up. Well, Judge Thatcher took it and invested it, and it earned us a dollar a day each, all year round. That was more than anybody knew what to do with. The Widow Douglas adopted me as her son, and said she’d civilize me. But it was hard living in that house all the time, since the widow was so dreadfully regular and proper in everything she did. So when I couldn’t stand it any longer, I took off. I got back into my old rags and my sugar barrel, and I was free and happy. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and told me he was going to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I’d go back to the widow and be respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and she called me plenty of other names too, but she never meant any harm by it. She put me in those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and feel squeezed up tight. Well, then the same old routine started over. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to show up on time. When you got to the table you couldn’t just start eating. You had to wait while the widow bowed her head and grumbled a little over the food, even though there wasn’t really anything wrong with it, except that everything was cooked separately. In a barrel of leftovers it’s different. Things get mixed together, the juices swap around, and it all tastes better.

After supper she got out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers. I was dying to find out all about him, but after a while she let slip that Moses had been dead for quite some time. After that I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t have any use for dead people.

Before long I wanted a smoke, and I asked the widow to let me. She wouldn’t. She said it was a nasty habit and not clean, and that I should try to quit. That’s just how some people are. They’re against a thing when they don’t know the first thing about it. Here she was, fussing over Moses, who was no relation of hers and no use to anybody, being dead, you see, and yet she found plenty to criticize in me for doing something that had some good in it. And she took snuff herself, too. Of course, that was fine, because she did it.

Her sister, Miss Watson, a pretty skinny old maid with spectacles on, had just come to live with her, and she went at me with a spelling book. She worked me fairly hard for about an hour, and then the widow made her let up. I couldn’t have stood much more. Then came another hour of deadly boredom, and I got fidgety. Miss Watson would say, “Don’t put your feet up there, Huckleberry,” and “Don’t slouch like that, Huckleberry—sit up straight,” and soon after, “Don’t yawn and stretch like that, Huckleberry—why don’t you try to behave?” Then she told me all about the bad place, and I said I wished I was there. That made her angry, but I didn’t mean anything by it. All I wanted was to go somewhere. All I wanted was a change, and I wasn’t picky. She said it was wicked to say what I said. She said she wouldn’t say it for anything in the world, because she was going to live so she could go to the good place. Well, I couldn’t see any advantage in going where she was going, so I decided I wouldn’t try for it. But I never told her so, because it would only cause trouble and wouldn’t do any good.

Now that she had a head start, she kept right on and described the good place in full. She said that all a person did there was wander around all day long with a harp, singing, forever and ever. So I wasn’t impressed. But I kept that to myself. I asked whether she figured Tom Sawyer would end up there, and she said not likely, not by a long shot. That pleased me, since I wanted him and me to stay together.

Miss Watson kept pecking away at me, and it got tiresome and lonely. After a while they brought the niggers in and had prayers, and then everybody went off to bed. I went up to my room with a candle stub and set it on the table. Then I sat down in a chair by the window and tried to think of something cheerful, but it was no use. I felt so lonely I almost wished I was dead. The stars were shining, and the leaves in the woods rustled so mournfully. Far off I heard an owl hooting about somebody who’d died, and a whippoorwill and a dog crying about somebody who was about to die. The wind kept trying to whisper something to me, and I couldn’t make out what, and that sent cold shivers over me. Then, way out in the woods, I heard the kind of sound a ghost makes when it wants to tell somebody what’s weighing on its mind but can’t make itself understood, so it can’t rest easy in its grave and has to wander around like that every night, grieving. I got so low and scared that I really wished I had some company. Soon a spider came crawling up my shoulder. I flicked it off, and it landed in the candle flame, and before I could move it was all shriveled up. Nobody had to tell me that was an awfully bad sign that would bring me bad luck, so I was scared and nearly shook my clothes right off. I got up and turned around in my tracks three times, crossing my chest every time. Then I tied a little lock of my hair with a thread to keep witches away. But I had no faith in it. That’s what you do when you’ve lost a horseshoe you found, instead of nailing it up over the door. But I’d never heard anybody say it was a way to keep off bad luck after you’d killed a spider.

I sat down again, shaking all over, and got out my pipe for a smoke, since the house was as still as death now and the widow wouldn’t find out. Well, after a long while I heard the clock far off in town go boom—boom—boom, twelve strokes, and then it was quiet again, quieter than ever. Soon I heard a twig snap down in the dark among the trees. Something was moving. I sat still and listened. Then I could just barely make out a “_me-yow! me-yow!_” down there. That was good! I said “_me-yow! me-yow!_” back, as softly as I could, and then I put out the light and scrambled out the window onto the shed. I slid down to the ground and crawled in among the trees, and sure enough, there was Tom Sawyer waiting for me.

chapters.title: Chapter II — The Boys Escape Jim
paragraphs: We tiptoed along a path through the trees toward the far end of the widow’s garden, ducking so the branches wouldn’t scrape our heads. As we were passing the kitchen, I tripped over a root and made a noise. We crouched down and lay still. Miss Watson’s big nigger, named Jim, was sitting in the kitchen doorway. We could see him pretty clearly, because there was a light behind him. He got up and stretched his neck out for about a minute, listening. Then he said:
“Who dah?”

He listened some more, then came tiptoeing over and stood right between us. We could almost have touched him. Well, it was probably minutes and minutes without a sound, and all of us so close together. A spot on my ankle started itching, but I didn’t dare scratch it. Then my ear started to itch, and then my back, right between the shoulders. It felt like I’d die if I couldn’t scratch. Well, I’ve noticed that plenty of times since. If you’re around fancy folks, or at a funeral, or trying to fall asleep when you’re not sleepy—anywhere it won’t do to scratch—you’ll itch in upwards of a thousand places. Soon Jim said:
“Hey, who’s that? Where are you? Dog my cats if I didn’t hear something. Well, I know what I’m gonna do: I’m gonna sit right here and listen till I hear it again.”

So he sat down on the ground between me and Tom. He leaned his back against a tree and stretched his legs out until one of them nearly touched one of mine. My nose started to itch. It itched until tears came into my eyes. But I didn’t dare scratch. Then it began to itch on the inside. Next I started itching underneath. I didn’t know how I was going to sit still. This misery went on for six or seven minutes, but it felt a lot longer. I was itching in eleven different places now. I figured I couldn’t stand it another minute, but I clenched my teeth hard and got ready to try. Just then Jim began to breathe heavily, and then he began to snore, and pretty soon I was comfortable again.

Tom gave me a signal, a little noise with his mouth, and we crept away on our hands and knees. When we were ten feet off, Tom whispered that he wanted to tie Jim to the tree for fun. But I said no. He might wake up and make a fuss, and then they’d find out I wasn’t in bed. Then Tom said he didn’t have enough candles and he would slip into the kitchen and get some more. I didn’t want him to try. I said Jim might wake up and come in. But Tom wanted to risk it, so we slid in there and got three candles, and Tom left five cents on the table to pay for them. Then we got out, and I was sweating to get away. But nothing would do for Tom except crawling over to where Jim was, on his hands and knees, to play a trick on him. I waited, and it seemed like a long time, with everything so still and lonely.

As soon as Tom was back, we hurried along the path, around the garden fence, and soon ended up on the steep top of the hill on the other side of the house. Tom said he’d slipped Jim’s hat off his head and hung it on a branch right over him, and Jim had stirred a little but hadn’t woken up. Afterward Jim said the witches had put a spell on him and put him in a trance, and rode him all over the state, and then set him back under the trees and hung his hat on a branch to show who’d done it. The next time Jim told it, he said they rode him down to New Orleans. After that, every time he told it, he stretched it a little more, until finally he said they rode him all over the world and nearly wore him to death, and his back was covered in saddle sores. Jim was awfully proud of it, and he got so he hardly noticed the other niggers. Niggers would come miles to hear Jim tell it, and he was looked up to more than any nigger in that country. Strange niggers would stand there with their mouths open and look him over as if he was a wonder. Niggers are always talking about witches in the dark by the kitchen fire. But whenever one of them was going on and acting like he knew all about such things, Jim would happen to walk in and say, “Hm! What you know ’bout witches?” and that nigger would be shut up and have to take a back seat. Jim always wore that five-cent piece around his neck on a string. He said it was a charm the devil had given him with his own hands, and the devil had told him he could cure anybody with it and call up witches whenever he wanted, just by saying something to it. But he never told anyone what he said to it. Niggers would come from all around and give Jim anything they had, just for a look at that five-cent piece. But they wouldn’t touch it, because the devil had had his hands on it. Jim was nearly ruined as a servant, because he got stuck-up from having seen the devil and been ridden by witches.

When Tom and I reached the top of the hill, we gazed down at the village and saw three or four lights flickering, where there were sick folks, maybe. Overhead the stars were sparkling fine, and down past the village lay the river, a full mile across, awfully quiet and grand. We climbed down the hill and found Jo Harper, Ben Rogers, and two or three other boys hiding in the old tanyard. We untied a skiff, rowed two and a half miles down the river to the big scar on the hillside, and landed.

We walked up to a clump of bushes, where Tom made everybody swear to keep the secret. Then he pointed out a hole in the hill, in the thickest part of the brush. We lit the candles and crawled inside on our hands and knees. After about two hundred yards the cave opened out. Tom felt his way among the passages and soon ducked under a wall where you’d never have guessed there was an opening. We followed a narrow stretch into a sort of room, all damp and clammy and cold, and stopped there. Tom said:
“All right, now we’re starting a band of robbers, and it’s called Tom Sawyer’s Gang. Anybody who wants to join has to swear an oath and sign his name in blood.”

Everybody was up for it. So Tom pulled out a sheet of paper with the oath already written on it and read it aloud. It swore every boy to stand by the band and never reveal its secrets. If anyone did harm to any boy in the band, then whichever boy was ordered to kill that person and his family had to carry it out, and he wasn’t allowed to eat or sleep until he had killed them and hacked a cross in their chests, which was the sign of the band. Nobody outside the band could use that mark, and if someone did, he would be taken to court; and if he did it a second time, he would be killed. And if any member of the band gave away the secrets, his throat would be cut, his carcass burned up and the ashes scattered everywhere, and his name struck from the list with blood and never spoken by the gang again. A curse would be put on it, and it would be forgotten forever.

Everybody said it was a truly beautiful oath, and they asked Tom whether he’d thought it all up himself. He said part of it, but the rest came out of pirate books and robber books, and every high-class gang had it.
Some of the boys thought it would be a good idea to kill the _families_ of boys who gave away the secrets. Tom said that was a fine idea, so he took a pencil and added it. Then Ben Rogers spoke up:
“What about Huck Finn? He doesn’t have any family. What are you going to do about him?”
“Well, doesn’t he have a father?” said Tom Sawyer.
“Sure, he’s got a father, but you can never find him these days. He used to lie around drunk with the hogs down at the tanyard, but nobody’s seen him around here for a year or more.”

They talked it over, and they were about to throw me out, because they said every boy had to have a family or somebody to kill, or it wouldn’t be fair to the others. Well, nobody could think of a way around it. They were all stumped and sat there silent. I was close to crying, but then I suddenly thought of something, and I offered them Miss Watson. They could kill her. Everybody said:
“Oh, she’ll do fine. That settles it. Huck can join.”
After that, each of them pricked a finger with a pin to draw blood for signing, and I put my mark on the paper.
“Now,” said Ben Rogers, “what line of business is this Gang in?”
“Nothing but robbery and murder,” Tom said.
“But who are we going to rob? Houses, or cattle, or—”

“Pshaw! Stealing cattle and that sort of thing isn’t robbery. It’s burglary,” said Tom Sawyer. “We’re not burglars. That has no style at all. We’re highwaymen. We stop stagecoaches and carriages on the road, wearing masks, and kill the people and take their watches and money.”
“Do we always have to kill the people?”
“Oh, certainly. It’s the best way. Some experts think otherwise, but mostly they say it’s best to kill them. The exception is a few that you bring to the cave and hold there until they’re ransomed.”
“Ransomed? What does that mean?”
“No idea. But it’s what they do. I’ve read it in books, so naturally we have to do it too.”
“But how can we do it if we don’t even know what it is?”
“Why, confound it, we’ve _got_ to do it! Didn’t I tell you it’s in the books? Do you want to start doing things differently from the books and make a big mess of everything?”

“Oh, that’s fine to _say_, Tom Sawyer, but how on earth are we supposed to ransom these fellows if nobody knows how it’s done? That’s the very thing _I_ want to find out. So what do you _figure_ it means?”
“Well, I can’t say. But maybe when you keep them until they’re ransomed, it means you hold on to them until they’re dead.”

“Now that’s more like it. That’ll do. Why couldn’t you have said so before? We’ll keep them until they’re ransomed to death. And a nuisance they’ll be, too, eating up everything and always trying to get loose.”
“What are you talking about, Ben Rogers? How can they get loose when there’s a guard watching them, ready to shoot them down if they move an inch?”

“A guard! Well, isn’t that _fine_. So somebody has to stay up all night with no sleep, just to watch them. I think that’s foolish. Why can’t somebody just take a club and ransom them the minute they get here?”

“Because it isn’t that way in the books, that’s why. Now, Ben Rogers, do you want to do things properly or don’t you? That’s the question. Don’t you think the people who wrote the books know what the right way is? Do you think _you_ can teach them anything? Not by a long shot. No, sir, we’ll just go ahead and ransom them the regular way.”
“All right. I don’t mind, but I still say it’s a fool way to do it. Say, do we kill the women too?”

“Well, Ben Rogers, if I were as ignorant as you, I’d keep quiet about it. Kill the women? No. Nobody ever saw anything like that in the books. You bring them to the cave and you’re always as polite as can be to them, and after a while they fall in love with you and never want to go home again.”

“Well, if that’s how it’s done, I agree, but I don’t believe in it. Pretty soon the cave will be so crowded with women and fellows waiting to be ransomed that there won’t be any room left for the robbers. But go ahead. I’ve got nothing more to say.”
Little Tommy Barnes had fallen asleep by now, and when they woke him up he was frightened. He cried and said he wanted to go home to his ma and didn’t want to be a robber anymore.

At that, they all laughed and called him a cry-baby. It made him furious, and he threatened to run off and spill every secret. But Tom handed him five cents to hush him up, and told us all to go home and gather again the next week to rob somebody and kill some people.

Ben Rogers explained that he could hardly ever get away, except on Sundays, so he wanted to start the following Sunday. The other boys all declared that doing it on a Sunday would be wicked, and that ended the argument. They promised to meet up and pick a day as soon as possible. After that we elected Tom Sawyer first captain and Jo Harper second captain of the Gang, and started for home.
I climbed up the shed and crept in through my window just before daybreak. My new clothes were all greasy and covered in clay, and I was dead tired.

chapters.title: Chapter III — A Good Going-over
paragraphs: Well, in the morning old Miss Watson gave me a good talking-to about my clothes. The widow didn’t scold, though. She just cleaned off the grease and clay and looked so sorry that I figured I would behave for a while if I could. Then Miss Watson took me into the closet and prayed over me, but nothing came of it. She told me to pray every day and I would get whatever I asked for. But that wasn’t so. I tried it. Once I got a fishing line, but no hooks, and a line was no good to me without hooks. I prayed for hooks three or four times, but somehow it never worked. Finally, one day, I asked Miss Watson to try praying for me, but she said I was a fool. She never told me why, and I couldn’t make it out at all.

One time I sat down back in the woods and had a long think about it. I said to myself, if a person can get anything they pray for, why doesn’t Deacon Winn get back the money he lost on pork? Why can’t the widow get back her silver snuffbox that was stolen? Why can’t Miss Watson get fatter? No, I said to myself, there’s nothing to it. I went and told the widow about it, and she said what a person could get by praying was “spiritual gifts.” That was too much for me, but she explained what she meant. I was supposed to help other people, do everything I could for them, look out for them all the time, and never think about myself. That included Miss Watson, as I understood it. I went out in the woods and turned it over in my mind for a long while, but I couldn’t see any benefit in it, except for the other people. So in the end I decided I wouldn’t worry about it anymore, but just let it go. Sometimes the widow would take me aside and talk about Providence in a way that made your mouth water, but then the next day Miss Watson would take hold and knock it all down again. I figured there must be two Providences, and a poor fellow would stand a pretty fair chance with the widow’s Providence, but if Miss Watson’s Providence got hold of him, there was no help for him anymore. I thought it all through and decided I would belong to the widow’s, if he wanted me, though I couldn’t see how he would be any better off than before, considering I was so ignorant and so kind of low-down and ornery.

Pap hadn’t been seen for more than a year, and that suited me fine. I didn’t want to see him anymore. Whenever he was sober and could lay hands on me, he used to beat me, though I spent most of my time in the woods whenever he was around. Well, about then he was found drowned in the river, about twelve miles above town, or so people said. They figured it was him, anyway. They said the drowned man was just his size, wore rags, and had uncommonly long hair, all of which fit pap. But they couldn’t make anything out from the face, because it had been in the water so long that it hardly looked like a face at all. They said he was floating on his back. They pulled him out and buried him on the bank. But I didn’t stay comfortable for long, because something occurred to me. I knew perfectly well that a drowned man doesn’t float on his back, but on his face. So I knew right then that this wasn’t pap, but a woman dressed up in a man’s clothes. And so I was uneasy again. I figured the old man would turn up again sooner or later, though I wished he wouldn’t.

We played robbers on and off for about a month, and then I quit. All the boys did. We hadn’t robbed anybody or killed anybody. We had only pretended. We used to jump out of the woods and go charging down on hog-drivers and on women in carts taking vegetables to market, but we never caught a single one of them. Tom Sawyer called the hogs “ingots” and the turnips and such “julery,” and we would go back to the cave and talk big about what we’d done and how many people we’d killed and marked. But I couldn’t see what we got out of it. One time Tom sent a boy running around town with a burning stick, which he called a slogan (it was the signal for the Gang to gather). Then he said his spies had given him secret news that the next day a whole crowd of Spanish merchants and rich A-rabs would camp in Cave Hollow with two hundred elephants, six hundred camels, and over a thousand “sumter” mules, all loaded down with di’monds, and they had only four hundred soldiers to guard them. So we would lie in ambuscade, as he called it, and kill the whole bunch and grab the loot. He said we had to polish up our swords and guns and get ready. He couldn’t even go after a turnip cart without having the swords and guns all scoured up for it, though they were only lath and broomsticks, and you could scrub at them until you rotted, and they still weren’t worth a mouthful of ashes more than they were before. I didn’t believe we could beat such a crowd of Spaniards and A-rabs, but I wanted to see the camels and elephants, so I was there the next day, Saturday, in the ambuscade. When we got the signal, we rushed out of the woods and down the hill. But there weren’t any Spaniards or A-rabs, and no camels or elephants either. It was nothing but a Sunday-school picnic, and only the youngest class at that. We broke it up and chased the children up the hollow, but all we got was some doughnuts and jam, though Ben Rogers got a rag doll, and Jo Harper got a hymnbook and a religious tract. Then the teacher charged in and made us drop everything and run.

I hadn’t seen any di’monds, and I told Tom Sawyer so. He said there were loads of them there anyway, and there were A-rabs there too, and elephants and so on. I asked why we couldn’t see them, then. He said that if I weren’t so ignorant and had read a book called Don Quixote, I would know without asking. He said it was all done by enchantment. There were hundreds of soldiers there, he said, and elephants and treasure and the rest, but we had enemies, which he called magicians, and they had turned the whole thing into a little children’s Sunday school, just out of spite. I said fine, then what we ought to do was go after the magicians. Tom Sawyer said I was a numskull.
“Why,” he said, “a magician could summon a whole bunch of genies, and they would chop you into hash before you could say Jack Robinson. They’re as tall as a tree and as big around as a church.”
“Well,” I said, “suppose we got some genies to help _us_. Couldn’t we beat the other crowd then?”
“How are you going to get them?”
“I don’t know. How do _they_ get them?”

“Why, they rub an old tin lamp or an iron ring, and then the genies come tearing in, with thunder and lightning ripping around and smoke rolling, and they do everything they’re told. They think nothing of yanking a shot-tower up by the roots and whacking a Sunday-school superintendent over the head with it, or any other man.”
“Who makes them tear around like that?”

“Why, whoever rubs the lamp or the ring. They belong to whoever rubs it, and they have to do whatever he says. If he tells them to build a palace forty miles long out of di’monds and fill it with chewing gum, or whatever you want, and bring an emperor’s daughter from China for you to marry, they have to do it, and they have to finish before sunup the next morning, too. And what’s more, they have to waltz that palace around the country to wherever you want it, you understand.”

“Well,” I said, “I think they’re a pack of fatheads for not keeping the palace themselves instead of giving it away like that. And what’s more, if I were one of them, I’d see him in Jericho before I’d drop my business and go to him just because he rubbed an old tin lamp.”
“Listen to you, Huck Finn! You’d _have_ to show up when he rubbed it, whether you liked it or not.”
“What! Me, as tall as a tree and as big as a church? All right, then, I _would_ come. But I bet I’d make that man climb the tallest tree in the country.”
“Shucks, there’s no use talking to you, Huck Finn. You don’t seem to know anything, somehow. You’re a perfect saphead.”

I chewed on all this for two or three days, and then I figured I ought to find out whether there was anything to it. I got hold of an old tin lamp and an iron ring, took them out in the woods, and rubbed and rubbed until I was sweating like an Injun, planning to build myself a palace and sell it. It was no use. Not one genie showed up. So I decided the whole business was just another of Tom Sawyer’s lies. He may have believed in the A-rabs and the elephants, but I think different. It had all the marks of a Sunday-school.

chapters.title: Chapter IV — Huck and the Judge
paragraphs: Well, three or four months went by, and winter was well along. I had been going to school nearly the whole time, and I could spell and read and write a little, and recite the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five. I don’t figure I could ever get any further than that if I lived forever. I don’t put much stock in mathematics, anyway.

I hated school at first, but after a while I got so I could put up with it. Whenever I got extra tired of it I skipped a day, and the whipping I got the next morning did me good and cheered me up. So the longer I went, the easier it got. I was getting used to the widow’s ways, too, and they didn’t rub me so raw. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed mostly felt tight and squeezing, but before the cold weather came I used to slip out and sleep in the woods now and then, and that was a rest to me. I liked the old ways best, but I was starting to like the new ones a little bit, too. The widow said I was coming along slow but sure, and doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I happened to knock over the salt-cellar. I grabbed for some salt as fast as I could, to throw over my left shoulder and head off the bad luck, but Miss Watson beat me to it and crossed me off. She says, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; what a mess you are always making!” The widow said a kind word for me, but that wasn’t going to keep off the bad luck, and I knew it well enough. After breakfast I went out feeling worried and shaky, wondering where the bad luck was going to land on me and what it would be. There are ways to head off some kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of those kinds, so I didn’t try anything. I just wandered along, low in spirits and keeping a lookout.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile, where you get through the high board fence. There was an inch of new snow on the ground, and I saw somebody’s tracks. They had come up from the quarry, stood around the stile for a while, and then gone on around the garden fence. It was strange that whoever it was hadn’t come in, after standing around like that. I couldn’t figure it out. It seemed very curious, somehow. I was about to follow the tracks around, but first I bent down to look at them. At first I didn’t notice anything, and then I did. In the left boot-heel there was a cross, made with big nails to keep off the devil.
I was on my feet in a second and scrambling down the hill. Every now and then I looked back over my shoulder, but I didn’t see anybody. I got to Judge Thatcher’s as fast as I could. He said:
“Goodness, my boy, you’re completely winded. Have you come about your interest?”
“No, sir,” I says. “Is there some for me?”

“Oh, yes. The half-year payment arrived last night—better than a hundred and fifty dollars. Quite a fortune for a boy. Let me invest it along with your six thousand. If you carry it off, you’ll only spend it.”
“No, sir,” I says, “spending it is the last thing I want. I don’t want any of it—not the six thousand, either. It’s yours if you’ll take it. I’m giving it to you, the six thousand and all.”
He looked surprised. He seemed unable to make sense of it. He says:
“Why, what do you mean, my boy?”
I says, “Please don’t ask me any questions about it. You’ll take it—won’t you?”
He says:
“Well, I’m puzzled. Is something the matter?”
“Just take it, please,” says I, “and don’t quiz me. That way I won’t have to tell you any lies.”
He thought it over for a while, and then he says:
“Oho-o! Now I follow you. It’s not a gift you want to make. You want to _sell_ me everything you own. That’s the sensible way.”
Then he scribbled a few lines on a sheet of paper, read them over to himself, and says:
“Now look here. It says ‘for a consideration.’ What that means is, I’ve bought the property off you and paid for it. This dollar is your payment. Go on, put your name to it.”
So I signed it and left.

Miss Watson’s nigger, Jim, had a hair-ball as big as your fist, taken out of the fourth stomach of an ox, and he used to work magic with it. He said there was a spirit inside it that knew everything. So that night I went to him and told him pap was back, because I had found his tracks in the snow. What I wanted to know was what pap was going to do, and whether he was going to stay. Jim got out his hair-ball, said something over it, then held it up and let it drop on the floor. It landed pretty solid and rolled only about an inch. Jim tried it again, and then once more, and it did exactly the same. Jim got down on his knees and put his ear against it and listened. But it was no use. He said it wouldn’t talk. He said sometimes it wouldn’t talk without money. I told him I had an old slick counterfeit quarter that was no good, because the brass showed through the silver a little. It wouldn’t pass anyhow, even if the brass didn’t show, because it was so slick it felt greasy, and that would give it away every time. (I figured I wouldn’t mention the dollar I got from the judge.) I said it was pretty bad money, but maybe the hair-ball would take it, since maybe it wouldn’t know the difference. Jim sniffed it and bit it and rubbed it, and said he would fix things so the hair-ball would think it was good. He said he would split open a raw Irish potato, put the quarter in between the halves, and leave it there all night. By morning you couldn’t see any brass, and it wouldn’t feel greasy anymore, so anybody in town would take it in a minute, let alone a hair-ball. Well, I had known before that a potato would do that, but I had forgotten it.

Jim slid the quarter under the hair-ball and got down to listen once more. This time the hair-ball was satisfied, he said, and it would tell my entire fortune if I wanted. I said to go ahead. So the hair-ball spoke to Jim, and Jim passed it along to me. He says:

“Yo’ ole father doan’ know yit what he’s a-gwyne to do. Sometimes he spec’ he’ll go ’way, en den agin he spec’ he’ll stay. De bes’ thing is to res’ easy en let de ole man do what he wants. Dey’s two angels hoverin’ roun’ him. One of ’em is white en shiny, en de other one is black. De white one gits him to go right fer a little while, den de black one sails in en busts it all up. Nobody can tell yit which one gwyne to git him in de end. But you is all right. You gwyne to have a lot o’ trouble in yo’ life, en a lot o’ joy. Sometimes you gwyne to git hurt, en sometimes you gwyne to git sick, but every time you’s gwyne to git well agin. Dey’s two gals flyin’ roun’ you in yo’ life. One of ’em’s light en de other one is dark. One is rich en de other one is po’. You’s gwyne to marry de po’ one first en de rich one later on. You wants to stay ’way from de water as much as you kin, en don’t take no risks, ’cause it’s written down in de book dat you’s gwyne to git hung.”
That night, when I lit my candle and went up to my room, there sat pap himself!

chapters.title: Chapter V — Huck’s Father
paragraphs: I had shut the door behind me. Then I turned around, and there he was. I used to be scared of him all the time, because he whipped me so much. I figured I was scared now, too. But in a minute I saw I was wrong—that is, after the first jolt, as you might say, when my breath sort of caught, since he was so unexpected. Right after that I saw I wasn’t scared of him enough to bother about.

He was nearly fifty, and he looked it. His hair was long and tangled and greasy, and it hung down so that his eyes shone through it as if he were hiding behind vines. It was all black, with no gray, and so were his long, matted whiskers. There was no color in his face, wherever his face showed. It was white, and not like another man’s white, but a white to turn your stomach, a white to make your skin crawl—a tree-toad white, a fish-belly white. As for his clothes, they were just rags, that was all. He had one ankle resting on the other knee. The boot on that foot was busted, and two toes stuck out, and he wiggled them now and then. His hat lay on the floor—an old black slouch hat with the top caved in, like a lid.

I stood there looking at him, and he sat there looking at me, with his chair tilted back a little. I put the candle down. I noticed the window was up, so he must have climbed in by way of the shed. He kept looking me up and down. After a while he says:
“Starchy clothes, very starchy. I suppose you figure you’re some kind of big-bug now, _don’t_ you?”
“Maybe I am, maybe I ain’t,” I says.

“Don’t you sass me,” says he. “You’ve taken on a whole heap of airs since I been off. I’ll cut you down to size before I’m through. They tell me you’re educated now, that you can read and write. Think you’re a better man than your father because he can’t? _I’ll_ beat that out of you. Who said you could go meddling with highfalutin foolishness like that, hey? Who said so?”
“The widow. She told me.”
“The widow, hey? And who gave the widow leave to poke her nose into what ain’t none of her business?”
“Nobody ever told her.”

“Well, I’ll teach her to meddle. And looky here—you quit that school, you hear? I’ll teach people to raise a boy to put on airs over his own father and act like he’s better’n what _he_ is. You let me catch you fooling around that school again, you hear? Your mother couldn’t read, and she couldn’t write, neither, before she died. Nobody in the family could before _they_ died. _I_ can’t, and here you are puffing yourself up like this. I ain’t the man to stand for it—you hear? Say, let me hear you read.”

I picked up a book and started in on something about General Washington and the wars. After I’d read about half a minute, he smacked the book with his hand and knocked it clear across the room. He says:

“Well, it’s true. You can do it. I wasn’t sure when you said so. Now listen here, you quit your frills. I ain’t standing for it. I’ll be watching for you, my smarty, and if I catch you anywhere near that school, I’ll give you a good hiding. Next thing, you’ll be getting religion, too. Never in my life saw a son like this.”
Next he grabbed a small blue and yellow picture showing some cows and a boy, and says:
“What’s this?”
“It’s something they gave me for learning my lessons well.”
He tore it up, and says:
“I’ll give you something better—I’ll give you a cowhide.”
He sat there mumbling and growling for a minute, and then he says:

“Well, ain’t you a perfumed dandy! A bed, and sheets and blankets, and a looking-glass, and a scrap of carpet on the floor—while your own father sleeps with the hogs at the tanyard. Never saw such a son. I’ll knock some of this nonsense out of you before I’m through, see if I don’t. Why, your airs never stop. They say you’re rich. Hey? What’s that about?”
“They lie—that’s what.”

“Looky here—mind how you talk to me. I’m standing about all I can stand now, so don’t give me no sass. I’ve been in town two days, and I ain’t heard nothing but how rich you are. I heard about it way down the river, too. That’s why I came. You get me that money tomorrow—I want it.”
“I ain’t got no money.”
“That’s a lie. Judge Thatcher has it. Go and get it. I want it.”
“I tell you I ain’t got any money. Go ask Judge Thatcher yourself, and he’ll say the same thing.”
“Fine. I will ask him, and I’ll squeeze it out of him, too, or find out why not. Now then, what have you got in your pocket? I want that.”
“I ain’t got but a dollar, and I want that for—”
“I don’t care what you want it for. Just hand it over.”

He took it and bit it to see if it was good, and then said he was going downtown to get some whisky, because he hadn’t had a drink all day. When he had stepped out onto the shed roof he stuck his head back in and cussed me for putting on frills and trying to be better than him. Then, when I figured he was gone, he came back and stuck his head in again and told me to remember about that school, because he was going to be waiting for me and whip me if I didn’t quit it.
The next day he was drunk, and he went to Judge Thatcher’s and bullied him and tried to make him hand over the money. But he couldn’t, and then he swore he’d make the law force him.

The judge and the widow went to court to get me taken away from him and have one of them made my guardian. But there was a new judge who had just arrived, and he didn’t know the old man. So he said courts shouldn’t step in and separate families if they could help it, and that he’d rather not take a child away from its father. So Judge Thatcher and the widow had to give up on the whole business.

The old man was so delighted he couldn’t keep still. He said he would thrash me black and blue unless I scraped up some money for him. So I borrowed three dollars from Judge Thatcher, and pap took it and got drunk. He went around blowing and cussing and whooping and carrying on, and he kept it up all over town, beating a tin pan, until nearly midnight. Then they locked him up, and the next day they hauled him before the court and locked him up again, this time for a week. But he said _he_ was satisfied. He was boss of his son, he said, and he’d make things hot for _him_.

When he got out, the new judge announced that he meant to make a man of him. So he took him home, cleaned him up and dressed him nicely, and sat him down at the family table for breakfast, dinner and supper, treating him like the finest pie in the pantry, so to speak. After supper the judge lectured him on temperance and such matters until the old man was in tears. He said he’d been a fool and thrown away his life, but now he was going to turn over a new leaf and become a man nobody would be ashamed of, and he hoped the judge would help him and not look down on him. The judge said he could hug him for saying so, and then _he_ started crying, and his wife started crying all over again. Pap said he’d always been a man people misunderstood, and the judge said he believed it. The old man said that what a fellow needed when he was down was sympathy, and the judge agreed, so they all cried again. When bedtime came, the old man stood up, held out his hand, and said:

“Look at it, ladies and gentlemen. Take hold of it and shake it. That was the hand of a hog, but it isn’t anymore. It’s the hand of a man who’s begun a new life, and he’ll die before he goes back. Mark my words, and don’t forget I said them. It’s a clean hand now. Shake it, and don’t be afraid.”

So they shook it, one after another all around the room, and cried. The judge’s wife kissed it. Then the old man signed a pledge, making his mark. The judge said it was the holiest moment on record, or something like that. Then they tucked the old man into a lovely room, the spare room, and sometime in the night he got terribly thirsty. He climbed out onto the porch roof, slid down a post, traded his new coat for a jug of forty-rod whisky, climbed back up, and had himself a fine old time. Toward daylight he crawled out again, drunk as a fiddler, rolled off the porch, broke his left arm in two places, and was nearly frozen to death when somebody found him after sunup. And when they went to look at that spare room, they had to take soundings before they could sail across it.
The judge was feeling rather sore about it. He said he supposed you might reform the old man with a shotgun, maybe, but he couldn’t think of any other way.

chapters.title: Chapter VI — He Went for Judge Thatcher
paragraphs: Well, before long the old man was up and about again. Then he took Judge Thatcher to court to make him hand over that money, and he came after me, too, for not quitting school. He caught me a couple of times and thrashed me, but I went to school anyway, and most of the time I dodged him or outran him. I hadn’t cared much about school before, but now I figured I’d go just to spite pap. The lawsuit was slow going. It seemed like they were never going to get started on it, so every now and then I’d borrow two or three dollars from the judge and give it to him, to keep from getting a whipping. Every time he got money he got drunk, every time he got drunk he raised Cain around town, and every time he raised Cain he landed in jail. It suited him fine. That kind of thing was right up his alley.

He started hanging around the widow’s place so much that she finally told him that if he didn’t quit hanging around there, she would make trouble for him. Well, _wasn’t_ he mad? He said he’d show everyone who was Huck Finn’s boss. So one day in the spring he lay in wait for me, caught me, and took me about three miles up the river in a skiff. We crossed over to the Illinois shore, where it was wooded and there were no houses except an old log hut, in a spot where the trees grew so thick you couldn’t find it unless you knew where it was.

He kept me with him all the time, and I never got a chance to run off. We lived in that old cabin, and every night he locked the door and put the key under his head. He had a gun that he’d stolen, I reckon, and we fished and hunted, and that’s what we lived on. Every so often he locked me in and walked three miles to the store at the ferry, where he traded fish and game for whisky. He’d bring it home, get drunk, have a good time, and beat me. The widow found out where I was after a while and sent a man over to try to get hold of me, but pap drove him off with the gun. It wasn’t long after that before I was used to being there, and I liked it, all except the whippings.

It was kind of lazy and jolly, lounging around comfortably all day, smoking and fishing, with no books and no studying. Two months or more went by, and my clothes turned into rags and dirt. I couldn’t see how I’d ever liked it so much at the widow’s, where you had to wash, eat off a plate, comb your hair, go to bed and get up at regular times, fuss over a book all the time, and have old Miss Watson picking at you constantly. I didn’t want to go back anymore. I had quit swearing because the widow didn’t like it, but now I took it up again because pap had no objection. All in all, it was pretty good living up there in the woods.

But after a while pap got too free with his hickory stick, and I couldn’t stand it. I was covered with welts. He also started going away a lot and locking me in. Once he locked me in and stayed gone three days. It was awfully lonesome. I figured he had drowned and I was never going to get out. I was scared. I made up my mind to work out some way of leaving. I’d tried many times to get out of that cabin, but I couldn’t find a way. There wasn’t a window big enough for a dog to squeeze through. I couldn’t climb up the chimney because it was too narrow. The door was made of thick, solid oak slabs. Pap was careful not to leave a knife or anything like it in the cabin when he was away. I reckon I had searched the place a hundred times, and I spent most of my time at it, since it was about the only way to pass the hours. But this time I finally found something: an old rusty wood saw with no handle, lying between a rafter and the roof boards. I greased it up and went to work. At the far end of the cabin, behind the table, an old horse blanket was nailed against the logs to keep the wind from blowing through the cracks and putting out the candle. I got under the table, lifted the blanket, and started sawing a section out of the big bottom log, big enough for me to crawl through. It was a good long job, but I was nearly done when I heard pap’s gun in the woods. I hid the signs of my work, dropped the blanket back, hid my saw, and soon pap came in.

Pap wasn’t in a good mood, which means he was his usual self. He said he’d been in town and everything was going wrong. His lawyer thought he’d win the lawsuit and get the money if they ever got the trial started, but there were ways of putting it off for a long time, and Judge Thatcher knew how to do it. He also said people were saying there would be another trial to take me away from him and make the widow my guardian, and they figured it would win this time. That shook me up quite a bit, because I didn’t want to go back to the widow’s and be so cooped up and “sivilized,” as they called it. Then the old man started cussing. He cussed everything and everybody he could think of, then cussed them all over again to make sure he hadn’t skipped anyone. After that he finished off with a general cuss all around, taking in a good many people whose names he didn’t know, and when he came to them he just called them what’s-his-name and carried right on cussing.

He said he’d like to see the widow get me. He said he would keep watch, and if they tried any such trick on him, he knew a place six or seven miles off where he could stash me, and they could hunt until they dropped and never find me. That made me uneasy again, but only for a minute. I figured I wouldn’t be around when he got the chance.

The old man sent me down to the skiff to fetch the things he’d bought. There was a fifty-pound sack of corn meal, a side of bacon, some ammunition, a four-gallon jug of whisky, an old book, and two newspapers for wadding, along with some tow. I carried up a load, then went back and sat on the bow of the skiff to rest. I thought it all over and decided I would take the gun and some fishing lines and head for the woods when I ran away. I figured I wouldn’t stay in one place, but just tramp straight across the country, mostly at night, hunting and fishing to stay alive, and get so far away that neither the old man nor the widow could ever find me again. I judged I would saw my way out and leave that night if pap got drunk enough, and I reckoned he would. I got so wrapped up in it that I didn’t notice how long I’d been sitting there until the old man hollered and asked whether I was asleep or drowned.

I got everything up to the cabin, and by then it was nearly dark. While I was cooking supper, the old man took a swig or two and got warmed up, and he started ripping and roaring again. He’d been drunk in town and had lain in the gutter all night, and he was a sight to see. You’d have thought he was Adam, he was so covered in mud. Whenever his liquor started to work, he almost always went after the government, and this time he said:

“Call this a government! Why, just look at it and see what it’s like. Here’s the law, all ready to take a man’s son away from him, a man’s own son, that he’s gone to all the trouble and worry and expense of raising. Yes, just when that man has finally got his son raised and ready to go to work and start doing something for _him_ and give him a rest, the law jumps him. And they call _that_ government! That’s not all, either. The law backs old Judge Thatcher and helps him keep me out of my property. Here’s what the law does: it takes a man worth six thousand dollars and more, and crams him into a rattletrap cabin like this, and lets him walk around in clothes that aren’t fit for a hog. They call that government! A man can’t get his rights in a government like this. Sometimes I’ve got a mighty notion to leave the country for good and all. Yes, and I _told_ them so. I told old Thatcher so to his face. Lots of them heard me and can tell you what I said. I said, for two cents I’d leave this blamed country and never come near it again. Those are the very words. I said, look at my hat, if you call it a hat. The lid sticks up and the rest of it slides down till it’s below my chin, and then it isn’t rightly a hat at all, but more like my head was shoved up through a joint of stovepipe. Look at it, I said, such a hat for me to wear, and I’d be one of the wealthiest men in this town if I could get my rights.

“Oh, yes, this is a wonderful government, just wonderful. Why, look here. There was a free nigger there from Ohio, a mulatto, nearly as white as a white man. He had the whitest shirt you ever saw on him, too, and the shiniest hat, and there isn’t a man in that town with clothes as fine as his. He had a gold watch and chain, and a silver-headed cane, the awfullest old gray-headed big shot in the State. And what do you think? They said he was a professor in a college, and could speak all kinds of languages, and knew everything. And that isn’t the worst of it. They said he could _vote_ when he was at home. Well, that finished me. I thought, what is this country coming to? It was election day, and I was just about to go and vote myself, if I hadn’t been too drunk to get there. But when they told me there was a State in this country where they’d let that nigger vote, I backed out. I said I’ll never vote again. Those are the very words I said, and they all heard me. The country can rot for all I care. I’ll never vote again as long as I live. And you should have seen the cool way of that nigger. Why, he wouldn’t have given me the road if I hadn’t shoved him out of the way. I said to the people, why isn’t this nigger put up at auction and sold? That’s what I want to know. And what do you suppose they said? Why, they said he couldn’t be sold until he’d been in the State six months, and he hadn’t been there that long yet. There, now, that’s a sample. They call that a government, when it can’t sell a free nigger until he’s been in the State six months. Here’s a government that calls itself a government, and acts like a government, and thinks it is a government, and yet it has to sit stock-still for six whole months before it can lay hold of a prowling, thieving, infernal, white-shirted free nigger, and—”

Pap was going on so hard that he never noticed where his old limber legs were taking him. He went head over heels over the tub of salt pork and skinned both shins, and the rest of his speech was the hottest kind of language, mostly thrown at the nigger and the government, though he gave the tub a share too, here and there. He hopped around the cabin a good deal, first on one leg and then on the other, grabbing first one shin and then the other, and finally he swung his left foot out all of a sudden and gave the tub a rattling kick. But that was poor judgment, because that was the boot with a couple of his toes poking out the front. So now he let out a howl that made a person’s hair stand on end, and down he went in the dirt, rolling around and clutching his toes, and the cussing he did then beat anything he had ever done before. He said so himself afterward. He had heard old Sowberry Hagan in his best days, and he said this beat him, too, but I reckon that was maybe piling it on a bit.

After supper Pap picked up the jug and announced that there was enough whisky in it for two drunks and one case of delirium tremens. That was always how he put it. I figured he’d be blind drunk in about an hour, and then I could steal the key or saw my way out, one or the other. He drank and drank, and after a while he tumbled onto his blankets, but my luck wasn’t running with me. He didn’t fall into a deep sleep. He was restless instead, groaning and moaning and tossing this way and that for a long time. Finally I got so sleepy that I couldn’t keep my eyes open no matter how hard I tried, and before I knew it I was sound asleep, with the candle still burning.

I don’t know how long I slept, but all of a sudden there was an awful scream and I was on my feet. There was Pap, wild-eyed, leaping around every which way and yelling about snakes. He said they were crawling up his legs. Then he’d jump and scream and say one had bitten him on the cheek, but I couldn’t see any snakes. He took off and ran around and around the cabin, hollering, “Take him off! Take him off! He’s biting me on the neck!” I never saw a man with such wild eyes. Before long he was all worn out and dropped down panting. Then he rolled over and over, amazingly fast, kicking things in every direction and striking and grabbing at the air and screaming that devils had hold of him. After a while he wore himself out and lay still, moaning. Then he lay stiller, and made no sound at all. I could hear the owls and the wolves far off in the woods, and it seemed terribly quiet. He was lying over in the corner. Presently he raised himself halfway and listened, with his head tilted to one side. He said, very low:

“Tramp, tramp, tramp. That’s the dead, tramp, tramp, tramp, coming for me. But I won’t go with them. Oh, they’re here! Don’t touch me, don’t! Take your hands off, they’re cold. Let go. Oh, leave a poor devil be!”

Next he dropped onto his hands and knees and crawled off, pleading with them to leave him be. He wrapped himself in his blanket and wormed under the old pine table, still pleading, and then he broke down crying. I could hear him sobbing right through the blanket.

After a while he rolled back out and sprang to his feet, wild-eyed, and when he saw me he came straight at me. He chased me around and around the room with a clasp-knife, calling me the Angel of Death and saying he’d kill me so I couldn’t come after him anymore. I begged and told him I was only Huck, but he laughed _such_ a screechy laugh, and roared and cussed, and kept right on chasing me. Once I turned sharp and ducked under his arm, and he grabbed me by the jacket between the shoulders. I thought I was done for, but I wriggled out of the jacket quick as lightning and saved myself. Before long he was tired out, and he dropped down with his back against the door and said he’d rest a minute and then kill me. He put his knife underneath him and said he’d sleep and get his strength back, and then we’d see who was who.

So he dozed off soon enough. After a while I took the old split-bottom chair and climbed up on it as quietly as I could, so as not to make any noise, and took down the gun. I ran the ramrod down the barrel to make sure it was loaded, then laid the gun across the turnip barrel, pointed at Pap, and sat down behind it to wait for him to move. And how slow and still the time did crawl along.

chapters.title: Chapter VII — Laying for Him
paragraphs: “Get up! What are you up to?”
I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to work out where I was. The sun was already up, and I’d been sound asleep. Pap was standing over me, looking sour and sick, too. He said:
“What are you doing with this gun?”
I figured he didn’t remember a thing about what he’d been doing, so I said:
“Somebody tried to get in, so I was lying in wait for him.”
“Why didn’t you wake me up?”
“Well, I tried to, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t budge you.”
“Well, fine. Quit standing there yapping all day. Get out there and see whether any fish are on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be there shortly.”

He unlocked the door and I hurried off up the riverbank. I noticed bits of branches and such floating down, along with some scraps of bark, so I knew the river had started to rise. I figured I’d be having a grand time if I were over in town. The June rise was always good luck for me, because as soon as it starts, cordwood comes floating down, and pieces of log rafts, sometimes a dozen logs together. All you have to do is catch them and sell them to the woodyards and the sawmill.

I went on up the bank with one eye out for Pap and the other out for whatever the rise might bring along. Then all of a sudden here came a canoe, and a beauty, too, about thirteen or fourteen foot long, riding high in the water like a duck. I dove off the bank headfirst like a frog, clothes and all, and swam for the canoe. I fully expected somebody to be lying down in it, because people often did that to fool folks, and when a fellow had rowed his skiff almost up to it they’d sit up and laugh at him. But it wasn’t like that this time. It was a drift canoe, sure enough, and I climbed in and paddled her ashore. I thought to myself, the old man will be glad when he sees this, since she’s worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore Pap wasn’t in sight yet, and as I was steering her into a little creek like a gully, all hung over with vines and willows, I got another idea. I figured I’d hide her well, and then, instead of heading for the woods when I ran off, I’d go down the river about fifty miles and camp in one place for good, and not have such a rough time tramping on foot.

It was pretty close to the shanty, and the whole time I thought I could hear the old man coming. But I got her hidden, and then I stepped out and peeked around a clump of willows, and there was the old man a little way down the path, drawing a bead on a bird with his gun. So he hadn’t seen anything.

When he came up I was hard at work pulling in a trotline. He scolded me a bit for being so slow, but I told him I’d fallen in the river and that was what took me so long. I knew he’d notice I was wet, and then he’d start asking questions. We took five catfish off the lines and went home.

After breakfast we lay down to sleep it off, both of us nearly worn out, and I got to thinking that if I could work out some way to keep Pap and the widow from trying to follow me, that would be a surer thing than trusting to luck to get far enough away before they missed me. You see, all kinds of things might happen. Well, for a while I couldn’t think of any way, but after a bit Pap sat up for a minute to drink another barrel of water, and he said:
“Next time a man comes prowling around here, you wake me up, you hear? That man wasn’t here for any good. I’d have shot him. Next time you wake me up, you hear?”
Then he dropped back down and went to sleep again. But what he’d said gave me the very idea I wanted. I told myself, I can fix it now so nobody will think of following me.

Around twelve o’clock we got up and went along the bank. The river was coming up fast, and plenty of driftwood was going by on the rise. Before long a piece of a log raft came along, nine logs fastened together. We went out in the skiff and towed it ashore. Then we had dinner. Anybody but Pap would have waited and watched the whole day, so as to catch more stuff, but that wasn’t Pap’s way. Nine logs was enough for one time, and he had to head right over to town and sell them. So he locked me in, took the skiff, and set off towing the raft at about half past three. I figured he wouldn’t be back that night. I waited until I reckoned he had a good head start, then got out my saw and went to work on that log again. He hadn’t even reached the other side of the river before I was out of the hole, and him and his raft were just a speck on the water, way off yonder.

First I hauled the sack of cornmeal over to the hidden canoe, pushed aside the vines and branches, and stowed it. The side of bacon went in the same way, then the whisky jug. Every scrap of coffee and sugar went too, and all the ammunition and the wadding. I took the bucket and the gourd, a dipper and a tin cup, my old saw, two blankets, the skillet and the coffeepot. I took fishlines and matches and anything else worth a cent. I stripped the place bare. I wanted an axe, but the only one was out at the woodpile, and I knew why I was leaving that. Last I carried out the gun, and I was finished.

I had worn down the ground quite a bit crawling out of the hole and dragging out so many things. So I fixed that up as well as I could from the outside, scattering dust over the spot to cover the smoothness and the sawdust. Then I set the piece of log back in its place and put two rocks under it and one against it to hold it there, since it was bent at that spot and didn’t quite touch the ground. If you stood four or five foot away and didn’t know it had been sawed, you’d never notice. Besides, this was the back of the cabin, and it wasn’t likely anybody would go poking around there.

It was grass all the way to the canoe, so I hadn’t left a track. I walked around to check. I stood on the bank and looked out over the river. All safe. So I took the gun and went a little way into the woods, and I was hunting around for some birds when I saw a wild pig. Hogs soon went wild in those bottoms after they’d gotten loose from the prairie farms. I shot this fellow and carried him back to the cabin.

I took the axe and smashed in the door. I beat it and hacked it up quite a bit while I was at it. I dragged the pig inside and took him nearly back to the table, and chopped into his throat with the axe, and laid him down on the ground to bleed. I say ground because that’s what it _was_: hard packed, with no boards. Well, next I took an old sack and filled it with big rocks, as many as I could drag, and I started it from the pig and dragged it to the door and through the woods down to the river and dumped it in, and down it sank, out of sight. You could easily see that something had been dragged across the ground. I sure did wish Tom Sawyer was there. I knew he’d take an interest in this kind of business and add the fancy touches. Nobody could outdo himself like Tom Sawyer at a thing like that.

Well, last of all I pulled out some of my hair, got the axe good and bloody, stuck the hair to the back of it, and slung the axe in the corner. Then I picked up the pig and held him against my chest with my jacket wrapped around him, so he couldn’t drip, until I got a good way below the house, and then I dumped him in the river. Now I thought of something else. So I went and got the bag of meal and my old saw out of the canoe and carried them to the house. I took the bag to where it used to stand and ripped a hole in the bottom of it with the saw, because there weren’t any knives and forks on the place. Pap did all his cooking with his clasp-knife. Then I carried the sack about a hundred yards across the grass and through the willows east of the house, to a shallow lake that was five miles wide and full of rushes, and ducks too, you might say, in season. A slough or creek led out of it on the other side and ran for miles, I don’t know where, but it didn’t go to the river. The meal sifted out and left a little trail all the way to the lake. I dropped Pap’s whetstone there too, so it would look like an accident. Then I tied up the rip in the meal sack with a string so it wouldn’t leak anymore, and took it and my saw back to the canoe.

By now it was nearly dark, so I let the canoe slip down the river to a spot under some willows hanging over the bank, and waited there for the moon to come up. I tied to a willow and ate a bite, then lay back in the canoe with a pipe to think up a plan. I reasoned that they’d follow the trail of that sack of rocks to the water and drag the river for me. They’d follow the meal trail to the lake and go poking down the creek after the robbers who’d killed me and carried off the goods. They’d never look in the river for anything except my dead body. Soon they’d tire of it and quit worrying about me. Fine. I could stop wherever I liked. Jackson’s Island suited me. I knew that island pretty well, and nobody ever went there. From there I could paddle to town at night, creep around, and pick up what I needed. Jackson’s Island was the place.

I was worn out, and before I knew it I’d dropped off. When I woke I couldn’t think where I was for a moment. I sat up and looked about, a bit frightened, and then it came back to me. The river looked miles and miles across. The moon was so bright that I could have counted the drift logs gliding by, black and silent, hundreds of yards out. Not a sound anywhere, and it looked late and even _smelled_ late. You know what I mean. I just don’t have the words for it.

I gave a big yawn and a stretch, and I was just about to untie and start off when I heard a sound far across the water. I listened. Before long I made it out. It was that dull, steady sound oars make in the rowlocks on a still night. I peeked out through the willow branches, and there it was, a skiff, way across the water. I couldn’t tell how many were in it. It kept coming, and when it was even with me I saw there was only one man in it. I thought, maybe it’s Pap, though I wasn’t expecting him. He drifted past below me with the current, and then he came swinging back up along the shore in the slack water, and he passed so close I could have reached out the gun and touched him. Well, it _was_ Pap, sure enough, and sober, too, going by the way he handled his oars.

I didn’t waste any time. In a minute I was gliding downstream, quiet but fast, in the shade of the bank. I went two and a half miles that way, then pushed out a quarter mile or more toward the middle of the river, because I’d soon be passing the ferry landing and somebody might spot me and call out. I drifted in among the driftwood, lay down flat in the bottom of the canoe, and let her float.

I lay there and had a good rest and a smoke on my pipe, gazing up at the sky, which didn’t have a cloud in it. The sky looks ever so deep when you’re lying on your back in the moonlight; I never knew that before. And how far a person can hear on the water on nights like that! I could hear people talking at the ferry landing, and every word they said, too. One man said the days were getting long and the nights short now. The other one said _this_ wasn’t one of the short ones, he figured—and then they laughed, and he said it over again, and they laughed again. Then they woke up another fellow and told him, and laughed, but he didn’t laugh. He snapped out something sharp and said to leave him alone. The first fellow said he planned to tell it to his old woman—she’d think it was pretty good—but he said that was nothing next to some of the things he’d said in his time. I heard one man say it was nearly three o’clock, and he hoped daylight wouldn’t take more than another week to get here. After that the talk drifted farther and farther off, until I couldn’t make out the words anymore. I could still hear the murmur, and a laugh now and then, but it sounded a long way away.

Now I was well below the ferry. I sat up, and there was Jackson’s Island, about two and a half miles downstream, thick with trees and rising out of the middle of the river, big and dark and solid, like a steamboat with no lights on. There was no sign of the sandbar at the head of it—that was all under water now.

It didn’t take me long to reach it. I shot past the head at a tearing pace, the current was so swift, and then I came into the slack water and landed on the Illinois side. I ran the canoe into a deep notch in the bank that I knew about. I had to part the willow branches to get in, and once I’d tied up, nobody could have seen the canoe from outside.

I climbed up and sat on a log at the head of the island and looked out over the big river, the black driftwood, and the town far across the water, three miles off, where three or four lights were twinkling. A huge lumber raft was about a mile upstream, drifting down, with a lantern in the middle of it. I watched it come creeping along, and when it was almost even with where I stood, I heard a man call, “Stern oars, there! Swing her head to starboard!” I heard it as plainly as if he’d been standing next to me.
The sky had turned a little gray, so I walked up into the woods and stretched out for a nap before breakfast.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII — Sleeping in the Woods
paragraphs: The sun was so high when I woke up that I figured it must be past eight o’clock. I lay there in the grass and the cool shade, thinking things over and feeling rested and rather comfortable and content. I could see the sun through a hole or two, but mostly there were big trees all around, and it was gloomy in among them. There were freckled patches on the ground where the light sifted down through the leaves, and the patches shifted about a little, which showed there was a breeze up above. A couple of squirrels sat on a branch and chattered at me in a very friendly way.

I was awfully lazy and comfortable and didn’t want to get up and cook breakfast. I was dozing off again when I thought I heard a deep “boom!” far up the river. I stirred myself, propped up on my elbow, and listened. Pretty soon I heard it again. I jumped up and looked out through a gap in the leaves, and I saw a cloud of smoke lying on the water a long way up, about even with the ferry. And there was the ferryboat, full of people, floating down. Now I understood what was going on. “Boom!” I saw white smoke spurt out of the ferryboat’s side. You see, they were firing a cannon over the water, trying to make my body come up to the top.

I was pretty hungry, but I couldn’t start a fire, because they might see the smoke. So I sat there watching the cannon smoke and listening to the booms. The river was a mile wide there, and it always looks pretty on a summer morning, so I was having a good enough time watching them hunt for my remains—if only I’d had a bite to eat. Then I happened to remember how they always put quicksilver in loaves of bread and set them afloat, because the loaves drift straight to a drowned body and stop right over it. So I said to myself, I’ll keep a lookout, and if any of those loaves are floating around after me, I’ll give them a chance. I moved to the Illinois edge of the island to see what luck I’d have, and I wasn’t disappointed. A big double loaf came along, and I nearly got it with a long stick, but my foot slipped and it floated farther out. Of course I was standing where the current runs closest to shore—I knew that much. But after a while another one came along, and this time I won. I pulled out the plug, shook out the little blob of quicksilver, and sank my teeth in. It was “baker’s bread”—what the rich folks eat, not any of your low-down corn pone.

I found a good spot among the leaves and sat on a log, munching the bread and watching the ferryboat, very well pleased. Then something occurred to me. I said to myself, I reckon the widow or the parson or somebody prayed that this bread would find me, and here it has gone and done it. So there’s no doubt there’s something to that business—that is, there’s something to it when somebody like the widow or the parson prays, but it doesn’t work for me, and I reckon it only works for the right kind of person.

I lit a pipe and had a good long smoke, and kept watching. The ferryboat was drifting with the current, and I figured I’d get a chance to see who was aboard when she came by, since she’d come in close, the same as the bread did. When she’d come pretty far down toward me, I put out my pipe, went to the place where I’d fished out the bread, and lay down behind a log on the bank in a little clearing. Where the log forked, I could peep through.

Before long she came drifting by, so close in that they could have laid down a plank and strolled ashore. Nearly everybody was on the boat: Pap, Judge Thatcher, Bessie Thatcher, Jo Harper, Tom Sawyer with his old Aunt Polly, Sid and Mary, and plenty of others. They were all talking about the murder, until the captain broke in:
“Keep your eyes peeled, now. The current hugs the shore right here, so he may have washed up and snagged in the brush along the water’s edge. I hope so, anyway.”

Well, I didn’t. They all pressed forward and leaned over the rails, practically in my face, silent, staring with everything they had. I could see every one of them just fine, but they couldn’t see me. Then the captain shouted:

“Stand clear!” and the cannon went off with such a blast right in front of me that the noise made me deaf and the smoke nearly blinded me, and I figured I was done for. If they’d had some bullets in it, I reckon they’d have gotten the corpse they were after. Well, I saw I wasn’t hurt, thank goodness. The boat floated on and went out of sight around the shoulder of the island. I could hear the booming now and then, farther and farther off, and after an hour I couldn’t hear it anymore. The island was three miles long. I figured they’d reached the lower end and were giving it up. But they weren’t done yet. They turned around the foot of the island and started up the channel on the Missouri side, under steam, booming once in a while as they went. I crossed over to that side and watched them. When they were even with the head of the island, they quit shooting, crossed over to the Missouri shore, and went home to town.

I knew I was safe now, since nobody else would come looking for me. I unloaded my gear from the canoe and made a snug camp in the thick woods. I stretched my blankets into a sort of tent and stowed my belongings under it so the rain couldn’t reach them. I caught a catfish and chopped him open with my saw, and around sundown I lit my campfire and ate supper. After that I set out a line to catch some fish for breakfast.

When it was dark I sat by my campfire smoking and feeling pretty well content. After a while, though, it got sort of lonesome, so I went and sat on the bank and listened to the current swishing along, and counted the stars and the drift logs and rafts that came down, and then went to bed. There’s no better way to pass the time when you’re lonesome. You can’t stay that way; you soon get over it.

That was how it went for three days and three nights, with no change at all. On the next day, though, I went exploring down the length of the island. I was the boss of it, since it all belonged to me, you might say, and I wanted to learn every corner of it, though mostly I just wanted something to fill the time. I found lots of strawberries, ripe and perfect, along with green summer grapes and green raspberries, and the green blackberries were only starting to show. I figured they’d all be useful sooner or later.

Well, I went poking along in the deep woods until I figured I wasn’t far from the lower end of the island. I had my gun along, but I hadn’t shot anything. It was for protection, and I thought I’d kill some game close to home. About then I nearly stepped on a good-sized snake, and it went sliding off through the grass and flowers, and I went after it, trying to get a shot. I hurried along, and all at once I jumped right onto the ashes of a campfire that was still smoking.

My heart jumped up into my lungs. I didn’t wait to look any further, but uncocked my gun and went sneaking back on tiptoe as fast as I could. Every now and then I stopped for a second among the thick leaves and listened, but my breath came so hard I couldn’t hear anything else. I slunk along a little farther, then listened again, and so on, and so on. If I saw a stump, I took it for a man. If I stepped on a stick and broke it, it felt as if somebody had cut one of my breaths in two and I’d only gotten half, and the short half, too.

When I got back to camp I wasn’t feeling very bold; I didn’t have much nerve left. But I told myself this was no time to be fooling around. So I loaded all my things into the canoe again to keep them out of sight, put out the fire, and scattered the ashes around to look like an old camp from last year, and then I climbed a tree.

I reckon I stayed up in that tree for two hours. I saw nothing and heard nothing—I only _thought_ I heard and saw about a thousand things. But I couldn’t stay up there forever, so finally I climbed down, though I stuck to the thick woods and kept watching the whole way. The only food I had was berries and the leftovers from breakfast.

Night came, and I was pretty hungry. As soon as it was good and dark, I pushed off before the moon came up and paddled across to the Illinois bank, a quarter of a mile or so. I went into the woods and cooked supper, and I’d nearly decided to stay there the whole night when I heard a _plunkety-plunk, plunkety-plunk_ and told myself, that’s horses. Then I heard voices. I threw everything back into the canoe as fast as I could and crept through the woods to learn what I could. I hadn’t gone far before I heard a man say:
“We’d better camp here if we can find a good spot. The horses are about worn out. Let’s look around.”
