I didn’t wait around, but shoved off and paddled away quietly. I tied up in my old spot and figured I’d sleep in the canoe.

I hardly slept. Somehow I couldn’t, with so much on my mind. Each time I woke up I felt sure somebody had a hand on my neck, so the sleep did me no good at all. At last I told myself, I can’t go on like this. I’m going to find out who’s here on the island with me, or die trying. Well, I felt better right away.

So I took my paddle and slid out from shore just a step or two, and then let the canoe drift down among the shadows. The moon was shining, and outside the shadows it made things nearly as bright as day. I poked along for the better part of an hour, with everything still as stones and sound asleep. By this time I was almost down to the lower end of the island. A cool little rippling breeze began to blow, and that was as good as saying the night was nearly over. I gave the paddle a turn and brought her nose to shore. Then I took my gun, slipped out, and went into the edge of the woods. I sat down on a log there and looked out through the leaves. I watched the moon go off duty and the darkness start to blanket the river. But in a little while I saw a pale streak over the treetops and knew the day was coming. So I took my gun and slipped off toward the place where I’d come across that campfire, stopping every minute or two to listen. But I had no luck somehow; I couldn’t seem to find the place. Then after a while, sure enough, I caught a glimpse of fire far off through the trees. I went toward it, cautious and slow. Soon I was close enough to have a look, and there lay a man on the ground. It nearly gave me the shivers. He had a blanket wrapped around his head, and his head was almost in the fire. I sat there behind a clump of bushes, about six feet from him, and kept my eyes on him steadily. It was getting to be gray daylight now. Pretty soon he yawned and stretched and threw off the blanket, and it was Miss Watson’s Jim! I bet I was glad to see him. I said:
“Hello, Jim!” and stepped out.
He jumped up and stared at me wildly. Then he dropped down on his knees, put his hands together, and said:

“Don’t hurt me—don’t! I ain’t never done no harm to a ghos’. I always liked dead folks, an’ done all I could for ’em. You go an’ git back in de river, where you b’longs, an’ don’t do nuffin’ to ol’ Jim, dat was always yo’ fren’.”

It didn’t take me long to make him understand I wasn’t dead. I was so glad to see Jim. I wasn’t lonesome anymore. I told him I wasn’t scared he’d tell anybody where I was. I kept on talking, but he just sat there looking at me and never said a word. Then I said:
“It’s broad daylight. Let’s have breakfast. Get your campfire going good.”
“What’s de use o’ buildin’ up a fire to cook strawberries an’ such truck? But you got a gun, ain’t you? Den we can git somethin’ better dan strawberries.”
“Strawberries and such truck,” I said. “Is that what you live on?”
“I couldn’t git nuffin else,” he said.
“Why, how long have you been on the island, Jim?”
“I come here de night after you was killed.”
“What, all this time?”
“Yes, indeedy.”
“And you haven’t had a thing to eat but that kind of garbage?”
“No, sah, nuffin else.”
“Well, you must be about starved, aren’t you?”
“I could eat a horse, I reckon. I think I could. How long you been on de island?”
“Since the night I got killed.”
“No! Why, what you been livin’ on? But you got a gun. Oh, yes, you got a gun. Dat’s good. Now you go kill somethin’ an’ I’ll build de fire.”

So we went over to where the canoe was. While he built a fire in a grassy clearing among the trees, I fetched cornmeal and bacon and coffee, the coffeepot and the frying pan, and sugar and tin cups. The nigger was knocked flat by all this, because he figured it was done by witchcraft. I caught a good big catfish, too, and Jim cleaned it with his knife and fried it.

When breakfast was ready, we stretched out on the grass and ate it piping hot. Jim dug in with everything he had, since he was nearly starved. Once we were pretty well stuffed, we lay back and took it easy. After a while Jim said:
“But look here, Huck, who was it dat got killed in dat shanty, if it wasn’t you?”
Then I told him the whole business, and he said it was clever. He said Tom Sawyer couldn’t have come up with a better plan than mine. Then I said:
“How did you come to be here, Jim, and how did you get here?”
He looked pretty uneasy and didn’t say anything for a minute. Then he said:
“Maybe I better not tell.”
“Why not, Jim?”
“Well, dere’s reasons. But you wouldn’t tell on me if I was to tell you, would you, Huck?”
“I’ll be darned if I would, Jim.”
“Well, I believe you, Huck. I—I _run off_.”
“Jim!”
“But remember, you promised you wouldn’t tell—you know you promised, Huck.”

“Well, I did. I said I wouldn’t, and I’ll keep my word. Honest _injun_, I will. People would call me a low-down Abolitionist and look down on me for keeping quiet—but that makes no difference. I’m not going to tell, and I’m not going back there, anyhow. So now let’s hear all about it.”

“Well, you see, it was like dis. Old missus—dat’s Miss Watson—she picks on me all de time and treats me pretty rough, but she always said she wouldn’t sell me down to Orleans. But I noticed dere was a nigger trader hangin’ around de place a lot lately, and I started gettin’ uneasy. Well, one night pretty late I creeps up to de door, and de door wasn’t shut all de way, and I hear old missus tellin’ de widow she’s gwine to sell me down to Orleans. She didn’t want to, but she could git eight hundred dollars for me, and it was such a big pile of money she couldn’t say no. De widow tried to git her to promise she wouldn’t do it, but I never waited to hear de rest. I lit out of dere mighty quick, I tell you.

“I took off and ran down de hill, figurin’ to steal a skiff along de shore somewhere above de town, but dere was still people up and about, so I hid in de old broke-down cooper shop on de bank to wait for everybody to go away. Well, I was dere all night. Dere was somebody around all de time. Along about six in de mornin’ skiffs started goin’ by, and by eight or nine every skiff dat went past was talkin’ about how your pap come over to town and said you was killed. Dese last skiffs was full of ladies and gentlemen goin’ over to see de place. Sometimes dey’d pull up at de shore and rest a while before dey started across, so from all de talk I come to know everythin’ about de killin’. I was powerful sorry you was killed, Huck, but I ain’t no more.

“I laid dere under de shavings all day. I was hungry, but I wasn’t scared, because I knowed old missus and de widow was gonna start for de camp meetin’ right after breakfast and be gone all day, and dey knows I go off with de cattle around daylight, so dey wouldn’t expect to see me around de place, and so dey wouldn’t miss me till after dark in de evenin’. De other servants wouldn’t miss me, because dey’d slip off and take a holiday as soon as de old folks was out of de way.

“Well, when it come dark I took off up de river road and went two miles or more, to where dere wasn’t no houses. I’d already made up my mind what I was gwine to do. You see, if I kept tryin’ to git away on foot, de dogs would track me. If I stole a skiff to cross over, dey’d miss dat skiff, you see, and dey’d know about where I’d land on de other side and where to pick up my trail. So I says, a raft is what I’m after. A raft don’t _make_ no track.

“After a while I see a light comin’ round de point, so I waded in and pushed a log ahead of me and swum more’n halfway across de river, and got in among de driftwood and kept my head down low, and kinda swum against de current till de raft come along. Den I swum to de back of it and grabbed hold. It clouded over and got pretty dark for a little while. So I climbed up and laid down on de planks. De men was all way yonder in de middle, where de lantern was. De river was risin’ and dere was a good current, so I figured by four in de mornin’ I’d be twenty-five miles down de river, and den I’d slip in just before daylight and swim ashore and take to de woods on de Illinois side.

“But I didn’t have no luck. When we was almost down to de head of de island, a man started comin’ toward de back with de lantern. I seen it was no use waitin’, so I slid overboard and struck out for de island. Well, I had a notion I could land most anywhere, but I couldn’t—de bank was too steep. I was almost to de foot of de island before I found a good place. I went into de woods and decided I wouldn’t fool with no more rafts, long as dey move de lantern around like dat. I had my pipe and a plug of dog-leg tobacco, and some matches in my cap, and dey wasn’t wet, so I was all right.”
“And so you haven’t had any meat or bread to eat all this time? Why didn’t you get mud turtles?”

“How you gwine to git ’em? You can’t sneak up on ’em and grab ’em, and how’s a body gwine to hit ’em with a rock? How could anybody do it in de night? And I wasn’t gwine to show myself on de bank in de daytime.”
“Well, that’s so. You must have had to stay in the woods the whole time, of course. Did you hear them firing the cannon?”
“Oh, yes. I knowed dey was after you. I seen ’em go by here—watched ’em through de bushes.”

A few young birds came along, fluttering a yard or two at a stretch and then settling. Jim said that meant rain was on the way. Young chickens flying like that were a sign of rain, he said, so he figured young birds meant the same. I was about to catch a few of them, but Jim wouldn’t allow it. He said it meant death. His father had been lying very sick once, he said, and some of them caught a bird, and his old granny declared his father would die, and he did.

Jim also said you must never count up the dishes you’re going to cook for dinner, because that brings bad luck. Shaking out the tablecloth after sundown did the same. And if a man kept a beehive and that man died, he said, somebody had to tell the bees before sunup the next morning, or the bees would all lose heart, stop working and die. Jim said bees never stung idiots, but I didn’t believe that, since I’d tried them lots of times myself and they never stung me.

A few of these I’d heard before, but not all. Jim knew signs of every kind. He claimed to know nearly everything. To me it seemed like every sign was about bad luck, so I asked him whether there were no signs of good luck. He answered:

“Mighty few—and _dey_ ain’t no use to a body. What you want to know when good luck’s a-comin’ for? Want to keep it away?” And he said: “If you got hairy arms and a hairy chest, it’s a sign you’s gwine to be rich. Well, dere’s some use in a sign like dat, ’cause it’s so far ahead. You see, maybe you got to be poor a long time first, and so you might git discouraged and kill yourself if you didn’t know by de sign dat you’s gwine to be rich someday.”
“Do you have hairy arms and a hairy chest, Jim?”
“What’s de use o’ askin’ dat question? Can’t you see I has?”
“Well, are you rich?”
“No, but I been rich once, and I’s gwine to be rich again. Once I had fourteen dollars, but I took to speculatin’ and got busted out.”
“What did you speculate in, Jim?”
“Well, first I tackled stock.”
“What kind of stock?”
“Why, livestock—cattle, you know. I put ten dollars in a cow. But I ain’t gwine to risk no more money in stock. De cow up and died on my hands.”
“So you lost the ten dollars.”
“No, I didn’t lose it all. I only lost about nine of it. I sold de hide and tallow for a dollar and ten cents.”
“That left you five dollars and ten cents. Did you speculate any more?”

“Yes. You know dat one-legged nigger dat belongs to old Mister Bradish? Well, he set up a bank, and he say anybody dat put in a dollar would git four dollars more at de end of de year. Well, all de niggers went in, but dey didn’t have much. I was de only one dat had much. So I held out for more dan four dollars, and I said if I didn’t git it I’d start a bank myself. Well, of course dat nigger wanted to keep me out of de business, because he says dere wasn’t business enough for two banks, so he say I could put in my five dollars and he pay me thirty-five at de end of de year.

“So I done it. Den I figured I’d invest de thirty-five dollars right off and keep things movin’. Dere was a nigger name’ Bob dat had caught hold of a wood flatboat, and his master didn’t know it. I bought it off him and told him to take de thirty-five dollars when de end of de year come. But somebody stole de flatboat dat night, and next day de one-legged nigger say de bank’s busted. So none of us got no money.”
“What did you do with the ten cents, Jim?”

“Well, I was gwine to spend it, but I had a dream, and de dream told me to give it to a nigger name’ Balum—Balum’s Ass dey call him for short. He’s one of dem chuckleheads, you know. But he’s lucky, dey say, and I seen I wasn’t lucky. De dream say let Balum invest de ten cents and he’d make a raise for me. Well, Balum he took de money, and when he was in church he hear de preacher say dat whoever give to de poor lend to de Lord, and is bound to git his money back a hundred times. So Balum he went and give de ten cents to de poor, and laid low to see what was gwine to come of it.”
“Well, what did come of it, Jim?”

“Nuffin never come of it. I couldn’t manage to collect dat money no way, and Balum couldn’t neither. I ain’t gwine to lend no more money without I see de security. Bound to git your money back a hundred times, de preacher says! If I could git de ten _cents_ back, I’d call it square and be glad of de chance.”
“Well, no harm done, Jim, if you’re bound to get rich again sooner or later.”
“Yes, and I’s rich now, come to look at it. I owns myself, and I’s worth eight hundred dollars. I wish I had de money, I wouldn’t want no more.”

chapters.title: Chapter IX — The Cave
paragraphs: I wanted to go and look at a spot near the middle of the island that I’d found while I was exploring. So we set out and got there soon enough, since the island was only three miles long and a quarter of a mile wide.

The place was a long, steep ridge, a hill about forty feet high. Getting to the top was rough going, with such steep sides and such thick bushes. We tramped and scrambled all over it, and finally we found a big cave in the rock, nearly at the top on the Illinois side. It was as big as two or three rooms bunched together, and Jim could stand straight up inside. It was cool in there. Jim wanted to carry our things in right away, but I said we didn’t want to be climbing up and down all the time.

Jim said that if we had the canoe hidden in a good place and all our things in the cave, we could run for it if anybody came to the island, and they would never find us without dogs. And besides, he said, those little birds had told us it was going to rain, and did I want our things to get wet?

So we went back and got the canoe, paddled up alongside the cave, and lugged all our things up there. Then we looked for a place close by to hide the canoe, among the thick willows. We took some fish off the lines and set the lines again, and started getting ready for dinner.
The cave’s entrance was big enough to roll a barrel through. On one side of it the floor stuck out a little, flat and a good place to build a fire. So we built one there and cooked dinner.

We spread the blankets on the cave floor for a carpet and ate our dinner there, with the rest of our things handy at the back. Before long the sky darkened and the thunder and lightning started, so the birds had been right. Right away the rain came, and it poured down like fury, and I never saw wind blow so hard. It was a regular summer storm. Everything outside would go so dark it looked blue-black, and lovely. The rain would come sweeping by so thick that trees a little way off looked faint and spidery. Then a blast of wind would arrive and bend the trees over and flip up the pale undersides of the leaves, and a real ripper of a gust would follow and set the branches thrashing their arms as if they’d gone wild. And then, just when it was at its bluest and blackest—_fst!_—everything was bright as glory, and you’d get a quick glimpse of treetops tossing around away off in the storm, hundreds of yards farther than you could see a moment before. In a second it was dark as sin again, and you’d hear the thunder let go with an awful crash and go rumbling, grumbling, tumbling down the sky toward the underside of the world, like empty barrels rolling down stairs—long stairs, where they bounce a lot, you know.
“Jim, this is nice,” I said. “There’s no place I’d sooner be than right here. Hand me another hunk of fish and some of that hot corn bread.”

“Well, you wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for Jim. You’d be down in dem woods wid no dinner, an’ gittin’ mos’ drownded too, dat you would, honey. Chickens knows when it’s gwine to rain, an’ so do de birds, chile.”

The river kept rising for ten or twelve days, until at last it spilled over its banks. The water stood three or four feet deep in the low parts of the island and on the Illinois bottomland. On that side it spread out many miles wide, but on the Missouri side the distance across was the same old half a mile, because the Missouri shore was nothing but a wall of high bluffs.

In the daytime we paddled the canoe all over the island. It was mighty cool and shady in the deep woods, even with the sun blazing outside. We wound in and out among the trees, and sometimes the vines hung so thick that we had to back up and go another way. On every old broken-down tree you could see rabbits and snakes and such. After the island had been flooded a day or two, they got so tame from hunger that you could paddle right up and put your hand on them if you wanted to. The snakes and turtles were the exception—they would slide off into the water. The ridge our cavern was on was full of them. We could have had pets enough if we’d wanted them.

One night we caught a little piece of a lumber raft, with nice pine planks. It was twelve feet wide and fifteen or sixteen feet long, and the top stood six or seven inches above the water—a solid, level floor. Sometimes we saw saw-logs go by in the daylight, but we let them go. We didn’t show ourselves in daylight.

Another night, up at the head of the island just before daylight, a frame house came floating down on the west side. It was two stories and tilted over quite a bit. We paddled out and climbed aboard, going in through an upstairs window. But it was still too dark to see, so we tied the canoe on and sat in her to wait for daylight.

Daylight started creeping in before we reached the foot of the island. Then we looked in through the window. We could pick out a bed, a table, two old chairs, and a lot of stuff lying around on the floor, and clothes hung against the wall. Something in the far corner looked like a man lying there. So Jim called out:
“Hello, you!”
It didn’t stir. So I hollered again, and then Jim said:
“Dat man ain’t sleepin’—he’s dead. Stay right here an’ I’ll go look.”
He went over, bent down, took a look, and said:
“It’s a dead man. Yes, indeedy, an’ naked too. He’s been shot in de back. I reck’n he’s been dead two or three days. Come in, Huck, but don’t look at his face—it’s too ghastly.”

I didn’t look at him at all. Jim threw some old rags over him, but he didn’t need to; I had no wish to see him. Heaps of greasy old cards lay scattered over the floor, along with old whisky bottles and a couple of masks made of black cloth, and the walls were covered with the most ignorant kind of words and pictures drawn in charcoal. Two dirty old calico dresses, a sun-bonnet, and some women’s underclothes hung on the wall, and some men’s clothing too. We put the whole lot into the canoe, since it might come in handy. A boy’s old speckled straw hat was on the floor, and I took that too. There was also a bottle that had held milk, with a rag stopper for a baby to suck on. We would have taken the bottle, but it was broken. There was a shabby old chest and an old hair trunk with broken hinges. They stood open, but nothing in them was worth anything. From the way things were scattered about, we figured the people had left in a hurry and hadn’t been able to carry off most of their stuff.

We took an old tin lantern, a butcher knife with no handle, a brand-new Barlow knife worth two bits in any store, a bunch of tallow candles, a tin candlestick, a gourd, a tin cup, a ratty old bedquilt off the bed, and a bag with needles and pins and beeswax and buttons and thread and all that kind of truck in it. We took a hatchet and some nails, a fishline as thick as my little finger with some monstrous hooks on it, a roll of buckskin, a leather dog collar, a horseshoe, and some vials of medicine with no labels on them. Just as we were leaving, I found a pretty good curry-comb, and Jim found a ratty old fiddle bow and a wooden leg. The straps were broken off the leg, but apart from that it was a good enough leg, though it was too long for me and not long enough for Jim, and we couldn’t find the other one, though we hunted all around.

So, all in all, we made a good haul. By the time we were ready to push off, we were a quarter of a mile below the island and it was pretty broad day. So I made Jim lie down in the canoe and cover up with the quilt, because if he sat up, people could tell he was a nigger from a good way off. I paddled over to the Illinois shore and drifted down almost half a mile while doing it. I crept up the slack water under the bank and had no accidents and saw nobody. We got home safe.

chapters.title: Chapter X — The Find
paragraphs: After breakfast I wanted to talk about the dead man and guess how he came to be killed, but Jim didn’t want to. He said it would bring bad luck. Besides, he said, the man might come and haunt us; he said a man who wasn’t buried was more likely to go haunting around than one who was planted and comfortable. That sounded pretty reasonable, so I said no more. But I couldn’t keep from thinking it over and wishing I knew who shot the man and why they did it.

We went through the clothes we’d taken and found eight dollars in silver sewed into the lining of an old blanket overcoat. Jim figured the people in that house had stolen the coat, because if they’d known the money was there, they wouldn’t have left it. I said I figured they killed him too, but Jim didn’t want to talk about that. I said:

“Now you call it bad luck, but what did you tell me when I brought in that snake-skin I found up on the ridge the day before yesterday? You said touching a snake-skin was the worst bad luck there is. Well, look at your bad luck! We’ve hauled in all this truck, and eight dollars on top of it. I’d like some bad luck like this every day, Jim.”
“Never you mind, honey, never you mind. Don’t you get too perky. It’s a-comin’. Mind, I’m tellin’ you, it’s a-comin’.”

And it did come. We had that talk on a Tuesday. Then, after dinner on Friday, we were lying around in the grass at the upper end of the ridge and ran out of tobacco. I went to the cavern to get some and found a rattlesnake in there. I killed him and curled him up on the foot of Jim’s blanket, looking ever so natural, thinking there’d be some fun when Jim found him there. By night I’d forgotten all about the snake. While I was striking a light, Jim threw himself down on the blanket, and the snake’s mate was there and bit him.

He leaped up yelling, and the first thing the light showed us was the varmint coiled and ready to strike again. I knocked him dead with a stick in a second, and Jim snatched up Pap’s whisky jug and started pouring it down his throat.

He had no shoes on, and the snake had got him right in the heel. That was all because I was fool enough to forget that a dead snake’s mate always comes to wherever you leave it and curls up beside it. Jim told me to cut the snake’s head off and throw it away, then skin the body and roast a piece. I did it, and he ate the meat and said it would help cure him. He also had me cut off the rattles and tie them around his wrist, saying that would help too. Then I slipped away quietly and flung the snakes far off into the bushes, because I wasn’t about to let Jim find out this was all my fault, not if I could help it.

Jim sucked and sucked at the jug, and now and then he lost his head and thrashed around and yelled, but every time he came to himself he went back to sucking at the jug. His foot swelled up pretty big, and so did his leg. But after a while the drunk began to take hold, so I judged he was all right. Still, I’d rather have been bit by a snake than drink Pap’s whisky.

Jim was laid up for four days and nights. Then the swelling was all gone and he was up and about again. I made up my mind I would never take hold of a snake-skin again, now that I’d seen what came of it. Jim said he reckoned I’d believe him next time. He also said that handling a snake-skin was such awful bad luck that maybe we hadn’t seen the end of it yet. He said he’d rather see the new moon over his left shoulder a thousand times than pick up a snake-skin in his hand. Well, I was starting to feel that way myself, though I’ve always figured that looking at the new moon over your left shoulder is one of the most careless and foolish things a person can do. Old Hank Bunker did it once and bragged about it, and in less than two years he got drunk and fell off the shot tower and flattened himself out until he was just a kind of layer, you might say. They slid him edgewise between two barn doors for a coffin and buried him that way, so they say, but I didn’t see it. Pap told me. Anyway, it all came of looking at the moon that way, like a fool.

Well, the days went by and the river went back down between its banks. About the first thing we did was bait one of the big hooks with a skinned rabbit, set it out, and catch a catfish as big as a man. He was six feet two inches long and weighed over two hundred pounds. We couldn’t handle him, of course; he would have flung us clear into Illinois. We just sat there and watched him rip and tear around until he drowned. We found a brass button in his stomach, and a round ball, and lots of rubbish. We split the ball open with the hatchet, and there was a spool inside. Jim said it must have been in there a long time, for the fish to coat it over like that and make a ball of it. It was as big a fish as was ever caught in the Mississippi, I reckon. Jim said he’d never seen a bigger one. He would have been worth a good deal over at the village. They sell a fish like that by the pound in the market house there, and everybody buys some. His meat’s as white as snow and makes a good fry.

The next morning I said things were getting slow and dull, and I wanted to stir something up. I said I reckoned I would slip across the river and find out what was going on. Jim liked that idea, but he said I must go in the dark and keep a sharp lookout. Then he thought it over and asked whether I couldn’t put on some of those old things and dress up like a girl. That was a good idea too. So we shortened one of the calico gowns, and I rolled my trouser legs up to my knees and climbed into it. Jim fastened it up the back with the hooks, and it was a fair fit. I put on the sun-bonnet and tied it under my chin, and anybody looking in to see my face would be looking down a length of stovepipe. Jim said hardly anybody would know me, even in the daytime. I practiced all day to get the hang of the clothes, and after a while I could do pretty well in them. Only Jim said I didn’t walk like a girl, and he said I must quit pulling up my gown to get at my trouser pocket. I took notice and did better.
Right after dark I set out in the canoe, heading up the Illinois shore.

I started across to the town from a little below the ferry landing, and the current carried me in at the bottom of the town. I tied up and walked along the bank. A light was burning in a little shanty that nobody had lived in for a long time, and I wondered who had moved in there. I slipped up and peeped in at the window. A woman about forty years old was in there, knitting by a candle on a pine table. I didn’t know her face. She was a stranger, because you couldn’t come up with a face in that town that I didn’t know. This was lucky, because I was losing my nerve. I was getting afraid I shouldn’t have come, since people might know my voice and find me out. But if this woman had been in such a little town for two days, she could tell me everything I wanted to know. So I knocked at the door and made up my mind not to forget I was a girl.

chapters.title: Chapter XI — Huck and the Woman
paragraphs: “Come in,” said the woman, and I did. She said, “Take a chair.”
I did. She looked me all over with her little shiny eyes and said:
“What might your name be?”
“Sarah Williams.”
“Where do you live? Around here?”
“No, ma’am. I’m from Hookerville, seven miles down the river. I’ve walked the whole way and I’m worn out.”
“Hungry, too, I reckon. I’ll find you something.”

“No, ma’am, I ain’t hungry. I was so starved I had to stop at a farm two miles back down the river, so I ain’t hungry anymore. That’s what made me so late. My mother’s laid up sick, with no money or anything, and I came to tell my uncle Abner Moore. She says he lives at the upper end of town. I’ve never been here before. Do you know him?”
“No, but I don’t know everybody yet. I haven’t lived here even two weeks. It’s a good long way to the upper end of town. You’d better stay here the night. Go on and take off your bonnet.”
“No,” I says. “I’ll sit and rest a bit, I figure, then move on. Dark doesn’t scare me.”

She said she wouldn’t let me go alone, but her husband would be home before long, maybe in an hour and a half, and she’d send him along with me. Then she started in about her husband, and her kin up the river, and her kin down the river, and how much better off they used to be, and how they wondered whether they’d made a mistake moving to our town instead of leaving well enough alone—and on and on, until I was afraid _I_ had made the mistake, coming to her to find out what was going on in town. But after a while she got around to Pap and the murder, and then I was pretty glad to let her rattle on. She told about me and Tom Sawyer finding the six thousand dollars (only she made it ten), and all about Pap and what a hard case he was, and what a hard case I was, and finally she reached the part where I got murdered. I says:
“Who did it? We’ve heard plenty about all this happening down in Hookerville, but we don’t know who it was that killed Huck Finn.”
“Well, I reckon there are quite a few people right here who’d like to know who killed him. Some think old Finn did it himself.”
“No—is that so?”
“Almost everybody thought so at first. He’ll never know how close he came to getting lynched. But before nightfall they changed their minds and decided it was a runaway nigger named Jim.”
“Why, _he_—”
I stopped short. I figured I’d better keep quiet. She ran right on and never noticed I had spoken at all:

“That nigger ran off the very night Huck Finn was killed. So there’s a reward out for him—three hundred dollars. And there’s a reward out for old Finn, too—two hundred dollars. You see, he came to town the morning after the murder and told everybody about it, and he went along on the ferryboat search, and right after that he up and left. By nightfall they wanted to lynch him, but he was gone, you see. Well, the next day they found out the nigger was gone, too; nobody had seen him since ten o’clock the night of the murder. So they put it on him, you see. And while everybody was all worked up about it, back comes old Finn the next day, blubbering to Judge Thatcher for money to hunt the nigger all over Illinois. The judge gave him some, and that evening he got drunk and hung around till after midnight with a couple of mighty rough-looking strangers, and then left with them. Well, he hasn’t come back since, and nobody expects him until this blows over a little, because people think now that he killed his own boy and set things up so folks would blame robbers, and then he’d get Huck’s money without having to fuss with a long lawsuit. People do say he wasn’t too good to do it. Oh, he’s sly, I reckon. If he stays away for a year he’ll be fine. You can’t prove a thing on him, you know. Everything will have calmed down by then, and he’ll walk right into Huck’s money as easy as pie.”
“Yes, I reckon so, ma’am. I don’t see anything to stop him. Has everybody stopped thinking the nigger did it?”
“Oh, no, not all of them. Plenty still think he did it. But they’ll have the nigger in hand soon enough, and maybe they can frighten a confession out of him.”
“Why, are they still after him?”

“Well, aren’t you the innocent one! Does three hundred dollars lie around every day for folks to pick up? Some people think the nigger isn’t far from here. I’m one of them—but I haven’t talked it around. A few days ago I was chatting with an old couple in the log shanty next door, and they happened to mention that hardly anybody ever goes to that island over yonder they call Jackson’s Island. Doesn’t anybody live there? says I. No, nobody, say they. I didn’t say any more, but I did some thinking. I was nearly sure I’d seen smoke over there, up near the head of the island, a day or two before that. So I says to myself, like as not that nigger’s hiding over there, and anyhow, says I, it’s worth the trouble to search the place. I haven’t seen any smoke since, so maybe he’s gone, if it was him. But my husband’s going over to look—him and another man. He’d gone up the river, but he got back today, and I told him the minute he got here two hours ago.”

I was so jumpy by now that I couldn’t sit still. My hands needed something to do, so I grabbed a needle off the table and tried to thread it. My hands trembled and I made a poor job of it. When the woman finally quit talking, I glanced up and found her eyeing me with a curious look and a faint smile. I set the needle and thread down, acted interested—and I was, too—and says:
“Three hundred dollars is a heap of money. I sure wish my mother could have it. Is your husband heading over there tonight?”
“Oh, yes. He and the man I mentioned went uptown to find a boat and try to borrow a second gun. They’ll cross over after midnight.”
“Couldn’t they see better if they waited until daylight?”
“Yes. And couldn’t the nigger see better, too? He’ll probably be asleep after midnight, and the men can creep through the woods and find his campfire, if he has one, all the easier for the dark.”
“I didn’t think of that.”
The woman kept studying me with that curious look, and I didn’t feel one bit comfortable. After a bit she says,
“What did you say your name was, honey?”
“M—Mary Williams.”

Somehow it didn’t seem to me that I’d said Mary the first time. I thought I’d said Sarah. So I didn’t look up, and I felt kind of cornered, and was afraid it showed on my face. I wished the woman would say something more, because the longer she sat quiet, the worse I felt. But then she says:
“Honey, didn’t you tell me Sarah when you first walked in?”
“Oh, yes, ma’am, I did. Sarah Mary Williams. Sarah’s my first name. Some folks call me Sarah, and some call me Mary.”
“Oh, so that’s how it is?”
“Yes, ma’am.”
That eased my mind a little, but I still wished I was somewhere else. I wasn’t ready to look up yet.

Well, the woman went on about how hard times were, and how poorly they had to live, and how the rats ran around as free as if the place belonged to them, and so forth and so on, and that settled me down again. She was right about the rats. Every so often you could see one stick his nose out of a hole in the corner. She said that when she was alone she had to keep things within reach to throw at them, or they’d never leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot, and said she was generally a good shot with it, but she’d wrenched her arm a day or two back and wasn’t sure she could aim true now. But she watched for her chance, and soon she banged away at a rat and missed him by a mile, and said “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to take a try at the next one. I wanted to get out of there before her husband came back, but of course I kept that to myself. I took the lead, and the first rat that poked out his nose, I let fly, and if he’d stayed put he’d have been one sick rat. She said that was first-rate, and she figured I’d get the next one. She fetched the lump of lead and brought it back, along with a hank of yarn she wanted help with. I held up both my hands and she looped the hank over them, and kept on talking about her own and her husband’s business. But she stopped to say:
“Watch out for those rats. You’d better keep the lead in your lap, where it’s handy.”

So right then she dropped the lump in my lap, and I squeezed my knees together over it while she kept talking. But it lasted only about a minute. Then she took the yarn off my hands, looked me square in the face, all friendly, and says:
“Come now, what’s your real name?”
“Wh—what, ma’am?”
“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—or something else?”
I trembled like a leaf, I reckon, and had no idea what to do. Still, I says:
“Please don’t tease a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in your way here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay right where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you, either. You just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it, and what’s more, I’ll help you. So will my old man, if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway apprentice, that’s all. It’s nothing. There’s no harm in it. You were treated badly, and you made up your mind to light out. Bless you, child, I wouldn’t tell on you. Tell me all about it now, that’s a good boy.”

So I said there wouldn’t be any use trying to keep up the act any longer, and I would just make a clean breast of it and tell her everything, but she mustn’t go back on her promise. Then I told her my father and mother were dead, and the law had bound me out to a mean old farmer in the country, thirty miles back from the river, and he treated me so badly I couldn’t stand it any longer. He went away for a couple of days, and so I took my chance, stole some of his daughter’s old clothes, and cleared out, and it had taken me three nights to cover the thirty miles. I traveled at night and hid and slept in the daytime, and the bag of bread and meat I brought from home lasted me the whole way, and I had plenty. I said I believed my uncle Abner Moore would take care of me, and that was why I’d headed for this town of Goshen.
“Goshen, child? This isn’t Goshen. This is St. Petersburg. Goshen is ten miles farther up the river. Who told you this was Goshen?”

“Why, a man I ran into at daybreak this morning, just as I was about to head into the woods for my usual sleep. He said that when the road split I should take the right fork, and five miles would bring me to Goshen.”
“He was drunk, I reckon. He told you exactly wrong.”
“Well, he sure acted drunk, but it doesn’t matter now. I need to get going. I’ll make Goshen before it’s light.”
“Wait just a minute. I’ll wrap up a bite for you to carry. You may be glad of it.”
So she packed me up a snack, and says:
“Say, when a cow is lying down, which end of her gets up first? Answer right away now—don’t stop to think it over. Which end gets up first?”
“The hind end, ma’am.”
“Well, then, a horse?”
“The front end, ma’am.”
“Which side of a tree does the moss grow on?”
“The north side.”
“Say fifteen cows are grazing on a hillside. How many of them have their heads turned the same way while they eat?”
“All fifteen, ma’am.”
“Well, I do believe you _have_ lived in the country. I was afraid you were trying to fool me again. Now, what’s your real name?”
“George Peters, ma’am.”

“Well, try to remember that, George. Don’t forget and say it’s Elexander before you leave, and then squirm out of it by saying George Elexander when I catch you. And don’t go around women in that old calico. You make a pretty poor girl, though you might fool men, maybe. Bless you, child, when you sit down to thread a needle, don’t hold the thread still and bring the needle up to it. Hold the needle still and poke the thread at it. That’s how a woman almost always does it, and a man always does it the opposite way. And when you throw something at a rat or whatever, go up on your tiptoes and swing your hand up over your head as clumsily as you can, and miss your rat by six or seven feet. Throw stiff-armed from the shoulder, as if there were a pivot there for it to turn on, the way a girl does, not from the wrist and elbow with your arm out to one side, the way a boy does. And mind this: when a girl tries to catch something in her lap, she spreads her knees apart. She doesn’t slam them together the way you did when you caught that lump of lead. Why, I took you for a boy when I saw you threading the needle, and I cooked up the other tests just to be sure. Now run along to your uncle, Sarah Mary Williams George Elexander Peters, and if you land in trouble, send word to Mrs. Judith Loftus, which is me, and I’ll do what I can to help you out. Follow the river road the whole way, and next time you go tramping, bring shoes and socks. The river road is rocky, and your feet will be a sight by the time you reach Goshen, I reckon.”

I climbed the bank about fifty yards, then looped back along my own tracks and crept down to my canoe, which was a good stretch below the house. I hopped in and shoved off in a hurry. I paddled upstream far enough to reach the head of the island, and then started across. I pulled off the sunbonnet, since I didn’t want blinders on just then. About halfway over, I heard the clock start to strike, so I stopped paddling to listen. The sound drifted faint over the water but clear—eleven. When I hit the head of the island I didn’t stop to catch my wind, though I was nearly spent. I pushed straight into the trees where my old camp used to be, and built a good fire on a high, dry spot.

Then I leaped back into the canoe and tore off toward our place, a mile and a half downstream, as fast as I could paddle. I landed, splashed through the woods and up the ridge, and into the cavern. There was Jim, stretched out on the ground, sound asleep. I shook him awake and says:
“Get up and move, Jim! Not a minute to waste. They’re coming after us!”

Jim never asked a question, and he never said a word, but the way he worked for the next half hour showed how scared he was. By that time everything we owned in the world was on our raft, and she was ready to be shoved out from the willow cove where she was hidden. The first thing we did was put out the campfire at the cavern, and after that we didn’t show a candle outside.

I paddled the canoe a little way out from shore and had a look around, but if there was a boat anywhere, I couldn’t make it out, because stars and shadows are no good to see by. Then we got the raft out and slid along in the dark under the trees, past the lower end of the island, dead quiet, without saying a word.

chapters.title: Chapter XII — Slow Navigation
paragraphs: It must have been nearly one o’clock by the time we finally got below the island, and the raft seemed to crawl. If a boat came along, we planned to jump into the canoe and make a run for the Illinois shore. It was a good thing no boat came, because it had never crossed our minds to put the gun in the canoe, or a fishing line, or anything to eat. We were in too much of a sweat to think of so many things. It wasn’t good sense to put _everything_ on the raft.

If the men went to the island, I expect they found the camp fire I built and sat up all night watching it for Jim to come back. Anyway, they kept away from us, and if my building that fire didn’t fool them, it wasn’t my fault. I played the trick on them as low-down as I knew how.

When the first streak of daylight showed, we tied up at a tow-head in a big bend on the Illinois side. We chopped off cottonwood branches with the hatchet and piled them over the raft, so it looked as if part of the bank had caved in there. A tow-head is a sandbar with cottonwoods growing on it as thick as the teeth of a harrow.

There were mountains on the Missouri shore and heavy woods on the Illinois side, and the channel ran along the Missouri shore at that spot, so we weren’t afraid anybody would stumble onto us. We lay there all day and watched the rafts and steamboats race down along the Missouri shore, while the steamboats headed upstream fought the big river out in the middle. I told Jim all about my jabbering with that woman. Jim said she was a smart one, and that if she had set out after us herself, she wouldn’t have sat down to watch a camp fire—no, sir, she’d have fetched a dog. Well, then, I said, why couldn’t she tell her husband to fetch a dog? Jim said he bet she thought of it by the time the men were ready to start, and he figured they must have gone up into town to get a dog and lost all that time. Otherwise we wouldn’t be here on a tow-head sixteen or seventeen miles below the village—no, indeed, we would be back in that same old town. So I said I didn’t care why they hadn’t caught us, as long as they hadn’t.

As it began to get dark, we poked our heads out of the cottonwood thicket and looked up and down and across the river. Nothing in sight, so Jim pulled up some of the top planks of the raft and built a snug wigwam to get under in blazing or rainy weather and to keep our things dry. He made a floor for the wigwam and raised it a foot or more above the raft, so now the blankets and all our gear were out of reach of the steamboat waves. Right in the middle of the wigwam we laid down a layer of dirt about five or six inches deep, with a frame around it to hold it in place. This was for building a fire on in wet or chilly weather, and the wigwam would keep the fire from being seen. We also made a spare steering-oar, because one of the others might get broken on a snag or something. We fixed up a short forked stick to hang the old lantern on, because we had to light the lantern whenever we saw a steamboat coming downstream, to keep from getting run over. We wouldn’t need to light it for boats going upstream unless we saw we were in what they call a “crossing.” The river was still pretty high, and the very low banks were still a little under water, so upstream boats didn’t always follow the channel but hunted for easy water.

On this second night we drifted between seven and eight hours, with a current running better than four miles an hour. We caught fish and talked, and every now and then we took a swim to keep from getting sleepy. It was kind of solemn, drifting down that big, still river, lying on our backs and looking up at the stars. We never felt like talking loud, and we didn’t laugh often, only a low little chuckle now and then. We had mighty good weather as a general thing, and nothing happened to us at all, that night or the next or the next.

Every night we passed towns, some of them way up on black hillsides, with nothing to see but a shiny bed of lights and not a single house. On the fifth night we passed St. Louis, and it looked like the whole world was lit up. Back in St. Petersburg they used to say there were twenty or thirty thousand people in St. Louis, but I never believed it until I saw that wonderful spread of lights at two o’clock on that still night. There wasn’t a sound; everybody was asleep.

Every night by then, around ten o’clock, I would slip ashore at some little village and buy ten or fifteen cents’ worth of meal or bacon or other food. Sometimes I lifted a chicken that wasn’t roosting comfortably and took him along. Pap always said to take a chicken when you get the chance, because even if you don’t want him yourself, you can easily find somebody who does, and a good deed is never forgotten. I never saw a time when pap didn’t want the chicken himself, but that’s what he used to say, anyway.

In the mornings before daylight I slipped into cornfields and borrowed a watermelon, or a muskmelon, or a pumpkin, or some new corn, or things like that. Pap always said there was no harm in borrowing things if you meant to pay them back some day. But the widow said it was nothing but a soft name for stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim said he figured the widow was partly right and pap was partly right, so the best thing would be for us to pick out two or three things from the list and say we wouldn’t borrow those anymore. Then he figured it wouldn’t do any harm to borrow the rest. So we talked it over all one night, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to give up the watermelons, or the cantaloupes, or the muskmelons, or what. But toward daylight we got it all settled to our satisfaction and decided to give up crabapples and persimmons. We hadn’t been feeling quite right before that, but now it was all comfortable. I was glad the way it turned out, too, because crabapples are never any good, and the persimmons wouldn’t be ripe for two or three months yet.
Now and then we shot a water bird that had gotten up too early in the morning or hadn’t gone to bed early enough in the evening. Taking it all around, we lived pretty high.

On the fifth night below St. Louis, we had a big storm after midnight, with a power of thunder and lightning, and the rain came down in a solid sheet. We stayed in the wigwam and let the raft look after itself. When the lightning flared, we could see a big straight river ahead and high, rocky bluffs on both sides. After a while I said, “Hel-_lo_, Jim, look over there!” It was a steamboat that had wrecked herself on a rock, and we were drifting straight down on her. The lightning showed her very plainly. She was leaning over, with part of her upper deck above water, and when the flashes came, you could see every little chimney-guy clean and clear, and a chair by the big bell with an old slouch hat hanging on the back of it.

Well, it was the middle of the night and stormy, and everything was so mysterious, and I felt just the way any other boy would have felt, seeing that wreck lying there so mournful and lonesome in the middle of the river. I wanted to get aboard and sneak around a little and see what was there. So I said:
“Let’s land on her, Jim.”
But at first Jim was dead set against it. He said:
“I don’t want to go fooling around no wreck. We’s doin’ mighty well, and we better let well enough alone, like de good book says. Likely as not dere’s a watchman on dat wreck.”

“Watchman, my grandmother,” I said. “There’s nothing to watch but the texas and the pilot-house, and do you think anybody’s going to risk his life for a texas and a pilot-house on a night like this, when the whole thing is likely to break up and wash down the river any minute?” Jim couldn’t say anything to that, so he didn’t try. “Besides,” I said, “we might borrow something worth having from the captain’s stateroom. Cigars, _I_ bet you—and they cost five cents apiece, cash on the barrelhead. Steamboat captains are always rich, and they get sixty dollars a month, and _they_ don’t care a cent what a thing costs, you know, as long as they want it. Stick a candle in your pocket. I can’t rest, Jim, till we’ve searched her. Do you think Tom Sawyer would ever walk past this? Not for pie, he wouldn’t. He’d call it an adventure—that’s what he’d call it—and he’d land on that wreck if it was the last thing he ever did. And wouldn’t he put on style about it? Wouldn’t he show off something fierce? Why, you’d think he was Christopher Columbus discovering Kingdom Come. I wish Tom Sawyer _was_ here.”

Jim grumbled a little but gave in. He said we mustn’t talk any more than we had to, and when we did, we had to keep it mighty low. The lightning showed us the wreck again just in time, and we caught hold of the starboard derrick and tied up there.

The deck was high out of the water on this side. We went creeping down the slope toward the port side in the dark, heading for the texas, feeling our way slowly with our feet and holding our hands out to fend off the guy ropes, because it was so dark we couldn’t see any sign of them. Pretty soon we bumped into the front end of the skylight and climbed up on it, and the next step brought us right in front of the captain’s door, which was open. And by golly, far down the texas hall we saw a light! In the same second, we thought we heard low voices in there!
Jim whispered that he was feeling powerful sick and told me to come along. I said all right and was about to start back for the raft, but just then I heard a voice wail out:
“Oh, please don’t, boys; I swear I’ll never tell!”
Another voice answered, pretty loud:

“That’s a lie, Jim Turner. You’ve pulled this act before. You always want more than your share of the loot, and you’ve always gotten it, too, because you swore that if you didn’t, you’d tell. But this time you’ve said it just one time too many. You’re the meanest, most treacherous hound in this country.”

By this time Jim was gone for the raft. I was just boiling over with curiosity. I told myself that Tom Sawyer wouldn’t back out now, so I wouldn’t either; I was going to see what was happening here. So I dropped onto my hands and knees in the narrow passage and crept toward the back in the dark, until there was only one stateroom between me and the cross-hall of the texas. There I saw a man stretched out on the floor, tied hand and foot, and two men standing over him. One of them held a dim lantern, and the other had a pistol. This one kept pointing the pistol at the head of the man on the floor and saying:
“I’d _like_ to! And I ought to, too—the mean skunk!”
Each time, the man on the floor would shrivel up and say, “Oh, please don’t, Bill; I ain’t ever going to tell.”
Every time he said it, the fellow holding the lantern would laugh and answer:

“Sure you ain’t! That’s the truest thing you ever said, you bet. Listen to him beg! And yet if we hadn’t gotten the best of him and tied him up, he’d have killed us both. And what _for?_ For nothing. Just because we stood up for our _rights_—that’s what for. But I’ll bet you ain’t going to threaten anybody anymore, Jim Turner. Put _away_ that pistol, Bill.”
Bill said:
“I don’t want to, Jake Packard. I’m for killing him—didn’t he kill old Hatfield the very same way? Don’t he deserve it?”
“Well, I don’t _want_ him killed, and I have my own reasons for it.”
“Bless your heart for those words, Jake Packard! I’ll never forget you as long as I live!” said the man on the floor, sort of blubbering.

Packard paid no attention to that. He hung his lantern on a nail and started toward where I was in the dark, motioning for Bill to follow. I scuttled backward as fast as I could for about two yards, but the boat slanted so much that I couldn’t make good time. To keep from getting run over and caught, I crawled into a stateroom on the high side. The man came feeling along in the dark, and when Packard reached my stateroom, he said:
“Here—come in here.”

In he came, and Bill after him. But before they got in, I was already up in the upper berth, cornered and sorry I’d come. Then they stood there with their hands on the edge of the berth and talked. I couldn’t see them, but I could tell where they were by the whisky they’d been drinking. I was glad I didn’t drink whisky, but it wouldn’t have made much difference anyway, because most of the time they couldn’t have treed me, since I didn’t breathe. I was too scared. Besides, a person _couldn’t_ breathe and listen to such talk. They talked low and in earnest. Bill wanted to kill Turner. He said:

“He’s said he’ll tell, and he will. Even if we gave him both our shares _now_, it wouldn’t make any difference after the fight and the way we’ve treated him. As sure as you’re born, he’ll turn State’s evidence. Now you listen to _me_. I’m for putting him out of his misery.”
“So am I,” said Packard, very quietly.
“Dang it, I’d started to think you weren’t. Well, then, that’s all right. Let’s go and do it.”

“Hold on a minute; I haven’t had my say yet. You listen to me. Shooting’s fine, but there are quieter ways if it’s _got_ to be done. What _I_ say is this: it isn’t smart to go courting a hangman’s rope when you can get what you’re after some other way that’s just as good and doesn’t put you at any risk. Ain’t that so?”
“You bet it is. But how are you going to manage it this time?”

“Well, here’s my idea. We’ll scramble around and gather up whatever loot we overlooked in the staterooms, and head for shore and hide it. Then we’ll wait. Now, I say it won’t be more than two hours before this wreck breaks up and washes down the river. See? He’ll be drowned, and he’ll have nobody to blame for it but himself. I figure that’s a considerable sight better than killing him. I’m against killing a man as long as you can get around it; it isn’t good sense, and it isn’t good morals. Ain’t I right?”
“Yes, I reckon you are. But suppose she _doesn’t_ break up and wash away?”
“Well, we can wait the two hours anyway and see, can’t we?”
“All right, then; come along.”
So they set off, and I took off in a cold sweat, scrambling forward. It was pitch dark there, but I whispered hoarsely, “Jim!” and he answered right at my elbow with a kind of moan, and I said:

“Quick, Jim, there’s no time for fooling around and moaning. There’s a gang of murderers in there, and if we don’t find their boat and cut her loose to drift down the river, so they can’t get away from the wreck, one of them’s going to be in a bad way. But if we do find their boat, we can put _all_ of them in a bad way, because the Sheriff will get them. Quick, hurry! I’ll search the port side, and you search the starboard. You start at the raft, and—”
“Oh, lordy, lordy me! _Raf’?_ Ain’ no raf’ no mo’! She done come loose en drifted off—en here we is!”

chapters.title: Chapter XIII — Escaping from the Wreck
paragraphs: Well, I caught my breath and nearly fainted. Trapped on a wreck with a gang like that! But this was no time to be fussing over my feelings. We _had_ to find that boat now, because we needed it ourselves. So we crept down the starboard side, shaking and quaking, and it was slow work. It seemed a week before we reached the stern. There was no sign of a boat. Jim said he didn’t think he could go any farther, he was so scared he had hardly any strength left. But I told him to come on, because if we got left on this wreck we were in real trouble. So on we crept again. We made for the stern of the texas and found it, and then we scrambled forward along the skylight, hanging on from shutter to shutter, since the edge of the skylight was under water. When we got pretty close to the cross-hall door, there was the skiff, sure enough! I could barely make her out. I felt so thankful. Another second and I’d have been aboard her, but just then the door opened. One of the men stuck his head out, only a couple of feet from me, and I thought I was done for. But he pulled it back in again and said:
“Get that blasted lantern out of sight, Bill!”
He threw a bag of something into the boat, then climbed in and sat down. It was Packard. Then Bill came out and got in too. Packard said, in a low voice:
“All set. Shove off!”
I could hardly hold on to the shutters, I was so weak. But Bill said:
“Wait a minute. Did you go through his pockets?”
“No. Didn’t you?”
“No. So he’s still got his share of the cash.”
“Well, then, come on. No sense taking the loot and leaving the money.”
“Say, won’t he get suspicious about what we’re up to?”
“Maybe he won’t. But we have to have it anyway. Come on.”
So they climbed out and went back inside.

The door slammed shut behind them, because it was on the tilted side of the boat. Half a second later I was in the skiff, and Jim came tumbling in after me. I whipped out my knife and cut the rope, and away we went!

We never touched an oar, and we didn’t speak or even whisper, or hardly breathe. We glided swiftly along in dead silence, past the tip of the paddle-box and past the stern. A second or two later we were a hundred yards below the wreck, and the darkness swallowed her up, every last trace of her. We were safe, and we knew it.

When we were three or four hundred yards downstream, we saw the lantern flash at the texas door for a second, like a little spark. That told us the rascals had found their boat missing, and were starting to understand that they were in just as much trouble as Jim Turner.

Then Jim took the oars, and we set out after our raft. This was the first time I started to worry about those men. I guess I hadn’t had time before. I began to think how dreadful it was, even for murderers, to be in such a fix. I told myself there was no saying I mightn’t turn out to be a murderer myself someday, and then how would _I_ like it? So I said to Jim:

“At the first light we see, we’ll land a hundred yards above or below it, somewhere that makes a good hiding place for you and the skiff. Then I’ll go and cook up some kind of story, and get somebody to go after that gang and rescue them from their scrape, so they can be hanged when their time comes.”

But that idea didn’t work out, because pretty soon it started to storm again, and this time worse than ever. The rain poured down, and not a light showed anywhere. Everybody was in bed, I guess. We went booming down the river, watching for lights and watching for our raft. After a long time the rain let up, but the clouds stayed, and the lightning kept whimpering. Then, after a while, a flash showed us a black shape floating ahead, and we steered for it.

It was the raft, and we were mighty glad to be back aboard her. Now we saw a light away down to the right, on shore, so I said I would go to it. The skiff was half full of loot that the gang had stolen from the wreck. We hustled it onto the raft in a pile, and I told Jim to float on down, show a light when he figured he’d gone about two miles, and keep it burning until I came. Then I took the oars and pushed off toward the light. As I got closer, three or four more showed up on a hillside. It was a village. I came in above the shore light, rested on my oars, and drifted. As I went by, I saw it was a lantern hanging from the jackstaff of a double-hulled ferryboat. I paddled around looking for the watchman, wondering where he slept, and after a while I found him perched on the bitts up front, with his head down between his knees. I gave his shoulder two or three little shoves and started to cry.
He woke up with a start, but when he saw it was only me, he gave a good yawn and stretch, and then he said:
“Hello, what’s up? Don’t cry, bub. What’s the trouble?”
I said:
“Pap, and Mam, and Sis, and—”
Then I broke down. He said:
“Oh, dang it, _don’t_ take on so. We all have our troubles, and this one will come out all right. What’s the matter with them?”
“They’re—they’re—are you the watchman of the boat?”

“Yes,” he said, looking fairly well pleased with himself. “I’m the captain and the owner and the mate and the pilot and the watchman and the head deckhand. And sometimes I’m the freight and passengers. I ain’t as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be so blamed generous and good to Tom, Dick and Harry as he is, and fling money around the way he does. But I’ve told him many a time that I wouldn’t trade places with him. Because, says I, a sailor’s life is the life for me, and I’m darned if _I’d_ live two miles out of town, where nothing ever happens, not for all his money and as much more on top of it. Says I—”
I broke in and said:
“They’re in an awful lot of trouble, and—”
“_Who_ is?”
“Why, Pap and Mam and Sis and Miss Hooker. And if you’d take your ferryboat and go up there—”
“Up where? Where are they?”
“On the wreck.”
“What wreck?”
“Why, there’s only one.”
“What, you don’t mean the _Walter Scott?_”
“Yes.”
“Good land! What in the world are they doing _there_?”
“Well, they didn’t go there on purpose.”
“I bet they didn’t! Why, great goodness, they haven’t got a chance if they don’t get off mighty quick! How in the world did they ever get into such a scrape?”
“Easy enough. Miss Hooker had been visiting in the town up there—”
“Yes, Booth’s Landing. Go on.”

“She was visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and just as evening was coming on she started across with her nigger woman in the horse ferry, to stay the night at her friend’s house, Miss What’s-her-name—I forget her name—and they lost their steering oar, and swung around and went floating down, stern first, about two miles, and got stuck on the wreck. The ferryman and the nigger woman and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker made a grab and got aboard the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we came along in our trading scow, and it was so dark we didn’t notice the wreck till we were right on it, and so _we_ got stuck too. But all of us were saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, he _was_ the best creature! I almost wish it had been me, I do.”
“My George! Never heard the beat of it. And what did you all do _then_?”

“Well, we hollered and carried on, but it’s so wide there that we couldn’t make anybody hear. So Pap said somebody had to get ashore and get help somehow. I was the only one who could swim, so I made a dash for it. Miss Hooker said that if I didn’t find help sooner, I should come here and look up her uncle, and he’d fix things. I reached land about a mile below, and I’ve been wandering around ever since, trying to get people to do something. But they said, ‘What, on such a night and in such a current? There’s no sense in it. Go for the steam ferry.’ Now if you’ll go and—”
“By Jackson, I’d _like_ to, and, blame it, I just might. But who in the dingnation is going to _pay_ me for it? Do you figure your pap can—”
“Why, _that’s_ all right. Miss Hooker told me, _particularly_, that her uncle Hornback—”

“Great guns! Is _he_ her uncle? Look here, you head for that light over yonder, and turn west when you get there, and about a quarter of a mile out you’ll come to the tavern. Tell them to send you out to Jim Hornback’s, and he’ll foot the bill. And don’t you dawdle, because he’ll want the news. Tell him I’ll have his niece safe before he can get to town. Hurry along, now. I’m going up around the corner here to rouse my engineer.”

I headed for the light, but as soon as he turned the corner I went back, got into my skiff and bailed her out. Then I pulled up the shore in the slack water about six hundred yards and tucked myself in among some wood boats, because I couldn’t rest easy until I saw the ferryboat start. But all in all, I felt rather comfortable about taking all this trouble for that gang, since not many would have done it. I wished the widow knew about it. I figured she’d be proud of me for helping those rapscallions, because rapscallions and deadbeats are the kind the widow and good people take the most interest in.

Well, before long, here came the wreck, dim and dusky, sliding along downstream! A kind of cold shiver went through me, and then I struck out for her. She was sitting very deep, and I saw right away there wasn’t much chance of anybody being alive in her. I rowed all around her and hollered a little, but there was no answer. All was dead still. I felt a little heavy-hearted about the gang, but not much, since I figured if they could stand it, so could I.

Then here came the ferryboat. So I shoved off for the middle of the river on a long slant downstream, and when I judged I was out of sight, I rested on my oars and looked back. I watched her go and sniff around the wreck for Miss Hooker’s remains, because the captain would know her uncle Hornback would want them. Then pretty soon the ferryboat gave it up and headed for shore, and I bent to my work and went booming down the river.

It did seem a powerfully long time before Jim’s light showed up, and when it did, it looked a thousand miles off. By the time I got there, the sky was starting to turn a little gray in the east. So we made for an island, hid the raft, sank the skiff, and turned in and slept like dead people.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV — A General Good Time
paragraphs: After a while, when we got up, we went through the loot the gang had stolen off the wreck. We found boots, and blankets, and clothes, and all sorts of other things, and a lot of books, and a spyglass, and three boxes of cigars. We had never been so rich before in either of our lives. The cigars were prime. We lazed around the woods all afternoon, talking, with me reading the books and having a generally good time. I told Jim all about what had happened inside the wreck and at the ferryboat, and I said these kinds of things were adventures. But he said he didn’t want any more adventures. He said that when I went into the texas and he crawled back to the raft and found her gone, he nearly died. He figured it was all up with _him_, whichever way things turned out, because if he didn’t get saved he would drown, and if he did get saved, whoever saved him would send him back home to collect the reward, and then Miss Watson would sell him South, for sure. Well, he was right. He was almost always right. He had an uncommonly level head, for a nigger.

I read Jim a good deal about kings and dukes and earls and such: how fancy they dressed, how much style they put on, and how they called each other your majesty and your grace and your lordship, and so on, rather than plain mister. Jim’s eyes bugged out, and he got real interested. He said:
“I never knowed dey was so many un um. I hain’t heared ’bout hardly none un um, ’cept ole King Sollermun, lessen you counts dem kings in a deck er k’yards. How much do a king git?”
“Get?” I said. “Why, they get a thousand dollars a month if they want it. They can have as much as they want. Everything belongs to them.”
“_Ain’_ dat gay? En what dey got to do, Huck?”
“_They_ don’t do a thing! Why, what a way to talk! They just sit around.”
“No! Is dat so?”

“Of course it is. They just sit around—except maybe when there’s a war, and then they go to the war. But other times they just lounge around, or go hawking—just hawking and sp— Sh! Did you hear a noise?”
We skipped out and looked, but it was nothing but the flutter of a steamboat’s wheel way off down the river, coming around the point. So we came back.

“Yes,” I said, “and other times, when things are dull, they fuss with the parliament, and if everybody doesn’t go along exactly right, he whacks their heads off. But mostly they hang around the harem.”
“Roun’ de which?”
“Harem.”
“What’s de harem?”
“It’s where he keeps all his wives. Don’t you know what a harem is? Solomon had one. He had about a million wives.”

“Well, now, dat’s right. I—I plum forgot. A harem’s jes’ a boa’din’-house, I reck’n. Dey mos’ likely has rackety times in de nussery. En de wives quarrels a heap, I reck’n, en dat make de racket wuss. Yit dey say Sollermun was de wises’ man dat ever lived. I doan’ b’lieve it. Bekase why: would a wise man want to live right in de middle er sich a blim-blammin’ all de time? No, sah, he wouldn’t. A wise man ’ud up en build hisself a boiler factory, en den he could shet _down_ de factory when he want a res’.”
“Well, but he _was_ the wisest man, anyway, because the widow told me so herself.”
“I doan care what de widder say. He _warn’t_ no wise man nuther. He got some er de dad-fetchedes’ ways I ever seen. You know ’bout dat chile he was gwyne to chop in two?”
“Yes, the widow told me the whole story.”

“_Well_, den! Ain’t dat de beatin’est notion in de whole worl’? You jes’ stop and look at it a minute. Dere’s de stump—dat’s one o’ de women; here’s you—dat’s de other one; I’s Sollermun; and dis dollar bill is de chile. Bofe o’ you says it’s yours. So what does I do? Does I go roun’ de neighbors lookin’ to fine out which one de bill _do_ belong to, and hand it to de right one, safe and sound, like anybody wid a lick o’ sense would? No; I grab dat bill and tear it in _two_, and give half to you and de other half to de other woman. Dat’s how Sollermun was gwine to do wid de chile. Now I wants to ask you: what good is dat half a bill? Can’t buy nuffin’ wid it. And what good is half a chile? I wouldn’t give a durn for a million o’ ’em.”
“Hang it, Jim, you’ve totally missed what I was getting at—you’re off by a thousand miles, blame it.”

“Who? Me? Go ’long. Doan’ talk to _me_ ’bout yo’ points. I reckon I knows sense when I sees it, and dere ain’t no sense in carryin’ on like dat. De fight warn’t ’bout half a chile, it was ’bout a whole chile; and a man who thinks he kin settle a fight ’bout a whole chile wid half a chile don’t know enough to come in out o’ de rain. Doan’ talk to me ’bout Sollermun, Huck, I knows him from de back.”
“But I’m telling you, you don’t get the point.”

“Blame de point! I reckon I knows what I knows. And mind you, de _real_ point is farther on—it’s deeper down. It lies in how Sollermun was raised. Take a man who’s got only one or two chillun: is dat man gwine to be wasteful wid chillun? No, he ain’t; he can’t afford it. _He_ knows what dey’re worth. But take a man who’s got ’bout five million chillun runnin’ roun’ de house, and it’s different. _He_ would as soon chop a chile in two as a cat. Dere’s plenty more. A chile or two, more or less, warn’t no matter to Sollermun, dad fetch him!”

I never saw such a nigger. Once he got a notion into his head, there was no getting it out again. He was the most down on Solomon of any nigger I ever saw. So I started talking about other kings and let Solomon drop. I told him about Louis Sixteenth, who got his head cut off in France a long time ago, and about his little boy, the dolphin, who would have been king, only they grabbed him and shut him up in jail, and some say he died there.
“Poor little fella.”
“Some folks say he escaped, though, and made his way over to America.”
“Dat’s good! But he’ll be mighty lonesome—dere ain’t no kings here, is dere, Huck?”
“No.”
“Den he can’t git no job. What’s he gwine to do?”
“Well, who knows? Some of them go to work as policemen, and some teach folks to speak French.”
“Huh? Huck, don’t dem French people speak de way we does?”
“_No_, Jim. If you heard them, you wouldn’t catch a single word.”
“Well, now, I’ll be ding-busted! How come?”
“_I_ don’t know, but it’s true. I picked up a little of their gabble out of a book. Suppose a man came up to you and said _Polly-voo-franzy_—what would you think?”
“I wouldn’t think nuffin’. I’d knock him upside de head—dat is, ’less he was white. I ain’t lettin’ no nigger call me dat.”
“Shucks, he isn’t insulting you. All he’s doing is asking whether you can speak French.”
“Well, den, why couldn’t he _say_ it?”
“Why, he _is_ saying it. That’s how a Frenchman _says_ it.”
“Well, it’s a blame ridiculous way, and I don’t want to hear no more ’bout it. Dere ain’t no sense in it.”
“Look here, Jim; does a cat talk the way we do?”
“No, a cat don’t.”
“Well, does a cow?”
“No, a cow don’t, neither.”
“Does a cat talk like a cow, or a cow talk like a cat?”
“No, dey don’t.”
“So it’s only right and natural that they talk unlike each other, isn’t it?”
“Course it is.”
“And isn’t it just as right and natural that a cat and a cow talk unlike _us?_”
“Why, most surely it is.”
“Well, then, why isn’t it natural and right for a _Frenchman_ to talk different from us? Answer me that.”
“Is a cat a man, Huck?”
“No.”
“Well, den, a cat talkin’ like a man makes no sense. Is a cow a man?—or is a cow a cat?”
“No, she’s neither one.”
“Well, den, she got no call to talk like one or de other. Now, is a Frenchman a man?”
“Yes.”
“_Well_, den! Dad blame it all, why don’t he _talk_ like one? Answer me _dat!_”
I saw there was no use wasting words—you can’t teach a nigger to argue. So I quit.

chapters.title: Chapter XV — Huck Loses the Raft
paragraphs: We figured three more nights would get us to Cairo, at the bottom of Illinois, where the Ohio River comes in, and that was where we were headed. We would sell the raft, catch a steamboat, and go way up the Ohio among the free States, and then we’d be out of trouble.

Well, the second night a fog started to roll in, and we steered for a tow-head to tie up to, since it wouldn’t do to try to run in a fog. But when I paddled ahead in the canoe with the line to make it fast, there was nothing but little saplings to tie to. I looped the line around one of them right at the edge of the cut bank, but the current was strong, and the raft came booming down so fast that she ripped it out by the roots and off she went. I saw the fog closing in, and it made me so sick and scared that I couldn’t move for almost half a minute, it seemed to me—and then there was no raft in sight; you couldn’t see twenty yards. I jumped into the canoe and ran back to the stern, grabbed the paddle, and pushed her back a stroke. But she didn’t budge. I was in such a hurry that I hadn’t untied her. I got up and tried to untie her, but I was so worked up and my hands shook so badly that I could hardly do a thing with them.

The moment I was loose I went after the raft, full speed, straight down along the tow-head. That worked fine for a while, but the tow-head was less than sixty yards long, and as soon as I shot past its lower end I was out in thick white fog, with no more notion of my direction than a corpse has.

Thinks I, it won’t do to paddle; the first thing I know I’ll run into the bank or a tow-head or something. I’ve got to sit still and drift, and yet it’s mighty fidgety business, holding your hands still at a time like that. I whooped and listened. Away down there somewhere I heard a small whoop, and my spirits came right up. I went tearing after it, listening hard to catch it again. The next time it came, I saw I wasn’t heading for it but off to the right of it. And the time after that I was heading off to the left of it—and not gaining on it much either, because I was flying around this way and that and the other, while it kept going straight ahead the whole time.

I sure wished that fool would think to beat on a tin pan, and keep beating it, but he never did, and it was the quiet stretches between the whoops that gave me all the trouble. Well, I fought along, and pretty soon I heard the whoop _behind_ me. I was tangled up good now. Either that was somebody else’s whoop, or I had gotten turned around.

I dropped the paddle. The whoop came again, still behind me but from a new spot. It kept coming and kept moving, and I kept answering, until at last it was ahead of me once more. That told me the current had turned the canoe’s nose downstream, and that I was fine if it was Jim calling and not some other raftsman. In a fog you can’t judge a voice at all, since nothing looks right or sounds right in one.

The whooping kept up, and about a minute later I came booming down upon a cut bank, where the big trees stood like smoky ghosts. The current flung me off to the left and rushed on through a crowd of snags that fairly roared, with the water tearing past them so hard.
A second or two later it was solid white and still again. I sat perfectly still then, listening to my heart thump, and I don’t believe I drew a breath while it thumped a hundred times.

Then I just gave up, because now I understood. That cut bank was an island, and Jim had gone down the far side of it. It was no tow-head you could drift past in ten minutes. It was covered with the tall timber of a real island, and could easily be five or six miles long and over half a mile wide.

I stayed quiet for roughly fifteen minutes, with my ears straining. All that time, of course, I was drifting at four or five miles an hour, but a person never thinks about that.
