You _feel_ as if you’re lying perfectly still on the water, and when a snag slips by, you don’t think about how fast _you’re_ moving—you gasp and think, my! look how that snag is racing. If you doubt that it’s dismal and lonesome to be out in a fog like that, alone at night, you just try it one time and see.

Next, for about half an hour, I whooped every now and then, until finally I heard an answer a long way off and tried to follow it, but I couldn’t manage it, and soon I figured I had drifted into a nest of tow-heads, because I got dim little glimpses of them on both sides of me—sometimes only a narrow channel between them, and some that I couldn’t see I knew were there because I could hear the current washing against the old dead brush and trash hanging over the banks. Well, it wasn’t long before I lost the whoops down among the tow-heads, and I only tried chasing them a little while anyway, because it was worse than chasing a Jack-o’-lantern. You never knew a sound to dodge around so, and swap places so quick and so often.

I had to scramble away from the bank pretty briskly four or five times, so as not to knock the islands out of the river. From that I guessed the raft must be bumping the bank now and then, since otherwise it would have pulled ahead out of earshot, being a bit faster than me.

Well, eventually I seemed to be out on the open river again, but I couldn’t hear a trace of a whoop anywhere. I figured Jim might have run onto a snag and that was the end of him. I was good and worn out, so I stretched out in the canoe and told myself I wouldn’t worry about it anymore. I didn’t mean to fall asleep, but I was so drowsy I couldn’t fight it, so I decided to take just one little cat-nap.

It must have been longer than a cat-nap, though, because when I woke up the stars were out bright, the fog had cleared off, and I was spinning around a big bend stern first. For a bit I had no idea where I was and thought I was dreaming. When things began to come back, they seemed to float up faint from some time last week.

It was a monstrous big river here, with the tallest, thickest timber on both banks—just a solid wall, as far as I could tell by the stars. I looked way down the river and saw a black speck on the water. I took off after it, but when I got there it was nothing but a couple of sawlogs fastened together. Then I saw another speck and chased that; then another, and this time I was right. It was the raft.

When I reached it, there was Jim, sitting with his head down between his knees, fast asleep, and his right arm hanging over the steering-oar. The other oar had been smashed off, and the raft was strewn with leaves, branches and dirt. So she’d been through a rough time.
I tied up and lay down on the raft right under Jim’s nose, and started yawning and stretching my fists out against Jim, and said:
“Hello, Jim, was I asleep? Why didn’t you wake me up?”

“Goodness gracious, is dat you, Huck? And you ain’t dead—you ain’t drowned—you’s back again? It’s too good to be true, honey, it’s too good to be true. Lemme look at you, chile, lemme feel you. No, you ain’t dead! You’s back again, alive and sound, jes’ de same ol’ Huck—de same ol’ Huck, thank goodness!”
“What’s the matter with you, Jim? Have you been drinking?”
“Drinkin’? Has I been drinkin’? Has I had a chance to be drinkin’?”
“Well, then, why are you talking so wild?”
“How does I talk wild?”
“_How?_ Well, haven’t you been carrying on about me coming back, and all that nonsense, like I’d gone off somewhere?”
“Huck—Huck Finn, look me in de eye; look right in my eye. _Ain’t_ you gone off somewheres?”
“Gone away? Why, what in the world do you mean? _I_ haven’t been gone anywhere. Where would I go?”
“Well, look here, boss, somethin’ is wrong, dere is. Is I _me_, or who _is_ I? Is I here, or where _is_ I? Now dat’s what I wants to know.”
“Well, you’re here all right, as far as I can see, but you’re a muddle-headed old fool, Jim.”
“I is, is I? Well, den, answer me dis: Didn’t you take de line out in de canoe so you could tie up to dat tow-head?”
“No, I didn’t. What tow-head? I haven’t seen any tow-head.”
“You ain’t seen no tow-head? Look here, didn’t de line pull loose and de raf’ go hummin’ down de river, and leave you and de canoe behind in de fog?”
“What fog?”

“Why, _de_ fog!—de fog dat’s been all roun’ us all night. And didn’t you whoop, and didn’t I whoop, till we got mixed up in de islands and one of us got lost and de other was jes’ as good as lost, ’cause he didn’t know where he wuz? And didn’t I bust up against a whole lot o’ dem islands and have a terrible time and mos’ git drowned? Now ain’t dat so, boss—ain’t it so? You answer me dat.”

“Well, this is too much for me, Jim. I haven’t seen any fog, or any islands, or any trouble, or anything. I’ve been sitting here talking with you all night until you dropped off to sleep about ten minutes ago, and I reckon I did the same. You couldn’t have gotten drunk in that time, so of course you’ve been dreaming.”
“Dad fetch it, how could I dream all dat in jes’ ten minutes?”
“Well, hang it all, you did dream it, because none of it happened.”
“But, Huck, it’s all jes’ as plain to me as—”
“It doesn’t matter how plain it is; there’s nothing to it. I know, because I’ve been right here the whole time.”
Jim didn’t say anything for about five minutes, but sat there studying it over. Then he said:
“Well, den, I reckon I did dream it, Huck; but dog my cats if it ain’t de powerfulest dream I ever saw. And I ain’t never had a dream before dat wore me out like dis one.”
“Oh, well, that’s all right, because a dream can wear a body out something awful sometimes. But this was a humdinger of a dream; tell me all about it, Jim.”

So Jim got started and told me the whole thing from beginning to end, just the way it happened, except he dressed it up quite a bit. Then he said he had to go ahead and “’terpret” it, because it had been sent as a warning. He said the first tow-head stood for a man who would try to do us some good, but the current was another man, one who would pull us away from him. The whoops were warnings that would come to us every so often, and if we didn’t work hard to understand them, they’d only lead us into bad luck instead of keeping us clear of it. The pile of tow-heads was the trouble we were going to run into with quarrelsome people and every kind of mean folks, but if we minded our own business and didn’t talk back and stir them up, we’d come through it and get out of the fog into the big clear river, which was the free States, and there wouldn’t be any more trouble.
The sky had turned pretty dark right after I climbed onto the raft, but now it was clearing up again.
“Well, that’s all explained well enough as far as it goes, Jim,” I says, “but what do _these_ things stand for?”
I meant the leaves and rubbish lying on the raft, and the broken oar. You could see them plain as day now.

Jim looked at the trash, then looked at me, then back at the trash. The dream had stuck in his head so hard that he couldn’t seem to shake it loose and fit the facts back into their places right away. But once he had the whole business straightened out, he looked at me steady, without a smile, and says:

“What dey stan’ for? I’s gwine to tell you. When I wuz all wore out from workin’ en hollerin’ for you, en I fell asleep, my heart wuz nearly broke, bekase you wuz los’, en I didn’ care no mo’ what happen’ to me en de raf’. En when I woke up en foun’ you back agin, all safe en soun’, de tears come, en I could a got down on my knees en kissed yo’ foot, I wuz so thankful. En all you wuz thinkin’ ’bout wuz how you could make a fool o’ ole Jim wid a lie. Dat truck over dere is _trash;_ en trash is what people is dat throws dirt on de head o’ dey fren’s en makes ’em ashamed.”

Then he rose slowly, crossed to the wigwam, and went inside, and he said nothing more than that. Nothing more was needed. I felt so low I could almost have kissed _his_ foot just to make him take it back.

It took me fifteen minutes to work myself up to going and humbling myself to a nigger; but I did it, and I was never sorry for it afterward, either. I didn’t play any more mean tricks on him, and I wouldn’t have played that one if I’d known it would make him feel that way.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI — Expectation
paragraphs: We slept most of the day and set out at night, a little way behind a monstrous long raft that took as long to go by as a parade. She had four long sweeps at each end, so we figured she carried thirty men, probably. She had five big wigwams on board, spaced far apart, an open campfire in the middle, and a tall flagpole at each end. She had a power of style. Being a raftsman on a craft like that really _amounted_ to something.

We drifted down into a big bend, and the night clouded over and turned hot. The river was very wide, with solid forest walling it in on both sides; you hardly ever saw a gap in the trees, or a light. We talked about Cairo and wondered if we’d know it when we reached it. I said we probably wouldn’t, because I’d heard there were only about a dozen houses there, and if they happened not to have their lights on, how would we know we were passing a town? Jim said that if the two big rivers came together there, that would show us. But I said we might think we were just passing the tip of an island and coming back into the same old river. That worried Jim, and me too. So what were we to do? I said we should paddle ashore the first time a light showed, and tell them Pap was coming along behind with a trading-scow, that he was new at the business, and that he wanted to know how far it was to Cairo. Jim thought it was a good idea, so we smoked on it and waited.

There wasn’t anything to do now but keep a sharp lookout for the town and not go past it without seeing it. Jim said he’d be sure to see it, because the minute he saw it he’d be a free man, but if he missed it he’d be back in slave country with no more chance at freedom. Every little while he jumps up and says:
“Dah she is!”

But it wasn’t. It was jack-o’-lanterns, or lightning bugs; so he sat back down and went on watching, the same as before. Jim said being so close to freedom made him tremble and feel feverish all over. Well, I can tell you it made me tremble and feel feverish all over, too, to hear him, because I was starting to get it through my head that he _was_ almost free—and who was to blame for that? Why, _me_. I couldn’t get that out of my conscience, no matter how I tried. It got to troubling me so that I couldn’t rest; I couldn’t stay still in one place. It had never come home to me before what this thing was that I was doing. But now it did, and it stayed with me and scorched me worse and worse. I tried to tell myself that _I_ wasn’t to blame, because _I_ hadn’t run Jim off from his rightful owner; but it was no use. Every time, my conscience spoke right up and said, “But you knew he was running for his freedom, and you could have paddled ashore and told somebody.” That was true—I couldn’t get around it any way at all. That was where it pinched. Conscience said to me, “What did poor Miss Watson ever do to you, that you could watch her nigger go off right under your eyes and never say one single word? What did that poor old woman do to you, that you could treat her so meanly? Why, she tried to teach you your book, she tried to teach you your manners, she tried to be good to you every way she knew how. _That’s_ what she did.”

I felt so mean and wretched that I nearly wished myself dead. I paced up and down the raft, cursing myself under my breath, and Jim paced past me the other way. Neither of us could hold still. Each time he danced around and cried, “Dah’s Cairo!” it hit me like a bullet, and I figured that if it _was_ Cairo, I’d die of misery on the spot.

All the while I was arguing with myself, Jim was talking out loud. He said that once he reached a free State, the first thing he’d do was begin saving money, and not spend one cent of it. When he had enough, he’d buy his wife, who belonged to a farm near Miss Watson’s place; then the two of them would work to buy the two children, and if their master refused to sell, they’d find an Abolitionist to go and steal them.

It nearly froze me to hear him talk like that. He would never have dared to talk that way in all his life before. Just look what a difference it made in him the minute he thought he was nearly free. It was just like the old saying: “Give a nigger an inch and he’ll take an ell.” Thinks I, this is what comes of my not thinking. Here was this nigger, whom I had as good as helped to run away, coming right out plain and saying he would steal his children—children who belonged to a man I didn’t even know, a man who had never done me any harm.

I was sorry to hear Jim say that; it brought him down so low. My conscience started stirring me up hotter than ever, until at last I said to it, “Leave me alone—it ain’t too late yet—I’ll paddle ashore at the first light and tell.” Right away I felt easy and happy and light as a feather. All my troubles were gone. I started watching sharp for a light, and sort of singing to myself. After a while one showed. Jim sings out:
“We’s safe, Huck, we’s safe! Jump up and crack yo’ heels! Dat’s de good ole Cairo at las’, I jis knows it!”
I says:
“Let me take the canoe and go look, Jim. Maybe it ain’t, you know.”
Up he jumped and got the canoe ready. He spread his old coat on the bottom for me to sit on, handed me the paddle, and as I shoved off, he says:

“Pooty soon I’ll be shoutin’ for joy, en I’ll say, it’s all on account o’ Huck; I’s a free man, en I never coulda been free ’cept for Huck; Huck done it. Jim ain’t never gwine forgit you, Huck; you’s de bes’ fren’ Jim ever had; en you’s de _only_ fren’ ole Jim got now.”

I was paddling away, all in a sweat to turn him in; but when he said this, it seemed to take all the starch right out of me. I slowed down then, and I wasn’t at all sure whether I was glad I had started or whether I wasn’t. When I was fifty yards off, Jim says:
“Dere you go, de ole true Huck; de on’y white genlman dat ever kep’ his promise to ole Jim.”

Well, I just felt sick. But I told myself I _had_ to do it—there was no getting _out_ of it. Right then a skiff came along with two men in it, carrying guns, and they stopped, and I stopped. One of them says:
“What’s that over there?”
“A piece of a raft,” I says.
“Are you on it?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Anybody else on it?”
“Just one, sir.”
“Well, five niggers broke away tonight, up past the head of the bend. This man of yours—is he white or black?”

I didn’t answer right away. I tried to, but the words wouldn’t come. For a second or two I tried to brace myself and spit it out, but I wasn’t man enough—didn’t have the nerve of a rabbit. I could see I was weakening; so I quit trying, and just up and said:
“He’s white.”
“I think we’ll go and see for ourselves.”
“I wish you would,” I said, “because it’s my pap over there, and maybe you could help me tow the raft in to where the light is. He’s sick—and so are Mam and Mary Ann.”
“Oh, the devil! We’re in a hurry, boy. But I suppose we have to. Come on, get to work with your paddle, and let’s go.”
I dug in with my paddle and they pulled on their oars. After we’d made a stroke or two, I says:
“Pap’ll be awful thankful, I can tell you. Everybody else clears out when I beg them to help tow the raft in, and I can’t manage it alone.”
“Well, that’s rotten mean of them. Peculiar, too. Say, boy, what’s wrong with your father?”
“It’s the—uh—the—well, it ain’t anything much.”
They stopped rowing. It was only a very little way to the raft now. One of them says:
“Boy, you’re lying. What _is_ wrong with your pap? Give us a straight answer, and you’ll be better off.”
“I will, sir, I will, honest—only please don’t go off and leave us. It’s the—the—gentlemen, if you’ll just row ahead and let me toss you the towline, you needn’t come anywhere near the raft—please.”

“Back off, John, back off!” cries one. They backed water. “Stay clear, boy—keep to the leeward side. Blast it, I’ll bet the wind has already blown it our way. Your pap’s got smallpox, and you know it full well. Why didn’t you just say so? Do you want to spread it everywhere?”
“Well,” I said, blubbering, “I told everybody before, and they just up and left us.”

“Poor devil, that’s fair enough. We’re truly sorry for you, but we—well, hang it, we don’t care to catch smallpox, you understand. Now listen, here’s what to do. Don’t try to land on your own, or you’ll wreck the whole thing. Drift on down about twenty miles and you’ll reach a town on the left bank. By then the sun will be well up, and when you ask for help, say your family’s all sick with chills and fever. Don’t be a fool again and let people guess the real trouble. We’re doing you a kindness here, so put twenty miles between us, that’s a good boy. Landing over where the light is wouldn’t help you—it’s just a wood-yard. Say, I imagine your father’s poor, and I must say he’s had hard luck. Look, I’ll lay a twenty-dollar gold piece on this board, and you pick it up as it floats past. I feel mighty low leaving you like this; but my kingdom! Nobody can play games with smallpox, don’t you see?”
“Wait, Parker,” the other man says, “here’s a twenty to go on the board from me, too. Good-bye, boy; do as Mr Parker says and you’ll come out all right.”
“Right you are, my boy—good-bye, good-bye. And if you spot any runaway niggers, fetch help and grab them, and you’ll earn some money.”
“Good-bye, sir,” I said; “no runaway niggers will slip past me if I can stop them.”

They rowed off and I climbed aboard the raft, feeling low and bad, because I knew perfectly well I had done wrong, and I could see it was no use for me to try to learn to do right; a person who doesn’t get _started_ right when he’s little hasn’t got a chance—when the pinch comes there’s nothing to back him up and keep him at his work, and so he gets beaten. Then I thought a minute, and said to myself, hold on; suppose you had done right and given Jim up, would you feel better than you do now? No, says I, I’d feel bad—I’d feel just the same as I do now. Well, then, says I, what’s the use of learning to do right when it’s trouble to do right and no trouble to do wrong, and the pay is just the same? I was stuck. I couldn’t answer that. So I figured I wouldn’t bother about it anymore, but from then on always do whichever came handiest at the time.
I stepped into the wigwam, but Jim wasn’t in it. I searched everywhere, and he was nowhere to be found. I says:
“Jim!”
“I’s right here, Huck. Is dey gone out o’ sight yit? Talk low, now.”
He was in the river, hanging on under the stern oar with only his nose above water. I told him they were gone from sight, and he climbed back onto the raft. He says:

“I heerd ev’ry word dey said, en I slid down in de water, ready to swim off for sho’ if dey come aboard. Den I’d a swum back to de raf’ once dey wuz gone. But lawsy, how you fooled ’em, Huck! Dat _wuz_ de cleverest dodge ever! I tell you, chile, I ’speck you saved ole Jim—ole Jim ain’t gwine forgit dat, honey.”

After that we talked over the money. It was a fine catch—twenty dollars each. Jim said we could buy deck passage on a steamboat now, and the money would carry us as far into the free States as we cared to go. He said another twenty miles wasn’t much for the raft to travel, but he wished we were there already.
Near daybreak we tied up, and Jim was extra careful about hiding the raft well. Then he spent the whole day tying our things into bundles and getting everything ready for us to quit rafting.
About ten that night, we came in sight of the lights of a town far off in a left-hand bend of the river.
I took the canoe and went off to ask about it. Soon I found a man out on the water in a skiff, setting a trot-line. I paddled up alongside and said:
“Mister, is that town Cairo?”
“Cairo? No. You must be a blame’ fool.”
“What town is it, mister?”
“If you want to know, go find out. Hang around here bothering me another half a minute and you’ll get something you won’t like.”
I paddled back to the raft. Jim was terribly let down, but I told him never mind, I reckoned Cairo would be the next place.

We passed another town before daylight, and I was about to go ashore again, but it stood on high ground, so I stayed put. Jim said there was no high ground around Cairo, and I had forgotten that. We lay up for the day on a tow-head pretty close to the left-hand bank. I was starting to suspect something, and so was Jim. I said:
“Maybe we slid right past Cairo in the fog that night.”
He said:
“Let’s not talk ’bout it, Huck. Po’ niggers just can’t have no luck. I allus had a feelin’ dat rattlesnake-skin warn’t finished wid its work.”
“I wish I’d never set eyes on that snake-skin, Jim—I truly wish I’d never even seen the thing.”
“It ain’t yo’ fault, Huck; you didn’t know. Quit blamin’ yo’self ’bout it.”
When daylight came, sure enough, there was the clear Ohio water along the shore, and out in the middle was the same old muddy river! So that was the end of Cairo.

We talked the whole thing over. We couldn’t go overland, and of course we couldn’t push the raft upstream. The only choice was to wait for dark, then start back in the canoe and take our chances. So we slept all day in the cottonwood thicket to be rested for the job. But when we went back to the raft around dark, the canoe was gone!

For a good while neither of us said a word. There was nothing to say. We both knew perfectly well that this was more of the rattlesnake-skin’s work, so what was the use of talking about it? It would only sound like we were finding fault, and that was bound to bring more bad luck—and keep on bringing it, until we learned to keep quiet.

After a while we talked over what we ought to do. We found that the only way was to keep drifting down on the raft until we had a chance to buy a canoe to go back in. We weren’t about to borrow one when nobody was around, the way Pap would have done, because that might send people after us.
So we pushed off on the raft after dark.
If anybody still doesn’t believe it’s foolish to handle a snake-skin, after everything that snake-skin did to us, they’ll believe it now if they read on and see what else it did.

The best place to buy a canoe is from rafts tied up at the shore. But we didn’t see any rafts tied up, so we kept going for three hours and more. Meanwhile the night turned gray and rather thick, which is the next worst thing to fog. You can’t make out the shape of the river, and you can’t see far. It got very late and quiet, and then a steamboat came up the river. We lit the lantern, figuring she would see it. Boats going upstream don’t usually come near us; they hug the bars and hunt for easy water under the reefs. But on nights like this they just bull straight up the channel, fighting the whole river.

We could hear her pounding along, but we didn’t get a good look at her until she was close. She was aimed right at us. They often do that to see how close they can come without touching; sometimes the wheel bites off a sweep, and then the pilot sticks his head out and laughs, thinking he’s mighty smart. Well, here she came, and we said she meant to shave past us, but she didn’t seem to be turning aside at all. She was a big one, and moving fast, looking like a black cloud with rows of glow-worms around it. Then all at once she loomed up, huge and terrifying, with a long row of open furnace doors shining like red-hot teeth, and her monstrous bows and guards hanging right over us. Somebody yelled at us, bells jingled to stop the engines, there was a racket of cussing and a hiss of steam—and as Jim dove off one side and I dove off the other, she came smashing straight through the raft.

I dove down, and I meant to find the bottom, too, because a thirty-foot wheel had to go over me and I wanted to give it plenty of room. I could always stay underwater for a minute; this time I reckon I stayed down a minute and a half. Then I shot up toward the top in a hurry, since I was nearly bursting. I popped out up to my armpits, blew the water out of my nose, and panted a bit. Of course the current was booming, and of course that boat started her engines again ten seconds after she stopped them, since they never cared much about raftsmen. So now she was churning away upriver, out of sight in the thick weather, though I could still hear her.

I yelled for Jim about a dozen times, but got no answer. So I grabbed a plank that bumped against me while I was treading water, and struck out for shore, shoving it ahead of me. But I could tell the current was drifting toward the left-hand shore, which meant I was in a crossing, so I changed course and went that way.

It was one of those long, slanting, two-mile crossings, so it took me a good while to get over. I landed safely and climbed up the bank. I couldn’t see more than a little way, but I went feeling along over rough ground for a quarter of a mile or more, and then I came on a big old-fashioned double log house before I even noticed it. I was about to rush past and get away, but a pack of dogs jumped out and began howling and barking at me, and I knew better than to move another step.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII — An Evening Call
paragraphs: About a minute later somebody spoke from a window, without putting his head out, and said:
“Quiet, boys! Who’s there?”
I said:
“It’s me.”
“Who’s me?”
“George Jackson, sir.”
“What do you want?”
“Nothing, sir. I only want to go on by, but the dogs won’t let me.”
“What are you doing, prowling around here this time of night, hey?”
“I wasn’t prowling, sir. I fell overboard off the steamboat.”
“Oh, you did, did you? Somebody strike a light. What did you say your name was?”
“George Jackson, sir. I’m only a boy.”

“Listen here: if you’re telling the truth, you don’t need to be afraid—nobody will hurt you. But don’t try to move; stay right where you are. Some of you wake up Bob and Tom and bring the guns. George Jackson, is there anybody with you?”
“No, sir, nobody.”
Now I could hear people stirring around in the house, and I saw a light. The man shouted:
“Get that light out of sight, Betsy, you old fool—have you no sense at all? Set it on the floor behind the front door. Bob, if you and Tom are ready, get into position.”
“All ready.”
“Now, George Jackson, do you know the Shepherdsons?”
“No, sir; I never heard of them.”

“Well, that may be so, and it may not. Now, everybody ready. Step forward, George Jackson. And mind, don’t hurry—come very slowly. If anybody’s with you, tell him to stay back—if he shows himself, he’ll be shot. Come along now. Come slow. Push the door open yourself—just enough to squeeze in, you hear?”

I didn’t hurry; I couldn’t have, even if I’d wanted to. I took slow steps, one at a time, and everything was silent except what I thought was my own heartbeat. The dogs were as quiet as the people, but they trailed along a little behind me. When I reached the three log doorsteps, I heard the door being unlocked, unbarred and unbolted. I laid my hand on it and pushed it open a crack, then a little more, until somebody said, “There, that’s enough—stick your head in.” I did, though I figured they meant to take it off.

The candle was on the floor, and there they all were, looking at me and me at them, for about a quarter of a minute. There were three big men with guns pointed at me, which made me flinch, I tell you. The oldest was gray and about sixty, and the other two were thirty or more—all of them fine and handsome. There was also the sweetest old gray-headed lady, and behind her two young women whom I couldn’t see very well. The old gentleman said:
“There; I reckon it’s all right. Come in.”

Once I was inside, the old gentleman locked the door, then barred it and bolted it. He told the young men to bring their guns in, and they all went into a big parlor with a new rag carpet on the floor and gathered in a corner away from the front windows—there weren’t any on the side. They held the candle up, studied me carefully, and all said, “Why, _he_ isn’t a Shepherdson—no, nothing about him looks like a Shepherdson.” Then the old man said he hoped I wouldn’t mind if he checked me for weapons, because he meant no harm—he only wanted to be sure. So he didn’t dig into my pockets, just patted the outside with his hands and said I was fine. He told me to relax and make myself at home, and to tell them all about myself. But the old lady spoke up:
“Why, bless you, Saul, the poor thing is as wet as can be; and don’t you suppose he might be hungry?”
“You’re right, Rachel—I forgot.”
So the old lady said:

“Betsy” (this was a nigger woman), “run and fetch him something to eat, as fast as you can, poor thing; and one of you girls go wake Buck and tell him—oh, here he comes now. Buck, take this little stranger, get him out of those wet clothes, and put him in some dry ones of yours.”

Buck looked about my age—thirteen or fourteen or thereabouts, though he was a little bigger than me. He had nothing on but a shirt, and his hair was a mess. He came in yawning and rubbing one fist in his eyes, and dragging a gun along with the other hand. He said:
“Ain’t there no Shepherdsons around?”
They told him no, it was a false alarm.
“Well,” he said, “if there had been any, I reckon I’d have got one.”
They all laughed, and Bob said:
“Why, Buck, they could have scalped us all, you were so slow getting here.”
“Well, nobody came to get me, and it ain’t right that I’m always kept out of things. I never get a chance.”
“Never mind, Buck, my boy,” the old man said, “your turn will come, all in good time, so don’t worry about that. Now off you go, and do what your mother told you.”

When we got upstairs to his room, he gave me a coarse shirt and a short jacket and some pants of his, and I put them on. While I was doing it, he asked me my name, but before I could tell him, he started telling me about a bluejay and a young rabbit he had caught in the woods the day before yesterday. Then he asked me where Moses was when the candle went out. I said I didn’t know; I’d never heard about it before, not at all.
“Well, guess,” he said.
“How am I supposed to guess,” I said, “when I never heard of it before?”
“But you can guess, can’t you? It’s easy.”
“_Which_ candle?” I said.
“Why, any candle,” he said.
“I don’t know where he was,” I said. “Where was he?”
“Why, he was in the _dark!_ That’s where he was!”
“Well, if you knew where he was, why did you ask me?”

“Why, blame it all, it’s a riddle, can’t you see? Say, how long are you staying? You’ve got to stay for good. We’ll have the grandest times—there’s no school now. Have you got a dog? I’ve got one, and he’ll jump in the river and bring out chips you throw in. Do you like fixing up your hair on Sundays and all that foolishness? Not me, you bet, but Ma makes me. Confound these old britches! I suppose I’d better put them on, but I’d rather not, it’s so warm. Ready? All right. Come on, old pal.”

Cold corn-pone, cold corned beef, butter and buttermilk—that is what they had for me down there, and I’ve never come across anything better since. Buck and his ma and all the rest of them smoked corncob pipes, except the nigger woman, who was gone, and the two young women. They all smoked and talked, and I ate and talked. The young women had quilts wrapped around them, with their hair hanging down their backs. They all asked me questions, and I told them how Pap and I and the whole family had been living on a little farm at the bottom of Arkansaw. My sister Mary Ann ran off and got married and was never heard of again, and Bill went to hunt for them and was never heard of again either. Tom and Mort died, and then there was nobody left but me and Pap, and he was worn down to nothing, on account of his troubles. So when he died, I took what was left, because the farm didn’t belong to us, and started up the river as a deck passenger, and fell overboard; and that was how I came to be there. So they said I could have a home there as long as I wanted it. By then it was nearly daylight, and everybody went to bed, and I went to bed with Buck. When I woke up in the morning, drat it all, I had forgotten what my name was. So I lay there about an hour trying to think, and when Buck woke up I said:
“Can you spell, Buck?”
“Yes,” he said.
“I bet you can’t spell my name,” I said.
“I bet you anything I can,” he said.
“All right,” I said, “go ahead.”
“G-e-o-r-g-e J-a-x-o-n—there now,” he said.
“Well,” I said, “you did it, but I didn’t think you could. It’s no easy name to spell—right off the bat, without studying.”
I wrote it down in private, because somebody might want _me_ to spell it next, and I wanted to be ready and rattle it off as if I were used to it.

It was a mighty nice family, and a mighty nice house too. I’d never seen a country house with so much style. The front door didn’t have an iron latch, or a wooden one with a buckskin string. It had a brass knob you turned, just like the houses in town. There wasn’t any bed in the parlor, or any sign of one, though plenty of parlors in town do have beds in them. The big fireplace had a brick floor, and the bricks were kept clean and red by pouring water on them and scrubbing them with another brick. Sometimes they washed them over with a red water-paint called Spanish-brown, the same as people do in town. The brass dog-irons were big enough to hold up a saw-log. In the middle of the mantelpiece stood a clock. The bottom half of its glass front had a town painted on it, with a round empty spot in the middle for the sun, and you could see the pendulum swinging behind it. It was beautiful to hear that clock tick. Sometimes, after one of those peddlers had come by and cleaned her up and got her working right, she’d start in and strike a hundred and fifty before she wore herself out. They wouldn’t have taken any money for her.

Well, on each side of the clock sat a big, outlandish parrot made of something like chalk and painted up gaudy. Next to one parrot was a cat made of crockery, and next to the other a crockery dog. When you pressed down on them they squeaked, but their mouths never opened and they didn’t look any different or any more interested. The squeak came out from underneath. Behind all these things a couple of big wild-turkey-wing fans were spread out. On the table in the middle of the room sat a lovely kind of crockery basket, piled high with apples, oranges, peaches and grapes. They were much redder and yellower and prettier than real fruit, but they weren’t real, because you could see where pieces had chipped off and shown the white chalk, or whatever it was, underneath.

The table had a beautiful oilcloth cover, painted with a red and blue spread-eagle and a painted border all the way around. They said it came all the way from Philadelphia. Books were stacked, perfectly squared, on each corner of the table. One was a big family Bible full of pictures. One was Pilgrim’s Progress, about a man who left his family, though it never said why. I read a good deal of it now and then. The statements were interesting, but tough. Another was Friendship’s Offering, full of beautiful stuff and poetry, but I didn’t read the poetry. Another was Henry Clay’s Speeches, and another was Dr. Gunn’s Family Medicine, which told you everything to do if a person was sick or dead. There was a hymn book too, and a lot of other books. There were also nice split-bottom chairs, perfectly sound, not sagging in the middle and busted like an old basket.

They had pictures hanging on the walls, mostly Washingtons and Lafayettes, battles, Highland Marys, and one called “Signing the Declaration.” Some were what they called crayons, drawn by one of the daughters, who was dead now. She did them all herself when she was only fifteen. They were different from any pictures I’d seen before, and blacker than usual. One showed a woman in a slim black dress, belted tight up under the armpits, with puffs like cabbages in the middle of the sleeves. She wore a big black scoop-shovel bonnet with a black veil, and her thin white ankles were crisscrossed with black tape, and she had tiny black slippers shaped like chisels. She was leaning thoughtfully on her right elbow against a tombstone, under a weeping willow, with her other hand hanging at her side holding a white handkerchief and a purse. Underneath the picture it said “Shall I Never See You More Alas.” Another showed a young lady with her hair combed straight up to the top of her head and knotted in front of a comb like the back of a chair. She was crying into a handkerchief, and in her other hand she held a dead bird lying on its back with its feet in the air. Underneath it said “I Shall Never Hear Your Sweet Chirrup More Alas.” In another a young lady sat at a window looking up at the moon, with tears running down her cheeks. She had an open letter in one hand, with black sealing wax showing on one edge, and she was pressing a locket on a chain against her mouth. Underneath it said “And Are You Gone Yes You Are Gone Alas.” I reckon these were all nice pictures, but somehow I didn’t take to them, because whenever I was feeling a little low they gave me the fan-tods. Everybody was sorry she died, because she’d planned a lot more of these pictures, and you could tell from what she’d finished what they had lost. But I figured that with her disposition she was having a better time in the graveyard. She had been working on what they said was her greatest picture when she took sick. Every day and every night she prayed to be allowed to live until she finished it, but she never got the chance. It showed a young woman in a long white gown, standing on the rail of a bridge, all ready to jump off, with her hair hanging down her back, looking up at the moon with tears running down her face. She had two arms folded across her chest, two stretched out in front, and two more reaching up toward the moon. The idea was to see which pair looked best and then scratch out all the other arms. But, as I was saying, she died before she made up her mind. Now they kept this picture over the head of the bed in her room, and every time her birthday came around they hung flowers on it. The rest of the time it was hidden behind a little curtain. The young woman in the picture had a nice, sweet face, but with so many arms she looked too spidery, it seemed to me.

While she was alive, this girl kept a scrap-book. She used to paste in obituaries, accidents and cases of patient suffering clipped from the _Presbyterian Observer_, and then write poetry after them out of her own head. It was very good poetry. This is what she wrote about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots, who fell down a well and drowned:
ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D
Did young Stephen fall ill? Did young Stephen die? Did sad hearts grow heavy? Did mourners cry?
No, that was not the fate Of Stephen Dowling Bots; Sad hearts did grow heavy, But not from sickness’ shots.
No whooping-cough shook his frame, Nor dreary measles spots; Not these harmed the sacred name Of Stephen Dowling Bots.
Scorned love did not bring woe To that head of curly knots, Nor stomach troubles laid him low, Young Stephen Dowling Bots.
Oh no. Then hear with tearful eye The fate I now will tell. His soul flew from this cold world by Falling down a well.
They pulled him out and drained him dry; Alas, it was too late. His spirit had gone to sport on high In the realms of the good and great.

If Emmeline Grangerford could write poetry like that before she was fourteen, there’s no telling what she might have done by and by. Buck said she could rattle off poetry like nothing. She never had to stop and think. He said she’d slap down a line, and if she couldn’t find anything to rhyme with it, she’d just scratch it out and slap down another and keep going. She wasn’t particular. She could write about anything you gave her, as long as it was sad. Every time a man died, or a woman, or a child, she was on hand with her “tribute” before the body was cold. She called them tributes. The neighbors said it was the doctor first, then Emmeline, then the undertaker. The undertaker only beat Emmeline once, and that was when she got stuck on a rhyme for the dead person’s name, which was Whistler. She was never the same after that. She never complained, but she sort of pined away and didn’t live long. Poor thing, many a time I made myself go up to the little room that used to be hers and get out her poor old scrap-book and read in it, when her pictures had been aggravating me and I’d soured on her a little. I liked that whole family, the dead ones too, and I wasn’t going to let anything come between us. Poor Emmeline wrote poetry about all the dead people while she was alive, and it didn’t seem right that nobody was left to write some about her now that she was gone. So I tried to sweat out a verse or two myself, but somehow I couldn’t make it go. They kept Emmeline’s room neat and nice, with everything in it fixed just the way she liked it when she was alive, and nobody ever slept there. The old lady looked after the room herself, though there were plenty of niggers, and she did a lot of her sewing there, and mostly read her Bible there.

Well, as I was saying about the parlor, the windows had beautiful curtains: white ones, painted with pictures of castles with vines running down the walls, and cattle coming down to drink. There was also a little old piano with tin pans inside it, I reckon, and nothing was ever as lovely as hearing the young ladies sing “The Last Link is Broken” and play “The Battle of Prague” on it. The walls of all the rooms were plastered, most of them had carpets on the floors, and the whole house was whitewashed outside.

It was a double house, and the wide open space between the two halves had a roof and a floor. Sometimes they set the table there in the middle of the day, and it was a cool, comfortable place. Nothing could be better. And wasn’t the cooking good, and bushels of it too!

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII — Col. Grangerford
paragraphs: Col. Grangerford was a gentleman, you see. He was a gentleman all the way through, and so was his family. He was well born, as the saying goes, and the Widow Douglas used to say that counts for as much in a man as in a horse. Nobody ever denied that she was from the first aristocracy in our town, and pap said the same, though he himself was no more quality than a mudcat. Col. Grangerford was very tall and very slim, with a dark, pale complexion and not a trace of red in it anywhere. Every morning he shaved his thin face clean. He had the thinnest lips and the thinnest nostrils, a high nose, heavy eyebrows, and the blackest eyes, sunk so deep that they seemed to be looking out at you from caverns, as you might say. His forehead was high, and his black, straight hair hung to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin. Every day of his life he put on a clean shirt and a full suit from head to foot, made of linen so white it hurt your eyes to look at it. On Sundays he wore a blue tail-coat with brass buttons, and he carried a mahogany cane with a silver head. There was no frivolishness about him, not a bit, and he was never loud. He was as kind as could be. You could feel that, you know, and so you trusted him. Sometimes he smiled, and that was good to see. But when he straightened up like a liberty-pole and the lightning began to flicker out from under his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree first and find out what was the matter afterward. He never had to tell anybody to mind their manners, because everybody behaved well wherever he was. Everybody loved having him around, too. He was sunshine most of the time, I mean he made it seem like good weather. When he turned into a cloudbank it got awful dark for half a minute, and that was enough. Nothing would go wrong again for a week.

When he and the old lady came down in the morning, the whole family rose from their chairs and wished them good day, and nobody sat down again until they had. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the decanter was, mixed a glass of bitters, and handed it to him. He held it in his hand and waited until Tom’s and Bob’s were mixed. Then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam,” and _they_ bowed the least bit in the world and said thank you, and all three drank. Then Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water over the sugar and the tiny bit of whisky or apple brandy in the bottom of their tumblers, and handed them to me and Buck, and we drank to the old people too.

Bob was the oldest and Tom came next. They were tall, handsome men with very broad shoulders, brown faces, and long black hair and black eyes. Like the old gentleman, they dressed in white linen from head to foot, and they wore broad Panama hats.

Then there was Miss Charlotte. She was twenty-five, tall and proud and grand, and as good as could be when she wasn’t stirred up. When she was, she had a look that would make you wilt where you stood, just like her father. She was beautiful.
Her sister, Miss Sophia, was beautiful too, but differently. She was gentle and sweet as a dove, and just twenty years old.

Every one of them had a personal nigger to wait on them, Buck included. Mine had a monstrous easy time of it, since I wasn’t used to having anyone do things for me, but Buck’s nigger was hopping around nearly all the time.
That was all the family there was now, but there used to be more: three sons, who got killed, and Emmeline, who died.

The old gentleman owned a lot of farms and over a hundred niggers. Sometimes a crowd of people would ride in on horseback from ten or fifteen miles around and stay five or six days. They had such junketings around the place and on the river, with dances and picnics in the woods in the daytime and balls at the house at night. These people were mostly kinfolks of the family, and the men brought their guns with them. It was a handsome lot of quality, I tell you.

Another clan of aristocracy lived around there, five or six families, mostly named Shepherdson. They were as high-toned and well born and rich and grand as the Grangerford tribe. The Shepherdsons and the Grangerfords used the same steamboat landing, about two miles above our house. So sometimes, when I went up there with a crowd of our folks, I saw a lot of the Shepherdsons there on their fine horses.
One day Buck and me were way out in the woods hunting when we heard a horse coming. We were crossing the road. Buck said:
“Quick! Jump for the woods!”

We did, and then peeked down through the leaves into the woods. Pretty soon a fine-looking young man came galloping down the road, sitting his horse easy and looking like a soldier. He had his gun resting across the front of his saddle. I had seen him before. It was young Harney Shepherdson. I heard Buck’s gun go off right beside my ear, and Harney’s hat flew off his head. He snatched up his gun and rode straight for the spot where we were hiding. But we didn’t wait around. We took off through the woods at a run. The woods weren’t thick, so I kept glancing back over my shoulder, ready to duck the bullet, and twice I saw Harney aim his gun at Buck. Then he rode off the way he had come—to get his hat, I reckon, but I couldn’t tell. We never stopped running till we got home. The old gentleman’s eyes blazed for a minute—it was pleasure, mostly, I judged—and then his face sort of smoothed over, and he said, kind of gentle:
“I don’t like that, shooting from behind a bush. Why didn’t you step out into the road, my boy?”
“Shepherdsons never do, father. They always grab every advantage they can.”

Miss Charlotte held her head up like a queen the whole time Buck was telling his story, and her nostrils flared and her eyes flashed. The two young men looked grim, but they never said a word. Miss Sophia went pale, but the color came back when she learned the man wasn’t hurt.
As soon as I could get Buck off alone, down by the corn-cribs under the trees, I said:
“Did you want to kill him, Buck?”
“Well, you bet I did.”
“What did he ever do to you?”
“Him? He never did a thing to me.”
“Then why did you want to kill him?”
“Why, no reason—it’s just because of the feud.”
“What’s a feud?”
“Why, where were you raised? Don’t you know what a feud is?”
“I never heard of one before. Tell me about it.”

“Well,” Buck said, “here’s how a feud goes. A man has a quarrel with another man and kills him. Then that man’s brother kills _him;_ then the other brothers, on both sides, go after one another; then the _cousins_ join in—and after a while everybody’s dead, and there ain’t any more feud. But it’s kind of slow and takes a long time.”
“Has this one been going on a long time, Buck?”

“Well, I should _say!_ It started thirty years ago, or somewhere around there. There was some trouble over something, and then a lawsuit to settle it. The suit went against one of the men, so he up and shot the man who won—which he would naturally do, of course. Anybody would.”
“What was the trouble about, Buck?—land?”
“I reckon maybe—I don’t know.”
“Well, who started the shooting? A Grangerford or a Shepherdson?”
“Lord, how would _I_ know? It was so long ago.”
“Doesn’t anybody know?”
“Oh, sure, pa knows, I reckon, and a few of the other old folks. But even they can’t tell you now what the row was over to begin with.”
“Have a lot of people been killed, Buck?”

“Yes, a good many funerals. But they don’t always kill. Pa’s got a few buckshot in him, but he don’t mind, since he don’t weigh much anyway. Bob’s been cut up some with a bowie knife, and Tom’s been hurt once or twice.”
“Has anybody been killed this year, Buck?”

“Yes, we got one and they got one. About three months ago my cousin Bud, fourteen years old, was riding through the woods on the other side of the river. He didn’t have any weapon with him, which was plain foolishness. In a lonesome stretch he heard a horse coming up behind him, and he saw old Baldy Shepherdson loping after him with a gun in his hand and his white hair flying in the wind. Instead of jumping off and running for the brush, Bud figured he could outrun him. So they raced, neck and neck, for five miles or more, with the old man gaining all the time. At last Bud saw it was no use, so he stopped and turned around to face him, so as to have the bullet holes in front, you know. The old man rode up and shot him down. But he didn’t get much chance to enjoy his luck, because inside of a week our folks laid _him_ out.”
“I’d say that old man was a coward, Buck.”

“I reckon he _wasn’t_ a coward. Not by a long shot. There ain’t a coward among those Shepherdsons—not a one. And there ain’t any cowards among the Grangerfords either. Why, one day that old man held his own in a fight for half an hour against three Grangerfords, and came out the winner. They were all on horseback. He climbed off his horse and got behind a little woodpile, and kept his horse in front of him to stop the bullets. But the Grangerfords stayed on their horses and rode circles around the old man, firing away at him, and he fired away at them. He and his horse both went home pretty full of holes and crippled, but the Grangerfords had to be _carried_ home—and one of them was dead, and another died the next day. No, sir. If a body’s out hunting for cowards, he don’t want to waste any time among those Shepherdsons, because they don’t breed that _kind_.”

The next Sunday we all rode to church, three miles away, every last one of us on horseback. The men brought their guns, and Buck did too, and they held them between their knees or leaned them close by against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same. The preaching was pretty ornery—all about loving your brother and other tiresome stuff like that. Still, everybody called it a fine sermon, and they chewed it over the whole way home. They had such a powerful lot to say about faith and good works and free grace and preforeordestination, and I don’t know what all, that to me it seemed about the roughest Sunday I had come across yet.

About an hour after dinner everybody was dozing around, some in their chairs and some in their rooms, and it got to be pretty dull. Buck and a dog were stretched out on the grass in the sun, sound asleep. I went up to our room and figured I’d take a nap myself. There was sweet Miss Sophia standing in her doorway, which was next to ours. She took me into her room and shut the door very softly, and asked me if I liked her, and I said I did. She asked if I would do something for her and not tell anybody, and I said I would. Then she said she had forgotten her Testament and left it on the church seat between two other books, and would I sneak out quietly, go fetch it for her, and not say anything to anybody. I said I would. So I slipped out and went up the road, and there wasn’t anybody at the church, except maybe a hog or two, since there wasn’t any lock on the door, and hogs like a plank floor in summertime because it’s cool. If you notice, most folks don’t go to church unless they have to; but a hog is different.

I said to myself, something’s up; it ain’t natural for a girl to be in such a sweat over a Testament. So I gave it a shake, and out dropped a little piece of paper with “_Half-past two_” written on it in pencil. I searched the book, but couldn’t find anything else. I couldn’t make anything of that, so I put the paper back in the book. When I got home and went upstairs, there was Miss Sophia in her doorway, waiting for me. She pulled me in and shut the door. Then she looked through the Testament till she found the paper, and as soon as she read it she looked glad. Before a body could think, she grabbed me and gave me a squeeze, and said I was the best boy in the world, and not to tell anybody. She was awful red in the face for a minute, and her eyes lit up, and it made her mighty pretty. I was pretty astonished, but when I got my breath back I asked her what the paper was about. She asked me if I had read it, and I said no. She asked if I could read writing, and I told her, “No, only coarse-hand.” Then she said the paper was nothing but a book-mark to keep her place, and I could go and play now.

I went off down to the river, thinking this over, and pretty soon I noticed that my nigger was following along behind me. When we were out of sight of the house, he glanced back and around for a second, and then came running up and said:
“Mars Jawge, come on down to de swamp wid me, en I’ll show you a whole pile o’ water-moccasins.”
I thought, now that’s mighty peculiar; he said the same thing yesterday. He ought to know nobody likes water-moccasins well enough to go looking for them. What is he up to, anyhow? So I told him:
“All right; lead the way.”

I followed him half a mile. Then he struck out across the swamp and waded ankle-deep for about another half mile. We came to a little flat piece of dry land, very thick with trees and bushes and vines, and he said:
“Jist push on in dere a few steps, Mars Jawge; dat’s whah dey is. I’s seen ’em already; I don’t keer to see ’em no mo’.”

Then he sloshed right along and went away, and pretty soon the trees hid him. I pushed a little way into the place and came to a small open patch, about as big as a bedroom, with vines hanging all around it. And there lay a man, fast asleep—and, by jings, it was my old Jim!

I woke him up, and I figured it would be a grand surprise to him to see me again, but it wasn’t. He nearly cried, he was so glad, but he wasn’t surprised. He said he had swum along behind me that night and heard me yell every time, but didn’t dare answer, because he didn’t want anybody to pick _him_ up and take him back into slavery. He said:

“I got hurt a little, en I couldn’t swim fas’, so I wuz way behine you by de end. When you got to shore I figgered I could ketch up wid you on land widout hollerin’ at you. But den I seen dat house, en I started goin’ slow. I wuz too fur off to hear what dey said to you—I wuz scared o’ de dogs. But when it got all quiet agin, I knowed you wuz inside, so I headed for de woods to wait fer daylight. Early in de mawnin’ some o’ de niggers come by, on dey way to de fields, en dey took me en showed me dis place, whah de dogs can’t track me on account o’ de water. En ev’ry night dey brings me food, en tells me how you’s gittin’ on.”
“Why didn’t you tell my Jack to bring me here sooner, Jim?”
“Well, I didn’t want to bother you, Huck, not till we could do sumfn—but we’s all right now. I been buyin’ pots en pans en grub, whenever I got a chanst, en fixin’ up de raf’ at night when—”
“_What_ raft, Jim?”
“Our ole raf’.”
“Do you mean to tell me our old raft wasn’t smashed to pieces?”

“No, she wasn’t. She got tore up a good bit—one end of her did. But dere wasn’t much harm done, ’cept our things wuz mos’ all los’. If we hadn’t dived so deep en swum so far under water, en de night hadn’t been so dark, en we hadn’t been so scared, en such pumpkin-heads, as de sayin’ goes, we’d a seen de raf’. But it’s jist as well we didn’t, ’cause now she’s all fixed up agin, mos’ as good as new, en we got a new lot o’ stuff to replace what wuz los’.”
“Well, how did you get the raft back, Jim—did you catch her?”

“How wuz I gwine to catch her, out in de woods? No. Some o’ de niggers found her stuck on a snag right here in de bend, en dey hid her in a creek amongst de willows. Dey wuz so much arguin’ over which one o’ dem she belonged to de mos’ dat I heard ’bout it purty soon. So I stepped in en settled de fuss by tellin’ ’em she don’t belong to none o’ dem, she belong to you en me. En I ast ’em, wuz dey gwine to grab a young white gentleman’s property en git a whippin’ for it? Den I gave ’em ten cents apiece, en dey wuz mighty well satisfied, en wished some mo’ rafts ’ud come along en make ’em rich agin. Dey’s mighty good to me, dese niggers is, en whatever I wants done, I don’t have to ask ’em twice, honey. Dat Jack’s a good nigger, en purty smart.”

“Yes, he is. He never told me you were here. He told me to come along and he’d show me a lot of water-moccasins. That way, if anything comes of this, he ain’t mixed up in it. He can say he never saw us together, and it’ll be the truth.”

I don’t want to talk much about the next day. I reckon I’ll keep it pretty short. I woke up about dawn and was going to roll over and go back to sleep, when I noticed how still it was—nobody seemed to be stirring. That wasn’t usual. Next I noticed that Buck was up and gone. Well, I got up, wondering, and went downstairs—nobody around, everything still as a mouse. It was the same outside. I thought, what does it mean? Down by the woodpile I ran across my Jack, and said:
“What’s it all about?”
He said:
“Don’t you know, Mars Jawge?”
“No,” I said, “I don’t.”

“Well, den, Miss Sophia’s run off! She sure has. She slipped off sometime in de night—nobody knows jist when. Run off to marry dat young Harney Shepherdson, you know—leastways, dat’s what dey figger. De fambly found out ’bout half an hour ago, maybe a little mo’, en I _tell_ you, dey didn’t waste no time. You never seen sich a rushin’ roun’ fer guns en hosses! De women folks gone to rouse up de relations, en ole Mars Saul en de boys grabbed dey guns en rode up de river road to try en ketch dat young man en kill him ’fo’ he kin git across de river wid Miss Sophia. I reckon dey’s gwine to be mighty rough times.”
“Buck went off without waking me up.”

“Well, I reckon he _did!_ Dey wasn’t gwine to drag you into it. Mars Buck loaded up his gun en swore he’d bring home a Shepherdson or bust. Well, dere’ll be plenty o’ dem dere, I reckon, en you bet he’ll bring one down if he gits a chanst.”

I took off up the river road as hard as I could go. By and by I began to hear guns a good way off. When I came in sight of the log store and the woodpile where the steamboats land, I worked my way along under the trees and brush until I reached a good spot. Then I climbed up into the fork of a cottonwood, out of reach, and watched. A little way in front of the tree there was a wood-rank four feet high, and at first I was going to hide behind that; but maybe it was luckier that I didn’t.

Four or five men were cavorting on their horses in the open ground in front of the log store, cussing and yelling, trying to get at two young fellows crouched behind the wood-rank next to the steamboat landing. They couldn’t do it. Whenever one of them showed himself on the river side of the pile, he got shot at. The two boys were squatting back to back behind the pile, so they could watch in both directions.

After a while the men quit their whooping and cavorting around and started riding toward the store. Then one of the boys raised his gun, took a steady aim over the wood-rank, and knocked one of the men out of his saddle. The rest all jumped off their horses, grabbed the wounded man, and started carrying him to the store; and that very minute the two boys took off running. They had made it halfway to my tree before the men noticed. Then the men saw them, jumped on their horses, and chased after them. They were gaining on the boys, but it didn’t do them any good; the boys had too big a lead. They reached the woodpile in front of my tree and ducked in behind it, so they had the advantage over the men again. One of the boys was Buck, and the other was a slim young fellow about nineteen years old.

The men raced around for a while, and then rode off. The minute they were out of sight, I called down to Buck and told him where I was. At first he couldn’t figure out where my voice was coming from up in the tree, and he was awfully surprised. He told me to keep a sharp lookout and let him know when the men showed up again; he said they were up to some kind of devilment and wouldn’t be gone long. I wished I was out of that tree, but I didn’t dare come down. Buck started to cry and rage, and swore that he and his cousin Joe (the other young fellow) would get even for this day yet. He said his father and his two brothers were killed, and two or three of the enemy. He said the Shepherdsons had waited in ambush for them. Buck said his father and brothers should have waited for their relatives—the Shepherdsons were too strong for them. I asked him what had become of young Harney and Miss Sophia. He said they had gotten across the river and were safe. I was glad of that; but the way Buck carried on because he hadn’t managed to kill Harney the day he shot at him—I never heard anything like it.

All of a sudden—bang! bang! bang!—three or four guns went off. The men had slipped around through the woods and come up from behind, on foot! The boys dove for the river, both of them hurt, and as they swam down with the current the men ran along the bank shooting at them and shouting, “Kill them, kill them!” It made me so sick I nearly fell out of the tree. I’m not going to tell _all_ that happened—it would make me sick again if I did. I wished I had never come ashore that night to see such things. I’ll never get rid of them—lots of times I dream about them.

I stayed in the tree until it started to get dark, too afraid to come down. Sometimes I heard guns far off in the woods, and twice I saw little gangs of men gallop past the log store with guns, so I figured the trouble was still going on. I felt terribly low, and I made up my mind I would never go near that house again, because I figured I was to blame somehow. I guessed that piece of paper meant Miss Sophia was supposed to meet Harney somewhere at half-past two and run off with him; and I guessed I should have told her father about that paper and the strange way she acted, and then maybe he would have locked her up, and this awful mess would never have happened.

When I got down out of the tree, I crept along the river bank a little way and found the two bodies lying at the water’s edge. I tugged at them until I got them ashore, then covered up their faces and got away as fast as I could. I cried a little while I was covering up Buck’s face, because he had been mighty good to me.

Night had just fallen. I stayed away from the house, cut through the woods, and made for the swamp. Jim wasn’t on his island, so I hurried off toward the creek and shoved my way through the willows, itching to climb aboard and leave that terrible country behind. The raft was gone! Lord, was I scared! For close to a minute I couldn’t catch my breath. Then I hollered out, and a voice answered, not twenty-five foot away:
“Lawsy mercy! Dat you, honey? Don’ make no noise.”
That was Jim’s voice—nothing had ever sounded so good to me. I ran a short way down the bank and climbed aboard, and Jim threw his arms around me and hugged me, he was that happy to see me. He said:

“Bless you, chile, I was plumb sho’ you’s dead again. Jack’s been here; he say he reck’n you’s been shot, ’cause you didn’ come home no mo’. So I’s jes’ dis minute startin’ de raf’ down toward de mouf er de crick, so’s to be all ready to shove out en leave soon as Jack come back en tells me for certain you _is_ dead. Lawsy, I’s mighty glad to have you back again, honey.”
I said:

“All right, that’s mighty good. They won’t find me, and they’ll think I’m dead and floated off down the river—there’s something up there that will make them think so. So don’t waste a minute, Jim. Just shove off for the big water as fast as you can.”

I couldn’t relax until the raft was two miles downstream and out in the middle of the Mississippi. Then we hung up our signal lantern and decided we were free and safe again. I hadn’t eaten a bite since yesterday, so Jim brought out some corn-dodgers, buttermilk, pork, cabbage and greens—nothing in the world tastes so good when it’s cooked right—and we talked and enjoyed ourselves while I ate my supper. I was powerful glad to be away from the feuds, and Jim was just as glad to be out of the swamp. We agreed that after all, there was no home like a raft. Other places feel so cramped and stuffy, but a raft never does. On a raft you feel mighty free and easy and comfortable.

chapters.title: Chapter XIX — Tying Up Day-times
paragraphs: Two or three days and nights went by; I reckon I could say they swam by, they slid along so quiet and smooth and lovely. Here is how we passed the time. It was a monstrous big river down there, sometimes a mile and a half wide. We ran at night and laid up and hid in the daytime. As soon as the night was nearly gone we stopped and tied up—nearly always in the dead water under a tow-head—and then cut young cottonwoods and willows and hid the raft under them. Then we set out the lines. Next we slid into the river and had a swim to freshen up and cool off; then we sat down on the sandy bottom, where the water was about knee deep, and watched the daylight come. Not a sound anywhere, perfectly still, just as if the whole world were asleep, except maybe the bullfrogs croaking now and then. The first thing you could see, looking out over the water, was a kind of dull line—that was the woods on the other side, and you couldn’t make out anything else. Then a pale place in the sky; then more paleness spreading around; then the river softened away off in the distance and wasn’t black anymore but gray. You could see little dark spots drifting along ever so far away—trading scows and such—and long black streaks that were rafts. Sometimes you could hear a sweep creaking, or voices all jumbled together, it was so still and sounds carried so far. After a while you could see a streak on the water, and from the look of the streak you knew there was a snag there, where the swift current breaks against it and makes the streak look that way. You see the mist curl up off the water, and the east turns red, and the river too, and you make out a log cabin at the edge of the woods, way over on the other bank—a woodyard, likely, piled up by those cheats so you could throw a dog through it anywhere. Then a nice breeze springs up and comes fanning you from over there, so cool and fresh and sweet-smelling from the woods and the flowers; but sometimes not, because they’ve left dead fish lying around, gars and such, and they get pretty rank. And next you’ve got the full day, and everything smiling in the sun, and the songbirds just going at it!

Once the sun was up, nobody would notice a little smoke, so we would pull some fish off the lines and cook a hot breakfast. After that we would sit and watch how lonesome the river was, and kind of laze along, and drift off to sleep before long. We’d wake up and look around for what had done it, and maybe spot a steamboat coughing upstream, so far over toward the other bank that all you could tell about her was whether she had a stern wheel or side wheels. Then for an hour there would be nothing to hear and nothing to see—just plain lonesomeness. Next a raft would slide past, way off yonder, and maybe a galoot on it chopping wood, since they nearly always are on a raft. You’d see the axe flash and come down, and hear nothing; you’d see it go up again, and not until it was over the man’s head would you hear the _k’chunk!_—the sound had needed all that time to cross the water. So we would pass the day, lazing about and listening to the quiet. Once there was a thick fog, and the rafts and boats that went by were beating tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run them down. One scow or raft passed so near we could hear the people talking and cussing and laughing, plain as anything, yet we couldn’t see a trace of them. It gave you the creeps; it was as if spirits were carrying on in the air. Jim said he believed it was spirits, but I told him:
“No. Spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

As soon as it was dark we shoved off. When we got her out to about the middle, we left her alone and let her float wherever the current wanted to take her. Then we lit our pipes and dangled our legs in the water and talked about all kinds of things. We went naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us—the new clothes Buck’s folks made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and anyway I never went much on clothes.

Sometimes we had the whole river to ourselves for the longest time. Across the water lay the banks and the islands, and maybe a spark that was a candle in a cabin window; and sometimes out on the river you could see a spark or two, on a raft or a scow, you understand, and maybe hear a fiddle or a song floating over from one of those boats. Living on a raft is lovely. Overhead was the sky, all speckled with stars, and we used to lie on our backs looking up at them and arguing over whether somebody made them or they just happened. Jim thought they were made, but I thought they happened; it seemed to me it would have taken far too long to _make_ so many. Jim said the moon might have _laid_ them. Well, that sounded fairly reasonable, so I didn’t argue, since I’ve seen a frog lay nearly as many, so of course it could be done. We also watched the falling stars and saw them streak down the sky. Jim thought they had spoiled and been tossed out of the nest.

Once or twice a night we would see a steamboat slipping along in the dark, and now and then she would belch a whole world of sparks out of her chimneys, and they would rain down on the river and look awful pretty. Then she would turn a corner, her lights would wink out and her noise shut off, and the river would be still again. A long while after she was gone, her waves would reach us and joggle the raft a bit, and after that you wouldn’t hear anything for who knows how long, except maybe frogs or something.

Past midnight the people on shore turned in, and for two or three hours the shores stayed dark, with no more sparks in the cabin windows. Those sparks worked as our clock: when the first one showed again, morning was on its way, and we went looking for a place to hide and tie up at once.

One morning around daybreak I found a canoe, crossed a chute to the mainland—only two hundred yards—and paddled a mile or so up a creek through the cypress woods, hoping to find some berries. I was just passing a place where a cowpath crossed the creek when a pair of men came pelting up the path, running as hard as their legs would carry them. I figured I was done for, because any time somebody was chasing somebody, I assumed it was _me_ they wanted—or maybe Jim. I was about to get out of there fast, but they were already close, and they hollered and begged me to save their lives. They said they hadn’t done anything and were being chased anyway, and that men and dogs were on their way. They wanted to hop right in, but I told them:

“Don’t do it. I can’t hear the dogs and horses yet, so you’ve got time to push through the brush and go up the creek a little way. Then take to the water and wade down to me and get in. That’ll throw the dogs off the scent.”

They did it, and as soon as they were aboard I lit out for our tow-head, and in about five or ten minutes we heard the dogs and the men far off, shouting. We heard them come toward the creek, but couldn’t see them; they seemed to stop and fool around for a while. Then, as we got farther and farther away all the time, we could hardly hear them at all. By the time we had left a mile of woods behind us and reached the river, everything was quiet, and we paddled over to the tow-head, hid in the cottonwoods, and were safe.

One of the men was seventy or so, bald, with very gray whiskers. He had on a battered old slouch hat, a greasy blue wool shirt, and ragged blue jeans trousers tucked into his boot-tops, with home-knit galluses—no, there was only one. Over his arm he carried a long-tailed blue jeans coat with shiny brass buttons, and each of the two men had a big, fat, shabby-looking carpet-bag.

The other man was about thirty, and just as poorly dressed. When we’d eaten breakfast we all took it easy and talked, and the first thing we learned was that the two of them were strangers to each other.
“What got you into trouble?” the baldhead asked the other fellow.

“Well, I’d been selling an article to take the tartar off the teeth—and it does take it off, all right, and usually the enamel along with it. But I stayed a night longer than I should have, and I was just slipping out of town when I ran into you on the trail this side of town, and you said they were coming and begged me to help you escape. So I told you I was expecting trouble myself and would scatter out _with_ you. That’s my whole story—what’s yours?

“Well, I’ve been running a little temperance revival over there for about a week, and I was the pet of all the women folks, big and little, because I was making it mighty hot for the drinkers, I _tell_ you. I was taking in as much as five or six dollars a night—ten cents a head, children and niggers free—and business kept growing, when somehow a little rumor went around last night that I had a habit of spending my spare time with a private jug on the sly. A nigger got me out of bed this morning and told me the people were gathering quietly with their dogs and horses. They’d be along pretty soon, he said, and give me about half an hour’s head start, and then hunt me down if they could. If they caught me, they’d tar and feather me and ride me out on a rail, sure. I didn’t wait for any breakfast—I wasn’t hungry.”
“Old man,” said the young one, “I reckon we could team up together. What do you think?”
“I ain’t against it. What’s your line of work, mainly?”

“Journeyman printer by trade. I do a little in patent medicines, and some acting—tragedy, you know. I try mesmerism and phrenology when there’s a chance, and teach a singing-and-geography school for a change. Once in a while I give a lecture—oh, I do lots of things, just about anything that comes along, so long as it ain’t work. What’s your racket?”

“I’ve done a good deal of doctoring in my time. Laying on of hands is my best hold—for cancer and paralysis and such things. And I can tell a fortune pretty well when I’ve got somebody along to dig up the facts for me. Preaching’s my line too, and working the camp meetings, and doing missionary work around the country.”
Neither of them said anything for a while. Then the young man heaved a sigh and said:
“Alas!”
“What are you alassing about?” says the baldhead.
“To think I should live to lead such a life, and be dragged down into such company.” And he started wiping the corner of his eye with a rag.
“Darn your hide, ain’t the company good enough for you?” says the baldhead, pretty sharp and stuck-up about it.

“Yes, it _is_ good enough for me. It’s as good as I deserve, for who brought me so low when I stood so high? _I_ did, myself. I don’t blame _you_, gentlemen—far from it. I don’t blame anybody. I deserve it all. Let the cold world do its worst. One thing I know: there’s a grave waiting for me somewhere. The world can go on just as it always has, and take everything from me—loved ones, property, everything—but it can’t take that. Someday I’ll lie down in it and forget it all, and my poor broken heart will be at rest.” He kept on wiping.
“Drat your poor broken heart,” says the baldhead. “What are you heaving your poor broken heart at _us_ for? _We_ ain’t done nothing.”
“No, I know you haven’t. I’m not blaming you, gentlemen. I brought myself down—yes, I did it myself. It’s right that I should suffer—perfectly right—and I make no complaint.”
“Brought down from where? Where did you fall from?”
“Ah, you wouldn’t believe me. The world never believes—let it pass—it’s no matter. The secret of my birth—”
“The secret of your birth! Do you mean to say—”
“Gentlemen,” says the young man, very solemnly, “I will tell it to you, because I feel I can trust you. By rights, I am a duke!”
Jim’s eyes popped wide when he heard that, and I reckon mine did as well. Then the baldhead says, “No! Surely you ain’t serious?”

“Yes. My great-grandfather, the eldest son of the Duke of Bridgewater, fled to this country near the end of the last century to breathe the pure air of freedom. He married here and died, leaving a son; his own father died about the same time. The second son of the late duke grabbed the titles and estates, and the infant who was the real duke was ignored. I am the direct descendant of that infant—I am the rightful Duke of Bridgewater. And here I am, forlorn, torn from my high estate, hunted by men, despised by the cold world, ragged, worn out, heartbroken, and brought down to the company of criminals on a raft!”

Jim felt sorry for him, no end, and so did I. We tried to cheer him up, but he said there wasn’t much point, since nothing could comfort him very much. What would do him more good than nearly anything, he said, was if we’d agree to recognize who he was. We told him we would, if he’d show us how. He said we should bow whenever we spoke to him and call him “Your Grace,” or “My Lord,” or “Your Lordship.” He wouldn’t object to plain “Bridgewater,” either, which, he said, was a title anyhow and not a name. And one of us should serve him at dinner and run any little errand he wanted run.

Well, that was easy enough, so we did it. Throughout dinner Jim hovered close by, serving him, and saying, “Will yo’ Grace take some o’ dis or some o’ dat?” and so on. Anybody could see how much the duke liked it.

But the old man got pretty quiet after a while. He didn’t have much to say, and he didn’t look too comfortable with all the fussing going on around that duke. He seemed to have something on his mind. So, along in the afternoon, he says:
“Listen, Bilgewater,” he says, “I’m terrible sorry for you, but you ain’t the only one who’s had that kind of trouble.”
“No?”
“No, you ain’t. You ain’t the only person who’s been dragged down wrongfully out of a high place.”
“Alas!”
“No, you ain’t the only one with a secret about his birth.” And, by jings, _he_ breaks down and cries.
