“Hold on! What do you mean?”
“Bilgewater, may I trust you?” says the old man, still half sobbing.
“Till my dying breath!” The duke grabbed the old man’s hand and squeezed it. “Tell me this secret of your existence. Speak!”
“Bilgewater, I am the late Dauphin!”
You bet, Jim and I stared this time. Then the duke says:
“You are what?”
“Indeed, my friend, I fear it is true. Before you at this very moment sits the poor lost Dauphin, Looy the Seventeen, son of Looy the Sixteen and Marry Antonette.”
“You? At your age? Never! You must be claiming to be the late Charlemagne, then, because you’d have to be six or seven hundred years old, at the very least.”

“Trouble has done it, Bilgewater. Trouble is what gave me these gray hairs and this early baldness. Yes, gentlemen, before you stands, in blue jeans and misery, the wandering, exiled, trampled, and suffering rightful King of France.”

Well, he cried and carried on so much that Jim and I hardly knew what to do. We felt so sorry for him—and so glad and proud to have him with us, too. So we went to work on him the same way we had with the duke, and tried to comfort _him_. But he said it was no use, that nothing but being dead and done with it all could do him any good. Still, he said it often made him feel easier and better for a while when people treated him according to his rights, and got down on one knee to speak to him, and always called him “Your Majesty,” and served him first at meals, and didn’t sit down in his presence until he told them to. So Jim and I set about majestying him, doing this and that and the other thing for him, and standing until he told us we could sit. This did him heaps of good, and he got cheerful and comfortable. But the duke kind of soured on him, and didn’t look at all satisfied with how things were going. Still, the king acted really friendly toward him, and said that the duke’s great-grandfather and all the other Dukes of Bilgewater had been thought a good deal of by _his_ father, and had been allowed to come to the palace quite often. But the duke stayed huffy for a good while, until finally the king says:

“Chances are we’ll be stuck together a darned long time on this here raft, Bilgewater, so what’s the use of your being sour? It’ll only make things uncomfortable. It ain’t my fault I wasn’t born a duke, and it ain’t your fault you wasn’t born a king—so what’s the use of worrying? Make the best of things the way you find them, says I—that’s my motto. This ain’t a bad thing we’ve landed in here—plenty of grub and an easy life. Come on, give me your hand, Duke, and let’s all be friends.”

The duke did it, and Jim and I were pretty glad to see it. It cleared away all the awkwardness, and we felt mighty good about it, because it would have been a miserable business to have any unfriendliness on the raft. What you want most of all on a raft is for everybody to be content and feel right and kindly toward the others.

It didn’t take me long to make up my mind that these liars weren’t kings or dukes at all, just low-down humbugs and frauds. But I never said anything and never let on. I kept it to myself, which is the best way, because then you don’t have any quarrels and don’t get into any trouble. If they wanted us to call them kings and dukes, I had no objection, as long as it kept the peace in the family. And there was no use telling Jim, so I didn’t tell him. If I never learned anything else from pap, I learned that the best way to get along with his kind of people is to let them have their own way.

chapters.title: Chapter XX — Huck Explains
paragraphs: They asked us a great many questions. They wanted to know why we covered the raft up that way, and why we laid by in the daytime instead of running—was Jim a runaway nigger? Says I:
“Goodness sakes, would a runaway nigger run _south?_”
No, they allowed he wouldn’t. I had to explain things somehow, so I says:

“My family lived in Pike County, Missouri, where I was born, and they all died off except me, pa, and my brother Ike. Pa decided he’d break up and move down to live with Uncle Ben, who’s got a little one-horse place on the river, forty-four miles below Orleans. Pa was pretty poor and owed some money, so by the time he’d paid up, nothing was left but sixteen dollars and our nigger, Jim. That wasn’t enough to carry us fourteen hundred miles, by deck passage or any other way. Well, when the river rose, pa got lucky one day and caught hold of this piece of raft, so we figured we’d float down to Orleans on it. But pa’s luck ran out. One night a steamboat plowed into the front corner of the raft, and we all went into the water and dove under the paddle wheel. Jim and I surfaced fine, but pa was drunk and Ike was only four, so neither of them ever came up. Well, for the next day or two we had plenty of trouble, since people kept rowing out in skiffs to take Jim away from me, claiming they believed he was a runaway nigger. So now we don’t travel in the daytime. At night they leave us alone.”
The duke says:

“Leave it to me to figure out a way we can run in the daytime if we want to. I’ll think it over—I’ll come up with a plan that’ll fix it. We’ll let it alone for today, because of course we don’t want to go past that town over there in daylight—it might not be healthy.”

Toward night it started to darken up and look like rain. The heat lightning was flickering low in the sky, and the leaves were beginning to shiver. It was going to be pretty ugly, that was easy to see. So the duke and the king went to inspecting our wigwam, to see what the beds were like. My bed was a straw mattress, better than Jim’s, which was stuffed with corn shucks. There are always cobs in a shuck mattress, and they poke into you and hurt, and when you roll over, the dry shucks sound like you’re rolling over in a pile of dead leaves. It makes such a rustling that you wake up. Well, the duke said he’d take my bed, but the king said he wouldn’t. He says:
“I would have thought the difference in rank would have suggested to you that a corn-shuck bed ain’t quite fit for me to sleep on. Your Grace will take the shuck bed yourself.”
Jim and I broke into a sweat again for a minute, afraid of more trouble between the two of them, so we were mighty relieved when the duke says:

“It is always my fate to be ground into the mud under the iron heel of oppression. Misfortune has broken my once proud spirit. I give in, I submit; it is my fate. I stand alone in the world—let me suffer; I can bear it.”

We pushed off as soon as it was good and dark. The king told us to keep well out toward the middle of the river and show no light until we were a long way below the town. After a while we saw the small cluster of lights—that was the town, you know—and slid past it, about half a mile out, with no trouble. When we were three-quarters of a mile below it, we hung up our signal lantern. Around ten o’clock the rain, wind, thunder and lightning all hit at once, so the king ordered us both to keep watch until the weather improved, and then he and the duke crept into the wigwam and went to sleep. I was off duty until twelve, but I wouldn’t have gone to bed even if I’d had one, since you don’t get to see a storm like that every day of the week, not by a long way. My souls, how the wind screamed! Every second or two a glare would light up the whitecaps for half a mile around, and you could see the islands looking dusty through the rain and the trees whipping about in the wind. Then comes a _h-whack!_—bum! bum! bumble-umble-um-bum-bum-bum-bum—and the thunder would go rumbling and grumbling off and fade out, and then _rip_ comes another flash and another sockdolager. Sometimes the waves nearly swept me off the raft, but I had no clothes on and didn’t care. Snags gave us no trouble, because the lightning kept glaring and flickering so steadily that we spotted them in plenty of time to swing her head one way or the other and miss them.

I had the middle watch, you know, but by then I was pretty sleepy, so Jim offered to take the first half for me. He was always mighty kind that way, Jim was. I crawled into the wigwam, but the king and the duke had their legs spread out so far that there was no room for me, so I lay down outdoors. The rain didn’t bother me, since it was warm, and the waves weren’t so high anymore. Around two they rose again, and Jim meant to wake me, but he changed his mind. He figured they weren’t high enough yet to do any harm. He was wrong, though, because pretty soon, out of nowhere, a regular ripper of a wave came along and washed me overboard. Jim nearly died laughing. He was the easiest nigger to set off laughing that ever lived, anyway.
I took the watch, and Jim lay down and snored away. After a while the storm let up for good, and when the first cabin light showed, I roused him and we slid the raft into a hiding place for the day.

After breakfast the king dug out a greasy old deck of cards, and he and the duke played seven-up for a while, a nickel a game. When they got tired of that, they said they ought to “lay out a campaign,” as they called it. The duke reached into his carpet-bag and pulled out a bundle of small printed handbills, and read them aloud. One said that “the celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris,” would “lecture on the Science of Phrenology” at such and such a place on the blank day of blank, with admission at ten cents, and would “furnish charts of character at twenty-five cents apiece.” The duke said that was _him_. Another bill named him as the “world-renowned Shakespearian tragedian, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London.” Other bills gave him a whole string of other names and had him doing other wonderful things, like finding water and gold with a “divining-rod” and “dissipating witch spells,” and so on. After a while he says:
“Still, the theatrical muse is the one closest to my heart. Have you ever walked the stage, Royalty?”
“No,” the king says.

“Then you shall, Fallen Grandeur, before three more days are out,” says the duke. “In the first good town we reach, we’ll rent a hall and perform the sword fight from Richard III. and the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet. How does that strike you?”

“I’m in, clear up to the hub, for anything that pays, Bilgewater. But you see, I don’t know nothing about play-actin’, and I hain’t seen much of it. I was too little when Pap had ’em at the palace. Reckon you can learn me?”
“Easy!”
“All right. I’m jist a-freezn’ for something new, anyhow. Le’s start right off.”
So the duke told him the whole story of who Romeo was and who Juliet was, and added that he was used to playing Romeo himself, so the king could take Juliet.
“But if Juliet’s s’posed to be a young gal, duke, my bald head and white whiskers are gonna look awful peculiar on her, I’d say.”

“No, don’t worry about that. These country hicks will never think of it. Besides, you’ll be in costume, and that makes all the difference in the world. Juliet is on a balcony, enjoying the moonlight before she goes to bed, and she’s wearing her nightgown and a ruffled nightcap. Here are the costumes for the parts.”

He pulled out two or three suits made of curtain calico, which he said was medieval armor for Richard III. and the other fellow, along with a long white cotton nightshirt and a ruffled nightcap to match. The king was satisfied. So the duke got out his book and read the parts aloud in the grandest, most spread-eagle style, prancing around and acting as he went to show how it had to be done. Then he handed the book to the king and told him to learn his part by heart.

There was a little one-horse town about three miles down the bend. After dinner the duke said he had worked out an idea for how we could run in daylight without putting Jim in danger, and he would go down to the town and take care of it. The king said he would go too, and see if he couldn’t pick up something for himself. We were out of coffee, so Jim said I had better go along with them in the canoe and buy some.

When we got there, nobody was stirring. The streets were empty and dead quiet, like a Sunday. In a back yard we found a sick nigger sunning himself, and he told us that everybody who wasn’t too young or too sick or too old had gone to a camp-meeting about two miles back in the woods. The king got directions and said he would go and work that camp-meeting for all it was worth, and I could come along too.

The duke said what he was after was a printing office. We found one, a tiny place up over a carpenter shop. The carpenters and printers had all gone to the meeting, and no doors were locked. It was a dirty, cluttered room, with ink smears and handbills all over the walls, showing pictures of horses and runaway niggers. The duke took off his coat and said he was all set now. So the king and I headed off for the camp-meeting.

We got there in about half an hour, soaked with sweat, because it was a terribly hot day. There must have been a thousand people there, from twenty miles around. The woods were full of teams and wagons tied up everywhere, the horses eating out of the wagon-troughs and stamping to keep the flies off. There were sheds built of poles and roofed with branches, where people sold lemonade and gingerbread, and there were heaps of watermelons and green corn and that kind of stuff.

The preaching went on under sheds of the same kind, only bigger, and they held whole crowds. The benches were made from the rough outer slabs of logs, with holes bored in the round side to stick in poles for legs. They had no backs. The preachers stood on high platforms at one end of the sheds. The women wore sun-bonnets, and some had on linsey-woolsey dresses, some gingham, and a few of the young ones calico. Some of the young men were barefoot, and some of the children wore nothing but a tow-linen shirt. A few of the old women were knitting, and some of the young folks were courting on the sly.

At the first shed we came to, the preacher was lining out a hymn. He would read out two lines, and everybody sang them. It was kind of grand to hear, there were so many of them and they sang so stirringly. Then he would read out two more for them to sing, and so on. The people got more and more worked up and sang louder and louder, and toward the end some started to groan and some started to shout. Then the preacher started to preach, and he went at it in earnest. He swayed first to one side of the platform and then the other, then leaned way out over the front of it, his arms and body moving all the time, shouting his words with all his might. Every now and then he would hold up his Bible, spread it open, and pass it around this way and that, shouting, “It’s the brazen serpent in the wilderness! Look upon it and live!” And the people would shout back, “Glory!—A-a-_men!_” So he went on, with the people groaning and crying and saying amen:

“Oh, come to the mourners’ bench! Come, you black with sin! (_amen!_) Come, you sick and sore! (_amen!_) Come, you lame and halt and blind! (_amen!_) Come, you poor and needy, sunk in shame! (_a-a-men!_) Come, all you who are worn and soiled and suffering!—Come with a broken spirit! Come with a contrite heart! Come in your rags and sin and dirt! The waters that cleanse are free, the door of heaven stands open—oh, step inside and be at rest!” (_a-a-men!_ _glory, glory, hallelujah!_)

And so on. You couldn’t make out what the preacher said anymore, for all the shouting and crying. People all over the crowd stood up and pushed their way, just by main strength, to the mourners’ bench with tears running down their faces. And when all the mourners had crowded up onto the front benches, they sang and shouted and threw themselves down on the straw, wild and crazy.

Well, the next thing I knew, the king had started in, and you could hear him over everybody. Then he went charging up onto the platform, and the preacher begged him to speak to the people, and he did. He told them he was a pirate, and had been a pirate for thirty years out in the Indian Ocean. His crew had been thinned out a good deal last spring in a fight, and he was home now to recruit some fresh men. Thank goodness, he had been robbed last night and put ashore from a steamboat without a cent, and he was glad of it. It was the most blessed thing that ever happened to him, because he was a changed man now, and happy for the first time in his life. Poor as he was, he was going to start right off and work his way back to the Indian Ocean, and spend the rest of his life turning the pirates onto the true path, because he could do it better than anybody else, knowing every pirate crew in that ocean. It would take him a long time to get there without money, but he would get there anyway, and every time he convinced a pirate he would say to him, “Don’t you thank me, don’t you give me any credit. It all belongs to those dear people at the Pokeville camp-meeting, born brothers and benefactors of the human race, and that dear preacher there, the truest friend a pirate ever had!”

Then he burst into tears, and so did everybody. Then somebody called out, “Take up a collection for him, take up a collection!” Half a dozen people jumped to do it, but somebody else called out, “Let _him_ pass the hat around!” Then everybody said so, the preacher too.

So the king went all through the crowd with his hat, wiping his eyes, blessing the people and praising them and thanking them for being so good to the poor pirates way off there. Every so often the prettiest girls, with tears running down their cheeks, would step up and ask if they could kiss him to remember him by, and he always let them. Some of them he hugged and kissed as many as five or six times. He was invited to stay a week, and everybody wanted him to live in their house and said they would count it an honor. But he said that since this was the last day of the camp-meeting he couldn’t do any good there, and besides, he was in a sweat to get to the Indian Ocean right away and go to work on the pirates.

When we got back to the raft and he sat down to count up, he found he had collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. On top of that, he had carried off a three-gallon jug of whisky that he found under a wagon when he was heading home through the woods. The king said that, taking it all around, it beat any day he had ever put in at the missionary business. He said there was no use arguing about it: heathens don’t amount to shucks next to pirates when it comes to working a camp-meeting.

The duke had been thinking _he’d_ done pretty well, until the king showed up, but after that he didn’t think so much of it. In that printing office he had set type and printed two small jobs for farmers, horse bills, and taken four dollars for them. He had also sold ten dollars’ worth of advertising space in the paper, which he said he would let them have for four dollars if they paid in advance, and they did. The paper cost two dollars a year, but he signed up three subscribers at half a dollar apiece, as long as they paid in advance. They had been going to pay in cordwood and onions, as usual, but he told them he had just bought the place and cut the price as low as he could afford, and would be running it for cash. He had also set up a little poem that he made himself, out of his own head, three verses, kind of sweet and sad, called “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart.” He left that all set up and ready to print in the paper, and charged nothing for it. Well, he had taken in nine dollars and a half altogether, and said he’d done a pretty fair day’s work for it.

Then he showed us one more little job he had printed and not charged for, since it was meant for us. It had a picture of a runaway nigger carrying a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with “$200 reward” printed under it. The words were all about Jim and described him down to the last detail. They said he had escaped last winter from St. Jacques’ plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, and had most likely gone north. Whoever caught him and sent him back would get the reward and expenses.

“Now,” says the duke, “from tonight on we can travel by day if we like. Whenever somebody comes in sight, we tie Jim up hand and foot with a rope and lay him in the wigwam. Then we show this handbill and say we caught him upriver, and we were too poor for a steamboat, so we got this little raft on credit from friends and are headed down to collect the reward. Handcuffs and chains would look better still on Jim, but they wouldn’t suit our story of being so poor. Too much like jewelry. Ropes are just the thing—we must preserve the unities, as we say on the boards.”

We all said the duke was pretty smart, and that there couldn’t be any trouble about running in the daytime. We figured we could make enough miles that night to get out of reach of the uproar we expected the duke’s work in the printing office to cause in that little town. After that we could go booming right along if we wanted.
We lay low and kept quiet, and never shoved off until nearly ten o’clock. Then we slid past, well away from the town, and didn’t hoist our lantern until we were completely out of sight of it.
When Jim called me to take the watch at four in the morning, he said:
“Huck, you reck’n we’s gwine to meet up wid any mo’ kings on dis trip?”
“No,” I says, “I reckon not.”
“Well,” he says, “dat’s fine, den. I don’t mine a king er two, but dat’s plenty. Dis one’s powerful drunk, en de duke ain’t much better.”

I learned that Jim had been trying to get the king to speak French, so he could hear how it sounded. But the king said he had lived in this country so long, and had so much trouble, that he’d forgotten how.

chapters.title: Chapter XXI — Sword Exercise
paragraphs: The sun was up by now, but we kept right on going and didn’t tie up. After a while the king and the duke came out looking pretty rumpled, but a swim after they jumped overboard perked them up a good deal. After breakfast the king sat down on the corner of the raft, pulled off his boots, rolled up his pants, and let his legs dangle in the water to be comfortable. He lit his pipe and started learning his Romeo and Juliet by heart. When he had it pretty well, he and the duke began to practice it together. The duke had to teach him every speech over and over, how to say it. He made him sigh and put his hand on his heart, and after a while said he was doing pretty well. “Only,” he says, “you mustn’t bellow out _Romeo!_ like that, like a bull. You must say it soft and sick and languishing, like this—R-o-o-meo! That’s the idea. Juliet is a dear, sweet, mere child of a girl, you know, and she doesn’t bray like a jackass.”

Next they got out a couple of long swords that the duke had made from oak laths, and started to practice the sword fight, with the duke calling himself Richard III. The way they laid on and pranced around the raft was grand to see. But after a while the king tripped and fell overboard. After that they took a rest and talked about all kinds of adventures they had had in other times along the river.
After dinner the duke says:
“Well, Capet, we’ll want this to be a first-class show, you know, so I think we’ll add a little something to it. We need a bit extra to give the audience when they call for encores, anyway.”
“What’s onkores, Bilgewater?”
The duke told him, and then says:
“I’ll answer them with the Highland fling or a sailor’s hornpipe. And you—now, let me think—ah, I have it—you can do Hamlet’s soliloquy.”
“Hamlet’s what?”

“Hamlet’s soliloquy, you understand, the most celebrated passage in all of Shakespeare. Ah, it’s sublime, sublime! It brings the house down every time. I don’t have it in the book—I only carry the one volume—but I believe I can piece it together from memory. Let me just pace back and forth a moment and see if I can summon it from the vaults of recollection.”

So he started marching up and down, thinking hard and scowling something terrible every few steps. Then he would hike his eyebrows way up, then press his hand against his forehead and stagger backward with a sort of moan, and after that he would sigh, and after that he’d pretend to wipe away a tear. It was a fine sight to see. Pretty soon he had it. He told us to pay attention. Then he struck a grand pose, with one leg pushed out in front, both arms stretched high, and his head tipped back to look at the sky; and then he started to rant and rave and grind his teeth, and from there to the end of the speech he howled and sprawled about and puffed out his chest, and he beat any acting _I_ ever saw before. This is the speech—I learned it easy enough, while he was teaching it to the king:

To be, or not to be; that is the bare bodkin That makes calamity of such a long life; For who would haul fardels, until Birnam Wood marches to Dunsinane, Except that dread of something after death Murders the innocent sleep, Great nature’s second course, And makes us prefer to sling the arrows of outrageous fortune Rather than flee to others we know nothing about. There’s the consideration that must make us pause: Wake Duncan with your knocking! I wish you could; For who would endure the whips and scorns of time, The oppressor’s wrong, the proud man’s insults, The law’s delay, and the quietus his pangs might take. In the dead waste and middle of the night, when churchyards gape In their usual suits of solemn black, Except that the undiscovered country, from whose border no traveler returns, Breathes contagion over the world, And so the native color of resolution, like the poor cat in the proverb, Is sicklied over with care. And all the clouds that hung low above our housetops, Looking at this, turn their currents awry, And lose the name of action. It is a consummation devoutly to be wished. But hush, here is the fair Ophelia: Open not your heavy marble jaws. But get you to a nunnery—go!

Well, the old man liked that speech, and before long he had it down so he could perform it first-rate. It seemed like he was born for it; and once he had his hand in and got excited, it was perfectly lovely the way he would rip and tear and rear up on his hind legs while he was delivering it.

The first chance we got, the duke had some show bills printed up; and after that, for two or three days while we drifted along, the raft was an uncommonly lively place, because there was nothing but sword-fighting and rehearsing—as the duke called it—going on all the time. One morning, when we were pretty far down in the state of Arkansaw, we came in sight of a little one-horse town in a big bend of the river. So we tied up about three-quarters of a mile above it, in the mouth of a creek that was closed in like a tunnel by cypress trees, and all of us but Jim took the canoe and went down to see whether the place offered any chance for our show.

We had mighty good luck. There was going to be a circus in town that afternoon, and the country people were already starting to come in, in all kinds of rickety old wagons and on horseback. The circus would leave before night, so our show had a pretty good chance. The duke rented the courthouse, and we went around and stuck up our bills. They read like this:

Shaksperean Revival!!! A Wonderful Attraction! One Night Only! The world-renowned tragedians, David Garrick the younger, of Drury Lane Theatre, London, and Edmund Kean the elder, of the Royal Haymarket Theatre, Whitechapel, Pudding Lane, Piccadilly, London, and the Royal Continental Theatres, present their sublime Shaksperean Spectacle entitled The Balcony Scene in Romeo and Juliet!!!
Assisted by the whole strength of the company! New costumes, new scenery, new appointments!
Also: The thrilling, masterly, and blood-curdling Broad-sword conflict In Richard III.!!!

also: (by special request,) Hamlet’s Immortal Soliloquy!! By the Illustrious Kean! Performed by him 300 nights in a row in Paris! For One Night Only, Owing to pressing European engagements! Admission 25 cents; children and servants, 10 cents.

Then we wandered around the town. The stores and houses were mostly old, rickety, dried-out frame buildings that had never been painted. They were set up three or four feet off the ground on stilts, to stay out of reach of the water when the river flooded. The houses had little gardens around them, but they hardly seemed to grow anything in them except jimpson weeds and sunflowers, along with ash piles, old curled-up boots and shoes, pieces of bottles, rags, and worn-out tinware. The fences were made of different kinds of boards, nailed on at different times, and they leaned every which way, with gates that usually had just one hinge—a leather one. Some of the fences had been whitewashed at some point, but the duke said that was back in Columbus’s time, most likely. There were usually hogs in the gardens, and people chasing them out.

All the stores were along one street. They had white homespun awnings out front, and the country people hitched their horses to the awning posts. Under the awnings sat empty dry-goods boxes, and loafers perched on them all day long, whittling them with their Barlow knives, chewing tobacco, gaping and yawning and stretching—a mighty sorry lot. They usually wore yellow straw hats nearly as wide as an umbrella, but no coats or waistcoats. They called each other Bill, and Buck, and Hank, and Joe, and Andy, and talked in a lazy drawl, and used a good many cuss words. There was about one loafer leaning against every awning post, and he nearly always had his hands in his trouser pockets, except when he took them out to lend a chew of tobacco or to scratch. What you heard from them all the time was:
“Gimme a chaw of tobacker, Hank.”
“Cain’t; I ain’t got but one chaw left. Ask Bill.”

Maybe Bill gives him a chaw; maybe he lies and says he ain’t got any. Some of those loafers never have a cent in the world, nor a chaw of tobacco of their own. They do all their chewing by borrowing. They say to a fellow, “I wish you’d lend me a chaw, Jack, I just this minute gave Ben Thompson the last chaw I had”—which is a lie nearly every time; it doesn’t fool anybody but a stranger; but Jack ain’t a stranger, so he says:

“_You_ gave him a chaw, did you? So did your sister’s cat’s grandmother. First you pay back all the chaws you already borrowed off me, Lafe Buckner, and then I’ll lend you a ton or two, and I won’t charge you any back interest, neither.”
“Well, I _did_ pay you back some of it once.”
“Yes, you did—about six chaws’ worth. You borrowed store tobacker from me and paid me back in nigger-head.”

Store tobacco is flat black plug, but these fellows mostly chew natural leaf, twisted up. When they borrow a chaw, they don’t usually cut it with a knife. They clamp the plug between their teeth and gnaw, and tug at it with their hands until it comes apart in two. Then sometimes the fellow who owns the tobacco gives the returned piece a sorrowful look, and says, sarcastic:
“Here, gimme the _chaw_, and you take the _plug_.”

Every street and lane was nothing but mud; there wasn’t a thing _but_ mud—mud black as tar and nearly a foot deep in some spots, and two or three inches deep in _every_ spot. Hogs lounged and grunted all over the place. You’d see a muddy sow with a litter of pigs come strolling lazily down the street and plop herself right down in the middle of it, so folks had to walk around her. She’d stretch out, shut her eyes, and flap her ears while the pigs nursed, looking as happy as if she were drawing a salary. Then pretty soon you’d hear a loafer holler, “Hi! _so_ boy! sic him, Tige!” and away the sow would go, squealing horribly, with a dog or two hanging from each ear and three or four dozen more running behind. And all the loafers would get up and watch till she was out of sight, laughing at the fun and looking thankful for the noise. Then they’d settle back down until the next dog fight. Nothing else could wake them up all over and make them happy all over the way a dog fight could—unless it was pouring turpentine on a stray dog and lighting him up, or tying a tin pan to his tail and watching him run himself to death.

On the river front, some of the houses stuck out over the bank, bowed and bent, and about ready to tumble in. The people had moved out of them. The bank had caved away under one corner of some others, and that corner hung out over nothing. People still lived in them, but it was dangerous, because sometimes a strip of land as wide as a house caves in all at once. Sometimes a belt of land a quarter of a mile deep will start to go, and cave and cave and cave until it has all fallen into the river in a single summer. A town like that has to keep moving back, and back, and back, because the river is always gnawing at it.

The closer it got to noon that day, the thicker the wagons and horses got in the streets, with more coming all the time. Families brought their dinners with them from the country and ate them in the wagons. There was a fair amount of whisky drinking going on, and I saw three fights. Pretty soon somebody sings out:
“Here comes old Boggs!—in from the country for his little monthly drunk. Here he comes, boys!”
All the loafers looked pleased; I guessed they were used to getting some fun out of Boggs. One of them says:
“Wonder who he’s a-gwyne to chaw up this time. If he’d chawed up every man he’s been a-gwyne to chaw up in the past twenty year, he’d be mighty famous by now.”
Another one says, “I wisht old Boggs would threaten me, ’cause then I’d know I wouldn’t die for a thousand year.”
Boggs comes charging along on his horse, whooping and yelling like an Indian, and hollering:
“Clear the track, thar. I’m on the war-path, and the price of coffins is a-gwyne up.”

He was drunk, rocking back and forth in his saddle, a man past fifty with a very red face. Everybody yelled at him and laughed at him and sassed him, and he sassed them right back. He said he’d deal with them and lay them out one at a time, in turn, but he couldn’t wait just now, because he’d come to town to kill old Colonel Sherburn, and his motto was, “Meat first, and spoon victuals to top off on.”
He saw me, and rode up and says:
“Whar’d you come from, boy? You ready to die?”
Then he rode on. I was scared, but a man says:
“He don’t mean nothing by it; he always carries on like that when he’s drunk. He’s the best-natured old fool in Arkansaw—never hurt nobody, drunk or sober.”
Boggs rode up to the biggest store in town, bent his head down to see under the hanging edge of the awning, and yells:
“Come on out, Sherburn! Come out and face the man you cheated. You’re the hound I’m after, and I’m a-gwyne to get you, too!”

And so he went on, calling Sherburn every name he could think of, with the whole street packed with people listening and laughing and egging him on. Pretty soon a proud-looking man of about fifty-five—and by far the best-dressed man in that town, too—steps out of the store, and the crowd falls back on each side to let him through. He says to Boggs, very calm and slow—he says:

“I’m sick of this, but I’ll put up with it until one o’clock. Until one o’clock, mind—no longer. If you open your mouth against me even once after that, you can’t travel so far that I won’t find you.”

Then he turns around and goes inside. The crowd looked very sober; nobody moved, and the laughing stopped. Boggs rode away cursing Sherburn at the top of his voice, all the way down the street; and soon back he comes and pulls up in front of the store, still going strong. Some men crowded around him and tried to make him hush, but he wouldn’t. They told him it would be one o’clock in about fifteen minutes, and so he _must_ go home—he must go right now. It was no use. He cussed with all his might, flung his hat down in the mud and rode over it, and in a minute off he went again, raging down the street with his gray hair streaming. Everybody who could get close to him did their best to talk him down off his horse, so they could lock him up and let him sober up; but it was no good—back up the street he would charge, and give Sherburn another cussing. Finally somebody says:
“Fetch his daughter!—quick, go get his daughter; sometimes he listens to her. If anybody can talk him around, she can.”

So somebody started off at a run. I walked down the street a little way and stopped. In about five or ten minutes, here comes Boggs again, but not on his horse. He was reeling across the street toward me, bareheaded, with a friend on each side holding his arms and hurrying him along. He was quiet and looked uneasy; and he wasn’t hanging back at all, but was doing some of the hurrying himself. Somebody sings out:
“Boggs!”

I looked across to see who had called, and it was Colonel Sherburn. He stood absolutely still in the street, one arm raised with a pistol in his right hand—not aimed, just held out with the barrel pointing up at the sky. In that very second I saw a young girl running toward us, with two men beside her. Boggs and his friends turned to see who had called him, and when they saw the pistol the men leaped aside, and the barrel came down, slow and steady, until it was level—both hammers cocked. Boggs throws both his hands up and says, “O Lord, don’t shoot!” Bang! goes the first shot, and he staggers backward, clawing at the air—bang! goes the second, and he drops onto his back on the ground, heavy and solid, arms flung wide. The young girl screamed and came running, and down she throws herself on her father, crying out, “Oh, he’s killed him, he’s killed him!” The crowd closed in around them, shoving and jamming each other with their necks craned to see, while the people up close tried to push them back, shouting, “Back, back! Give him air, give him air!”
Colonel Sherburn threw his pistol down on the ground, turned on his heel, and walked away.

They carried Boggs into a little drugstore, with the crowd pressing in around them and the whole town trailing along. I hurried over and grabbed a good spot at the window, close enough to see everything inside. They laid him on the floor with one big Bible under his head and another one opened and spread across his chest. First, though, they ripped his shirt open, and I saw where one of the bullets had gone in. He took about a dozen long gasps, his chest raising the Bible when he breathed in and lowering it again when he breathed out. After that he lay still. He was dead. Then they pulled his daughter away from him while she screamed and cried, and led her off. She was about sixteen, sweet and gentle-looking, but terribly pale and frightened.

Well, before long the whole town was there, squirming and squeezing and pushing and shoving to reach the window and get a look. But the people who had spots wouldn’t give them up, and the folks behind kept saying, “Say, now, you’ve looked long enough, you fellows. It ain’t right and it ain’t fair for you to stand there the whole time and never give anybody else a chance. Other folks have their rights just like you do.”

There was a lot of arguing back and forth, so I slipped out, figuring there might be trouble. The streets were full and everybody was worked up. Everyone who had seen the shooting was telling how it happened, and around each of them stood a big crowd, craning their necks to listen. One tall, skinny man with long hair and a big white fur stovepipe hat pushed back on his head, carrying a cane with a crooked handle, marked on the ground the spots where Boggs had stood and where Sherburn had stood. People followed him from one spot to the other, watching everything he did, nodding their heads to show they understood, and bending over a little with their hands on their thighs to watch him mark the places with his cane. Then he stood up stiff and straight where Sherburn had stood, frowning, with his hat brim pulled down over his eyes, and called out, “Boggs!” He swung his cane down slowly until it was level and said, “Bang!” Then he staggered backwards, said “Bang!” again, and fell flat on his back. The people who had seen it said he did it perfectly, that it was exactly how it all happened. Then a good dozen of them pulled out their bottles and treated him.

Well, before long somebody said Sherburn ought to be lynched. Within a minute everybody was saying it, and off they went, furious and yelling, tearing down every clothesline they came to so they could use it for the hanging.

chapters.title: Chapter XXII — Sherburn
paragraphs: They swarmed toward Sherburn’s house, whooping and raging like Indians. Everything in their way had to clear out or get run over and trampled to mush, and it was terrible to see. Children ran ahead of the mob, screaming and trying to get out of the way. Every window along the road was full of women’s heads, there were nigger boys in every tree, and bucks and wenches looking over every fence. Whenever the mob got close to them, they would break and scatter back out of reach. Lots of the women and girls were crying and carrying on, scared half to death.

They crowded up in front of Sherburn’s fence, packed together as tight as they could jam, and the noise was so loud you couldn’t hear yourself think. It was a little yard, only twenty feet across. Some of them shouted, “Tear down the fence! Tear down the fence!” Then came a racket of ripping and tearing and smashing, and down it went, and the front of the crowd began to roll in like a wave.

Just then Sherburn steps out onto the roof of his little front porch with a double-barreled gun in his hand, and takes his stand, perfectly calm and deliberate, without saying a word. The racket stopped, and the wave drew back.

Sherburn didn’t say a word. He just stood there, looking down at them. The silence was awful, eerie and uncomfortable. Sherburn moved his eyes slowly along the crowd, and wherever his gaze landed, people tried a little to stare him down, but they couldn’t. They dropped their eyes and looked sneaky. Then, after a while, Sherburn sort of laughed. It wasn’t the pleasant kind. It was the kind that makes you feel the way you do when you bite into bread with sand in it.
Then he says, slow and scornful:

“You, lynch somebody? That’s laughable. You, with enough nerve to lynch a _man!_ You’re brave enough to tar and feather poor, friendless women who get run out of other towns and wander in here, and from that you decided you had the guts to put your hands on a _man?_ Why, a _man_ is perfectly safe in the hands of ten thousand of your kind—so long as it’s daylight and you’re not standing behind him.

“Do I know you? I know you down to the bone. I was born and raised in the South, and I’ve lived in the North too, so I know what the average man is like, wherever you go. He’s a coward. Up North, he lets anyone who feels like it trample him, then goes home and prays to be given a meek spirit so he can stand it. Down South, a single man, all alone, has held up a stagecoach full of men in broad daylight and robbed every one. Your newspapers have called you a brave people so many times that you believe you _are_ braver than anyone else—but you’re exactly as brave as everybody, and not a bit braver. Why don’t your juries hang murderers? Because they’re afraid the man’s friends will shoot them in the back, in the dark—and that’s precisely what those friends _would_ do.

“So they always let the man go free, and then a _man_ goes out in the night, with a hundred masked cowards behind him, and lynches the rascal. Your mistake is that you didn’t bring a man with you. That’s one mistake, and the other is that you didn’t come in the dark and bring your masks. You brought _part_ of a man—Buck Harkness, there—and if you hadn’t had him to get you started, you’d have wasted it all on blowing off steam.

“You didn’t want to come. The average man doesn’t like trouble and danger. _You_ don’t like trouble and danger. But if only _half_ a man—like Buck Harkness, there—shouts ‘Lynch him! Lynch him!’ you’re afraid to back down. You’re afraid you’ll be found out for what you are—_cowards_—and so you raise a yell, hang on to that half-a-man’s coattail, and come raging up here, swearing what big things you’re going to do. The most pitiful thing there is, is a mob. That’s what an army is—a mob. Soldiers don’t fight with courage they were born with, but with courage borrowed from the crowd and from their officers. But a mob with no _man_ at the head of it is _beneath_ pitiful. Now what you should do is tuck your tails between your legs, go home, and crawl into a hole. If any real lynching is going to be done, it will be done in the dark, Southern style, and when those men come, they’ll bring their masks and a _man_ along. Now _leave_—and take your half-a-man with you”—and as he said this he tossed his gun up across his left arm and cocked it.

The crowd washed back all at once, then broke apart and went tearing off every which way. Buck Harkness ran after them, looking pretty cheap. I could have stayed if I’d wanted to, but I didn’t want to.

I went to the circus and hung around the back until the watchman walked by, and then I ducked in under the tent. I had my twenty-dollar gold piece and some other money, but I figured I’d better save it. There’s no telling how soon you’ll need it, away from home and among strangers like that. You can’t be too careful. I’m not against spending money on circuses when there’s no other way, but there’s no sense in _wasting_ it on them.

It was a real bully circus. It was the grandest sight ever, when they all came riding in, two by two, a gentleman and a lady side by side. The men wore just their drawers and undershirts, with no shoes or stirrups, and rested their hands easy and comfortable on their thighs. There must have been twenty of them. Every lady had a lovely complexion and was perfectly beautiful, and they looked just like a bunch of real, honest-to-goodness queens, dressed in clothes that cost millions of dollars and covered all over with diamonds. It was a powerful fine sight. I never saw anything so lovely. And then one by one they stood up on their horses and went weaving around the ring, so gentle and wavy and graceful. The men looked ever so tall and airy and straight, with their heads bobbing and skimming along way up there under the tent roof, and every lady’s rose-petal dress floated soft and silky around her hips, and she looked like the loveliest parasol.

Then they sped up, faster and faster, all of them dancing, kicking one foot out into the air and then the other. The horses leaned further and further, and the ring-master circled the center pole, cracking his whip and calling “Hi!—hi!” with the clown tossing out jokes behind him. After a while every rider let go of the reins, and each lady set her fists on her hips and each gentleman folded his arms, and my, how the horses did lean over and hump up! Then, one after the other, they all hopped down into the ring and took the sweetest bow I ever saw, and scampered out, while everybody clapped and went just about wild.

Well, all through the circus they did the most astonishing things, and all the while that clown carried on so much it nearly killed the people. The ring-master couldn’t say a word to him without the clown being right back at him, quick as a wink, with the funniest things anybody ever said. How he could ever _think_ of so many of them, so suddenly and so perfectly, was something I couldn’t understand at all. Why, I couldn’t have thought of them in a year. And by and by a drunk man tried to get into the ring. He said he wanted to ride, and that he could ride as well as anybody who ever lived. They argued with him and tried to keep him out, but he wouldn’t listen, and the whole show came to a standstill. Then the people started to holler at him and make fun of him, and that made him mad, and he began to rant and rage. That stirred up the crowd, and a lot of men started climbing down off the benches and swarming toward the ring, saying, “Knock him down! Throw him out!” and one or two women began to scream. So then the ring-master made a little speech. He said he hoped there wouldn’t be any disturbance, and that if the man would promise not to cause any more trouble, he would let him ride, if he thought the man could stay on the horse. So everybody laughed and said all right, and the man got on. The minute he was on, the horse began to snort and buck and jump and prance around, with two circus men hanging on to his bridle trying to hold him, and the drunk man clinging to his neck, his heels flying in the air with every jump, and the whole crowd on their feet, shouting and laughing till the tears rolled down. And at last, sure enough, despite everything the circus men could do, the horse broke loose and away he went like blazes, round and round the ring, with that drunk lying on top of him and hanging on to his neck, first one leg dangling almost to the ground on one side and then the other leg on the other side, and the people just going crazy. It wasn’t funny to me, though. I was all of a tremble to see how much danger he was in. But pretty soon he struggled up and got astride and grabbed the bridle, reeling this way and that. The next minute he sprang up, dropped the bridle, and stood! And the horse was going like a house on fire, too. He just stood up there, sailing around as easy and comfortable as if he’d never been drunk in his life. And then he began to pull off his clothes and fling them away. He shed them so thick they almost clogged the air, and altogether he shed seventeen suits. And then there he was, slim and handsome, dressed in the gaudiest and prettiest outfit you ever saw. He lit into that horse with his whip and made him fairly hum, and finally he skipped off, made his bow, and danced off to the dressing room, with everybody howling with pleasure and astonishment.

Then the ring-master saw how he’d been fooled, and he _was_ the sickest ring-master you ever saw, I reckon. Why, it was one of his own men! The man had thought up that whole joke by himself and never let on to anybody. Well, I felt sheepish enough to be taken in like that, but I wouldn’t have been in that ring-master’s place for a thousand dollars. I don’t know. There may be bullier circuses than that one, but I’ve never come across them yet. Anyway, it was plenty good enough for _me;_ and wherever I run across it, it can have all of _my_ business every time.

Well, that night we put on _our_ show, but there were only about twelve people there, just enough to pay expenses. And they laughed the whole time, which made the duke mad. Everybody left before the show was over, except one boy, who was asleep. So the duke said these Arkansaw lunkheads couldn’t rise to Shakespeare. What they wanted was low comedy, and maybe something rather worse than low comedy, he figured. He said he could size up their taste. So the next morning he got some big sheets of wrapping paper and some black paint, drew up some handbills, and stuck them up all over the village. The bills said:

AT THE COURT HOUSE! FOR 3 NIGHTS ONLY! _The World-Renowned Tragedians_ DAVID GARRICK THE YOUNGER! AND EDMUND KEAN THE ELDER! _Of the London and Continental Theatres_, In their Thrilling Tragedy of THE KING’S CAMELOPARD OR THE ROYAL NONESUCH!!! _Admission 50 cents_.
Then at the bottom was the biggest line of all, which said:
LADIES AND CHILDREN NOT ADMITTED.
“There,” he said, “if that line doesn’t draw them in, I don’t know Arkansaw!”

chapters.title: Chapter XXIII — Sold
paragraphs: Well, all day long he and the king were hard at work, rigging up a stage and a curtain and a row of candles for footlights. That night the house was packed full of men in no time. When the place couldn’t hold any more, the duke quit tending the door, went around the back way, came out onto the stage, and stood in front of the curtain. He made a little speech praising this tragedy, saying it was the most thrilling one ever. He went on bragging about the tragedy, and about Edmund Kean the Elder, who was to play the main part in it. At last, when he’d gotten everybody’s expectations up high enough, he rolled up the curtain, and the next minute the king came prancing out on all fours, naked. He was painted all over in rings and stripes, in all sorts of colors, as splendid as a rainbow. And—but never mind the rest of his outfit. It was just wild, but it was awfully funny. The people nearly killed themselves laughing. When the king finished capering and capered off behind the scenes, they roared and clapped and stormed and guffawed until he came back and did it over again, and after that they made him do it one more time. Well, it would make a cow laugh to see the antics that old idiot cut up.

Then the duke lets the curtain down, bows to the crowd, and announces that the great tragedy will be played only two nights more, on account of pressing engagements in London, where the seats are already all sold for it at Drury Lane. Then he bows again, and says that if he has managed to please and instruct them, he’ll be deeply obliged if they’ll mention it to their friends and get them to come see it.
Twenty people hollered out:
“What, is it over? Is that _all?_”

The duke says yes. Then there was a fine commotion. Everybody yells, “Cheated!” and jumps up mad, and they head for that stage and those tragedians. But a big, fine-looking man jumps up on a bench and shouts:

“Hold on! Just a word, gentlemen.” They stopped to listen. “We’ve been cheated—cheated badly. But we don’t want to be the laughingstock of this whole town, I reckon, and never hear the end of it as long as we live. _No_. What we want is to walk out of here quietly, praise this show to everybody, and get the _rest_ of the town cheated too! Then we’ll all be in the same boat. Isn’t that sensible?” (“You bet it is!—the judge is right!” everybody yells.) “All right, then—not a word about being cheated. Go on home, and tell everybody to come see the tragedy.”

The next day you couldn’t hear anything around that town except how splendid that show was. The house was jammed again that night, and we cheated that crowd the same way. When me and the king and the duke got back to the raft, we all had supper. Then, around midnight, they made Jim and me back her out, float her down the middle of the river, and bring her in and hide her about two miles below town.

The third night the house was packed again—and these weren’t newcomers this time, but people who’d been at the show the other two nights. I stood by the duke at the door, and I saw that every man who went in had his pockets bulging, or something wrapped up under his coat—and I saw it wasn’t perfume, either, not by a long shot. I smelled rotten eggs by the barrel, and spoiled cabbages, and such things; and if I know the signs of a dead cat being around, and I bet I do, there were sixty-four of them that went in. I squeezed in there for a minute, but it was too mixed up for me, and I couldn’t stand it. Well, when the place couldn’t hold any more people, the duke gave a fellow a quarter and asked him to mind the door for a minute, and then he started around to the stage door, with me behind him. But as soon as we turned the corner and were in the dark, he said:
“Walk fast now until you’re away from the houses, and then run for the raft like the devil is after you!”

I did it, and he did the same. We reached the raft at the same moment, and in less than two seconds we were gliding downstream, all dark and still, edging toward the middle of the river, with nobody saying a word. I figured the poor king was in for a rough time with the audience, but it was nothing of the sort. Pretty soon he crawled out from under the wigwam and said:
“Well, how did the old thing turn out this time, duke?”
He hadn’t been up in town at all.

We never showed a light until we were about ten miles below the village. Then we lit up and ate supper, and the king and the duke nearly laughed themselves to pieces over the way they’d treated those people. The duke said:

“Greenhorns, blockheads! _I_ knew the first night’s crowd would keep their mouths shut and let the rest of the town walk right into it. And I knew they’d be lying in wait for us on the third night, figuring it was _their_ turn. Well, so it is their turn, and I’d pay good money to find out what they’ll take for it. I’d dearly like to see what they’re making of their big opportunity. They can turn it into a picnic if they like—they brought plenty of food.”
Those rascals took in four hundred and sixty-five dollars in those three nights. I never saw money hauled in by the wagonload like that before. Later, when they were asleep and snoring, Jim said:
“Don’t it surprise you, de way dem kings carries on, Huck?”
“No,” I said, “it doesn’t.”
“Why don’t it, Huck?”
“No, because it comes with the breed, that’s why. They’re all the same, I figure.”
“But, Huck, dese kings of ourn is regular rascals. Dat’s jist what dey is. Dey’s regular rascals.”
“Well, that’s what I’m saying. Kings are mostly rascals, as far as I can make out.”
“Is dat so?”

“Read about them sometime and you’ll see. Look at Henry the Eighth; this one of ours is a Sunday-school superintendent next to _him_. And look at Charles the Second, and Louis the Fourteenth, and Louis the Fifteenth, and James the Second, and Edward the Second, and Richard the Third, and forty more; besides all those Saxon heptarchies that used to tear around so in old times and raise Cain. My, you ought to have seen old Henry the Eighth when he was in bloom. He _was_ a blossom. He used to marry a new wife every day and chop off her head the next morning. And he’d do it just as casually as if he was ordering eggs. ‘Fetch up Nell Gwynn,’ he says. They fetch her up. Next morning, ‘Chop off her head!’ And they chop it off. ‘Fetch up Jane Shore,’ he says, and up she comes. Next morning, ‘Chop off her head’—and they chop it off. ‘Ring for Fair Rosamun.’ Fair Rosamun answers the bell. Next morning, ‘Chop off her head.’ And he made every one of them tell him a story every night, and he kept that up until he’d grabbed a thousand and one stories that way, and then he put them all in a book and called it Domesday Book—which was a good name, and it said what it was. You don’t know kings, Jim, but I do, and this old rip of ours is one of the cleanest I’ve come across in history. Well, Henry gets an idea he wants to start some trouble with this country. How does he go about it—give notice?—give the country a chance? No. All of a sudden he heaves all the tea in Boston Harbor overboard, and slaps together a declaration of independence, and dares them to come and fight. That was _his_ style—he never gave anybody a chance. He suspected his father, the Duke of Wellington. Well, what did he do? Ask him to come out and show himself? No—he drowned him in a barrel of sweet wine, like a cat. Suppose people left money lying around where he was—what did he do? He grabbed it. Suppose he made a deal to do a job, and you paid him, and didn’t sit there and make sure he did it—what did he do? He always did the opposite. Suppose he opened his mouth—what then? If he didn’t shut it again mighty quick, he’d lose a lie every time. That’s the kind of bug Henry was; and if we’d had him along instead of our kings, he’d have fooled that town a lot worse than ours did. I don’t say ours are lambs, because they aren’t, when you come right down to the cold facts; but they’re nothing next to that old ram, anyway. All I say is, kings are kings, and you have to make allowances. Take them all around, they’re a mighty ornery lot. It’s the way they’re raised.”
“But dis one do _smell_ so much like de nation, Huck.”
“Well, they all do, Jim. _We_ can’t help the way a king smells; history doesn’t say how to.”
“Now de duke, he’s a tolerble likely man in some ways.”
“Sure, a duke is different. Only not by much. This one is a pretty rough specimen for a duke. When he’s drunk, a near-sighted man couldn’t tell him from a king.”
“Well, whatever, I doan’ hanker after no mo’ of um, Huck. Dese here is all I kin stan’.”
“Same with me, Jim. But they’re stuck to us now, so we have to keep in mind what they are and put up with them. I sometimes wish we’d hear about a country that has run out of kings.”
Where was the use in telling Jim these two weren’t real kings and dukes? It wouldn’t have helped any. Besides, it was exactly as I’d said: nobody could tell them from the real thing.

I fell asleep, and Jim didn’t wake me for my turn at watch. He did that a lot. When I came to at daybreak, there he sat with his head hanging between his knees, moaning and grieving to himself. I didn’t say anything or let on that I’d noticed. I knew what it was about. He was thinking of his wife and children, far away up the river, and he felt low and homesick, never having been away from home in all his life. And I honestly believe he cared as much for his family as white people do for theirs. It doesn’t seem natural, but I reckon it’s true. Nights, when he thought I was sleeping, he often moaned and grieved like that, and said, “Po’ little ’Lizabeth! Po’ little Johnny! It’s mighty hard; I spec’ I ain’t ever gwyne to see you no mo’, no mo’!” He was a mighty good nigger, Jim was.
But this time I somehow got to talking with him about his wife and young ones, and after a while he said:

“What make me feel so bad dis time is, I hear sumpn over yonder on de bank, like a whack, er a slam, jist a minute ago, en it put me in mind of de time I treat my little ’Lizabeth so ornery. She warn’t but ’bout fo’ year ole, en she catch de sk’yarlet fever, en had a powerful hard time of it; but she got well, en one day she was a-stannin’ aroun’, en I tell her, I say:
“‘Shet de do’.’
“She never did it; jis’ stood dah, sorter smilin’ up at me. Dat make me mad; en I tell her agin, mighty loud, I say:
“‘Doan’ you hear me?—shet de do’!’
“She jis’ stood de same way, kinder smilin’ up. I was a-bilin’! I say:
“‘I lay I _make_ you mind!’

“En wid dat I give her a slap side de head dat sont her sprawlin’. Den I went off into de yuther room, en I was gone ’bout ten minutes; en when I come back, dat do’ was a-stannin’ open _yit_, en dat chile stannin’ right dah in it, a-lookin’ down and mournin’, wid de tears runnin’ down. My, but I _was_ mad! I was fixin’ to go for dat chile, but jis’ den—dat do’ open inwards—jis’ den, de wind come along en slam it shut behind de chile, ker-_blam!_—en my lan’, de chile never move’! My breff pretty nigh jump outer me; en I feel so—so—I doan’ know _how_ I feel. I crope out, all a-tremblin’, en sneak aroun’ en open dat do’ easy en slow, en stick my head in behind de chile, soft en quiet, en all at once I say _pow!_ jis’ as loud as I could yell. _She never budge!_ Oh, Huck, I bust out cryin’ en snatch her up in my arms, en say, ‘Oh, de po’ little thing! May de Lord God Amighty forgive po’ ole Jim, ’cause he never gwyne to forgive hisself as long’s he live!’ Oh, she was plumb deef en dumb, Huck, plumb deef en dumb—en me a-treatin’ her dat way!”

chapters.title: Chapter XXIV — Jim in Royal Robes
paragraphs: The next day, toward night, we tied up under a little willow-covered sandbar out in the middle of the river, where there was a village on each side, and the duke and the king began to plan how to work those towns. Jim spoke to the duke and said he hoped it wouldn’t take more than a few hours, because it got mighty heavy and tiresome for him to lie all day in the wigwam tied up with the rope. You see, when we left him all alone we had to tie him, because if anybody happened on him by himself and not tied, it wouldn’t look much like he was a runaway nigger, you know. So the duke said it _was_ kind of hard to have to lie roped all day, and he’d figure out some way around it.

He was uncommonly clever, the duke was, and he soon hit on one. He dressed Jim up in King Lear’s costume—a long gown of curtain calico, and a white horsehair wig and whiskers. Then he took his theater paint and painted Jim’s face and hands and ears and neck all over a dead, dull, solid blue, like a man who’s been drowned nine days. Blamed if he wasn’t the horriblest-looking sight I ever saw. Then the duke took a shingle and wrote out a sign on it, like this:
_Sick Arab—but harmless when not out of his head._

Then he nailed the shingle to a lath and stood the lath up four or five feet in front of the wigwam. Jim was satisfied. He said it beat lying tied up for years on end, and shaking all over at every sound. The duke told him to relax and take it easy, and if anybody came poking around, he should jump out of the wigwam, put on a bit of a show, and howl once or twice like a wild animal, and the duke figured they’d run off and leave him in peace. That was sound reasoning, as far as it went; but most people wouldn’t hang around waiting for him to howl. Why, he didn’t just look dead; he looked a good deal worse than that.

These rascals wanted to try the Nonesuch again, because there was so much money in it, but they decided it wouldn’t be safe, since the news might have worked its way down the river by now. They couldn’t hit on any plan that suited them exactly. So at last the duke said he reckoned he’d take it easy and work his brains for an hour or two, and see if he couldn’t cook up something for the Arkansaw village; and the king said he’d go over to the other village with no plan at all, just trust Providence to lead him to something profitable—meaning the devil, I reckon. We had all bought store clothes where we stopped last, and now the king put his on and told me to put mine on. I did it, of course. The king’s clothes were all black, and he did look really fancy and stiff. I never knew before how clothes could change a person. Why, before, he looked like the orneriest old rip that ever lived; but now, when he took off his new white beaver hat and bowed and smiled, he looked so grand and good and pious that you’d say he’d walked right out of the ark, and maybe was old Leviticus himself. Jim cleaned up the canoe, and I got my paddle ready. There was a big steamboat sitting at the shore way up under the point, about three miles above the town. It had been there a couple of hours, taking on freight. The king said:
“The way I’m dressed, I reckon I’d better come in from St. Louis or Cincinnati, or some other big city. Make for the steamboat, Huckleberry; we’ll ride her down to the village.”

Nobody had to tell me twice to go for a steamboat ride. I landed half a mile above the village, then went scooting along the high bank in the slack water. Soon we came upon a nice, harmless-looking young country fellow sitting on a log and mopping the sweat off his face, since the weather was powerful warm. Two big carpet-bags sat next to him.
“Run her nose in to shore,” the king said. I did it. “Where are you bound, young man?”
“For the steamboat; going to Orleans.”
“Get aboard,” said the king. “Hold on a minute, my servant will help you with those bags. Jump out and help the gentleman, Adolphus”—meaning me, I saw.

I did, and then the three of us started up the road again. The young fellow was mighty grateful. He said it was hard work lugging his baggage in this kind of weather. He asked the king where he was headed, and the king told him he’d come down the river and landed at the other village that morning, and now he was going a few miles up the road to see an old friend on a farm. The young fellow said:

“When I first laid eyes on you, I said to myself, ‘That’s Mr. Wilks, sure enough, and he’s come mighty close to getting here in time.’ But then I thought again, ‘No, I reckon it isn’t him, or he wouldn’t be paddling up the river.’ You _aren’t_ him, are you?”

“No, my name’s Blodgett—Elexander Blodgett—_Reverend_ Elexander Blodgett, I s’pose I have to say, since I’m one o’ the Lord’s poor servants. But I can feel just as sorry for Mr. Wilks for not getting here in time, all the same, if he’s lost anything by it—which I hope he hasn’t.”

“Well, he won’t lose any property by it, because he’ll get all of that all right. But he’s missed seeing his brother Peter die—which he may not mind, there’s no telling about that—but his brother would’ve given anything in this world to see _him_ before he died. He never talked about anything else these last three weeks. They hadn’t seen each other since they were boys together—and Peter never saw his brother William at all—that’s the deaf and dumb one—William’s not more than thirty or thirty-five. Peter and George were the only ones who came out here. George was the married brother; he and his wife both died last year. Harvey and William are the only ones left now. And like I was saying, they haven’t gotten here in time.”
“Did anybody send them word?”

“Oh, yes. A month or two back, when Peter first came down sick, he said right then he had a feeling he wouldn’t pull through this time. See, he was pretty old, and George’s girls were too little to keep him much company, except Mary Jane, the red-headed one. So he got kind of lonesome after George and his wife passed on, and he didn’t seem to care much whether he lived. He was desperate to see Harvey—and William too, for that matter—because he was one of those people who just can’t bear to make a will. He left Harvey a letter, and said it told where his money was hidden, and how he wanted the rest of the property split so George’s girls would be provided for—since George left them nothing. And that letter was the only thing they could get him to put pen to.”
“Why do you reckon Harvey hasn’t come? Where does he live?”
“Oh, he lives in England—Sheffield—he preaches there—he’s never been in this country. He hasn’t had much time—and besides, he may not have gotten the letter at all, you know.”
“What a shame he couldn’t have lived to see his brothers, poor soul. So you’re bound for Orleans, you say?”
“Yes, but that’s only part of it. I’m taking a ship next Wednesday for Rio de Janeiro, where my uncle lives.”
“That’s a pretty long trip. But it’ll be lovely; I wish I was going. Is Mary Jane the oldest? How old are the others?”
“Mary Jane is nineteen, Susan is fifteen, and Joanna is around fourteen—she’s the one who gives her time to good works, and she has a harelip.”
“Poor things! Left alone in the cold world like that.”

“Well, it could be worse. Old Peter had friends, and they won’t let those girls come to any harm. There’s Hobson, the Baptist preacher; Deacon Lot Hovey; Ben Rucker; Abner Shackleford; Levi Bell, the lawyer; Dr. Robinson; their wives; the widow Bartley; and—well, plenty more. But those are the ones Peter was closest to, and the ones he sometimes mentioned in his letters home. So Harvey will know who to turn to when he gets here.”

Well, the old man kept up his questions until he’d wrung that young fellow dry. Blamed if he didn’t ask after every person and every thing in that whole blessed town, and all about the Wilkses. He asked about Peter’s trade, which was tanning; and George’s, which was carpentry; and Harvey’s, which was preaching as a dissenting minister; and so on, and so on. Then he said:
“Why’d you want to walk all the way up here to catch the steamboat?”

“Because she’s a big Orleans boat, and I was afraid she might not stop at the village. Boats that are loaded deep won’t stop when you hail them. A Cincinnati boat will, but this one’s out of St. Louis.”
“Was Peter Wilks well off?”
“Oh, yes, quite well off. He owned houses and land, and folks figure he left three or four thousand in cash stashed away somewhere.”
“When did you say he died?”
“I didn’t say, but it was last night.”
“The funeral’s tomorrow, I suppose?”
“Yes, around the middle of the day.”
“Well, it’s all terribly sad; but we all have to go, sooner or later. So what we need to do is be prepared; then we’re all right.”
“Yes, sir, that’s the best way. Ma always used to say that.”

By the time we reached the boat she was nearly done loading, and soon she pulled out. The king never said anything about going aboard, so I lost my ride after all. Once the boat was gone, the king made me paddle another mile up to a lonesome spot, and then he climbed ashore and said:

“Now hurry back, right away, and bring the duke up here, and the new carpet-bags. And if he’s gone over to the other side, go over there and get him. And tell him to dress himself up, no matter what. Move along, now.”

I could see what _he_ was up to, but I never said anything, of course. When I got back with the duke, we hid the canoe, and then the two of them sat down on a log, and the king told him everything, just the way the young fellow had told it—every last word. And the whole time he was doing it, he tried to talk like an Englishman, and he did it pretty well, too, for a bum. I can’t imitate him, so I’m not going to try; but he really did it pretty well. Then he said:
“How are you at playing deaf and dumb, Bilgewater?”
The duke told him to leave that to him; he said he’d played a deaf and dumb person on the theatrical stage. So then they waited for a steamboat.

Around the middle of the afternoon a couple of little boats came along, but they weren’t coming from far enough upriver. At last a big one came, and they hailed her. She sent out her yawl, and we went aboard. She was from Cincinnati, and when they found out we only wanted to go four or five miles, they were boiling mad, and cussed us out, and said they wouldn’t put us ashore. But the king stayed calm. He said:
“If gentlemen can afford to pay a dollar a mile apiece to be picked up and set down in a yawl, a steamboat can afford to carry them, can’t it?”
So they cooled down and said all right, and when we got to the village they rowed us ashore in the yawl. About two dozen men came flocking down when they saw the yawl coming, and the king said:
“Can any of you gentlemen tell me where Mr. Peter Wilks lives?” They glanced at one another and nodded, as if to say, “What did I tell you?” Then one of them said, kind of soft and gentle:
“I’m sorry, sir. All we can tell you is where he _lived_ as of yesterday evening.”
Quick as a wink, the rotten old creature fell completely to pieces. He collapsed against the man, rested his chin on his shoulder, bawled down his back, and said:
“Alas, alas! Our poor brother, gone, and we never got to see him! Oh, it is too, _too_ hard!”

Then he turned around, blubbering, and made a lot of idiotic signs to the duke with his hands, and blamed if _he_ didn’t drop a carpet-bag and burst out crying. If they weren’t the most outrageous pair, those two frauds, of any I ever ran across.

Well, the men crowded around and felt for them, and said all sorts of kind things, and hauled their carpet-bags up the hill for them, and let them lean on their shoulders and cry. They told the king all about his brother’s final moments, and the king passed it all along again on his fingers to the duke, and the pair of them carried on over that dead tanner as if they’d lost the twelve disciples. Well, if I ever saw anything like it, I’m a nigger. It was enough to make a body ashamed of the human race.

chapters.title: Chapter XXV — Is It Them?
paragraphs: The news spread over the whole town in two minutes. You could see people pelting down the street from every which way, some of them still pulling on their coats. Pretty soon we were in the middle of a crowd, and all that tramping sounded like soldiers on the march. Windows and dooryards were full, and every minute somebody would call out over a fence:
“Is it _them?_”
And somebody hurrying along in the crowd would call back:
“You bet it is.”

By the time we reached the house, the street out front was jammed, and the three girls stood in the doorway. Mary Jane _was_ red-headed, but that didn’t matter; she was awfully beautiful, her face and eyes lit up like glory, she was so happy her uncles had come. The king opened his arms, and Mary Jane leaped into them, and the harelip leaped at the duke, and there they _went_! Just about everybody, the women anyway, cried for joy to see them meet at last and have such a fine time of it.

Then the king nudged the duke privately—I saw him do it—and looked around and spotted the coffin over in the corner, on two chairs. So he and the duke, each with one hand across the other’s shoulder and the other hand at his eyes, walked slowly and solemnly over there. Everybody drew back to give them room, and all the talk and noise stopped, and people said “Sh!” and all the men took their hats off and bowed their heads, so you could have heard a pin drop. And when they got there, they bent over and looked in the coffin, and took one look, and then they burst out crying so loud you could nearly have heard them in Orleans. Then they put their arms around each other’s necks and hung their chins over each other’s shoulders. And for three minutes, or maybe four, I never saw two men leak the way they did. And mind you, everybody was doing the same, and the place got so damp I never saw anything like it. Then one of them got on one side of the coffin and the other on the other side, and they knelt down and rested their foreheads on the coffin, and pretended to pray silently to themselves. Well, when it came to that, it worked on the crowd like nothing you ever saw, and everybody broke down and went to sobbing right out loud—the poor girls, too. And nearly every woman went up to the girls without saying a word and kissed them solemnly on the forehead, and then put her hand on their heads and looked up toward the sky with the tears running down, and then burst out and went off sobbing and mopping her face, and gave the next woman a turn. I never saw anything so disgusting.

Well, after a while the king got up and came forward a little, and worked himself up and slobbered out a speech, all full of tears and flapdoodle. He said it was a sore trial for him and his poor brother to lose the deceased, and to miss seeing the deceased alive after the long journey of four thousand miles, but that it was a trial sweetened and made holy for them by this dear sympathy and these sacred tears. So he thanked them from his heart and from his brother’s heart, because out of their mouths they couldn’t, words being too weak and cold—and all that kind of rot and slush, until it was just sickening. And then he blubbered out a pious, goody-goody Amen, and let himself go and cried fit to bust.

The second he finished, somebody in the crowd started singing the doxology, and everybody joined in as loud as they could. It warmed you through and made you feel as good as church letting out. Music _is_ a good thing. After all that soul-butter and hogwash, I never saw anything freshen the air so, or sound so honest and fine.

Then the king started working his jaw again, and said how he and his nieces would be glad if a few of the main friends of the family would take supper with them that evening and help sit up with the remains of the deceased. He said if his poor brother lying over there could speak, he knew whom he would name, because they were names very dear to him, and mentioned often in his letters. So he would name the same, to wit, as follows, namely:—Rev. Mr. Hobson, and Deacon Lot Hovey, and Mr. Ben Rucker, and Abner Shackleford, and Levi Bell, and Dr. Robinson, and their wives, and the widow Bartley.

Rev. Hobson and Dr. Robinson were off at the far end of town, hunting together—I mean the doctor was sending some sick man off to the next world, and the preacher was pointing him the right way. Lawyer Bell had gone to Louisville on business. But the rest were there, and they all came up and shook the king’s hand and thanked him and talked with him. Then they shook the duke’s hand and said nothing, just kept smiling and bobbing their heads like a pack of sapheads, while he made all kinds of signs and said “Goo-goo—goo-goo-goo” the whole time, like a baby who can’t talk yet.
