So the king blathered along, and managed to ask about pretty much every person and dog in town by name, and mentioned all sorts of little things that had happened at one time or another in the town, or to George’s family, or to Peter. And he always acted like Peter had written him those things; but that was a lie. He got every blessed one of them from that young flathead we paddled up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane fetched the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and wept over it. It left the dwelling-house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls. It left the tanyard (doing a good business), plus some other houses and land (worth about seven thousand) and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William. And it said the six thousand in cash was hidden down in the cellar. So these two frauds said they’d go bring it up, and keep everything square and aboveboard, and told me to come along with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag, they dumped it out on the floor. It was a lovely sight, all those yellow-boys. My, how the king’s eyes did shine! He clapped the duke on the shoulder and said:
“Oh, _this_ ain’t nothin’ to brag about! Oh, no, I reckon not! Why, Bilji, it’s better than the Nonesuch, _ain’t_ it?”
The duke said it did. They pawed at the yellow-boys, let them run through their fingers, and let them jingle down onto the floor. Then the king said:

“Ain’t no use talkin’. Bein’ brothers of a rich dead man, and standin’ in for the foreign heirs he left behind, is the line of work for you and me, Bilge. This here comes of trustin’ in Providence. It’s the best way in the long run. I’ve tried ’em all, and there ain’t a better one.”
Most folks would have been happy with the pile and taken it on trust. But no, they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came out four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king said:
“Dern him! Where in the world did that four hundred and fifteen dollars get to, I wonder?”
They fretted over it for a while and hunted all over the place for it. Then the duke said:
“Well, he was a mighty sick man, and likely he just made a mistake. I reckon that’s how it was. The best thing is to let it go and keep quiet about it. We can spare it.”

“Oh, shucks, sure, we can _spare_ it. I don’t care nothin’ about that—it’s the _count_ I’m thinkin’ of. We want to be awful square and open and aboveboard here, you know. We want to lug this money upstairs and count it in front of everybody—then there ain’t nothin’ suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”
“Hold on,” said the duke. “Let’s make up the shortage,” and he started hauling yellow-boys out of his pocket.

“That’s a mighty fine idea, duke—you _have_ got a rattlin’ clever head on you,” said the king. “Blest if the old Nonesuch ain’t helpin’ us out again,” and _he_ started hauling out yellow-jackets and stacking them up.
It nearly broke them, but they made up the full six thousand, clean and clear.
“Say,” said the duke, “I’ve got another idea. Let’s go upstairs and count this money, and then turn right around and _give it to the girls_.”

“Good land, duke, let me hug you! That’s the most dazzlin’ idea a man ever had. You’ve certainly got the most astonishin’ head I ever saw. Oh, this is the boss trick, no mistake about it. Let ’em bring on their suspicions now if they want to—this’ll knock ’em flat.”

When we got upstairs, everybody gathered around the table, and the king counted the money and stacked it, three hundred dollars to a pile—twenty fine little piles. Everybody stared at it hungrily and licked their lips. Then they raked it all back into the bag, and I saw the king start puffing himself up for another speech. He said:

“Friends all, my poor brother lyin’ over yonder has been generous to those he’s left behind in this vale of sorrows. He has been generous to these poor little lambs that he loved and sheltered, and who are left fatherless and motherless. Yes, and those of us who knew him know he would have been _more_ generous to them if he hadn’t been afraid of wounding his dear William and me. Now, _wouldn’t_ he? There ain’t a question about it in _my_ mind. Well, then, what kind of brothers would stand in his way at such a time? And what kind of uncles would rob—yes, _rob_—such poor sweet lambs as these, that he loved so, at such a time? If I know William—and I _think_ I do—he—well, I’ll just ask him.” He turned around and began making a lot of signs to the duke with his hands, and the duke stared at him, stupid and thick-headed, for a while. Then all of a sudden he seemed to catch on, and jumped at the king, goo-gooing with all his might for joy, and hugged him about fifteen times before he let go. Then the king said, “I knew it. I reckon _that’ll_ convince anybody how _he_ feels about it. Here, Mary Jane, Susan, Joanna, take the money—take it _all_. It’s the gift of him who lies over yonder, cold but joyful.”

Mary Jane ran to him, Susan and the hare-lip ran to the duke, and I never saw such hugging and kissing in my life. Everybody crowded around with tears in their eyes and nearly shook the hands off those frauds, saying over and over:
“You _dear_ good souls!—how _lovely!_—how _could_ you!”

Well, pretty soon everybody was talking about the deceased again, and how good he was, and what a loss he was, and all that. Before long a big, iron-jawed man pushed his way in from outside and stood there listening and looking, not saying a word. Nobody said anything to him, either, because the king was talking and they were all busy listening. The king was saying—right in the middle of something he’d started—

“—them bein’ particular friends of the deceased. That’s why they’re invited here this evenin’. But tomorrow we want _all_ to come—everybody. For he respected everybody and liked everybody, and so it’s fittin’ that his funeral orgies should be public.”

And so he went mooning on and on, loving the sound of his own voice, and every little while he dragged in his funeral orgies again, until the duke couldn’t stand it any longer. He wrote on a little scrap of paper, “_obsequies_, you old fool,” folded it up, and went goo-gooing and reaching it over people’s heads to the king. The king read it, stuck it in his pocket, and said:
“Poor William, afflicted as he is, his _heart’s_ always right. He asks me to invite everybody to the funeral—wants me to make ’em all welcome. But he needn’t have worried—it’s just what I was doin’.”
Then he wandered along again, perfectly calm, and went on dropping in his funeral orgies every now and then, just like before. And when he did it the third time, he said:

“Now, I say orgies, and I don’t say it ’cause it’s the ordinary word—it ain’t; obsequies is the ordinary word—but orgies is the correct one. Folks in England don’t use obsequies no more; it’s died out over there. Orgies is what we say now. It’s better, too, ’cause it hits what you mean more exactly. The word’s built out of the Greek _orgo_, outside, open, abroad, and the Hebrew _jeesum_, to plant, cover up; hence in_ter._ So, you see, a funeral orgy is an open, public funeral.”

That man was the _worst_ I’d ever run across. Well, the iron-jawed man just laughed straight in his face, and everybody was shocked. They all cried out, “Why, _doctor!_” and Abner Shackleford spoke up:
“Robinson, haven’t you heard the news? This is Harvey Wilks.”
The king smiled eagerly, stuck out his flipper, and said:
“Can this be my poor brother’s dear good friend, the physician? I—”

“Get your hands off me!” the doctor snapped. “_You_ talk like an Englishman, do you? That’s the worst imitation I ever listened to. _You_, Peter Wilks’s brother! You’re a fraud, and that’s all you are!”

Well, how they all carried on! They crowded around the doctor and tried to calm him down. They tried to explain how Harvey had shown in forty ways that he _was_ Harvey, and knew everybody by name, and even the names of the dogs, and they begged and _begged_ him not to hurt Harvey’s feelings and the poor girl’s feelings, and all that. But it was no use. He stormed right on, and said any man who pretended to be an Englishman and couldn’t imitate the way they talk any better than that was a fraud and a liar. The poor girls were clinging to the king and crying, and all of a sudden the doctor turned on _them_. He said:

“I was your father’s friend and I’m yours. As a friend—an honest one, who wants to shield you from harm and trouble—I’m warning you: turn your backs on that scoundrel and have nothing to do with him. He’s an ignorant tramp, with his idiotic Greek and Hebrew, as he calls it. He’s about the thinnest impostor there is. He turned up here with a handful of empty names and facts he gathered somewhere, and you mistake them for _proofs_, while these foolish friends of yours, who ought to know better, help you deceive yourselves. Mary Jane Wilks, you know I’m your friend, and an unselfish one. Now hear me out. Throw this pitiful rascal out of the house—I _beg_ you to. Will you?”
Mary Jane drew herself up, and my, she was handsome! She said:

“_This_ is my answer.” She picked up the bag of money, put it into the king’s hands, and said, “Here’s six thousand dollars. Invest it for me and my sisters however you like, and don’t give us a receipt for it.”

Then she wrapped one arm around the king, while Susan and the hare-lip did the same on his other side. Everybody applauded and stamped on the floor like a perfect storm, and the king lifted his head and smiled proudly. The doctor said:
“Very well. I wash _my_ hands of the whole business. But mark my words, all of you: there’s a day coming when the thought of this one will turn your stomachs.” And out he went.
“All right, doctor,” said the king, sort of mocking him. “We’ll try to get ’em to send for you.” That made them all laugh, and they said it was a first-rate hit.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVI — A Pious King
paragraphs: Well, when they were all gone, the king asked Mary Jane how they were fixed for spare rooms. She said she had one spare room, which would do for Uncle William, and she’d give her own room to Uncle Harvey, since it was a little bigger. She would move in with her sisters and sleep on a cot. And up in the attic was a little cubbyhole with a straw bed in it. The king said the cubbyhole would do for his valley—meaning me.

So Mary Jane took us upstairs and showed them their rooms, which were plain but nice. She said she’d have her dresses and a lot of other things taken out of her room if they were in Uncle Harvey’s way, but he said they weren’t. The dresses hung along the wall, and in front of them was a curtain made of calico that hung down to the floor. There was an old hair trunk in one corner and a guitar case in another, and all sorts of little knickknacks and gimcracks around, the kind girls use to brighten up a room. The king said all those things made it homier and more pleasant, so she shouldn’t disturb them. The duke’s room was pretty small, but plenty good enough, and so was my cubbyhole.

That night they put on a big supper, and all those men and women came. I stood behind the chairs of the king and the duke and served them, while the niggers served everyone else. Mary Jane sat at the head of the table with Susan next to her. She went on about how dreadful the biscuits were, how stingy the preserves, and how poor and tough the fried chickens—all that kind of rot that women always say when they’re fishing for compliments. And the guests all knew it was tiptop and said so. “How _do_ you get your biscuits so nicely browned?” they asked, and “Wherever, for goodness’ sake, did you find these amazing pickles?” and every other scrap of humbug talk, just the way people always do at a supper, you know.

When it was all over, the hare-lip and I ate supper in the kitchen off the leftovers, while the others helped the niggers clean up. The hare-lip started pumping me about England, and I’ll be blamed if I didn’t think the ice was getting mighty thin sometimes. She said:
“Did you ever see the king?”
“Who? William the Fourth? Well, I bet I have—he goes to our church.” I knew he’d been dead for years, but I never let on. So when I said he goes to our church, she said:
“What—regularly?”
“Yes—regularly. His pew is right across from ours, on the other side of the pulpit.”
“I thought he lived in London?”
“Well, he does. Where _would_ he live?”
“But I thought _you_ lived in Sheffield?”
I saw I was in a pinch. I had to pretend to choke on a chicken bone, to buy time to think how to get out of it. Then I said:
“What I mean is, he attends our church regularly when he’s staying in Sheffield. That’s only in the summer, when he comes there for the sea baths.”
“Why, how you talk—Sheffield isn’t on the sea.”
“Well, who said it was?”
“Why, you did.”
“I did _not_.”
“You did!”
“I didn’t.”
“You did.”
“I never said anything of the kind.”
“Well, what _did_ you say, then?”
“I said he comes to take the sea _baths_—that’s what I said.”
“Well, then, how can he take the sea baths if it isn’t on the sea?”
“Look here,” I said. “Have you ever seen any Congress-water?”
“Yes.”
“Well, did you have to go to Congress to get it?”
“Why, no.”
“Well, then, William the Fourth doesn’t have to travel to the sea for a sea bath, either.”
“How does he get it, then?”

“The same way people down here get Congress-water—in barrels. There in the palace at Sheffield they’ve got furnaces, and he wants his water hot. They can’t boil that much water way off there at the sea. They don’t have the equipment for it.”
“Oh, now I get it. You might have told me that to begin with, and spared us the time.”
When she said that, I knew I was out of the woods again, and I felt comfortable and glad. Next she said:
“Do you go to church, too?”
“Yes—regularly.”
“Where do you sit?”
“Why, in our pew.”
“_Whose_ pew?”
“Why, _ours_—your Uncle Harvey’s.”
“His? What does _he_ want with a pew?”
“He wants it to sit in. What did you _think_ he wanted with it?”
“Why, I thought he’d be in the pulpit.”
Confound him, I’d forgotten he was a preacher. I saw I was in a pinch again, so I faked another chicken bone and got more time to think. Then I said:
“Blame it, do you suppose there’s only one preacher to a church?”
“Why, what do they want with more?”
“What! To preach in front of a king? Never met a girl like you. They keep seventeen of them, at the very least.”
“Seventeen! My land! I wouldn’t sit through a string of preachers like that, not even if it was the only way I’d ever get to glory. It must take them a week!”
“Shucks, they don’t _all_ preach on the same day—just _one_ of them does.”
“Well, then, what do the rest of them do?”
“Oh, not much. Lounge around, pass the plate, and one thing or another. But mainly they don’t do anything.”
“Well, then, what are they _for?_”
“Why, they’re for _style_. Don’t you know anything?”
“Well, I don’t care to know anything so foolish as that. Tell me about servants in England. Are they treated any better than we treat our niggers?”
“_No!_ Over there a servant is nobody. They’re treated worse than dogs.”
“But don’t they get time off, like we do at Christmas, and New Year’s week, and the Fourth of July?”

“Oh, just listen to that! Anybody could tell _you’ve_ never been to England. Why, Hare-l—why, Joanna, they never see a holiday from one year’s end to the next. They never go to the circus, or the theater, or nigger shows, or anywhere.”
“Or church?”
“Or church.”
“But _you_ always went to church.”

Well, I was caught again. I’d forgotten I was the old man’s servant. But the next minute I whirled into a kind of explanation of how a valley was different from a common servant and _had_ to go to church whether he wanted to or not, and sit with the family, because it was the law. But I didn’t do it very well, and when I finished I could see she wasn’t satisfied. She said:
“Honest Injun, now, haven’t you been telling me a pack of lies?”
“Honest Injun,” I said.
“None of it at all?”
“None of it at all. Not a lie in it,” I said.
“Lay your hand on this book and say it.”
It turned out to be only a dictionary, so I put my hand on it and swore. After that she seemed a bit more satisfied, and said:
“All right, I’ll believe part of it. But I’ll be switched if I’ll believe the rest.”

“What is it you won’t believe, Joe?” said Mary Jane, stepping in with Susan right behind her. “It isn’t right or kind of you to talk to him that way. He’s a stranger, and he’s a long way from his own people. How would you like it if somebody treated you like that?”

“That’s you all over, Maim—always charging in to help somebody before they’re even hurt. I haven’t done a thing to him. He told some whoppers, I reckon, and I said I wasn’t going to swallow every bit of it. That’s every last thing I _did_ say. I reckon he can stand a little something like that, can’t he?”

“I don’t care if it was little or big. He’s a stranger in our house, and it wasn’t decent of you to say it. If you were in his place, it would shame you. So you shouldn’t say anything to another person that will make _them_ feel ashamed.”
“But, Mam, he said—”
“It makes no difference what he _said_—that isn’t the point. The point is that you treat him _kindly_, and don’t say things that remind him he isn’t in his own country or among his own folks.”
I said to myself, _this_ is the kind of girl I’m letting that old reptile rob of her money!
Then Susan _she_ sailed in, and believe me, she gave Hare-lip a real scolding, the kind that would wake the dead!
And here was _another_ girl, I thought, that I was letting him cheat out of her money!
Then Mary Jane took her own turn, and went at her sweet and lovely again, which was her way. By the time she was done, there was hardly anything left of poor Hare-lip. So she started to bawl.
“All right, then,” said the other girls. “Now you just ask his pardon.”
And she did, too, and she did it beautifully. She did it so beautifully that it was a pleasure to hear, and I wished I could tell her a thousand lies so she could do it again.

I said to myself, this is _another_ one I’m letting him rob of her money. And when she was finished, they all just about bent over backward to make me feel at home and to let me know I was among friends. I felt so rotten and low and mean that I said to myself, my mind’s made up. I’ll get that money away from them for these girls, or bust.

So then I lit out—for bed, I said, meaning sometime or other. Once I was alone, I started thinking the whole thing over. I asked myself, should I go to that doctor in private and give these frauds away? No, that won’t do. He might let on who told him, and then the king and the duke would make things hot for me. Should I go in private and tell Mary Jane? No, I don’t dare. Her face would tip them off for sure. They’ve got the money, and they’d slip right out of town and get away with it. And if she went and fetched help, I’d be tangled up in the business before it was over, I figured. No, there’s only one good way. I’ve got to steal that money somehow, and I’ve got to steal it in a way that keeps them from suspecting me. They’ve got a good thing going here, and they won’t leave until they’ve squeezed this family and this town for all it’s worth, so I’ll find my chance soon enough. I’ll steal it and hide it, and sometime later, when I’m way down the river, I’ll write Mary Jane a letter and tell her where it is. But it would be better to get it tonight if I can, because maybe the doctor hasn’t eased off as much as he pretends. He might still scare them out of here.

So I thought, I’ll go and search their rooms. Upstairs the hall was dark. I found the duke’s room and started feeling around in it with my hands. Then I remembered that the king wasn’t the sort to let anybody else look after that money but himself, so I went to his room and started feeling around there. But I could see I couldn’t get anywhere without a candle, and of course I didn’t dare light one. So I figured I had to do the other thing—lie in wait and eavesdrop. About then I heard their footsteps coming, and I was going to duck under the bed. I reached for it, but it wasn’t where I thought it was. What I did touch was the curtain that hung over Mary Jane’s dresses, so I jumped in behind that, snuggled in among the gowns, and stood there perfectly still.

They came in and shut the door, and the first thing the duke did was get down and look under the bed. I was glad then that I hadn’t found the bed when I wanted it. And yet, you know, it comes naturally to hide under the bed when you’re up to something private. Then they sat down, and the king said:
“Well, what is it? And keep it pretty short, because we’d be better off down there whooping up the mourning than up here giving them a chance to talk about us.”
“Well, here it is, Capet. I’m uneasy. I’m not comfortable. That doctor is weighing on my mind. I wanted to know your plans. I’ve got an idea, and I think it’s a sound one.”
“What is it, duke?”

“That we ought to slip out of here before three in the morning and hurry down the river with what we’ve got. Especially since we got it so easy—_handed_ back to us, thrown at our heads, you might say, when of course we expected to have to steal it back. I’m for quitting and clearing out.”
That made me feel pretty bad. An hour or two earlier it would have been a little different, but now I felt bad and let down. The king burst out and said:

“What! And not sell off the rest of the property? March away like a pack of fools and leave eight or nine thousand dollars’ worth of property lying around, just begging to be scooped up? And all of it good, salable stuff, too.”
The duke grumbled and said the bag of gold was plenty. He didn’t want to go any deeper, and he didn’t like the idea of robbing a lot of orphans of _everything_ they owned.

“Why, how you talk!” said the king. “We won’t rob them of a thing but this money. The people who _buy_ the property are the ones who’ll suffer. As soon as it’s found out that we didn’t own it—which won’t be long after we’ve cleared out—the sale won’t be valid, and it’ll all go back to the estate. These orphans will get their house back again, and that’s plenty for _them._ They’re young and spry, and they can easily earn a living. _They’re_ not going to suffer. Why, just think—there are thousands and thousands who aren’t nearly so well off. Bless you, _they_ have nothing to complain about.”
Well, the king talked him dizzy, and at last he gave in. He said all right, but he believed it was blamed foolishness to stay, with that doctor hanging over them. But the king said:
“Curse the doctor! Why should we care about _him?_ Don’t we have all the fools in town on our side? And isn’t that a big enough majority in any town?”
So they got ready to go downstairs again. The duke said:
“I don’t think we put that money in a good place.”
That cheered me up. I’d begun to think I wasn’t going to get any kind of hint to help me. The king said:
“Why?”

“Because from now on Mary Jane will be in mourning, and the first thing you know, the nigger who tidies up the rooms will get an order to box up these clothes and put them away. And do you think a nigger can come across money and not borrow some of it?”

“Your head’s on straight again, duke,” said the king, and he came fumbling under the curtain two or three feet from where I stood. I pressed tight against the wall and kept very still, though I was trembling. I wondered what those fellows would say to me if they caught me, and I tried to think what I should do if they did. But the king got the bag before I could think more than half a thought, and he never suspected I was there. They pushed the bag through a rip in the straw mattress under the feather bed and crammed it in a foot or two among the straw. They said it was all right now, because a nigger only makes up the feather bed and turns the straw mattress over about twice a year, so there was no danger of it getting stolen now.

But I knew better. I had it out of there before they were halfway downstairs. I felt my way up to my little attic room and hid it there until I could get a chance to do something better. I decided I should hide it somewhere outside the house, because if they missed it they would tear the house apart. I knew that very well. Then I lay down with all my clothes on, but I couldn’t have gone to sleep if I’d wanted to, I was in such a sweat to get the business finished. After a while I heard the king and the duke come upstairs. So I rolled off my pallet and lay with my chin at the top of my ladder, and waited to see if anything would happen. But nothing did.
So I held on until all the late noises had stopped and the early ones hadn’t started yet. Then I slipped down the ladder.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVII — The Funeral
paragraphs: I crept to their doors and listened. They were snoring. So I tiptoed along and got downstairs all right. There wasn’t a sound anywhere. I peeked through a crack in the dining-room door and saw the men who were watching over the corpse, all sound asleep in their chairs. The door into the parlor, where the corpse lay, was open, and there was a candle in both rooms. I went on past, and the parlor door was open, but I saw there was nobody in there but what was left of Peter, so I pushed on by. But the front door was locked, and the key wasn’t there. Just then I heard somebody coming down the stairs behind me. I ran into the parlor and took a quick look around, and the only place I could see to hide the bag was in the coffin. The lid was pushed back about a foot, so I could see the dead man’s face down in there, with a wet cloth over it, and his shroud on. I tucked the money bag in under the lid, just past where his hands were crossed. They were so cold that it made my skin crawl. Then I ran back across the room and in behind the door.

It was Mary Jane who was coming. She walked to the coffin on tiptoe, knelt, and looked in. Then she lifted her handkerchief to her face, and I could tell she had started crying, though I couldn’t hear it, since her back was toward me. I slid out. On my way past the dining room I wanted to be sure the watchers hadn’t noticed me, so I peeked through the crack, and all was well. Not one of them had stirred.

I slipped up to bed, feeling pretty blue that the thing had played out this way after I’d gone to so much trouble and run so much risk over it. I said to myself, if it could stay where it is, that would be fine, because when we got a hundred miles or two down the river I could write back to Mary Jane, and she could dig him up again and get it. But that isn’t what’s going to happen. What’s going to happen is that the money will be found when they come to screw on the lid. Then the king will get it again, and it will be a long time before he gives anybody another chance to snatch it from him. Of course I _wanted_ to slide down and get it out of there, but I didn’t dare try it. Every minute it was getting closer to morning, and pretty soon some of those watchers would begin to stir, and I might get caught—caught with six thousand dollars in my hands that nobody had hired me to look after. I don’t want to be mixed up in any business like that, I told myself.

When I came downstairs in the morning, the parlor was shut up and the watchers were gone. There was nobody around but the family, the widow Bartley and our bunch. I watched their faces to see if anything had happened, but I couldn’t tell.

Toward the middle of the day the undertaker came with his helper. They set the coffin in the middle of the room on a couple of chairs, then arranged all our chairs in rows and borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, the parlor and the dining room were full. I saw that the coffin lid was just as it had been before, but I didn’t dare look in under it with folks around.

Then the people began to flock in. The beats and the girls took seats in the front row at the head of the coffin, and for half an hour the people filed slowly past in a single line and looked down at the dead man’s face for a minute. Some of them dropped a tear. It was all very quiet and solemn, with only the girls and the beats holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bent and sobbing a little. There was no other sound but feet scraping on the floor and noses being blown, because people always blow their noses more at a funeral than anywhere else except church.

When the place was packed full, the undertaker slid around in his black gloves with his soft, soothing ways, putting on the last touches and getting people and things all shipshape and comfortable, making no more noise than a cat. He never spoke. He moved people around, squeezed in latecomers, and opened up passageways, and he did it all with nods and signals of his hands. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the softest, gliding-est, stealthiest man I ever saw, and there was no more smile in him than in a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeum, a sickly one, and when everything was ready a young woman sat down and worked it. It was pretty squeaky and colicky, and everybody joined in and sang, and Peter was the only one who had a good thing, to my way of thinking. Then the Reverend Hobson opened up, slow and solemn, and started to talk, and right away the most outrageous racket broke out in the cellar that anyone ever heard. It was only one dog, but he made a terrible din and kept it up without a stop. The parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait, because you couldn’t hear yourself think. It was downright awkward, and nobody seemed to know what to do. But pretty soon they saw that long-legged undertaker give the preacher a sign, as much as to say, “Don’t you worry, just leave it to me.” Then he bent low and started to glide along the wall, with only his shoulders showing above the people’s heads. He glided along, with the uproar and racket getting worse all the time, and when he had gone around two sides of the room he vanished down the cellar stairs. About two seconds later we heard a whack, and the dog finished with one or two amazing howls, and then everything went dead still, and the parson picked up his solemn talk where he’d left off. A minute or two later the undertaker’s back and shoulders came gliding along the wall again. He glided and glided around three sides of the room, and then he straightened up, cupped his hands around his mouth, stretched his neck out toward the preacher over the people’s heads, and said in a kind of coarse whisper, “_He had a rat!_” Then he ducked down and glided back along the wall to his place. You could see it was a great satisfaction to the people, because naturally they’d wanted to know. A little thing like that costs nothing, and it’s just the little things that make a man looked up to and liked. There wasn’t a more popular man in town than that undertaker.

Well, the funeral sermon was very good, but awfully long and tiresome, and then the king shoved in and delivered some of his usual rubbish. At last the job was done, and the undertaker began to creep up on the coffin with his screwdriver. I was in a sweat by then, and I watched him pretty close. But he never touched anything. He just slid the lid along, soft as mush, and screwed it down tight and fast. So there I was! I didn’t know whether the money was in there or not. Suppose somebody had swiped that bag on the sly, I said to myself. Then how was I supposed to know whether to write to Mary Jane or not? Suppose she dug him up and found nothing, what would she think of me? Blame it, I thought, I might get hunted down and thrown in jail. I’d better lie low and keep quiet and not write at all. The whole thing was awfully tangled now. Trying to make it better, I’d made it a hundred times worse, and I wished to goodness I’d just left it alone, drat the whole business!
They buried him, and we came back to the house, and I went to studying faces again. I couldn’t help it, and I couldn’t rest easy. But nothing came of it. The faces didn’t tell me anything.

That evening the king went visiting around and sweetened everybody up and made himself ever so friendly. He let it be known that his congregation over in England would be worried sick about him, so he had to hurry and settle up the estate right away and head home. He was very sorry to be so rushed, and so was everybody else. They wished he could stay longer, but they said they could see it couldn’t be done. And he said of course he and William would take the girls home with them, and that pleased everybody too, because then the girls would be well provided for and among their own relations. It pleased the girls, too. It tickled them so much that they clean forgot they’d ever had a trouble in the world, and they told him to sell out as quick as he liked, because they’d be ready. Those poor things were so glad and happy that it made my heart ache to see them being fooled and lied to like that, but I couldn’t see any safe way for me to step in and change the tune.

Well, I’ll be blamed if the king didn’t put up the house and the niggers and all the property for auction right away. The sale was set for two days after the funeral, though anybody who wanted to could buy privately beforehand.

So the next day after the funeral, around noon, the girls’ joy got its first jolt. A couple of nigger traders came along, and the king sold them the niggers cheap, for three-day drafts, as they call it, and off they went, the two sons up the river to Memphis and their mother down the river to Orleans. I thought those poor girls and those niggers would break their hearts with grief. They cried all over each other and carried on so much that it almost made me sick to watch. The girls said they’d never dreamed of the family being separated or sold away from the town. I’ll never get it out of my memory, the sight of those poor miserable girls and niggers hanging around each other’s necks and crying. I don’t think I could have stood it, and I’d have had to burst out and tell on our gang, if I hadn’t known the sale wasn’t worth anything and the niggers would be back home in a week or two.

The whole thing caused a big stir in town, too, and quite a few people came right out and said it was a scandal to separate the mother from her children that way. It hurt the frauds a little, but the old fool just bulldozed ahead, no matter what the duke said or did, and I tell you, the duke was powerfully uneasy.
The next day was auction day. At broad daylight in the morning the king and the duke came up to the garret and woke me, and I could tell from their looks that there was trouble. The king said:
“Were you in my room the night before last?”
“No, your majesty.” That was how I always addressed him whenever nobody but our gang was around.
“Were you in there yesterday or last night?”
“No, your majesty.”
“Honor bright, now. No lies.”
“Honor bright, your majesty, it’s the truth. I haven’t set foot near your room since Miss Mary Jane showed it to you and the duke.”
Then the duke said:
“Have you seen anybody else go in there?”
“No, your grace, not that I remember, I believe.”
“Stop and think.”
I studied on it a while and saw my chance. Then I said:
“Well, I saw the niggers go in there several times.”
Both of them gave a little start, looking as if this was the last thing they’d expected, and then as if it was exactly what they’d expected. Then the duke said:
“What, _all_ of them?”
“No, not all at once, anyway. That is, I don’t think I ever saw them all come _out_ at once except one time.”
“Hello! When was that?”
“It was the day of the funeral, in the morning. It wasn’t early, because I overslept. I was just starting down the ladder, and I saw them.”
“Well, go on, _go_ on! What did they do? How did they act?”

“They didn’t do anything. They didn’t act like much of anything, as far as I could see. They tiptoed away, so I could tell easily enough that they’d slipped in there to tidy up your majesty’s room, or something, thinking you were up. They found you _weren’t_ up, so they were hoping to slip out of trouble without waking you, if they hadn’t already woken you.”

“Great guns, _this_ is a fine mess!” said the king, and both of them looked pretty sick and rather silly. They stood there thinking and scratching their heads for a minute, and then the duke let out a kind of raspy little chuckle and said:

“It does beat all how neatly the niggers played their hand. They pretended to be _sorry_ they were leaving this part of the country! And I believed they _were_ sorry, and so did you, and so did everybody. Don’t ever tell _me_ again that a nigger has no talent for the stage. Why, the way they played that scene would fool _anybody_. In my opinion, there’s a fortune in them. If I had money and a theater, I wouldn’t want a better act than that. And here we’ve gone and sold them for a song. Yes, and we’re not even allowed to sing the song yet. Say, where _is_ that song, that draft?”
“In the bank, waiting to be collected. Where _else_ would it be?”
“Well, _that’s_ all right then, thank goodness.”
I said, kind of timid:
“Has something gone wrong?”
The king whirled on me and snapped:

“None of your business! You keep your mouth shut and mind your own affairs, if you’ve got any. As long as you’re in this town, don’t you forget _that_. You hear?” Then he said to the duke, “We’ll just have to swallow it and say nothing. Mum’s the word for _us_.”
As they started down the ladder, the duke chuckled again and said:
“Quick sales _and_ small profits! Yes, sir, that’s a fine way to do business.”
v
The king snarled at him and said:
“I was trying to do what was best by selling them off so quick. If the profits turned out to be none, lacking considerably, and none to carry, is that my fault any more than it’s yours?”
“Well, _they’d_ still be in this house and we _wouldn’t_ be, if my advice had been listened to.”

The king sassed back as much as was safe for him, and then swung around and lit into _me_ again. He gave me a tongue-lashing for not coming and _telling_ him I’d seen the niggers come out of his room acting that way. He said any fool would have _known_ something was up. And then he turned around and cussed out _himself_ for a while, and said it all came of him not sleeping in and taking his natural rest that morning, and he’d be blamed if he’d ever do it again. So they went off grumbling, and I felt dreadfully glad that I’d pinned it all on the niggers and still hadn’t done the niggers any harm by it.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVIII — The Trip to England
paragraphs: Before long it was getting-up time. So I came down the ladder and started for downstairs, but as I came to the girls’ room, the door was open, and I saw Mary Jane sitting by her old hair trunk, which was open. She’d been packing things in it, getting ready to go to England. But now she had stopped, with a folded gown in her lap, and had her face in her hands, crying. I felt awful bad to see it. Anybody would. I went in and said:
“Miss Mary Jane, you hate to see people in trouble, and so do _I_, mostly. Tell me what’s wrong.”

So she did. And it was about the niggers. I’d just expected it. She said the lovely trip to England was nearly spoiled for her. She didn’t know _how_ she was ever going to be happy there, knowing that the mother and the children were never going to see each other again. And then she burst out crying harder than ever, threw up her hands, and said:
“Oh, dear, dear, to think they’re never _ever_ going to see each other again!”
“But they _will_, and inside of two weeks, and I _know_ it!” I said.
Laws, the words were out before I had time to think! And before I could move an inch, she flung her arms around my neck and begged me to say it _again_, say it _again_, say it _again!_

I saw I’d spoken too fast and said too much, and I was in a tight spot. I asked her to let me think a minute, and she sat there, very impatient and excited and pretty, but looking kind of happy and relieved, like a person who’s just had a tooth pulled. So I set about studying it out. I said to myself, I reckon a body who up and tells the truth when he’s in a tight place is taking an awful lot of risks, though I haven’t had any experience and can’t say for certain. But it looks that way to me, anyhow. And yet here’s a case where I’m blessed if the truth doesn’t look better to me, and actually _safer_, than a lie. I must put that away in my mind and think it over some other time, it’s so strange and out of the ordinary. I never saw anything like it. Well, at last I said to myself, I’m going to take the chance. I’ll up and tell the truth this time, though it does seem a lot like sitting down on a keg of gunpowder and lighting it just to see where you’ll land. Then I said:
“Miss Mary Jane, is there somewhere a short way outside town where you could stay for three or four days?”
“Yes, Mr. Lothrop’s. Why?”

“Never mind why yet. Suppose I explain how I know the niggers will see each other again inside of two weeks, right here in this house, and _prove_ it to you. Will you go to Mr. Lothrop’s and stay four days?”
“Four days!” she said. “I’ll stay a year!”

“All right,” I said. “All I want from you is your word. I’d rather have it than another man’s kiss-the-Bible oath.” She smiled and blushed very sweetly, and I said, “If you don’t mind, I’ll shut the door and bolt it.”
Then I went back and sat down again, and said:

“Don’t you holler. Just sit still and take it like a man. I’ve got to tell you the truth, and you’ll want to brace yourself, Miss Mary, because it’s a bad kind and it’s going to be hard to take, but there’s no help for it. These uncles of yours aren’t your uncles at all. They’re a couple of frauds, regular deadbeats. There, now we’re over the worst of it. You can stand the rest fairly easy.”

It jolted her something awful, of course, but I was over the shallow water now, so I kept right on, with her eyes blazing higher and higher all the time. I told her every blessed thing, from where we first ran into that young fool heading for the steamboat, clear through to where she threw herself on the king’s chest at the front door and he kissed her sixteen or seventeen times. Then up she jumped, with her face on fire like a sunset, and said:
“The brute! Come on, don’t waste a minute, not a _second_. We’ll have them tarred and feathered and thrown in the river!”
I said:
“Sure thing. But do you mean that before you go to Mr. Lothrop’s, or—”

“Oh,” she said, “what am I _thinking_ about!” And she sat right down again. “Don’t mind what I said, please don’t. You _won’t_, now, _will_ you?” She laid her silky hand on mine in such a way that I said I would die first. “I never thought, I was so stirred up,” she said. “Now go on, and I won’t do that anymore. You tell me what to do, and whatever you say, I’ll do it.”

“Well,” I said, “those two frauds are a rough gang, and I’m fixed so that I have to travel with them a while longer, whether I want to or not. I’d rather not tell you why. If you were to blow the whistle on them, this town would get me out of their claws and _I’d_ be all right, but there’s another person you don’t know about who’d be in big trouble. Well, we have to save _him_, don’t we? Of course. Well, then, we won’t blow the whistle on them.”

Saying those words put a good idea in my head. I saw how maybe I could get Jim and me rid of the frauds. I could get them jailed here, and then we’d leave. But I didn’t want to run the raft in the daytime with nobody aboard to answer questions but me, so I didn’t want the plan to start working until pretty late tonight. I said:
“Miss Mary Jane, here’s a plan, and it means you won’t be stuck at Mr. Lothrop’s very long, either. What’s the distance?”
“Just under four miles—straight out in the country, back that way.”

“Good, that’ll do. Now you head out there and lie low until nine or half-past tonight, and then get them to bring you home again—tell them you thought of something. If you’re back here before eleven, put a candle in this window. If I haven’t shown up, wait until eleven, and _then_ if I still haven’t shown up, it means I’m gone, out of the way, and safe. Then you come out and spread the news around, and get these frauds thrown in jail.”
“All right,” she says, “I’ll do it.”
“And if it happens that I don’t get away, and get picked up along with them, you have to stand up and say I told you the whole business ahead of time, and you have to back me up as much as you can.”
“Back you up! Of course I will. They won’t lay a finger on you!” she says, and I could see her nostrils flare and her eyes flash as she said it.

“If I get away, I won’t be here,” I says, “to prove these scoundrels aren’t your uncles, and I couldn’t do it if I _was_ here. I could swear they were crooks and loafers, that’s all, though that counts for something. Well, there are others who can prove it better than I can, and nobody’s going to doubt them as fast as they’d doubt me. I’ll tell you how to find them. Give me a pencil and a piece of paper. There—‘_Royal Nonesuch, Bricksville_.’ Put it away and don’t lose it. When the court wants to find out something about these two, have them send to Bricksville and say they’ve got the men who played the Royal Nonesuch, and ask for some witnesses—why, you’ll have that whole town down here before you can hardly blink, Miss Mary. And they’ll come boiling down, too.”
I figured we had everything pretty well settled now. So I says:

“Just let the auction go right ahead, and don’t worry. Nobody has to pay for what they buy until a whole day after the auction, since it was announced so quickly, and those two aren’t leaving town until they get that money. The way we’ve fixed it, the sale won’t count, and they won’t _get_ any money. It’s just like what happened with the niggers—that wasn’t a real sale, and the niggers will be back before long. Why, they can’t even collect the money for the _niggers_ yet—they’re in the worst kind of trouble, Miss Mary.”
“All right,” she says. “I’ll go down and eat breakfast first, and after that I’ll set off for Mr. Lothrop’s.”
“No, _that_ isn’t the way to do it, Miss Mary Jane,” I says, “not by any means. Go _before_ breakfast.”
“Why?”
“What did you think I wanted you to go for in the first place, Miss Mary?”
“Well, I never thought about it—and now that I do, I don’t know. What was it?”

“Why, it’s because you aren’t one of these poker-faced people. I couldn’t ask for a better book than your face. Anybody can sit down and read it as easy as big print. Do you think you could face your uncles when they come to kiss you good morning, and never—”
“Stop, stop, that’s enough! Yes, I’ll leave before breakfast—I’ll be glad to. And leave my sisters with them?”

“Yes; don’t worry about them. They’ll have to put up with it a while longer. They might get suspicious if all of you went. I don’t want you to see them, or your sisters, or anybody in this town. If a neighbor asked how your uncles were this morning, your face would give something away. No, you go right ahead, Miss Mary Jane, and I’ll handle all of them. I’ll tell Miss Susan to give your love to your uncles and say you’ve gone away for a few hours to get some rest and a change of scene, or to see a friend, and that you’ll be back tonight or early in the morning.”
“Saying I’ve gone to visit a friend is fine, but I won’t send my love to those two.”

“Well, then, it won’t be.” It was well enough to tell _her_ so—no harm in it. It was a small thing and no trouble, and it’s the small things that make life smoother for people, down here below. It would ease Mary Jane’s mind, and it wouldn’t cost a cent. Then I says: “There’s one more thing—that bag of money.”
“Well, they have it, and I feel like a fool when I think of _how_ they got hold of it.”
“No, you’re wrong there. They haven’t got it.”
“Why, who has it?”

“I wish I could say, but I can’t. I _had_ it, since I stole it from them, and I stole it to hand over to you. I know where I hid it, but I’m afraid it’s gone from there now. I’m terribly sorry, Miss Mary Jane, as sorry as a person can be. I did the best I could, honestly. I almost got caught, and I had to stuff it into the first spot I came across and run—and it was a bad spot.”
“Oh, don’t blame yourself—that’s a shame, and I won’t let you. There was nothing you could do; it wasn’t your fault. Where did you hide it?”

I didn’t want to get her thinking about her troubles again, and I couldn’t bring myself to say what would make her picture that corpse lying in the coffin with the bag of money on his stomach. So for a minute I said nothing; then I says:
“I’d rather not _say_ where I put it, Miss Mary Jane, if you’ll excuse me. But I’ll write it on a scrap of paper, and you can read it while you’re riding to Mr. Lothrop’s, if you like. Will that do?”
“Oh, yes.”
So I wrote: “I put it in the coffin. It was there when you sat crying beside it, deep in the night. I was hiding behind the door, and my heart ached for you, Miss Mary Jane.”

It made my eyes water a little to remember her crying there all alone in the night, with those devils lying right under her own roof, shaming her and robbing her. And when I folded the paper and gave it to her, I saw tears come into her eyes, too. She shook my hand hard, and says:

“_Good_-bye. I’ll do everything exactly the way you said. And even if I never see you again, I won’t forget you, and I’ll think about you many and many a time, and I’ll _pray_ for you, too!”—and then she was gone.

Pray for me! I figured if she really knew me, she’d pick a job more her own size. But I bet she did it, all the same—she was just that kind. She had the nerve to pray for Judas if she took the notion; she never backed down from anything, I’d say. Say what you like, but in my opinion she had more spunk than any girl I ever saw; in my opinion she was just full of spunk. It sounds like flattery, but it isn’t. And when it comes to beauty—and goodness, too—she beats them all. I haven’t seen her since the moment I watched her go out of that door. No, I haven’t seen her since, but I reckon I’ve thought of her many and many a million times, and of her saying she would pray for me. And if I’d ever thought it would do her any good for me to pray for _her_, I’ll be darned if I wouldn’t have done it or burst trying.
Well, Mary Jane slipped out the back way, I guess, because nobody saw her go. When I ran into Susan and the hare-lip, I says:
“What’s the name of those people across the river that you all go to see sometimes?”
They says:
“There are several, but mostly it’s the Proctors.”
“That’s it,” I says. “It had slipped my mind. Well, Miss Mary Jane asked me to tell you she’s rushed over there in a great hurry—somebody in that family is sick.”
“Which one?”
“I don’t know; at least, I sort of forget. But I think it’s—”
“Good heavens, I hope it isn’t _Hanner?_”
“I’m sorry to say it,” I says, “but Hanner’s the very one.”
“Good gracious, and she was perfectly well just last week! Is it serious?”
“There’s no word for how bad. They sat up with her all night, Miss Mary Jane said, and they don’t think she’ll last many hours.”
“Just think of that! What’s the matter with her?”
I couldn’t think of anything sensible right off the bat like that, so I says:
“Mumps.”
“Mumps, my foot! Nobody sits up with people who have the mumps.”
“They don’t, do they? You can bet they do with _these_ mumps. These mumps are something else. It’s a brand-new kind, Miss Mary Jane said.”
“How is it a new kind?”
“Because it’s mixed up with other things.”
“What other things?”
“Well, measles, and whooping cough, and erysipelas, and consumption, and yellow jaundice, and brain fever, and I don’t know what all.”
“Good land! And they call that the _mumps?_”
“That’s what Miss Mary Jane said.”
“Well, what in the world do they call it the _mumps_ for?”
“Because it _is_ the mumps, that’s why. That’s what it starts with.”

“Well, that doesn’t make any sense. A person might stub his toe, and take poison, and fall down the well, and break his neck, and bust his brains out, and somebody comes along and asks what killed him, and some numskull up and says, ‘Why, he stubbed his _toe_.’ Would there be any sense in that? _No_. And there’s no sense in _this_, either. Is it catching?”

“Is it _catching?_ Why, what a thing to say. Is a _harrow_ catching—in the dark? If you don’t get snagged on one tooth, you’re bound to on another, aren’t you? And you can’t get away from that tooth without dragging the whole harrow along, can you? Well, this kind of mumps is a kind of harrow, you might say—and it’s no slouch of a harrow, either, once you get it hooked on good.”
“Well, it’s awful, _I_ think,” says the hare-lip. “I’ll go to Uncle Harvey and—”
“Oh, sure,” I says, “I _would_. Of _course_ I would. I wouldn’t lose any time.”
“Well, why wouldn’t you?”

“Think it over for a moment and you may see why. Your uncles have to hurry back to England, don’t they? And would they be so mean as to sail off and make you travel all that way alone? _You_ know they’d wait for you. That much is clear. Your uncle Harvey’s a preacher, right? Fine. Now, would a _preacher_ lie to a steamboat clerk? Would he lie to a _ship clerk?_—just to get Miss Mary Jane on board? You know he wouldn’t. So what _will_ he do? He’ll say, ‘It’s a great pity, but my church business will have to manage as best it can, since my niece has been exposed to the dreadful pluribus-unum mumps, and it’s my bounden duty to stay right here and wait the three months it takes to find out whether she’s caught it.’ But never mind, if you really think it’s best to tell your uncle Harvey—”
“Shucks, and sit around here wasting time when we could all be having a fine time in England while we waited to find out whether Mary Jane has it or not? Why, you talk like a fool.”
“Well, still, maybe you ought to tell a few of the neighbors.”
“Would you listen to that. You’re the dumbest person alive. Can’t you _see_ that _they’d_ go and spread it? The only way is to tell nobody at _all_.”
“Well, maybe you’re right—yes, I think you _are_ right.”
“Still, I guess we should let Uncle Harvey know she’s gone out for a little while, so he won’t fret about her?”

“Yes, Miss Mary Jane wanted you to. She says, ‘Give Uncle Harvey and William my love and a kiss, and tell them I’ve gone across the river to see Mr.’—Mr.—what _is_ the name of that rich family your uncle Peter thought so highly of?—the one that—”
“Why, you must mean the Apthorps, mustn’t you?”

“Of course. Confound those names, a person can never keep them in mind, half the time. Yes, she said to tell them she’s gone to ask the Apthorps to be sure to come to the auction and buy this house, since she figured her uncle Peter would sooner see them have it than anyone. She’ll stay with them until they promise to come, and then, if she isn’t worn out, she’ll come home; if she is, she’ll be back in the morning regardless. She said not to mention the Proctors at all, just the Apthorps—which will be perfectly true, because she _is_ going there to talk about them buying the house. I know, because she told me herself.”
“Fine,” they said, and hurried off to find their uncles, to deliver the love and the kisses and the message.

Everything was fine now. The girls wouldn’t say anything, because they wanted to go to England; and the king and the duke would rather have Mary Jane off working for the auction than within reach of Doctor Robinson. I felt very good. I figured I’d done it pretty neatly—I reckoned Tom Sawyer couldn’t have done it any neater himself. Of course he would have thrown more style into it, but I can’t do that very handily, not having been raised to it.

Well, they held the auction in the public square, toward the end of the afternoon, and it dragged on and on. The old man was on hand, looking as sanctimonious as ever, up there beside the auctioneer, chipping in a little Scripture now and then, or some goody-goody saying. The duke was going around making sad cooing noises for sympathy all he knew how, and generally spreading himself.

But after a while the thing dragged to an end, and everything was sold—everything but a small, worthless lot in the graveyard. So they had to get rid of _that_ too—I never saw such a giraffe as the king for wanting to swallow _everything_. Well, while they were at it, a steamboat landed, and in about two minutes up came a crowd whooping and yelling and laughing and carrying on, and singing out:
“_Here’s_ your rival outfit! Here are two sets of heirs to old Peter Wilks—pay your money and take your pick!”

chapters.title: Chapter XXIX — Contested Relationship
paragraphs: They were bringing along a very nice-looking old gentleman, and a nice-looking younger one with his right arm in a sling. And, my goodness, how the people yelled and laughed, and kept it up. But I didn’t see any joke in it, and I figured it would be hard for the duke and the king to see one, either. I expected them to turn pale. But no, not a bit of pale did _they_ turn. The duke never let on that he suspected what was up, but just went around cooing, happy and satisfied, like a jug gurgling out buttermilk. As for the king, he just gazed and gazed sorrowfully at the newcomers, as if it gave him a stomach-ache in his very heart to think there could be such frauds and rascals in the world. Oh, he did it admirably. Lots of the leading people gathered around the king, to let him see they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely puzzled. Pretty soon he began to speak, and I could tell right away that he talked like an Englishman—not the king’s way, though the king’s _was_ pretty good for an imitation. I can’t give the old gentleman’s words, and I can’t imitate him, but he turned around to the crowd and says, about like this:

“This is a surprise I wasn’t expecting, and I’ll admit, plain and honest, that I’m not well prepared to meet it or answer it. My brother and I have had misfortunes. He’s broken his arm, and our baggage was put off at a town up the river last night, by mistake, in the middle of the night. I am Peter Wilks’s brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can’t hear or speak—and can’t even make signs worth much, now that he has only one hand to make them with. We are who we say we are, and in a day or two, when I get the baggage back, I can prove it. Until then I won’t say another word, but will go to the hotel and wait.”
So he and the new dummy started off, and the king laughed and blurted out:

“Broke his arm—_very_ likely, _isn’t_ it?—and mighty convenient, too, for a fraud who has to make signs and never learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s _very_ good!—and very clever—under the _circumstances!_”

So he laughed again, and so did everybody else, except three or four, or maybe half a dozen. One of these was the doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman with an old-fashioned carpet-bag, made of carpet cloth, who had just stepped off the steamboat and was talking to the doctor in a low voice, glancing at the king now and then and nodding. That was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville. Another was a big, rough, husky fellow who had walked up and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now. When the king finished, this husky man spoke up:
“Say, look here. If you’re Harvey Wilks, when did you get to this town?”
“The day before the funeral, friend,” says the king.
“But what time of day?”
“In the evenin’—’bout an hour or two before sundown.”
“_How_ did you come?”
“I came down on the Susan Powell from Cincinnati.”
“Well, then, how did you end up at the Point in the _mornin_’—in a canoe?”
“I wasn’t up at the Point in the mornin’.”
“That’s a lie.”
Several men leaped in front of him and begged him not to speak like that to an old man, and a preacher at that.

“Preacher be hanged! The man’s a fraud and a liar. He was at the Point that mornin’. I live up there, don’t I? I was there, and so was he, and I _saw_ him. He showed up in a canoe with Tim Collins and a boy.”
The doctor spoke up:
“Hines, would you recognize that boy if he stood in front of you?”
“I reckon I would, though I’m not sure. Why, there he is now. I’d know him easy.”
He was pointing at me. The doctor said:

“Neighbors, I don’t know whether the new pair are frauds or not, but if _these_ two aren’t frauds, then I’m an idiot, that’s all. I think it’s our duty to make sure they don’t get away from here until we’ve looked into this. Come along, Hines, and the rest of you too. We’ll take these fellows to the tavern and confront them with the other pair, and I reckon we’ll find out _something_ before we’re through.”
The crowd loved it, though maybe the king’s friends didn’t, and off we all went. It was about sundown. The doctor led me along by the hand. He was kind enough, but he never let _go_ of my hand.
We all crowded into a big room at the hotel, lit some candles, and brought in the new pair. First the doctor said:

“I’d hate to be too rough on these two men, but _I_ say they’re frauds, and they could have partners we’ve never heard of. If so, won’t those partners run off with the bag of gold Peter Wilks left behind? That’s quite possible. If these men are honest, they won’t mind sending for the money and letting us keep it safe until they’ve cleared themselves—am I right?”
Everyone agreed. So I figured they had our gang cornered right from the start. But the king only put on a sorrowful face and said:

“Gentlemen, I wish the money was there, for I have no wish to stand in the way of a fair, open, out-and-out investigation of this miserable business. But, alas, the money ain’t there. You can send and see, if you want to.”
“Where is it, then?”

“Well, when my niece gave it to me to keep for her, I took it and hid it inside the straw mattress of my bed. I didn’t want to put it in a bank for the few days we’d be here, and I thought the bed was a safe place, us not bein’ used to niggers and supposin’ them honest, like servants in England. The niggers stole it the very next mornin’, after I’d gone downstairs, and when I sold ’em I hadn’t missed the money yet, so they got clean away with it. My servant here can tell you about it, gentlemen.”

The doctor and several others said “Shucks!” and I could see nobody quite believed him. One man asked me if I saw the niggers steal it. I said no, but I saw them sneaking out of the room and hurrying away, and I never thought anything of it, except that I figured they were afraid they’d woken up my master and were trying to get away before he made trouble for them. That was all they asked me. Then the doctor whirled on me and said:
“Are _you_ English, too?”
I said yes, and he and some others laughed and said, “Nonsense!”

Well, then they dove into the general investigation, and there we were, hour after hour, and nobody said a word about supper or even seemed to think of it. They kept at it and kept at it, and it _was_ the most tangled-up business you ever saw. They made the king tell his story, and they made the old gentleman tell his. Anybody but a pack of prejudiced fools would have _seen_ that the old gentleman was telling the truth and the other one was lying. After a while they called me up to tell what I knew. The king gave me a sideways look out of the corner of his eye, so I knew well enough to talk on his side. I started telling about Sheffield, and how we lived there, and all about the English Wilkses, and so on. But I hadn’t gotten very far before the doctor began to laugh, and Levi Bell, the lawyer, said:
“Sit down, my boy. I wouldn’t strain myself if I were you. I reckon you’re not used to lying. It doesn’t come easily to you. What you need is practice. You do it pretty awkwardly.”
I didn’t give a hang for the praise, but I was glad to be excused all the same.
The doctor started to say something, then turned and said:
“If you had been in town at the start, Levi Bell—” The king broke in and held out his hand, saying:
“Why, is this my poor dead brother’s old friend, the one he wrote about so often?”

The lawyer and the king shook hands, and the lawyer smiled and looked pleased. They talked together for a while, then stepped off to one side and talked in low voices. At last the lawyer spoke up and said:
“That’ll settle it. I’ll take the order and send it along with your brother’s, and then they’ll know it’s all right.”

So they got some paper and a pen, and the king sat down, twisted his head to one side, chewed his tongue, and scrawled something. Then they handed the pen to the duke—and for the first time the duke looked sick. But he took the pen and wrote. Then the lawyer turned to the new old gentleman and said:
“Now you and your brother, sir, each write a line or two and put your names to it.”
The old gentleman wrote, but not a soul could make it out. The lawyer looked thoroughly astonished and said:

“Well, that beats _me_”—and he pulled a bundle of old letters out of his pocket and looked them over, then looked at the old man’s writing, and then at _them_ again. Then he said: “These old letters are from Harvey Wilks. And here are _these_ two handwritings, and anybody can see _they_ didn’t write them” (the king and the duke looked fooled and foolish, I tell you, to see how the lawyer had taken them in), “and here is _this_ old gentleman’s handwriting, and anybody can tell easily enough _he_ didn’t write them—the fact is, the scratches he makes aren’t really _writing_ at all. Now, here are some letters from—”
The new old gentleman said:
“If you please, let me explain. Nobody can read my handwriting except my brother there, so he does my copying for me. It’s _his_ hand you have there, not mine.”
“_Well!_” said the lawyer. “This _is_ a state of affairs. I have some of William’s letters, too, so if you’ll get him to write a line or so, we can com—”
“He _can’t_ write with his left hand,” the old gentleman answered. “With his right, you’d find he wrote his own letters and mine as well. Compare them both, please—one hand wrote them all.”
The lawyer did so, and said:

“I believe that’s right—and if it isn’t, there’s a much stronger resemblance than I had noticed before, anyway. Well, well, well! I thought we were right on the track of an answer, but it’s partly gone to pieces. Still, _one_ thing is proved—_these_ two aren’t Wilkses, either of them”—and he wagged his head toward the king and the duke.

Well, what do you think? That pigheaded old fool _still_ wouldn’t give in! He really wouldn’t. He said it wasn’t a fair test. He said his brother William was the worst joker in the world, and hadn’t even _tried_ to write—he could see William was going to play one of his jokes the minute he put pen to paper. And so he warmed up and went on warbling and warbling until he was actually starting to believe what he was saying _himself_. But pretty soon the new gentleman broke in and said:
“Something has occurred to me. Is anyone here who helped lay out my br—who helped prepare the late Peter Wilks for his burial?”
“Yes,” says somebody. “Ab Turner and I did. We’re both here.”
Then the old man turned toward the king and said:
“Maybe this gentleman can say what was tattooed across his chest?”

Blamed if the king didn’t have to brace himself mighty quick, or he’d have caved in like a riverbank the current has cut out from under, it hit him so suddenly. And mind you, it was the kind of blow that would make almost _anybody_ cave in, to get hit with something so solid without any warning, because how was _he_ supposed to know what was tattooed on the man? He turned a little white; he couldn’t help it. It was mighty still in there, with everybody leaning forward a little and staring at him. I said to myself, _Now_ he’ll throw in the towel—there’s no more use. Well, did he? You can hardly believe it, but he didn’t. I reckon he figured he’d keep the thing going until he wore those people out, so they’d thin out, and he and the duke could break loose and get away. Anyway, he sat there, and pretty soon he began to smile and said:

“Mf! That’s a _very_ hard question, _ain’t_ it! _Yes_, sir, I can say what’s tattooed on his chest. A small, thin, blue arrow, that’s all. Unless you look close, you won’t see it. _Now_ what do you say, hey?”
Well, _I_ never saw anything like that old blister for plain, out-and-out nerve.
The new old gentleman turned briskly to Ab Turner and his partner, his eyes lit up as if he figured he’d caught the king _this_ time, and said:
“There! You heard him. Was any such mark on Peter Wilks’s chest?”
Both of them spoke up and said:
“We didn’t see any such mark.”

“Good!” the old gentleman said. “What you _did_ see on his chest was a small, faint P, then a B (an initial he gave up when he was young), then a W, with dashes in between, like so: P—B—W”—and he drew them that way on a scrap of paper. “Come now, isn’t that what you saw?”
Both of them spoke up again and said:
“No, we _didn’t_. We never saw any marks at all.”
Well, the whole room _was_ in an uproar now, and they hollered:

“The whole _bilin_’ of ’em are frauds! Let’s duck ’em! Let’s drown ’em! Let’s ride ’em out on a rail!” and everybody was whooping at once, and there was a rattling uproar. But the lawyer jumped up on the table and yelled:
“Gentlemen—gentle_men!_ Listen to me for one word—just a _single_ word—if you PLEASE! There’s still one way. Let’s go dig up the corpse and see for ourselves.”
That won them over.
“Hooray!” they all shouted and were starting right off, but the lawyer and the doctor called out:
“Hold on, hold on! Grab all four of these men and the boy, and bring _them_ along, too!”
“We’ll do it!” they all shouted. “And if we don’t find those marks, we’ll lynch the whole gang!”

I _was_ scared now, I can tell you. But there was no escaping. They gripped every one of us and marched us off to the graveyard, a mile and a half down the river, with the whole town trailing behind, since we made plenty of noise and it was only nine at night.
As we went past our house, I wished I hadn’t sent Mary Jane out of town, because now if I could have tipped her the wink, she’d have come running to save me and expose our frauds.

Well, we swarmed down the river road, carrying on like wildcats, and to make it scarier the sky was darkening, the lightning was starting to wink and flicker, and the wind was shivering through the leaves. This was the worst trouble and the most dangerous I’d ever been in, and I was kind of stunned. Everything was going so differently from what I had planned. Instead of being fixed so I could take my own time if I wanted, see all the fun, and have Mary Jane at my back to save me and set me free when the pinch came, here was nothing in the world between me and sudden death except those tattoo marks. If they didn’t find them—

I couldn’t stand to think about it, yet I couldn’t think about anything else. It kept getting darker, a fine time to slip away from the crowd, but that big husky, Hines, held my wrist, and you might as well try to slip away from Goliath. He hauled me along, he was so worked up, and I had to run to keep up with him.

When they got there, they swarmed into the graveyard and flooded over it like a river overflowing its banks. When they reached the grave, they found they had about a hundred times as many shovels as they needed, but nobody had thought to bring a lantern. They went ahead and started digging by the flicker of the lightning anyway, and sent a man to the nearest house, half a mile off, to borrow one.

So they dug and dug like crazy, and it got awfully dark, and the rain started, and the wind swished and swooshed along, and the lightning came faster and faster, and the thunder boomed. But those people took no notice of any of it, they were so wrapped up in this business. One minute you could see everything, every face in that big crowd and the shovelfuls of dirt sailing up out of the grave, and the next second the dark wiped it all out and you couldn’t see anything at all.

At last they got the coffin out and started unscrewing the lid, and then there was such crowding and shouldering and shoving to squeeze in and get a look that you never saw the like, and in the dark it was terrible. Hines hurt my wrist something awful, pulling and yanking on it, and I reckon he forgot I even existed, he was so worked up and out of breath.
All at once the lightning poured down a whole flood of white glare, and somebody yelled out:
“Good Lord, look! The bag of gold is right there on his chest!”
Hines whooped like everybody else, dropped my wrist, and gave a great heave to force his way in for a look. As for how fast I bolted and scrambled for the road in the dark, nobody can tell you.

I had the road all to myself, and I fairly flew. Well, I had it to myself except for the thick darkness, the flashes every now and then, the drumming of the rain, the thrashing of the wind and the cracking of the thunder; and as sure as you’re born, I sure did make time!

When I got to town I saw there wasn’t a soul out in the storm, so I didn’t bother with back streets but pounded straight down the main one. As I came up toward our house, I aimed my eye at it and kept it there. No light; the house was all dark, which made me feel sorry and let down, though I couldn’t say why. But then, just as I was sailing past, _flash_, the light came on in Mary Jane’s window! My heart swelled up so sudden I thought it would burst; and in the same second the house and everything was behind me in the dark, and never again would it be ahead of me in this world. She _was_ the best girl I ever saw, and she had the most nerve.

As soon as I was far enough above the town to make out the towhead, I began watching sharp for a boat to borrow, and the first time the lightning showed me one that wasn’t chained, I grabbed it and pushed off. It was a canoe, tied with nothing but a rope. The towhead was an awfully long way off, out in the middle of the river, but I didn’t waste any time; and by the time I reached the raft I was so worn out that I would have lain down to rest and gasp if I could have afforded it. But I couldn’t. As I jumped aboard I shouted:
“Get out here, Jim, and set her loose! Glory be to goodness, we’re rid of them!”

Jim jumped up and came at me with both arms stretched wide, he was so full of joy. But when the lightning lit him up, my heart leaped into my mouth and I fell overboard backwards, because I forgot he was made up as old King Lear and a drowned Arab all in one, and it nearly scared the stuffing out of me. But Jim fished me out, and was about to hug me and bless me and all that, he was so glad I was back and we were rid of the king and the duke, but I said:
“Not now! Save it for breakfast, save it for breakfast! Cut her loose and let her drift!”

So in two seconds we were sliding off down the river, and it _did_ feel so good to be free again, all by ourselves on the big river with nobody to bother us. I had to skip around a bit and jump up and click my heels a few times—I couldn’t help it; but around the third click I heard a sound I knew mighty well, and I held my breath and listened and waited. Sure enough, when the next flash burst out over the water, there they came!—pulling hard on their oars and making their skiff fairly hum! It was the king and the duke.
I sank down onto the planks right then and gave up, and I had to fight hard to keep from bawling.

chapters.title: Chapter XXX — The King Went for Him
paragraphs: When they climbed aboard, the king came straight at me, shook me by the collar, and said:
“So ye tried to slip away from us, did ye, ye pup! Sick of our company, are ye?”
I said:
“No, your majesty, we weren’t—_please_ don’t, your majesty!”
“Then talk fast and tell us what ye were thinkin’, or I’ll rattle the insides right out o’ ye!”

“Honest, I’ll tell you everything just the way it happened, your majesty. The man who was holding me was very good to me. He kept saying he had a boy about my size who died last year, and he was sorry to see a boy in such a dangerous fix. And when they were all taken by surprise, finding the gold and rushing at the coffin, he let go of me and whispered, ‘Run for it now, or they’ll hang you, sure!’ and I took off. It didn’t seem any good for _me_ to stay—_I_ couldn’t do anything, and I didn’t want to be hanged if I could get away. So I never stopped running till I found the canoe; and when I got here I told Jim to hurry, or they’d catch me and hang me yet, and I said I was afraid you and the duke weren’t alive anymore, and I was awful sorry, and so was Jim, and he was awful glad when we saw you coming. You can ask Jim if I’m not telling the truth.”
Jim backed me up; the king told him to shut his mouth and sneered, “Oh, sure, that sounds _very_ believable!” He gave me another shake and said he figured he’d drown me. But the duke spoke up:
“Turn the boy loose, you old fool! Would _you_ have acted any different? When you got free, did you go looking for _him_? _I_ don’t recall that you did.”
So the king let go of me and started cursing that town and everybody in it. But the duke said:

“You’d be a whole lot better off giving _yourself_ a good cursing, because you’re the one who has earned it most. From the very start you haven’t done a single thing with any sense in it, except coming out so cool and brazen with that imaginary blue-arrow mark. That _was_ clever—it was downright first-rate; and it’s what saved us. If it hadn’t been for that, they’d have jailed us until those Englishmen’s baggage arrived—and then the penitentiary, you bet! But that trick led them off to the graveyard, and the gold did us an even bigger favor; because if those excited fools hadn’t let go of everything and rushed in for a look, we’d be sleeping in our neckties tonight—neckties guaranteed to _wear_, too—longer than _we’d_ need them.”
They were quiet for a minute, thinking; then the king said, kind of absent-minded:
“Hmph! And we figured the _niggers_ stole it!”
That made me squirm!
“Yes,” said the duke, slow and deliberate and sarcastic, “_we_ did.”
After about half a minute the king drawled out:
“At least, _I_ did.”
The duke said, in the same tone:
“On the contrary, _I_ did.”
The king bristled a little, and said:
“Look here, Bilgewater, what are ye gettin’ at?”
The duke said, pretty briskly:
“Since it comes to that, maybe you’ll let me ask what _you_ were getting at?”
“Bah!” said the king, very sarcastic. “But _I_ don’t know—maybe you were asleep, and didn’t know what you were about.”
Now the duke bristled up, and said:
“Oh, stop this blasted nonsense! Do you take me for a plain fool? You think _I_ don’t know who stuck that money in the coffin?”
“_Oh_, you know, all right! You know because you put it there yourself!”
“That’s a lie!”—and the duke went for him. The king shouted:
“Take your hands off!—let go of my throat!—I take it all back!”
The duke said:
“Well, then, you admit it first. Say that you _did_ stash that money there, planning to ditch me some day, sneak back, dig it up and keep every cent.”
“Hold on one minute, duke. Answer me one question, straight and fair. Say you didn’t put the money there, and I’ll take your word for it and unsay everything I said.”
“Why, you old scoundrel, I did not, and you know it. So there!”
“Well, then, I believe you. But answer me just this one more—now _don’t_ get mad—didn’t you have it in your mind to take the money and hide it?”
The duke didn’t say anything for a little while; then he said:
“Well, I don’t care if I _did_; I didn’t _do_ it, anyway. But you not only had it in mind, you _did_ it.”
“May I never die if I did it, duke, and that’s honest. I won’t say I wasn’t _going_ to do it, because I _was_; but you—I mean somebody—beat me to it.”
“That’s a lie! You did it, and you’ve got to _say_ you did it, or—”
