The king began to gurgle, and then he gasped out:
“Enough!—_I admit it!_”
That was a great relief to hear. I felt a good deal better than I had a minute before. So the duke let go of him and said:

“If you ever deny it again, I’ll drown you. It’s _good_ for you to sit there and blubber like a baby—it’s only right, after the way you’ve acted. I never saw such an old ostrich for wanting to gobble up everything—and me trusting you all the time like you were my own father. You ought to be ashamed of yourself, standing by and hearing it pinned on a lot of poor niggers, and never saying a word for them. It makes me feel ridiculous to think I was fool enough to _believe_ that rubbish. Curse you, I can see now why you were so anxious to make up the deficit—you wanted to get hold of whatever money I’d made from the Nonesuch and one thing and another, and scoop up the _whole lot!_”
The king said, timidly, still sniffling:
“Why, duke, it was you who said to make up the deficit; it wasn’t me.”

“Dry up! I don’t want to hear another word out of you!” said the duke. “And _now_ you see what you _got_ for it. They’ve got all their own money back, and all of _ours_ except a shekel or two _besides_. Go on to bed, and don’t you deficit me any more deficits as long as you live!”

The king crept off to the wigwam and comforted himself with his bottle, and soon the duke got busy with _his_. Within half an hour they were thick as thieves again, and the more they drank, the more affectionate they grew, until they dropped off snoring in each other’s arms. They both got very mellow, but I noticed the king never got so mellow that he forgot to remember not to deny hiding the money-bag again. That put my mind at ease. Of course, once they were snoring, Jim and I had a long chat, and I told him the whole story.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXI — Ominous Plans
paragraphs: For days and days we didn’t dare stop at any town; we kept right on down the river. We were in the South now, in warm weather, and a mighty long way from home. We began to come to trees with Spanish moss on them, hanging down from the branches like long gray beards. It was the first I ever saw it growing, and it made the woods look solemn and gloomy. The frauds figured they were out of danger now, so they started working the villages again.

First they gave a lecture on temperance; but it didn’t bring in enough for the two of them to get drunk on. Then in another village they started a dancing school; but they knew no more about dancing than a kangaroo does, so at their first prance the general public jumped in and pranced them out of town. Another time they tried yellocution, but they hadn’t yellocuted long before the audience got up and gave them a solid good cursing and made them clear out. They tried missionary work, and mesmerizing, and doctoring, and fortune-telling, and a little of everything; but they never seemed to have any luck. So at last they were just about dead broke, and they lay around the raft as she floated along, thinking and thinking and never saying a word, half a day at a time, dreadfully blue and desperate.

And then finally they changed their ways and started huddling together in the wigwam, murmuring low and secretive for two or three hours on end. Jim and I got uneasy, because we didn’t like the look of it. We figured they were scheming some new mischief, worse than any before. We chewed it over and over and finally decided they must be planning to burgle somebody’s house or store, or to start making fake money, or some such thing. That scared us pretty good, and we agreed we would have nothing whatever to do with such business, and that the first real chance we got, we would shake them off and clear out, leaving them behind. Well, early one morning we hid the raft somewhere safe, about two miles below a poor, shabby little village called Pikesville. The king went ashore and told us both to stay out of sight while he walked up to town and sniffed around to learn whether word of the Royal Nonesuch had reached there yet. (“Looking for a house to rob, you _mean_,” I said to myself; “and when you’ve finished robbing it, you’ll come back here and wonder where me and Jim and the raft got to—and wondering is all you’ll get.”) He said that if he wasn’t back by noon, the duke and I could take it that all was well, and we should come on up.

So we stayed where we were. The duke fretted and sweated around and was in a mighty sour mood. He scolded us for everything, and we couldn’t seem to do anything right; he found fault with every little thing. Something was brewing, sure. I was good and glad when midday came and there was no king; at least we’d have a change—and maybe a chance for _the_ change on top of it. So the duke and I went up to the village and hunted around for the king, and after a while we found him in the back room of a little low saloon, very drunk, with a bunch of loafers hounding him for sport, and he cursing and threatening with all his might, and so drunk he couldn’t walk and couldn’t do anything to them. The duke started abusing him as an old fool, and the king started sassing back, and the minute they were well into it, I took off and ran for all I was worth, and flew down the river road like a deer, because I saw our chance; and I made up my mind it would be a long day before they ever saw me and Jim again. I got down there all out of breath but loaded up with joy, and shouted:
“Set her loose, Jim! We’re all right now!”

But nobody answered, and nobody came out of the wigwam. Jim was gone! I let out a yell—then another—then a third; I ran this way and that through the woods, hollering and shrieking, but it did no good. Old Jim was gone. Then I sat down and cried; I couldn’t stop myself. But I couldn’t stay sitting for long. Soon I went out to the road, trying to work out what I ought to do, and came across a boy walking along. I asked whether he’d seen a strange nigger in such-and-such clothes, and he said:
“Yes.”
“Where?” I said.
“Over at Silas Phelps’ place, two miles down from here. He’s a runaway nigger, and they’ve caught him. You looking for him?”

“You bet I haven’t! I ran into him in the woods an hour or two ago, and he said if I yelled he’d cut my liver out. He told me to lie down and stay put, and I did. I’ve been there ever since, too scared to come out.”
“Well,” he says, “you don’t need to be scared anymore, because they’ve caught him. He ran off from down South somewhere.”
“Good thing they caught him.”
“I _reckon_ it is! There’s a two hundred dollar reward on him. It’s like finding money lying in the road.”
“It sure is—and _I_ could have had it, if I’d been big enough. I saw him _first_. Who caught him?”
“Some old fellow, a stranger. He sold his claim on him for forty dollars, because he has to go up the river and can’t wait around. Imagine that! You bet _I’d_ wait, even if it took seven years.”
“Same here, every time,” says I. “But maybe his claim isn’t worth any more than that, if he’ll sell it so cheap. Maybe there’s something crooked about it.”

“But it _is_, though—straight as a string. I saw the handbill myself. It tells all about him, down to the last detail—describes him like a portrait, and names the plantation he came from, below New Or_leans_. No sirree _bob_, there’s no trouble with _that_ deal, you bet. Say, give me a chew of tobacco, will you?”

I didn’t have any, so he left. I went back to the raft and sat down in the wigwam to think. But I couldn’t think of anything. I thought until my head was sore, and I still couldn’t see any way out of the trouble. After this whole long trip, and after everything we’d done for those scoundrels, it had all come to nothing, everything smashed and ruined, because they had the heart to play a trick like that on Jim and make him a slave again for the rest of his life, among strangers, too, for forty dirty dollars.

At one point I told myself it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave back home near his family, since he _had_ to be a slave anyway. So I figured I should write a letter to Tom Sawyer and ask him to tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I soon gave that idea up, for two reasons. She’d be angry and disgusted at his wickedness and ingratitude for running away from her, and she’d sell him straight down the river again. And even if she didn’t, everybody naturally looks down on an ungrateful nigger, and people would make Jim feel it all the time, so he’d feel low and disgraced. And then think of _me!_ It would get around that Huck Finn had helped a nigger to freedom, and if I ever saw anybody from that town again, I’d be ready to drop down and lick his boots for shame. That’s just how it is: a person does something low-down, and then doesn’t want to face the consequences. He thinks that as long as he can hide it, it’s no disgrace. That was exactly my fix. The more I studied on it, the more my conscience ground away at me, and the more wicked and low and miserable I felt. And finally it hit me all at once that here was the plain hand of Providence slapping me in the face, letting me know that somebody up in heaven had been watching my wickedness the whole time, while I was stealing a poor old woman’s nigger who had never done me any harm. Now I was being shown that there’s One who is always on the lookout, and who won’t allow such wretched doings to go just so far and no further. I nearly dropped in my tracks, I was so scared. Well, I did my best to soften it up for myself somehow, by saying I’d been raised wicked and so wasn’t so much to blame. But something inside me kept saying, “There was Sunday school, you could have gone to it, and if you had, they’d have taught you there that people who act the way you’ve been acting about that nigger go to everlasting fire.”

It made me shiver. I about decided to pray, and see whether I could stop being the sort of boy I was and turn into a better one. So I got down on my knees. But no words came. Why not? There was no sense trying to hide it from Him. Nor from _me_, either. I knew very well why. My heart wasn’t right, I wasn’t being square, I was playing double. I was pretending to give up sin, but deep inside I was clinging to the biggest one of all. I was trying to make my mouth _say_ I would do the right and clean thing, and go write to that nigger’s owner and tell her where he was. But way down in me I knew it was a lie, and He knew it. You can’t pray a lie—I found that out.

So there I was, full of trouble, as full as a person can be, with no idea what to do. Then at last an idea came, and I told myself, I’ll go write the letter—and _then_ see whether I can pray. And it was astonishing: right away I felt light as a feather, and all my troubles were gone. So I found a piece of paper and a pencil, and sat down, glad and excited, and wrote:
Miss Watson, your runaway nigger Jim is two miles below Pikesville, where Mr. Phelps has got hold of him. He will hand him over for the reward if you send for him.
_Huck Finn._

I felt good, and washed clean of sin, for the first time in my life, and I knew I could pray now. But I didn’t do it right away. I laid the paper down and sat there thinking—thinking how good it was that all this had happened the way it did, and how close I’d come to being lost and going to hell. And I kept on thinking. And I got to thinking about our trip down the river, and I saw Jim in front of me all the time: in the daytime and the night, sometimes in moonlight, sometimes in storms, with us floating along, talking and singing and laughing. But somehow I couldn’t find any place that would harden me against him, only the other kind. I’d see him standing my watch on top of his own, instead of calling me, so I could keep sleeping. I’d see how glad he was when I came back out of the fog, and when I came to him again in the swamp, up where the feud was, and times like that. He always called me honey, and petted me, and did everything he could think of for me, and was always so good. And finally I came to the time I saved him by telling the men we had smallpox aboard, and how grateful he was, and how he said I was the best friend old Jim ever had in the world, and the _only_ one he has now. And then I happened to look around and see that paper.

It was a tight spot. I picked it up and held it in my hand. I was trembling, because I had to decide, once and for all, between two things, and I knew it. I thought it over for a minute, sort of holding my breath, and then I said to myself:
“All right, then, I’ll _go_ to hell”—and tore it up.

They were awful thoughts and awful words, but they were said. And I let them stay said, and never thought another word about reforming. I shoved the whole business out of my head, and told myself I’d go back to wickedness, which was my line, since I’d been raised to it, and the other wasn’t. And for a start, I would go to work and steal Jim out of slavery again; and if I could think up anything worse, I’d do that too. Because as long as I was in it, and in it for good, I might as well go the whole hog.

Then I started thinking about how to go at it, and turned over a good many ways in my mind, and at last settled on a plan that suited me. So I took note of a wooded island a little way down the river, and as soon as it was good and dark I slipped out with my raft, headed for it, hid the raft there, and turned in. I slept the whole night, got up before daylight, ate my breakfast, put on my store clothes, tied up some other clothes and odds and ends in a bundle, and took the canoe and made for shore. I landed below where I figured Phelps’s place was, hid my bundle in the woods, then filled the canoe with water, loaded rocks into her, and sank her where I could find her again when I wanted her. That was about a quarter of a mile below a little steam sawmill on the bank.

Then I set off up the road, and as I went by the mill I noticed a sign on it that said “Phelps’s Sawmill.” Two or three hundred yards farther along I came to the farmhouses and kept my eyes open, but nobody was around, even though it was full daylight by now. I didn’t mind, though, since I didn’t want to meet anybody yet—I only wanted to look the place over. My plan was to arrive there from the village, not from downriver. So I took a look and kept walking, straight into town. Well, the first man I saw when I got there was the duke. He was pasting up a bill for the Royal Nonesuch—three nights only—just like that other time. _They_ had some nerve, those frauds! I was practically on top of him before I could slip away. He looked astonished, and says:
“Hel-_lo!_ Where did _you_ come from?” Then he says, sort of glad and eager, “Where’s the raft?—did you leave her in a good place?”
I says:
“Why, that’s just what I was going to ask your grace.”
Then he didn’t look so happy, and says:
“What made you think of asking _me?_” he says.

“Well,” I says, “when I saw the king in that grog shop yesterday, I said to myself, we can’t get him home for hours, not till he sobers up. So I went loafing around town to pass the time and wait. A man came up and offered me ten cents to help him row a skiff across the river and back to fetch a sheep, so I went along. But as we were dragging the sheep to the boat, the man left me holding the rope and went around behind to shove him along, and the sheep was too strong for me, jerked loose, and ran, and we went after him. We didn’t have a dog, so we had to chase him all over the countryside until we wore him out. We didn’t catch him until dark. Then we ferried him over, and I started down for the raft. When I got there and saw it was gone, I said to myself, ‘They’ve gotten into trouble and had to leave, and they’ve taken my nigger, who’s the only nigger I have in the world, and now I’m in a strange country with no property left, nor anything else, and no way to make a living.’ So I sat down and cried. I slept in the woods all night. But what _did_ become of the raft, then?—and Jim—poor Jim!”

“Blamed if _I_ know—the raft, I mean. That old fool had made a deal and gotten forty dollars. When we found him in the grog shop, the loafers had been flipping half-dollars against him and had won every cent except what he’d spent on whisky. When I got him home late last night and the raft was gone, we said, ‘That little rascal stole our raft, ditched us, and ran off down the river.’”
“Why would I ditch my own _nigger_?—the only nigger I had in the world, and all the property I had.”

“We never thought of that. The fact is, I guess we’d come to think of him as _our_ nigger. Yes, we did—goodness knows we had trouble enough over him. So when we saw the raft was gone and we were flat broke, there was nothing to do but give the Royal Nonesuch another try. And I’ve been scraping along ever since, dry as a powder horn. Where’s that ten cents? Hand it over.”

I had plenty of money, so I gave him the ten cents, but I begged him to spend it on something to eat and give me some, because it was all the money I had and I hadn’t eaten anything since yesterday. He didn’t say a word. The next minute he whirls on me and says:
“Do you think that nigger would squeal on us? We’d skin him if he did!”
“How can he squeal? Didn’t he run off?”
“No! That old fool sold him and never shared a cent with me, and now the money’s gone.”
“_Sold_ him?” I says, and I started bawling. “Why, he was _my_ nigger, and that was my money! Where is he?—I want my nigger back.”
“Well, you can’t _have_ your nigger, so dry up that blubbering. Listen here—would _you_ dare squeal on us? Blamed if I’d trust you. Why, if you were ever to squeal on us—”
He stopped, but I had never seen the duke look so ugly in the eyes before. I went on whimpering, and says:
“I don’t want to squeal on anybody, and I haven’t got time to, anyhow. I’ve got to go out and find my nigger.”
He looked kind of bothered, and stood there with his bills fluttering on his arm, thinking, with his forehead wrinkled up. At last he says:
“Here’s what I’ll do. We’ve got to stay here three days. Promise me you won’t squeal, and won’t let the nigger squeal either, and I’ll tell you where he is.”
So I promised, and he says:

“A farmer named Silas Ph—” and then he broke off. You see, he’d begun telling me the truth, but when he stopped like that and started studying and thinking again, I guessed he’d changed his mind. And he had. He didn’t trust me. He wanted to be sure I was out of the way for all three days. So after a bit he says:
“The man who bought him is Abram Foster—Abram G. Foster—and he lives forty miles from here, out in the country on the Lafayette road.”
“All right,” I says, “I can do it on foot in three days. I’ll leave this very afternoon.”

“No, you won’t, you’ll start _now;_ and don’t you waste any time about it, either, or do any blabbing on the way. Just keep a tight tongue in your head and keep moving, and then you won’t get into trouble with _us_, understand?”
That was the order I wanted, and it was the one I’d been playing for. I wanted to be left free to carry out my plans.

“So clear out,” he says. “And you can tell Mr. Foster whatever you like. Maybe you can get him to believe Jim _is_ your nigger—some idiots don’t require papers—at least I’ve heard there are such people down South here. And when you tell him the handbill and the reward are fake, maybe he’ll believe you when you explain why we had them printed. Go on now, and tell him anything you want to. But mind you don’t flap your jaw _between_ here and there.”

So I took off and headed for the back country. I didn’t look behind me, but I had a feeling he was watching me go. I knew I could wear him out, though. I walked a good mile straight out into the country before I stopped. Then I circled back through the woods toward the Phelps place. I figured I’d better get started on my plan right away, no fooling around, because I wanted to keep Jim quiet until those fellows could clear out. I didn’t want any trouble with their kind. I’d seen all I ever wanted to see of them, and I wanted to be completely rid of them.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXII — Still and Sunday-like
paragraphs: When I got there, everything was still and Sunday-like, hot and sunny. The field hands had gone off to the fields, and the air was full of the faint droning of bugs and flies, the kind of sound that makes the place feel so lonesome, as if everybody’s dead and gone. And if a breeze slips by and shivers the leaves, it makes you feel sad, because it seems like spirits whispering, spirits that have been dead ever so many years, and you always think they’re talking about _you_. Mostly it makes a person wish _he_ was dead too, and finished with it all.

Phelps’ place was one of those little one-horse cotton plantations, and they all look alike. A rail fence ran around a two-acre yard. There was a stile made of logs sawed off and stood on end in steps, like barrels of different heights, for climbing over the fence, and for the women to stand on when they’re about to jump onto a horse. There were a few sickly patches of grass in the big yard, but mostly it was bare and smooth, like an old hat with the fuzz rubbed off. There was a big double log house for the white folks, built of hewed logs with the cracks stuffed with mud or mortar, and those mud stripes had been whitewashed at some time or other. There was a round-log kitchen, joined to the house by a wide, open passage with a roof over it. Behind the kitchen stood a log smokehouse. On the other side of the smokehouse were three little log nigger-cabins in a row, and one little hut all by itself, way down against the back fence. Some outbuildings sat a little way down on the other side. Next to the little hut were an ash-hopper and a big kettle for boiling soap. By the kitchen door was a bench with a bucket of water and a gourd. A hound was asleep there in the sun, and more hounds were asleep all around. About three shade trees stood far off in one corner, and in one spot by the fence there were some currant and gooseberry bushes. Outside the fence were a garden and a watermelon patch. Then the cotton fields began, and past the fields, the woods.

I went around and climbed over the back stile by the ash-hopper, and started toward the kitchen. When I’d gone a little way I heard the dull hum of a spinning wheel, rising in a wail and then sinking away again. Right then I knew for certain that I wished I was dead, because that _is_ the loneliest sound in the whole world.

I kept right on walking. I had no particular plan. I was just trusting Providence to put the right words in my mouth when the time came, because I’d noticed that Providence always did put the right words in my mouth as long as I left it alone.

When I was about halfway there, first one hound and then another got up and came at me. Of course I stopped, faced them, and stood still. And what a racket they made! In about fifteen seconds I was the hub of a wheel, you might say, with spokes made of dogs. Fifteen of them were packed in a circle around me, necks and noses stretched up toward me, barking and howling, and more were on their way. You could see them sailing over fences and around corners from everywhere.

A nigger woman came tearing out of the kitchen with a rolling pin in her hand, hollering, “Get away, _you_ Tige! You Spot! Get away, sah!” She gave first one and then another a whack and sent them yelping off, and the rest followed. A moment later half of them came back, wagging their tails around me and making friends. There’s no harm in a hound, anyway.

Behind the woman came a little nigger girl and two little nigger boys, wearing nothing but tow-linen shirts. They hung on to their mother’s dress and peeped out at me from behind her, shy, the way they always do. And then the white woman came running from the house, about forty-five or fifty years old, bareheaded, with her spinning stick in her hand. Her little white children came behind her, acting just the way the little niggers were. She was smiling so hard she could barely stand, and she said:
“It’s _you_, at last!—_isn’t_ it?”
“Yes’m” was out of my mouth before I’d thought.

She grabbed me and hugged me tight. Then she took both my hands and shook and shook them, and the tears welled up in her eyes and ran over. She couldn’t seem to hug and shake me enough, and she kept saying, “You don’t look as much like your mother as I expected you would, but land sakes, I don’t care about that, I’m _so_ glad to see you! Dear, dear, I could just eat you up! Children, it’s your cousin Tom! Say hello to him.”
But they dropped their heads, poked their fingers in their mouths, and ducked out of sight behind her. So she rattled on:
“Lize, hurry now and fix him a hot breakfast this minute. Or did you eat on the boat already?”

I said I’d had it on the boat. So she started for the house, leading me by the hand with the children trailing after us. When we got inside she sat me down in a split-bottomed chair, and sat herself down on a little low stool right in front of me, holding both my hands, and said:

“Now I can get a _good_ look at you. Goodness me, I’ve been hungry for this a great many times, all these long years, and at last it’s come! We’ve been expecting you for two days and more. What kept you? Did the boat run aground?”
“Yes’m—she—”
“Don’t say ‘yes’m.’ Say ‘Aunt Sally.’ Where did she run aground?”

I didn’t really know what to say, because I didn’t know whether the boat would have been coming up the river or down. But I go a good deal by instinct, and my instinct said she’d be coming up, from down toward Orleans. That didn’t help me much, though, since I didn’t know the names of any sandbars down that way. I saw I’d have to make up a sandbar, or else forget the name of the one we ran aground on, or—Then I hit on an idea and brought it out:
“It wasn’t the grounding. That only held us up a little. We blew out a cylinder head.”
“Good gracious! Was anybody hurt?”
“No’m. Killed a nigger.”

“Well, that’s lucky, since people do sometimes get hurt. Two years ago last Christmas, your uncle Silas was heading up from Newrleans aboard the old _Lally Rook_ when she blew a cylinder head and crippled a man. I believe he died later. He was a Baptist. Your uncle Silas was acquainted with a family in Baton Rouge who were well acquainted with his people. Yes, I remember now, he _did_ die. Mortification set in, and they had to amputate him. It didn’t save him, though. Yes, mortification, that was what it was. He turned blue all over and died in the hope of a glorious resurrection. They say he was a sight to behold. Your uncle has been up to town every day to fetch you. He went off again not more than an hour ago, and he’ll be back any minute. You must have passed him on the road, didn’t you? A man getting on in years, with a—”

“No, I didn’t see anybody, Aunt Sally. The boat landed right at daylight. I left my baggage on the wharf boat and went looking around town and out a little way in the country, to pass the time and not get here too soon. So I came in by the back way.”
“Who did you give the baggage to?”
“Nobody.”
“Why, child, it’ll be stolen!”
“Not where _I_ hid it, I reckon,” I said.
“How did you get breakfast so early on the boat?”
That was getting to be pretty thin ice, but I said:
“The captain saw me standing around and told me I’d better eat something before I went ashore. So he took me into the texas, to the officers’ lunch, and gave me all I wanted.”

I was getting so uneasy I couldn’t listen properly. All the while my mind was on the children. I wanted to get them off to one side and pump them a little, to find out who I was. But I couldn’t get a chance, because Mrs. Phelps kept right on talking. Pretty soon she sent cold chills shooting down my back, because she said:

“But here we are running on like this, and you haven’t told me a word about Sis, or any of them. Now I’ll rest my works a little, and you start up yours. Just tell me _everything_. Tell me all about every last one of them, and how they are, and what they’re doing, and what they told you to tell me, and everything else you can think of.”

Well, I saw I was up a stump, and up it good. Providence had stood by me this far all right, but now I was stuck hard and fast aground. I saw it was no use trying to go ahead. I’d _got_ to give up. So I told myself, here’s another place where I’ve got to risk the truth. I opened my mouth to begin, but she grabbed me and hustled me in behind the bed, and said:
“Here he comes! Duck your head lower. There, that’s enough. He can’t see you now. Don’t let on you’re here. I’m going to play a joke on him. Children, not a word out of you.”
I saw I was in a fix now. But there was no use worrying. There was nothing to do but hold still and try to be ready to jump clear when the lightning struck.
I got just one little glimpse of the old gentleman when he came in, and then the bed hid him. Mrs. Phelps jumped up to meet him, and said:
“Has he come?”
“No,” said her husband.
“Good-_ness_ gracious!” she cried. “Whatever in the world can have happened to him?”
“I can’t imagine,” said the old gentleman. “And I must say it makes me dreadfully uneasy.”
“Uneasy!” she said. “I’m ready to go out of my mind! He _must_ have come, and you missed him on the road. I _know_ it’s so. Something tells me so.”
“Why, Sally, I _couldn’t_ miss him on the road. _You_ know that.”
“But oh, dear, dear, what _will_ Sis say! He must have come! You must have missed him. He—”

“Oh, don’t make me any more upset than I already am. I can’t make head or tail of it. I’m at my wit’s end, and I’ll admit I’m plain scared. But there’s no hope that he’s come, because he _couldn’t_ have come without my seeing him. Sally, it’s awful, just awful. Something has happened to the boat, I’m sure of it!”
“Why, Silas! Look over there! Up the road! Isn’t that somebody coming?”

He sprang to the window at the head of the bed, and that gave Mrs. Phelps the chance she wanted. She bent down quick at the foot of the bed and gave me a tug, and out I came. When he turned back from the window, there she stood, beaming and smiling like a house on fire, and me beside her, looking pretty meek and sweaty. The old gentleman stared and said:
“Why, who’s that?”
“Who do you think it is?”
“I haven’t any idea. Who _is_ it?”
“It’s _Tom Sawyer!_”

By jings, I nearly sank through the floor! But there was no time to swap knives. The old man grabbed my hand and shook it, and kept on shaking. And all the while the woman danced around and laughed and cried, and then they both fired off questions about Sid, and Mary, and the rest of the tribe.

But if they were joyful, that was nothing next to how I felt. It was like being born again, I was so glad to learn who I was. Well, they clung to me for two hours. By the time my chin was too tired to move another inch, I had told them more about my family—the Sawyer family, I mean—than could ever have happened to six Sawyer families put together. I also explained how we blew out a cylinder head at the mouth of White River and spent three days fixing it. That worked out fine, first-rate, since _they_ had no idea it wouldn’t take three days to fix. If I’d called it a bolt head it would have done just as well.

Now I was feeling pretty comfortable down one side and pretty uncomfortable up the other. Being Tom Sawyer was easy and comfortable, and it stayed that way until after a while I heard a steamboat coughing its way down the river. Then I thought, suppose Tom Sawyer is on that boat? And suppose he walks in here any minute and calls out my name before I can wink at him to keep quiet? Well, I couldn’t _have_ it that way. It wouldn’t do at all. I had to go up the road and waylay him. So I told the folks I reckoned I’d go up to town and fetch down my baggage. The old gentleman wanted to go along with me, but I said no, I could drive the horse myself, and I’d rather he didn’t go to any trouble over me.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIII — A Nigger Stealer
paragraphs: So I set out for town in the wagon, and when I was about halfway there I saw another wagon coming. Sure enough, it was Tom Sawyer. I stopped and waited until he came alongside. I said, “Hold on!” and his wagon pulled up next to mine. His mouth dropped open like a trunk lid and stayed that way. He swallowed two or three times, like a person with a dry throat, and then said:
“I never did you any harm. You know that. So what do you want to come back and haunt _me_ for?”
I said:
“I haven’t come back. I haven’t been _gone_.”
When he heard my voice it steadied him some, but he still wasn’t satisfied. He said:
“Don’t you play any tricks on me, because I wouldn’t on you. Honest Injun now, you’re not a ghost?”
“Honest Injun, I’m not,” I said.
“Well—I—I—well, that ought to settle it, of course, but somehow I just can’t understand it. Look here, weren’t you ever murdered _at all?_”
“No. I was never murdered at all. I fooled them. Come over here and feel me if you don’t believe it.”

So he did, and that satisfied him. He was so glad to see me again he didn’t know what to do with himself. And he wanted to hear all about it right off, because it was a grand adventure, and mysterious, and so it hit him right where he lived. But I said to leave it till later. I told his driver to wait, and we drove off a little way, and I told him what kind of fix I was in and asked what he reckoned we’d better do. He said to let him alone a minute and not disturb him. So he thought and thought, and pretty soon he said:

“It’s all right. I’ve got it. Take my trunk in your wagon and pretend it’s yours. You turn back and dawdle along slowly, so you’ll get to the house about when you should. I’ll go on toward town a bit, then make a fresh start and get there a quarter or half an hour after you. You don’t need to let on you know me at first.”
I said:

“All right, but wait a minute. There’s one more thing, something that _nobody_ knows but me. There’s a nigger here that I’m trying to steal out of slavery, and his name is _Jim_—old Miss Watson’s Jim.”
He said:
“What! Why, Jim is—”
He stopped and got to thinking. I said:

“_I_ know what you’re going to say. You’ll say it’s a dirty, low-down business. Well, what if it is? _I_’m low-down, and I’m going to steal him, and I want you to keep quiet and not let on. Will you?”
His eyes lit up, and he said:
“I’ll _help_ you steal him!”

Well, I let go of everything then, like I’d been shot. It was the most astonishing thing I ever heard anybody say, and I have to admit Tom Sawyer dropped a good deal in my opinion. Still, I couldn’t believe it. Tom Sawyer, a _nigger stealer!_
“Oh, come on!” I said. “You’re joking.”
“No, I’m not joking, either.”
“All right, then,” I said, “joking or not, if you hear anybody talking about a runaway nigger, don’t forget that _you_ don’t know anything about him, and _I_ don’t know anything about him.”

Then we lifted the trunk into my wagon, and he drove off his way and I drove mine. But of course I forgot all about driving slow, I was so glad and so full of thoughts, and I got home way too quick for a trip that long. The old gentleman was at the door, and he said:

“Well, this is wonderful! Who would have thought that mare had it in her? I wish we’d timed her. And she hasn’t sweated a hair, not one. It’s wonderful. Why, I wouldn’t take a hundred dollars for that horse now, I honestly wouldn’t, and yet I’d have sold her for fifteen before, and figured that was all she was worth.”

That was all he said. He was the most innocent, best old soul I ever saw. But that wasn’t surprising, because he wasn’t only a farmer, he was a preacher too. He had a little one-horse log church out back of the plantation, which he’d built himself at his own expense, to serve as a church and a schoolhouse. He never charged anything for his preaching, and it was worth every penny. There were plenty of other farmer-preachers like him, doing it the same way, all through the South.
About half an hour later Tom’s wagon pulled up at the front stile, and Aunt Sally saw it through the window, since it was only about fifty yards off, and said:
“Somebody’s here! Now who could it be? My goodness, I do believe it’s a stranger. Jimmy” (that was one of the children) “run tell Lize to set another place for dinner.”

Everybody rushed for the front door, because of course a stranger doesn’t turn up _every_ year, and when one does, he’s a bigger event than the yellow fever. Tom was over the stile and heading for the house, the wagon was rattling back up the road toward the village, and all of us were bunched up in the front doorway. Tom had his store-bought clothes on, and an audience, and that was always a treat for Tom Sawyer. In a situation like that, it was no trouble for him to put on as much style as the occasion called for. He wasn’t a boy to sneak up that yard like a sheep. No, he came along calm and important, like the ram. When he got in front of us he lifted his hat, ever so gracious and delicate, as if it were the lid of a box with butterflies asleep inside that he didn’t want to wake, and said:
“Mr. Archibald Nichols, I presume?”
“No, my boy,” said the old gentleman, “I’m sorry to say your driver has fooled you. Nichols’s place is another three miles down the road. Come in, come in.”
Tom glanced back over his shoulder and said, “Too late. He’s out of sight.”
“So he has, my son. Now you’re coming in to eat dinner with us, and afterward we’ll hitch up the team and drive you down to Nichols’s.”
“Oh, I _can’t_ put you to so much trouble. I couldn’t think of it. I’ll walk. I don’t mind the distance.”
“But we won’t _let_ you walk. It wouldn’t be Southern hospitality. Come right in.”

“Oh, _do_,” said Aunt Sally. “It’s no trouble to us at all, none in the world. You _must_ stay. It’s a long, dusty three miles, and we _can’t_ let you walk. Besides, I already told them to put out another plate when I saw you coming, so you mustn’t disappoint us. Come right in and make yourself at home.”

So Tom thanked them warmly and politely, let himself be persuaded, and came in. Once he was inside, he said he was a stranger from Hicksville, Ohio, and that his name was William Thompson. Then he made another bow.

Well, he went on and on and on, making up stories about Hicksville and everybody in it that he could think of, while I got a little nervous and wondered how this was going to help me out of my scrape. At last, still talking away, he leaned over and kissed Aunt Sally right on the mouth, then settled back comfortably in his chair and was going on with his talk. But she jumped up and wiped it off with the back of her hand, and said:
“You outrageous puppy!”
He looked sort of hurt, and said:
“I’m surprised at you, ma’am.”
“You’re surpri—Why, who do you take me for? I’ve half a mind to grab you and—Tell me, what do you mean by kissing me?”
He looked sort of humble, and said:
“I didn’t mean anything, ma’am. I didn’t mean any harm. I—I—thought you’d like it.”
“You born fool!” She snatched up the spinning stick, and it seemed to take everything she had not to crack him with it. “Whatever made you think I’d enjoy that?”
“Well, I don’t know. Only they—they—told me you would.”
“_They_ told you I would. Whoever said that is _another_ lunatic. Never in my life have I heard the like. Just who is _they?_”
“Why, everybody. They all said so, ma’am.”
She could barely hold herself in. Her eyes snapped, and her fingers twitched like she wanted to scratch him, and she said:
“Who is ‘everybody’? Give me their names, or there’ll be one fewer idiot around here.”
He stood up looking distressed, and fumbled with his hat, and said:
“I’m sorry. I never expected this. They told me to. Every one of them said, go on, kiss her, she’ll like it. All of them said so. But I’m sorry, ma’am, and I’ll never do it again. Honest, I won’t.”
“You won’t, won’t you? Well, I should _think_ you won’t!”
“No, ma’am, I’m honest about it. I’ll never do it again, until you ask me.”
“Until I _ask_ you! Well, in all my born days I never saw the like! I bet you’ll be the Methuselah of numskulls in all creation before I ever ask you, or the likes of you.”

“Well,” he said, “it surprises me so. I can’t make it out, somehow. They said you would, and I thought you would. But—” He stopped and looked slowly around, as if he hoped to run across a friendly eye somewhere, and landed on the old gentleman’s, and said, “Didn’t _you_ think she’d like me to kiss her, sir?”
“Why, no. I—I—well, no, I believe I didn’t.”
Then he turned the same look around to me, and said:
“Tom, didn’t _you_ think Aunt Sally would throw open her arms and cry, ‘Sid Sawyer—’”
“My land!” she said, cutting in and jumping at him. “You impudent young rascal, to fool a person like that—” And she was about to hug him, but he held her off, and said:
“No, not until you’ve asked me first.”

So she didn’t waste any time, but asked him, and hugged him and kissed him over and over, and then passed him along to the old man, who took what was left. And once they’d calmed down a bit, she said:
“Well, bless me, what a surprise! We weren’t expecting _you_ at all, just Tom. Sis never wrote a word to me about anyone coming except him.”

“That’s because nobody meant for anyone but Tom to come,” he said. “But I begged and begged, and at the last minute she let me come too. So on the way down the river, Tom and I thought it would be a first-rate surprise if he came to the house first, and I tagged along later and dropped in, pretending to be a stranger. But it was a mistake, Aunt Sally. This isn’t a healthy place for a stranger to come.”

“No, not for impudent whelps, Sid. You ought to have your jaws boxed. I haven’t been so put out since I don’t know when. But I don’t care, I don’t mind how it came about. I’d put up with a thousand such jokes to have you here. Well, to think of that performance! I won’t deny it, I was nearly petrified with astonishment when you gave me that smack.”

We had dinner out in the wide open passage between the house and the kitchen, and there was enough on that table for seven families, and all of it hot too. None of that limp, tough meat that’s been left in a cupboard in a damp cellar all night and tastes like a hunk of old cold cannibal in the morning. Uncle Silas said a pretty long blessing over it, but it was worth it, and it didn’t cool the food a bit, the way I’ve seen that sort of interruption do plenty of times. We talked a great deal all afternoon, and Tom and I were on the lookout the whole time, but it was no use. They just never happened to mention any runaway nigger, and we were afraid to try to steer the talk that way. But at supper that night, one of the little boys said:
“Pa, can’t Tom and Sid and me go to the show?”

“No,” said the old man, “I don’t think there’s going to be one, and you couldn’t go if there was, because the runaway nigger told Burton and me all about that scandalous show, and Burton said he’d tell the people. So I expect they’ve run those outrageous loafers out of town by now.”

So there it was! But _I_ couldn’t help it. Tom and I were to sleep in the same room and the same bed, so, being tired, we said good night and went up right after supper, then climbed out the window and down the lightning-rod and headed for town. I didn’t believe anybody was going to give the king and the duke a warning, and if I didn’t hurry up and give them one, they were sure to get into trouble.

On the road Tom told me all about how everyone figured I’d been murdered, and how Pap disappeared soon after and never came back, and what a stir there was when Jim ran away. And I told Tom all about our Royal Nonesuch scoundrels, and as much of the raft trip as I had time for. Then we hit the town and went up through the middle of it. It was a good half past eight by then. Here came a raging rush of people with torches, whooping and yelling like mad, banging tin pans and blowing horns. We jumped to one side to let them pass, and as they went by I saw they had the king and the duke sitting astraddle on a rail. I knew it _was_ the king and the duke, though they were covered in tar and feathers and didn’t look like anything human in the world. They just looked like a couple of monstrous big soldier-plumes. Well, it made me sick to see it. I felt so sorry for those poor pitiful rascals that it seemed like I could never hold anything against them again. It was a dreadful thing to see. Human beings _can_ be awfully cruel to one another.

We saw we were too late and couldn’t do any good. We asked some stragglers about it, and they said everybody had gone to the show looking perfectly innocent, and kept quiet and out of sight until the poor old king was in the middle of his capering on the stage. Then somebody gave a signal, and the whole house rose up and went for them.

So we poked along back home, and I wasn’t feeling as cocky as I had been before, but kind of low and humble and to blame, somehow, even though _I_ hadn’t done anything. But that’s always the way. It makes no difference whether you do right or wrong, a person’s conscience has no sense, and goes after him _anyway_. If I had a yellow dog that knew no more than a person’s conscience does, I would poison him. It takes up more room than all the rest of a person’s insides, and yet it’s no good, nohow. Tom Sawyer says the same.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIV — The Hut by the Ash Hopper
paragraphs: We stopped talking and got to thinking. After a while Tom said:
“Listen, Huck, how foolish of us not to think of it sooner! I bet I know where Jim is.”
“No! Where?”
“In that hut down by the ash-hopper. Think about it. During dinner, didn’t you see a nigger man carry some food in there?”
“Yes.”
“What did you think the food was for?”
“For a dog.”
“So did I. Well, it wasn’t for a dog.”
“Why?”
“Because part of it was watermelon.”
“So it was, and I noticed it. Well, it’s amazing that I never thought how a dog wouldn’t eat watermelon. It shows how a person can look at something and not see it, both at once.”

“Now, the nigger opened the padlock to go in and locked it again on his way out. And around the time we left the table, he brought Uncle a key, the same one, I bet. Watermelon points to a man, the lock points to a prisoner, and it’s not likely there are two prisoners on a small plantation like this, among people so kind and good. Jim is the prisoner. Fine. I’m glad we worked it out like detectives. I wouldn’t trade that for any other method. So you use your brain and figure out a plan to steal Jim, and I’ll figure out one too, and we’ll go with the one we like better.”

What a head for just a boy to have! If I had Tom Sawyer’s head I wouldn’t trade it for being a duke, or the mate of a steamboat, or a clown in a circus, or anything else I can think of. I started thinking up a plan, but only to be doing something. I knew perfectly well where the right plan was going to come from. Pretty soon Tom said:
“Ready?”
“Yes,” I said.
“All right. Let’s hear it.”

“Here’s my plan,” I said. “It’s easy to find out whether it’s Jim in there. Then tomorrow night I’ll bring up my canoe and fetch my raft over from the island. Then on the first dark night, we lift the key from the old man’s britches once he’s in bed, and push off down the river with Jim on the raft, hiding by day and moving by night, just as Jim and I did before. Wouldn’t that work?”

“_Work?_ Of course it would work, like rats fighting. But it’s much too simple. There’s nothing _to_ it. What’s the point of a plan that takes no more effort than that? It’s as mild as goose-milk. Huck, it wouldn’t stir up any more talk than burgling a soap factory.”
I didn’t say anything, because I wasn’t expecting anything different. But I knew perfectly well that whenever he got _his_ plan ready, it wouldn’t have any of those objections.

And it didn’t. He told me his plan, and I saw at once that it was worth fifteen of mine for style, and would set Jim free just as well as mine would, and might get us all killed on top of it. So I was satisfied, and told him we’d go ahead with it. I won’t describe it here, since I knew it wouldn’t stay as it was. I knew he’d keep altering it every which way as we went, and throwing in new nonsense whenever he found the chance. And that’s exactly what he did.

One thing was dead certain: Tom Sawyer was in earnest, and he really was going to help steal that nigger out of slavery. That was the part I couldn’t get over. Here was a boy who was respectable and well brought up, with a good name to lose and folks back home with good names too. He was bright, not thickheaded; he knew things, he wasn’t ignorant; he wasn’t mean, he was kind. And yet here he was, with no more pride or sense of right or feeling than to lower himself to this business, and bring shame on himself and his family in front of everybody. I _couldn’t_ make sense of it, no way at all. It was outrageous, and I knew I ought to up and tell him so, and be his true friend by letting him quit right where he was and save himself. And I _did_ start to tell him, but he shut me up and said:
“Don’t you think I know what I’m doing? Don’t I usually know what I’m doing?”
“Yes.”
“Didn’t I _say_ I was going to help steal the nigger?”
“Yes.”
“_Well_, then.”

That was all he said, and all I said. There wasn’t any use saying more, because when Tom said he’d do a thing, he always did it. But _I_ couldn’t figure out why he was willing to get mixed up in this, so I let it drop and didn’t trouble myself about it anymore. If he was set on having it that way, _I_ couldn’t stop him.

When we got home the house was dark and quiet, so we went on down to the hut by the ash-hopper to look it over. We cut through the yard to see what the hounds would do. They knew us, and made no more noise than country dogs always make when something passes in the night. At the cabin we examined the front and both sides. On the side I didn’t know—the north side—we found a square window hole, pretty high up, with only one sturdy board nailed across it. I said:
“This is the very thing. The hole’s big enough for Jim to squeeze through if we pry that board off.”
Tom said:
“That’s as simple as tic-tac-toe, three-in-a-row, and as easy as skipping school. I should _hope_ we can think up something a little more complicated than _that_, Huck Finn.”
“Well, then,” I said, “what about sawing him out, like I did when I faked my own murder?”
“That’s more _like_ it,” he said. “It’s really mysterious and troublesome and good,” he said, “but I bet we can find a way that takes twice as long. There’s no hurry. Let’s keep looking around.”

Between the hut and the fence, at the back, there was a lean-to made of planks that joined the hut at the eaves. It was as long as the hut but narrow, only about six feet wide. Its door was at the south end and had a padlock on it. Tom went over to the soap kettle and rummaged around until he came back with the iron thing they use to lift the lid. He used it to pry out one of the staples. The chain fell down, and we opened the door, went in, shut it behind us, and struck a match. We saw that the shed was only built up against the cabin and had no connection with it. It had no floor, and there was nothing in it except some old rusty, worn-out hoes and spades and picks and a crippled plow. The match went out, and so did we. We shoved the staple back in, and the door was locked as good as ever. Tom was delighted. He said:
“Now we’ve got it figured. We’ll _dig_ him out, and it’ll take about a week!”

Then we started for the house. I went in by the back door—all you have to do is pull a buckskin latch-string, since they don’t lock the doors—but that wasn’t romantic enough for Tom Sawyer. Nothing would do but he had to climb up the lightning rod. He got halfway up about three times and slid back down every time, and the last time he nearly knocked his brains out, so he figured he’d have to give it up. But once he’d rested, he decided to give it one more try for luck, and this time he made it to the top.

In the morning we were up at daybreak and down at the nigger cabins to pet the dogs and make friends with the nigger who fed Jim—if it _was_ Jim who was being fed. The niggers were just finishing breakfast and heading out to the fields. Jim’s nigger was piling a tin pan with bread and meat and other things, and while the others were leaving, the key came down from the house.

This nigger had a good-natured, dim-witted face, and his hair was all tied up in little bunches with thread. That was to keep witches away. He said the witches had been pestering him terribly these nights, making him see all sorts of strange things and hear all sorts of strange words and noises, and he didn’t believe he’d ever been witched so long in his life. He got so worked up and went on so about his troubles that he forgot what he’d been about to do. So Tom said:
“What’s the grub for? Are you going to feed the dogs?”
A slow smile spread across the nigger’s face, like when you heave a brickbat into a mud puddle, and he said:
“Yes, Mars Sid, _a_ dog. Strange dog, too. Do you want to come and look at him?”
“Yes.”
I nudged Tom and whispered:
“You’re going in now, right here at daybreak? _That_ wasn’t the plan.”
“No, it wasn’t, but it’s the plan _now_.”
So, drat him, we went along, though I didn’t like it much. When we got inside we could hardly see a thing, it was so dark. But Jim was there, sure enough, and he could see us, and he cried out:
“Why, _Huck!_ And good _lan’!_ Ain’t that Mister Tom?”
I knew just how it would go. I’d expected it. _I_ didn’t know what to do, and if I had, I couldn’t have done it, because that nigger broke in and said:
“Why, gracious sakes! Does he know you gen’lmen?”
We could see fairly well now. Tom studied the nigger, steady and kind of wondering, and said:
“Does _who_ know us?”
“Why, dis-yer runaway nigger.”
“I don’t think he does. But what put that in your head?”
“What _put_ it there? Didn’t he just this minute holler like he knowed you?”
Tom said, in a puzzled sort of way:
“Well, that’s mighty strange. _Who_ sang out? _When_ did he sing out? _What_ did he sing out?” Then he turned to me, perfectly calm, and said, “Did _you_ hear anybody sing out?”
Of course there was only one thing to say, so I said:
“No, _I_ haven’t heard anybody say anything.”
Then he turned to Jim and looked him over as if he’d never seen him before, and said:
“Did you sing out?”
“No, sah,” said Jim. “_I_ hain’t said nothing, sah.”
“Not a word?”
“No, sah, I hain’t said a word.”
“Have you ever seen us before?”
“No, sah, not as _I_ knows on.”
So Tom turned back to the nigger, who looked wild and upset, and said, rather sternly:
“What’s the matter with you, anyway? What made you think somebody sang out?”

“Oh, it’s them dad-blamed witches, sah, and I wish I was dead, I do. They’s always at it, sah, and they near kill me, they scare me so. Please don’t tell nobody ’bout it, sah, or old Mars Silas he’ll scold me, ’cause he says there _ain’t_ no witches. I just wish to goodness he was here now—_then_ what would he say! I bet he couldn’t find no way around it _this_ time. But it’s always just so: folks that’s _set_ stays set. They won’t look into nothing and find it out for theirselves, and when _you_ find it out and tell ’em ’bout it, they don’t believe you.”
Tom gave him a dime and said we wouldn’t tell anybody. He told him to buy more thread to tie up his hair with, and then he looked at Jim and said:

“I wonder if Uncle Silas will hang this nigger. If I caught a nigger so ungrateful he’d run off, _I_ wouldn’t turn him over to anybody, I’d hang him myself.” And while the nigger stepped to the door to look at the dime and bite it to see if it was real, Tom whispered to Jim:
“Don’t ever let on you know us. And if you hear digging at night, that’s us. We’re going to set you free.”

Jim only had time to grab our hands and squeeze them. Then the nigger came back, and we said we’d come again some time if he wanted us to. He said he did, especially after dark, because the witches went after him mostly in the dark, and it was good to have folks around then.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXV — Escaping Properly
paragraphs: It was still almost an hour till breakfast, so we left and struck off into the woods. Tom said we had to have _some_ light to dig by, and a lantern gives too much and might get us into trouble. What we needed was a pile of those rotten chunks of wood called fox-fire, which just give off a soft kind of glow when you put them in a dark place. We gathered an armful and hid it in the weeds, then sat down to rest, and Tom said, rather dissatisfied:

“Blame it, this whole business is just as easy and awkward as can be. That makes it terribly hard to cook up a hard plan. There’s no watchman to drug—and there _ought_ to be a watchman. There isn’t even a dog to feed a sleeping potion to. And there’s Jim chained by one leg, with a ten-foot chain, to the leg of his bed. Why, all you have to do is lift up the bedstead and slip the chain off. And Uncle Silas trusts everybody. He sends the key out with that pumpkin-headed nigger and doesn’t send anybody to watch the nigger. Jim could have gotten out of that window hole before now, only there’d be no use trying to travel with a ten-foot chain on his leg. Why, drat it, Huck, it’s the stupidest arrangement I ever saw. You have to invent _all_ the difficulties. Well, we can’t help it. We have to do the best we can with the materials we’ve got. Anyhow, there’s one good thing: there’s more honor in getting him out through a whole lot of difficulties and dangers when not one of them was supplied to you by the people whose duty it was to supply them, and you had to think them all up out of your own head. Now just look at the lantern. When you come right down to the cold facts, we simply have to _pretend_ a lantern is risky. Why, we could work by a torchlight parade if we wanted to, _I_ believe. Now, while I think of it, we have to hunt up something to make a saw out of the first chance we get.”
“What do we want a saw for?”
“What do we _want_ one for? Don’t we have to saw the leg off Jim’s bed, to get the chain loose?”
“Why, you only just said anybody could lift the bedstead and slide the chain off.”

“Well, if that isn’t just like you, Huck Finn. You _can_ come up with the most baby-school ways of going at a thing. Haven’t you ever read any books at all?—Baron Trenck, or Casanova, or Benvenuto Cellini, or Henri IV, or any of those heroes? Who ever heard of springing a prisoner in a fussy old-maid way like that? No. The way all the top authorities do it is to saw the bed leg in two and leave it just so, then swallow the sawdust so nobody finds it, and rub dirt and grease over the cut so the sharpest seneschal alive can’t tell it’s been sawed and thinks the leg is perfectly solid. Then on the night you’re ready, you kick the leg, down it goes, you slide your chain off, and that’s that. All that’s left is to tie your rope ladder to the battlements and shinny down, breaking your leg in the moat—because a rope ladder is always nineteen feet too short, you know—and there are your horses and your faithful vassals, who scoop you up, throw you over a saddle, and off you go to your native Languedoc, or Navarre, or wherever it is. It’s splendid, Huck. I wish this cabin had a moat. If we have time on the night of the escape, we’ll dig one.”
I said:
“Why would we want a moat, when we’re going to sneak him out from underneath the cabin?”
But he never heard a word. He had forgotten me and everything else, and sat with his chin in his hand, thinking. Before long he sighed and shook his head, then sighed again, and said:
“No, it wouldn’t do—there isn’t enough necessity for it.”
“For what?” I said.
“Why, for sawing Jim’s leg off,” he said.
“Good land!” I said. “Why, there isn’t _any_ necessity for it. And why would you want to saw his leg off, anyway?”

“Well, some of the best authorities have done it. They couldn’t get the chain off, so they just cut off their hand and bolted. And a leg would be better still. But we’ll have to let that go. There isn’t necessity enough in this case, and besides, Jim’s a nigger and wouldn’t understand the reasons for it, or how it’s the custom in Europe. So we’ll let it go. But here’s one thing: he can have a rope ladder. We can tear up our sheets and make him one easy enough. And we can send it to him in a pie. That’s how it’s mostly done. And I’ve eaten worse pies.”
“Why, Tom Sawyer, what a thing to say,” I said. “Jim has no use for a rope ladder.”
“He _does_ have use for it. How _you_ talk, you ought to say. You don’t know anything about it. He’s _got_ to have a rope ladder. They all do.”
“What in the world can he _do_ with it?”

“_Do_ with it? He can hide it in his bed, can’t he? That’s what they all do, and _he’s_ got to do it too. Huck, you never seem to want to do anything the regular way. You’re always wanting to start something new. Suppose he _doesn’t_ do anything with it? Isn’t it there in his bed, as a clue, after he’s gone? And don’t you think they’ll want clues? Of course they will. And you wouldn’t leave them any? That would be a _fine_ how-do-you-do, _wouldn’t_ it! I never heard of such a thing.”

“Well,” I said, “if it’s in the rules, and he’s got to have it, all right, let him have it. I don’t want to go against any rules. But there’s one thing, Tom Sawyer: if we go tearing up our sheets to make Jim a rope ladder, we’re going to get in trouble with Aunt Sally, as sure as you’re born. Now the way I see it, a hickory-bark ladder costs nothing and wastes nothing, and it’s just as good for loading up a pie and hiding in a straw mattress as any rag ladder you could start. And as for Jim, he hasn’t had any experience, so _he_ doesn’t care what kind of a—”
“Oh, shucks, Huck Finn, if I was as ignorant as you, I’d keep my mouth shut—that’s what _I’d_ do. Who ever heard of a state prisoner escaping on a hickory-bark ladder? It’s just ridiculous.”
“All right, Tom, have it your way. But if you want my advice, you’ll let me borrow a sheet off the clothesline.”
He said that would work. It gave him another idea, and he said:
“Borrow a shirt, too.”
“What would we want with a shirt, Tom?”
“To give Jim something to keep his journal on.”
“Journal, my foot. _Jim_ can’t write.”
“Suppose he _can’t_ write. He can still make marks on a shirt, can’t he, if we make him a pen from an old pewter spoon or a chunk of old iron barrel hoop?”
“Why, Tom, we could yank a feather out of a goose and make him a better pen, and faster, too.”

“_Prisoners_ don’t have geese wandering around the dungeon keep for them to pluck pens from, you chucklehead. They _always_ make their pens from the hardest, toughest, most aggravating piece of old brass candlestick or the like that they can lay hands on. And it takes them weeks and weeks and months and months to file it down, too, because they have to do it by rubbing it against the wall. _They_ wouldn’t use a goose quill even if they had one. It ain’t proper.”
“All right, then, what do we make his ink out of?”

“Plenty of prisoners make it from iron rust and tears, but that’s the ordinary kind, and what women use. The best authorities use their own blood. Jim can do that. And when he wants to send out some little ordinary mysterious message, to let the world know where he’s being held captive, he can scratch it on the bottom of a tin plate with a fork and toss it out the window. The Man in the Iron Mask always did that, and it’s a mighty good way, too.”
“Jim ain’t got any tin plates. They feed him out of a pan.”
“That’s nothing. We can get him some.”
“Nobody could _read_ his plates, though.”

“That’s got nothing to _do_ with it, Huck Finn. _He_ only has to write on the plate and toss it out. Nobody _has_ to be able to read it. Half the time nobody can make out a word a prisoner scratches on a tin plate, or on anything else.”
“Then what’s the point of wasting the plates?”
“Why, blast it all, they ain’t the _prisoner’s_ plates.”
“But they’re _somebody’s_ plates, ain’t they?”
“Well, so what if they are? Why would the _prisoner_ care whose—”
He stopped right there, because we heard the breakfast horn blowing, so we hurried off to the house.

Later in the morning I borrowed a sheet and a white shirt off the clothesline. I found an old sack and put them in it, and then we went down and got the fox-fire and put that in as well. I called it borrowing, because that was what Pap always called it, but Tom said it wasn’t borrowing, it was stealing. He said we were playing prisoners, and prisoners don’t care how they get a thing as long as they get it, and nobody blames them for it, either. It ain’t any crime for a prisoner to steal what he needs to escape with, Tom said. It’s his right. So as long as we were playing prisoners, we had every right to steal anything on this place that we had the slightest use for in getting ourselves out of prison. He said that if we weren’t prisoners it would be a very different matter, and nobody but a mean, low person would steal when he wasn’t a prisoner. So we agreed we would steal everything that came handy. And yet he made a terrible fuss one day after that, when I stole a watermelon out of the nigger-patch and ate it. He made me go and give the niggers a dime, without telling them what it was for. Tom said what he meant was that we could steal anything we _needed_. Well, I said, I needed the watermelon. But he said I didn’t need it to get out of prison, and that was where the difference lay. He said that if I’d wanted it to hide a knife in, and smuggle it to Jim to kill the seneschal with, that would have been all right. So I let it go at that, though I couldn’t see any advantage in playing a prisoner if I had to sit down and chew over a pile of fancy hair-splitting like that every time I saw a chance to grab a watermelon.

Well, like I was saying, that morning we waited until everybody had settled down to their work and there was nobody in sight around the yard. Then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I stood off a little way to keep watch. After a while he came out, and we went and sat on the woodpile to talk. He said:
“Everything’s ready now except the tools, and those are easy to fix.”
“Tools?” I said.
“Yes.”
“Tools for what?”
“To dig with, of course. Surely you don’t figure we’re going to _chew_ him out?”
“Them old busted picks and such lying in there, ain’t they good enough to dig a nigger loose?” I said.
He turned to me with a look so pitying it would make a person cry, and said:

“Huck Finn, have you _ever_ heard of a prisoner who had picks and shovels and every modern convenience in his wardrobe for digging his way out? Now answer me this, if you’ve got a speck of reason in you: how would _that_ give him any chance of being a hero? They might as well hand him the key and be done. Picks and shovels! A king wouldn’t be given those.”
“Fine,” I said, “if picks and shovels are out, what is it we do want?”
“A couple of case knives.”
“To dig the foundations out from under that cabin?”
“Yes.”
“Dang it, Tom, that’s foolish.”

“It doesn’t matter how foolish it is. It’s the _right_ way, and it’s the proper way. And there ain’t any _other_ way that _I_ ever heard of, and I’ve read all the books that tell anything about these matters. They always dig out with a case knife, and not through dirt, mind you. Usually it’s through solid rock. And it takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, forever and ever. Why, look at that prisoner in the bottom dungeon of the Castle d’If, in the harbor of Marseilles, who dug himself out that way. How long was _he_ at it, would you guess?”
“I don’t know.”
“Well, guess.”
“I don’t know. A month and a half?”
“_Thirty-seven years_, and he came out in China. _That’s_ the kind of job I mean. I wish the bottom of _this_ fortress was solid rock.”
“_Jim_ don’t know anybody in China.”
“What’s _that_ got to do with anything? That other fellow didn’t either. You’re forever drifting off after some side question. Why can’t you keep to the point?”
“All right. _I_ don’t care where he comes out, so long as he _comes_ out, and I reckon Jim don’t either. But there’s one thing, anyhow: Jim’s too old to be dug out with a case knife. He won’t last.”
“He will too _last_. Surely you don’t think a _dirt_ foundation is going to eat up thirty-seven years?”
“How long will it take, Tom?”

“Well, we can’t risk taking as long as we ought to, because it might not be long before Uncle Silas hears from down there by New Orleans. He’ll hear that Jim ain’t from there. Then his next move will be to advertise Jim, or something like that. So we can’t risk taking as long to dig him out as we should. By rights I figure we ought to take a couple of years, but we can’t. Things being so uncertain, here’s what I recommend: we really do dig in, as fast as we can, and afterward we can _pretend_, to ourselves, that we were at it for thirty-seven years. Then we can snatch him out and rush him away the first time there’s an alarm. Yes, I reckon that’s the best way.”

“Now there’s some _sense_ in that,” I said. “Pretending doesn’t cost anything, and pretending ain’t any trouble. And if it matters, I don’t mind pretending we were at it a hundred and fifty years. It wouldn’t strain me any, once I got the hang of it. So I’ll mosey along now and swipe a couple of case knives.”
“Swipe three,” he said. “We need one to make a saw out of.”
“Tom, if it ain’t against the rules and sinful to suggest it,” I said, “there’s an old rusty saw blade over yonder, stuck under the siding behind the smokehouse.”
He looked kind of tired and discouraged, and said:
“It’s no use trying to teach you anything, Huck. Run along and swipe the knives, three of them.” So I did.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVI — The Lightning Rod
paragraphs: As soon as we figured everybody was asleep that night, we went down the lightning rod and shut ourselves up in the lean-to. We got out our pile of fox-fire and went to work. We cleared everything out of the way along the middle of the bottom log, a space of four or five feet. Tom said we were right behind Jim’s bed now, and we’d dig in under it. When we were through, nobody in the cabin could ever know there was a hole there, because Jim’s bed quilt hung down almost to the ground, and you’d have to lift it up and look underneath to see the hole. So we dug and dug with the case knives until almost midnight. By then we were dog-tired and our hands were blistered, and you could hardly see that we’d done anything. At last I said:
“This ain’t a thirty-seven-year job. This is a thirty-eight-year job, Tom Sawyer.”
He didn’t say anything. But he sighed, and pretty soon he quit digging, and for a good little while I knew he was thinking. Then he said:

“It’s no use, Huck. It ain’t going to work. If we were prisoners it would, because then we’d have as many years as we wanted and no hurry. We’d only get a few minutes to dig each day, while they were changing the guard, so our hands wouldn’t get blistered, and we could keep it up right along, year in and year out, and do it right, the way it ought to be done. But _we_ can’t fool around. We have to rush. We ain’t got time to spare. If we put in another night this way, we’d have to stop for a week to let our hands heal. We couldn’t touch a case knife with them sooner.”
“Well, then, what are we going to do, Tom?”
“I’ll tell you. It ain’t right, and it ain’t moral, and I wouldn’t want it to get out. But there’s just the one way: we have to dig him out with the picks and _pretend_ they’re case knives.”

“_Now_ you’re _talking!_” I said. “Your head gets clearer and clearer all the time, Tom Sawyer. Picks are the thing, moral or no moral. And as for me, I don’t care a straw about the morality of it, anyhow. When I set out to steal a nigger, or a watermelon, or a Sunday-school book, I ain’t one bit particular how it’s done, so long as it’s done. What I want is my nigger. Or what I want is my watermelon. Or what I want is my Sunday-school book. And if a pick’s the handiest thing, then a pick is what I’m going to dig that nigger or that watermelon or that Sunday-school book out with. And I don’t give a dead rat what the authorities think about it, either.”

“Well,” he said, “there’s an excuse for picks and pretending in a case like this. If there weren’t, I wouldn’t approve of it, and I wouldn’t stand by and watch the rules get broken, because right is right and wrong is wrong, and a person has no business doing wrong when he ain’t ignorant and knows better. It might do for _you_ to dig Jim out with a pick, _without_ any pretending, because you don’t know any better. But it wouldn’t do for me, because I do know better. Give me a case knife.”
He had his own right beside him, but I handed him mine. He flung it down and said:
“Give me a _case knife_.”
I didn’t know what to do, but then I thought of something. I scratched around among the old tools, found a pickax, and gave it to him. He took it and went to work and never said a word.
He was always that particular. Full of principle.

So then I got a shovel, and we picked and shoveled by turns and made the dirt fly. We stuck to it for about half an hour, which was as long as we could stand up, but we had a good-sized hole to show for it. When I got upstairs I looked out the window and saw Tom doing his level best to climb the lightning rod, but he couldn’t manage it, his hands were so sore. At last he said:
“It’s no use. It can’t be done. What do you figure I’d better do? Can’t you think of any way?”
“Yes,” I said, “but I reckon it ain’t proper. Come up the stairs and pretend it’s a lightning rod.”
So he did.

The next day Tom stole a pewter spoon and a brass candlestick out of the house, to turn into pens for Jim, along with six tallow candles. I loafed around the nigger cabins, waiting for my chance, and swiped three tin plates. Tom said that wasn’t enough. I told him nobody was ever going to find the plates Jim threw out, since they’d drop into the dog-fennel and jimpson weeds beneath the window hole, and we could carry them back for Jim to use again. That satisfied Tom. Then he said:
“Now the thing to work out is how to get the things to Jim.”
“Carry them in through the hole,” I said, “once it’s done.”

He only looked scornful, and said something about how nobody ever heard of such an idiotic idea, and then he went to studying on it. After a while he said he had worked out two or three ways, but there was no need to decide on any of them yet. He said we had to tell Jim first.

That night we went down the lightning rod a little after ten, taking one of the candles along. We listened under the window hole and heard Jim snoring, so we tossed the candle in, and it didn’t wake him. Then we lit into the digging with the pick and shovel, and in about two and a half hours the job was done. We crept in under Jim’s bed and into the cabin, felt around until we found the candle, and lit it. We stood over Jim a while and saw that he looked hearty and healthy, and then we woke him up gently and gradually. He was so glad to see us he nearly cried. He called us honey and every pet name he could think of, and he wanted us to hunt up a cold chisel right then, cut the chain off his leg, and clear out without losing any time. But Tom showed him how against the rules that would be, and sat down and told him all about our plans, and how we could change them in a minute any time there was an alarm. He told Jim not to be the least bit afraid, because we would see that he got away, _sure_. So Jim said it was all right, and we sat there and talked over old times for a while. Then Tom asked a lot of questions, and Jim told him that Uncle Silas came in every day or two to pray with him, and Aunt Sally came in to see whether he was comfortable and had plenty to eat, and that both of them were as kind as could be. Then Tom said:
“_Now_ I see how to manage it. We’ll send you things through them.”
I said, “Don’t do any such thing. It’s one of the most jackass ideas I ever came across.” But he paid no attention to me and went right on. That was his way once he’d got his plans set.

So Tom explained to Jim how we’d have to sneak in the rope-ladder pie and the other big things through Nat, the nigger who brought him his meals. Jim had to keep a sharp lookout, not act surprised, and never let Nat see him opening them. The small things we’d slip into Uncle Silas’s coat pockets, and Jim would have to steal them out from there. We’d also tie things to Aunt Sally’s apron-strings, or drop them in her apron pocket if we got the chance. Tom told him what each thing would be and what it was for, and how to keep a journal on his shirt in his own blood, and all the rest of it. He told Jim everything. Jim couldn’t see much sense in most of it, but he figured we were white folks and knew better than he did, so he was satisfied and said he’d do it all exactly the way Tom said.

Jim had plenty of corn-cob pipes and tobacco, so we had a real good friendly time. Then we crawled back out through the hole and went home to bed, with hands that looked like something had chewed on them. Tom was in high spirits. He said it was the best fun he’d ever had in his life, and the most intellectual. He said that if he could only see a way to manage it, we’d keep it going all the rest of our lives and leave Jim to our children to set free, because he believed Jim would like it better and better the more he got used to it. He said it could be stretched out to as much as eighty years that way, and it would be the best time on record. And he said it would make every one of us who had a hand in it famous.

In the morning we went out to the woodpile and chopped the brass candlestick into handy pieces, and Tom put them in his pocket along with the pewter spoon. Then we went over to the nigger cabins. While I kept Nat’s attention away, Tom pushed a piece of candlestick into the middle of a corn-pone in Jim’s pan, and we went along with Nat to see how it would work. It worked beautifully. When Jim bit into it, it nearly knocked all his teeth out, and nothing could have worked better. Tom said so himself. Jim never let on that it was anything but a bit of rock, or something of that kind that’s always getting into bread, you know. But after that he never bit into anything without first jabbing his fork into it in three or four places.

While we were standing there in the dim light, a couple of hounds came pushing in from under Jim’s bed, and they kept on piling in until there were eleven of them. There was hardly room in there to breathe. Good grief, we’d forgotten to fasten the door of the lean-to! The nigger Nat only hollered “Witches” once, then keeled over on the floor among the dogs and started groaning as if he were dying. Tom yanked the door open and threw out a slab of Jim’s meat. The dogs went after it, and in two seconds Tom was out the door himself and back in again with it shut, and I knew he’d fastened the other door too. Then he went to work on the nigger, coaxing and petting him and asking if he’d been imagining things again. Nat sat up, blinked around, and said:

“Mars Sid, you gwyne say I’s a fool, but ef I didn’t see mos’ a million dogs, er devils, er somethin’, I hope I drops dead right heah where I’s standin’. I did, fo’ sho’. Mars Sid, I _felt_ um—I _felt_ um, sah! Dey was all ovah me. Dad fetch it, I jis’ wants one chance to lay my han’s on one er dem witches—jis’ one chance—dat’s all _I_ asks. But mos’ly I wants dem to let me be, I does.”
Tom said:
“Well, I’ll tell you what _I_ think. Why do they come here right at this runaway nigger’s breakfast-time? Because they’re hungry, that’s why. Make them a witch pie. That’s what _you_ ought to do.”
“But my lan’, Mars Sid, how’s _I_ gwyne make ’m a witch pie? I doan’ know de fust thing ’bout it. I nevah even hearn tell er sich a thing befo’.”
