“Well, then, I’ll have to make it myself.”
“You’ll do it, honey?—will you really? I’ll wusshup de very groun’ you walks on, I will!”

“All right, I’ll do it, since it’s you, and you’ve been good to us and shown us the runaway nigger. But you have to be mighty careful. When we come around, turn your back to us. Then whatever we’ve put in the pan, act like you never saw it. And don’t look when Jim empties the pan, either—something might happen, I don’t know what. And above everything, don’t you go _touching_ the witch-things.”
“_Touch_ ’m, Mars Sid? Whatever _is_ you talkin’ ’bout? I wouldn’ lay a finger on um, not fo’ ten hund’d thous’n billion dollars, I wouldn’t.”

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVII — The Last Shirt
paragraphs: So that was settled. Then we went to the rubbage-pile in the back yard, where they throw the old boots, rags, broken bottles, worn-out tin things and all such trash. We scratched around there and found an old tin washpan, and plugged up the holes as best we could so it could bake the pie. We took it down to the cellar and stole it full of flour, then started for breakfast. On the way we found a couple of shingle-nails, which Tom said would come in handy for a prisoner to scratch his name and sorrows on the dungeon walls. One we dropped in Aunt Sally’s apron pocket, which was hanging on a chair, and the other we stuck in the band of Uncle Silas’s hat, which was on the bureau. We’d heard the children say that their pa and ma were going to the runaway nigger’s cabin this morning. Then we went in to breakfast, and Tom dropped the pewter spoon in Uncle Silas’s coat pocket. Aunt Sally hadn’t come yet, so we had to wait a little while.

When she did come, she was hot and red and cross, and could hardly wait for the blessing to be over. Then she started pouring out coffee with one hand and rapping the nearest child on the head with her thimble with the other, and said:
“I’ve searched high and low, and for the life of me I can’t think what _has_ become of your other shirt.”

My heart dropped down among my lungs and livers and things, and a hard piece of corn-crust started down my throat after it, met a cough on the way, and was shot across the table. It hit one of the children in the eye and curled him up like a fishing-worm, and he let out a yell the size of a warwhoop. Tom turned kind of blue around the gills, and it all added up to a pretty serious state of affairs for about a quarter of a minute. I’d have sold out for half price if there’d been a bidder. But after that we were all right again. It was the sudden surprise of it that left us so cold. Uncle Silas said:
“It’s most remarkably strange, and I can’t make it out. I know perfectly well I took it _off_, because—”

“Because you’ve only got one _on_. Just _listen_ to the man! _I_ know you took it off, and I’ve got better proof than your absent-minded memory, too, because it was hanging on the clothesline yesterday—I saw it there myself. But now it’s gone, and that’s all there is to it. You’ll just have to wear a red flannel one till I can find time to sew a new one. And that’ll be the third I’ve made in two years. It keeps a body running to keep you in shirts, and what you manage to _do_ with them all, I can’t imagine. You’d think you could learn to take some sort of care of them, at your age.”

“I know, Sally, and I do try my best. But it can’t be altogether my fault, because you know I never see them or touch them except when they’re on me, and I don’t believe I’ve ever lost one _off_ of me yet.”

“Well, it isn’t _your_ fault if you haven’t, Silas. You’d have done it if you could, I expect. And the shirt isn’t all that’s gone, either. There’s a spoon gone, and _that_ isn’t all. There were ten, and now there are only nine. The calf got the shirt, I suppose, but the calf certainly never took the spoon.”
“Why, what else is gone, Sally?”

“Six _candles_ are gone, that’s what. The rats could have got the candles, and I expect they did. I wonder they don’t carry off the whole place, the way you’re always about to stop up their holes and never do. And if they weren’t fools they’d sleep in your hair, Silas, and _you’d_ never find it out. But you can’t blame the _spoon_ on the rats, and that I _know_.”
“Well, Sally, I’m at fault, and I admit it. I’ve been careless. But I won’t let tomorrow go by without stopping up those holes.”
“Oh, don’t hurry; next year will do. Matilda Angelina Araminta _Phelps!_”
Whack came the thimble, and the child snatched her hand out of the sugar-bowl without any fooling around. Just then the nigger woman stepped into the passage and said:
“Missus, dey’s a sheet gone.”
“A _sheet_ gone! Well, for goodness’ sake!”
“I’ll stop up those holes _today_,” said Uncle Silas, looking sorrowful.
“Oh, _do_ be quiet!—do you suppose the rats took the _sheet? Where’s_ it gone, Lize?”
“Lawsy, Miss’ Sally, I ain’ got no notion. She wuz hangin’ on de clo’sline yistiddy, but now she done gone: she ain’ out dah no mo’.”
“I do believe the world _is_ coming to an end. In all my born days I _never_ saw anything like it. A shirt, and a sheet, and a spoon, and six can—”
“Missus,” said a young yaller wench, coming in, “a brass cannelstick is miss’n.”
“Get out of here, you hussy, or I’ll take a skillet to you!”

Well, she was just boiling. I began to look for a chance to sneak out and head for the woods until the weather calmed down. She kept right on raging, running her rebellion all by herself, with everybody else meek and quiet. At last Uncle Silas, looking kind of foolish, fished that spoon out of his pocket. She stopped with her mouth open and her hands in the air, and as for me, I wished I was in Jerusalem or somewheres. But not for long, because she said:
“It’s _just_ as I expected! So it was in your pocket the whole time. And likely you’ve got the other things in there too. How did it get in there?”

“I really don’t know, Sally,” he said, sort of apologizing, “or you know I would tell you. I was studying my text in Acts Seventeen before breakfast, and I suppose I put it in there without noticing, meaning to put my Testament in. It must be so, because my Testament isn’t in there. But I’ll go and see. If the Testament is where I had it, I’ll know I didn’t put it in, and that will show that I laid the Testament down and picked up the spoon, and—”
“Oh, for goodness’ sake! Give a body a rest! Go on now, the whole lot of you, and don’t come near me again until I’ve got my peace of mind back.”

_I’d_ have heard her if she’d only said it to herself, let alone out loud, and I’d have got up and obeyed her if I’d been dead. As we were passing through the sitting-room, the old man picked up his hat, and the shingle-nail fell out on the floor. He just picked it up and laid it on the mantel-shelf without saying a word, and went out. Tom saw him do it, remembered about the spoon, and said:

“Well, there’s no use sending things by _him_ anymore. He isn’t reliable.” Then he said: “But he did us a good turn with the spoon, anyway, without knowing it, so we’ll go and do him one without _him_ knowing it—stop up his rat-holes.”

There were a great many of them down in the cellar, and it took us a whole hour, but we did the job tight and good and shipshape. Then we heard steps on the stairs, so we blew out our light and hid. Here came the old man with a candle in one hand and a bundle of stuff in the other, looking as absent-minded as the year before last. He went mooning around, first to one rat-hole and then another, till he’d been to every one. Then he stood there about five minutes, picking tallow drips off his candle and thinking. Then he turned slowly and dreamily toward the stairs, saying:
“Well, for the life of me, I can’t recall when I did it. I could prove to her now that the rats weren’t to blame. But never mind—let it go. I don’t suppose it would do any good.”
And so he went off upstairs, mumbling to himself, and then we left. He was a mighty nice old man, and he always is.

Tom was a good deal bothered about what to do for a spoon, but he said we had to have one, so he thought it over. When he had worked it out, he told me what we were to do. Then we went and waited around the spoon-basket till we saw Aunt Sally coming. Tom began counting the spoons and laying them out to one side, and I slid one of them up my sleeve. Tom said:
“Why, Aunt Sally, there are only nine spoons _still_.”
She said:
“Go on and play, and don’t bother me. I know better. I counted them myself.”
“Well, Aunty, I’ve counted them twice, and _I_ only get nine.”
She was out of all patience, but of course she came over and counted them herself—anybody would.
“I declare to goodness there _are_ only nine!” she said. “Why, what in the world—plague _take_ the things, I’ll count them again.”
So I slipped the one I had back in, and when she was done counting, she said:
“Hang the troublesome trash, there are _ten_ now!” and she looked huffy and bothered both. But Tom said:
“Why, Aunty, _I_ don’t think there are ten.”
“You numskull, didn’t you see me _count_ them?”
“I know, but—”
“Well, I’ll count them _again_.”

So I swiped one, and they came out nine, the same as the other time. Well, she _was_ in a tearing rage, trembling all over she was so mad. But she counted and counted till she got so addled that she’d sometimes start counting the _basket_ as a spoon. So three times they came out right, and three times they came out wrong. Then she grabbed up the basket and slammed it across the house, knocking the cat galley-west. She told us to clear out and let her have some peace, and said that if we came bothering her again between then and dinner she’d skin us. So we had the extra spoon, and we dropped it in her apron pocket while she was giving us our sailing orders, and Jim got it all right, along with her shingle-nail, before noon. We were very well satisfied with this business, and Tom said it was worth twice the trouble it took. He said that _now_ she could never count those spoons the same way twice to save her life, and wouldn’t believe she’d counted them right even if she _did;_ and that after she’d just about counted her head off for the next three days, he figured she’d give it up and offer to kill anybody who ever asked her to count them again.

So that night we hung the sheet back on the clothesline and swiped another one out of her closet. We kept putting it back and stealing it again for a couple of days, until she lost track of how many sheets she had. By then she didn’t _care_ anymore, and she wasn’t going to worry herself sick over it, and she wouldn’t count them again for anything in the world. She’d rather die first.

So now we were in good shape with the shirt and the sheet and the spoon and the candles, thanks to the calf and the rats and all that mixed-up counting. As for the candlestick, it didn’t matter much, and it would blow over sooner or later.

But that pie was a real job. We had no end of trouble with it. We set up way down in the woods and cooked it there, and we got it done at last, and it turned out very well, too. But it took more than one day, and we used up three washpans full of flour before we were through. We got burned pretty much all over, here and there, and the smoke nearly put our eyes out. You see, all we wanted was a crust, and we couldn’t get it propped up right, and it kept caving in. But of course we thought of the right way finally, which was to cook the ladder right inside the pie. So the second night we went in to Jim, tore the sheet up into little strips, and twisted them together, and long before daylight we had a lovely rope that you could have hung a person with. We pretended it took nine months to make.

In the forenoon we carried it down to the woods, but it wouldn’t fit into the pie. Since it was made from a whole sheet, there was enough rope for forty pies if we’d wanted them, with plenty left over for soup, or sausage, or anything else you like. We could have had a whole dinner out of it.

But we didn’t need it. All we needed was just enough for the pie, so we threw the rest away. We didn’t bake any of the pies in the washpan, because we were afraid the solder would melt. But Uncle Silas had a fine brass warming pan with a long wooden handle that he thought a great deal of, because it had belonged to one of his ancestors and had come over from England with William the Conqueror, in the _Mayflower_ or one of those early ships. It was hidden away in the attic with a lot of other old pots and things that were valuable, not because they were any good (they weren’t), but because they were relics, you know. We sneaked it out, in secret, and took it down there. It failed on the first pies, because we didn’t know how to use it, but it came up smiling on the last one. We lined it with dough, set it in the coals, loaded it up with the rag rope, put a dough roof on top, shut the lid, and piled hot embers over it. Then we stood off five feet, holding the long handle, cool and comfortable, and in fifteen minutes it turned out a pie that was a pleasure to look at. But anybody who ate it would want to bring along a couple of kegs of toothpicks. If that rope ladder wouldn’t cramp him down to business, I don’t know anything about what I’m talking about, and it would give him enough stomachache to last till next time, too.

Nat didn’t look when we put the witch pie in Jim’s pan. We put the three tin plates in the bottom of the pan, under the food, and so Jim got everything just fine. As soon as he was alone he broke into the pie, hid the rope ladder inside his straw mattress, scratched some marks on a tin plate, and threw it out of the window hole.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVIII — The Coat of Arms
paragraphs: Making those pens was a terribly tough job, and so was the saw, and Jim figured the inscription would be the toughest of all. That’s the one the prisoner has to scratch on the wall. But he had to have it. Tom said he’d _got_ to. There was never a state prisoner who didn’t scratch his inscription to leave behind, along with his coat of arms.

“Look at Lady Jane Grey,” he says. “Look at Gilford Dudley. Look at old Northumberland! Why, Huck, suppose it _is_ a lot of trouble? What are you going to do about it? How are you going to get around it? Jim’s _got_ to do his inscription and his coat of arms. They all do.”
Jim says:
“Why, Mars Tom, I ain’t got no coat o’ arms. I ain’t got nuffin but dis here ole shirt, en you knows I got to keep de journal on dat.”
“Oh, you don’t understand, Jim. A coat of arms is something very different.”
“Well,” I says, “Jim’s got a point, anyhow, when he says he has no coat of arms. He hasn’t.”
“I reckon _I_ knew that,” Tom says, “but you bet he’ll have one before he leaves this place, because he’s going out _right_, and there won’t be any flaws in his record.”

So while Jim and I filed away at the pens, each of us with a brickbat, Jim making his out of the brass and me making mine out of the spoon, Tom set to work thinking up the coat of arms. After a while he said he’d come up with so many good ones he hardly knew which to take, but there was one he reckoned he’d settle on. He says:

“On the shield we’ll put a bend _or_ in the dexter base and a saltire _murrey_ in the fess, with a dog, couchant, as the common charge, and under his paw a chain embattled, standing for slavery. Then a chevron _vert_ in a chief engrailed, and three invected lines on a field _azure_, with the nombril points rampant on a dancette indented. For the crest, a runaway nigger, _sable_, bundle over his shoulder, on a bar sinister. Then a couple of gules for supporters, which is you and me. The motto is _Maggiore fretta, minore atto._ I got it out of a book, and it means the more haste, the less speed.”
“Geewhillikins,” I says, “and what in the world does all the rest of it mean?”
“We haven’t got time to bother with that,” he says. “We’ve got to dig in like all git-out.”
“Well, tell me just _some_ of it, then,” I says. “What’s a fess?”
“A fess is—well, a fess is—look, _you_ don’t need to know. I’ll show him how to make one when he gets to that part.”
“Aw, Tom,” I says, “you could just tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”
“Oh, _I_ don’t know that either. But he’s got to have one. Every nobleman does.”
That was Tom all over. When he didn’t feel like explaining something, he just wouldn’t, and you could pester him for a week without making any difference.

Now that he had the whole coat-of-arms business settled, he started in to finish the rest of that part of the work, which was to plan a mournful inscription. He said Jim had to have one, the same as they all did. He made up a bunch, wrote them out on a paper, and read them off, like this:
1. _Here a captive heart burst._
2. _Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and his friends, wasted away his sorrowful life._
3. _Here a lonely heart was broken, and a worn-out spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years alone in captivity._
4. _Here, with no home and no friends, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, a noble stranger perished, the natural son of Louis XIV._

Tom’s voice shook while he was reading them, and he nearly broke down. When he finished he couldn’t possibly decide which one Jim should scratch on the wall, they were all so good. But finally he allowed that Jim could scratch them all on. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch such a pile of stuff onto the logs with a nail, and besides, he didn’t know how to make letters. But Tom said he’d mark them out for him, and then all he’d have to do was follow the lines. Then pretty soon he says:
“Come to think of it, the logs won’t do. They don’t have log walls in a dungeon. We’ve got to cut the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll fetch a rock.”

Jim said the rock was worse than the logs. He said it would take him such an awful long time to cut them into a rock that he’d never get out. But Tom said he’d let me help him do it. Then he took a look to see how Jim and I were getting along with the pens. It was mighty tedious, hard work, and slow, and it gave my hands no chance to get over the sores, and we didn’t seem to be making any headway to speak of. So Tom says:

“I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the mournful inscriptions, and one rock can do both jobs. Down at the mill there’s a great big grindstone. We’ll swipe it, carve all the things on it, and file the pens and the saw on it, too.”

It was no bad idea, and it was no bad grindstone either, so we decided to tackle it. It wasn’t quite midnight yet, so we left Jim at work and headed for the mill. We swiped the grindstone and set out to roll it home, but it was an awfully tough job. Sometimes, no matter what we did, we couldn’t keep it from falling over, and it came close to mashing us every time. Tom said it was going to get one of us, sure, before we were through. We got it halfway, and then we were completely worn out and nearly drowned in sweat. We saw it was no use, and we’d have to go and fetch Jim. So he lifted up his bed and slid the chain off the bed leg, wrapped it round and round his neck, and we crawled out through our hole and went down there. Jim and I laid into that grindstone and walked it along like it was nothing, while Tom supervised. He could out-supervise any boy I ever saw. He knew how to do everything.

Our hole was pretty big, but not big enough for the grindstone. Jim grabbed the pick, though, and had it wide enough in no time. Then Tom marked the designs out on the stone with the nail and put Jim to work on them. The nail was his chisel, and his hammer was an iron bolt from the rubbish in the lean-to. Tom told him to keep at it until his candle burned out, and then go to bed, hide the grindstone under his straw mattress, and sleep on it. Then we helped him fasten his chain back on the bed leg, and we were ready for bed ourselves. But Tom thought of something, and says:
“You got any spiders in here, Jim?”
“No, sah, thank goodness I ain’t, Mars Tom.”
“All right, we’ll get you some.”
“But bless you, honey, I don’ _want_ none. I’s ’fraid o’ dem. I’d jis’ as soon have rattlesnakes aroun’.”
Tom thought for a minute or two, and says:
“That’s a fine idea. And I reckon somebody’s done it before. They _must_ have. It stands to reason. Yes, that’s a first-rate idea. Where would you keep it?”
“Keep what, Mars Tom?”
“Why, a rattlesnake.”
“Lord have mercy, Mars Tom! If a rattlesnake ever come in here, I’d go bustin’ right out thoo dat log wall, I would, haid first.”
“Why, Jim, after a little while you wouldn’t be afraid of it. You could tame it.”
“_Tame_ it!”

“Yes, and it’s easy. Every animal is thankful for kindness and petting, and not one of them would _think_ of hurting somebody who pets them. Any book will tell you so. Try it, that’s all I ask, for just two or three days. Why, before long you can get him to love you, and sleep with you, and never leave your side for a minute, and let you wind him around your neck and stick his head in your mouth.”

“_Please_, Mars Tom, _don_’ talk so! I can’t _stan’_ it! He’d _let_ me stick his head in my mouf, as a favor, would he? I bet he’d wait a powerful long time ’fo’ I _ast_ him. En on top o’ dat, I don’ _want_ him sleepin’ wid me.”

“Jim, quit being so silly. A prisoner’s _got_ to have some sort of dumb pet. And if nobody has ever tried a rattlesnake, then you’d win more glory by being the first one to do it than by anything else you could think of to save your life.”
“Mars Tom, I don’ _want_ no glory like dat. De snake bite Jim’s chin clean off, and den _whah_ is de glory? No, sah, I won’t have no sich doin’s.”
“Blame it, can’t you _try?_ I only _want_ you to try. You don’t have to keep it up if it doesn’t work.”

“But it’s all over fo’ me if dat snake bite me while I’s tryin’ him out. Mars Tom, I’ll tackle mos’ anything dat ain’t onreasonable, but if you en Huck bring a rattlesnake in here fo’ me to tame, I’s gwine to _leave_, and dat’s _shore_.”

“Well, then, forget it, forget it, if you’re going to be so pigheaded. We can get you some garter snakes instead. You can tie buttons on their tails and make believe they’re rattlesnakes, and I reckon that’ll have to do.”
“I can stan’ _dem_, Mars Tom, but I tell you, I could get along fine widout ’em. I never knowed befo’ it was so much bother en trouble to be a prisoner.”
“Well, it _always_ is, when it’s done properly. Are there any rats around here?”
“No, sah, I ain’t seen none.”
“Well, we’ll get you some rats.”

“Why, Mars Tom, I don’ _want_ no rats. Dey’s de dadblamedest creeturs to bother a body, en run aroun’ all over him, en bite his feet when he’s tryin’ to sleep, dat I ever see. No, sah, gimme garter snakes if I’s got to have ’em, but don’ gimme no rats. I ain’t got no use fo’ ’em, hardly.”

“But, Jim, you _got_ to have them. They all do. So don’t make any more fuss about it. Prisoners are never without rats. There isn’t a single case of it. And they train them, and pet them, and teach them tricks, and they get as friendly as flies. But you have to play music for them. You got anything to play music on?”
“I ain’t got nuffin but a coarse comb en a piece o’ paper, en a juice harp. But I reckon dey wouldn’ take no stock in a juice harp.”

“Sure they would. _They_ don’t care what kind of music it is. A jew’s harp is plenty good enough for a rat. All animals like music, and in a prison they just dote on it, especially painful music, and a jew’s harp can’t give you any other kind. It always interests them, and they come out to see what’s the matter with you. Yes, you’re all set, you’re fixed up fine. Sit on your bed at night before you go to sleep, and again early in the morning, and play your jew’s harp. Play ‘The Last Link Is Broken.’ That tune will pull in a rat quicker than anything. After you’ve played about two minutes, you’ll see all the rats and snakes and spiders and things start to worry about you, and come running. They’ll just fairly swarm all over you and have a grand time.”

“Yes, _dey_ will, I reckon, Mars Tom, but what kine o’ time is _Jim_ havin’? I’ll be blest if I kin see de good in it. But I’ll do it if I got to. Better keep de animals happy, I reckon, en have no trouble in de house.”
Tom waited and thought it over, to see if there wasn’t anything else, and pretty soon he says:
“Oh, I forgot one thing. Do you suppose you could grow a flower in here?”
“I don’ know, Mars Tom, maybe I could. But it’s tolable dark in heah, en I ain’ got no use fo’ no flower, nohow, en she’d be a powerful sight o’ trouble.”
“Well, try it anyway. Other prisoners have done it.”
“One o’ dem big mullen-stalks dat looks like a cat-tail would grow in heah, Mars Tom, I reckon, but she wouldn’t be wuth half de trouble she’d cost.”

“Don’t you believe it. We’ll bring you a little one, and you plant it in that corner over there and raise it. And don’t call it mullen. Call it Pitchiola, because that’s its proper name when it’s in a prison. And you’ve got to water it with your tears.”
“Why, I got plenty of spring water, Mars Tom.”
“You don’t _want_ spring water. You’ve got to water it with your tears. That’s how they always do it.”
“Why, Mars Tom, I bet you I kin raise one o’ dem mullen-stalks twice as fast on spring water as another man kin _start_ one on tears.”
“That ain’t the point. You _have_ to do it with tears.”
“She’ll die on my han’s, Mars Tom, she sholy will, kase I don’ hardly ever cry.”

That stumped Tom. But he thought it over and then said Jim would have to make do with an onion as best he could. He promised to slip down to the nigger cabins in the morning and drop one, private, in Jim’s coffee-pot. Jim said he’d “just as soon have tobacco in his coffee.” Then he found so much to complain about, between the work and bother of raising the mullen, and playing the jew’s harp for the rats, and petting and flattering the snakes and spiders and such, on top of all the other work he had to do on pens and inscriptions and journals and things, that being a prisoner was more trouble and worry and responsibility than anything he’d ever taken on. Tom nearly lost all patience with him. He said Jim had more fine chances loaded onto him than any prisoner ever had in the world to make a name for himself, and he didn’t know enough to appreciate them, so they were pretty much wasted on him. Jim felt sorry then, and said he wouldn’t carry on like that anymore. After that, Tom and I headed off to bed.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIX — Rats
paragraphs: In the morning we walked up to the village and bought a wire rat-trap and brought it back. We unstopped the best rat-hole, and in about an hour we had fifteen of the finest rats you ever saw. Then we put the trap in a safe place under Aunt Sally’s bed. But while we were off hunting spiders, little Thomas Franklin Benjamin Jefferson Elexander Phelps found it there and opened the door to see if the rats would come out, and they did. Aunt Sally came in, and when we got back she was standing on top of the bed raising Cain, while the rats did what they could to keep her from getting bored. So she took the hickory to both of us and dusted our jackets. Then it took us a good two hours to catch another fifteen or sixteen, drat that meddlesome cub, and they weren’t the best ones either, because the first haul had been the pick of the flock. I never saw a finer lot of rats than that first haul.

We got a splendid stock of assorted spiders and bugs and frogs and caterpillars and one thing and another. We nearly got a hornet’s nest too, but we didn’t. The family was at home. We didn’t give up right away but stuck with them as long as we could, figuring either we’d tire them out or they’d tire us out, and they did. Then we got some allycumpain and rubbed it on the spots, and we were just about all right again, except we couldn’t sit down comfortably. So then we went after the snakes, and we grabbed a couple of dozen garter snakes and house snakes and put them in a bag and left it in our room. By then it was suppertime, and we’d put in a rattling good honest day’s work. Hungry? Oh, no, I reckon not! And when we went back up, there wasn’t a blessed snake in the bag. We hadn’t tied the sack half tight, and they’d worked their way out and left. But it didn’t matter much, because they were still somewhere on the premises, so we figured we could get some of them again. No, there was no real shortage of snakes around that house for quite a while. You’d see them dripping from the rafters and other places every now and then, and they usually landed in your plate or down the back of your neck, and mostly where you didn’t want them. Well, they were handsome and striped, and there wasn’t any harm in a million of them. But that made no difference to Aunt Sally. She despised snakes, whatever the breed, and she couldn’t stand them any way you could fix it. Every time one of them flopped down on her, it didn’t matter what she was doing, she would drop that work and light out. I never saw such a woman. You could hear her whoop all the way to Jericho. You couldn’t get her to pick one up with the tongs. And if she turned over in bed and found one there, she’d scramble out and let out a howl that would make you think the house was on fire. She upset the old man so much that he said he could almost wish there had never been any snakes created. Why, even after every last snake had been gone from the house for a whole week, Aunt Sally wasn’t over it yet. She was nowhere near over it. When she was sitting there thinking about something, you could touch the back of her neck with a feather and she’d jump right out of her stockings. It was very curious. But Tom said all women were just like that. He said they were made that way for some reason or other.

We got a whipping every time one of our snakes crossed her path, and she said those whippings were nothing compared to what she’d do if we ever filled the place with them again. I didn’t mind the whippings, because they didn’t amount to anything. What I minded was the trouble of laying in another supply. But we got them in, and all the other creatures too, and you never saw a cabin as cheerful as Jim’s when they all swarmed out for the music and went for him. Jim didn’t like the spiders, and the spiders didn’t like Jim, so they’d lie in wait for him and make it mighty hot for him. He said that between the rats and the snakes and the grindstone there was hardly any room left in the bed for him, and when there was, a body couldn’t sleep, it was so lively. It was always lively, he said, because _they_ never all slept at the same time but took turns. When the snakes were asleep, the rats were on deck, and when the rats turned in, the snakes came on watch. So he always had one gang under him, in his way, and the other gang having a circus over him, and if he got up to hunt for a new place, the spiders would take a chance at him as he crossed over. He said if he ever got out this time, he’d never be a prisoner again, not even for a salary.

Well, by the end of three weeks everything was in pretty good shape. The shirt had been sent in early, baked in a pie, and every time a rat bit Jim, he would get up and write a little in his journal while the ink was fresh. The pens were made, and the inscriptions and the rest were all carved on the grindstone. The bed-leg was sawed in two, and we had eaten up the sawdust, which gave us the most amazing stomachache. We figured we were all going to die, but we didn’t. It was the most undigestible sawdust I ever saw, and Tom said the same.

But like I was saying, we had all the work done at last, and we were all pretty worn out, Jim most of all. The old man had written a couple of times to the plantation below Orleans, asking them to come and get their runaway nigger, but he hadn’t gotten any answer, because there wasn’t any such plantation. So he decided he would advertise Jim in the St. Louis and New Orleans papers. When he mentioned the St. Louis ones, it gave me the cold shivers, and I saw we had no time to lose. So Tom said it was time for the nonnamous letters.
“What are those?” I says.

“They’re warnings, to let people know something’s up. It’s done one way sometimes and another way other times, but there’s always some spy lurking about who tips off the governor of the castle. When Louis XVI. was getting ready to light out of the Tooleries, it was a servant-girl who tipped them off. That’s a mighty good method, and so are the nonnamous letters, so we’ll use both. And the custom is for the prisoner’s mother to swap clothes with him. She stays behind, and he slips out wearing her dress. We’ll do that as well.”
“Hold on, Tom, why would we want to _warn_ anybody that something’s up? Let them figure it out themselves. That’s their lookout.”

“Yes, I know, but you can’t depend on them. That’s how they’ve acted from the very start. They left us to do _everything_. They’re so trusting and thick-headed they don’t notice anything at all. So if we don’t _give_ them notice, there won’t be anybody or anything to interfere with us, and then after all our hard work and trouble, this escape will go off perfectly flat. It won’t amount to anything. There won’t be anything _to_ it.”
“Well, as for me, Tom, that’s how I’d like it.”
“Shucks!” he says, and looked disgusted. So I says:
“I ain’t going to make any complaint. Whatever way suits you suits me. But what are you going to do about the servant-girl?”
“That’s you. In the middle of the night you sneak in and lift that yaller girl’s frock.”
“Why, Tom, that’ll cause trouble the next morning, because she probably don’t have any but that one.”
“I know. But you’ll only need it for fifteen minutes, long enough to carry the nonnamous letter and push it under the front door.”
“All right, then, I’ll do it. But I could carry it just as easy in my own clothes.”
“You wouldn’t look like a servant-girl _then_, would you?”
“Maybe not, but nobody’s going to see how I look, _anyhow_.”
“That has nothing to do with it. All we have to do is our _duty_, and not worry about whether anybody _sees_ us do it or not. Don’t you have any principle at all?”
“Fine, I won’t say another word. I’ll be the servant-girl. Who plays Jim’s mother?”
“I’m his mother. I’ll swipe a gown from Aunt Sally.”
“Well, that means you’ll have to stay behind in the cabin once me and Jim get out.”

“Not on your life. I’ll pack Jim’s clothes with straw and lay them on his bed, and that stands for his mother in disguise. Jim will take the nigger woman’s gown off me and put it on, and then all of us will evade together. A prisoner of style doesn’t escape, he evades. That’s what it’s always called when a king gets away, for instance. Same goes for a king’s son, and it doesn’t matter whether he’s a natural one or an unnatural one.”
So Tom wrote the nonnamous letter. That night I snatched the yaller wench’s frock, put it on, and pushed the letter under the front door, just as Tom had told me to. It read:
_Look out. Something bad is cooking. Keep your eyes open._ UNKNOWN FRIEND

The next night we stuck up a picture of a skull and crossbones, which Tom drew in blood, on the front door, and the night after that, one of a coffin on the back door. I never saw a family in such a sweat. They couldn’t have been more scared if the place had been full of ghosts lying in wait behind everything and under the beds and shivering through the air. If a door banged, Aunt Sally jumped and said “ouch!” If anything fell, she jumped and said “ouch!” If you happened to touch her when she wasn’t noticing, she did the same. She couldn’t face in any direction and be satisfied, because she figured there was something behind her every time, so she was always whirling around suddenly and saying “ouch,” and before she’d gotten two-thirds of the way around, she’d whirl back and say it again. She was afraid to go to bed, but she didn’t dare sit up. So the thing was working very well, Tom said. He said he never saw anything work more satisfactorily. He said it showed it was done right.

Then he said it was time for the grand finale! So the very next morning, at the crack of dawn, we got another letter ready. We were wondering what to do with it, because we’d heard them say at supper that they were going to put a nigger on watch at both doors all night. Tom climbed down the lightning-rod to spy around, and the nigger at the back door was asleep, so he stuck the letter in the back of his neck and came back. This letter said:

Do not give me away, I want to be your friend. A desprate gang of cutthroats from over in the Indian Territory is going to steal your runaway nigger tonight. They have been scaring you on purpose so you will stay inside the house and leave them be. I am one of that gang, but I have got religgion and want to quit and live honest again, so I will tell you their helish plan. They will creep down from the north along the fence at midnight exact, with a false key, and go into the nigger’s cabin to take him. I am supposed to hang back and blow a tin horn if I see any danger. But instead I will BA like a sheep once they are in, and not blow at all. Then while they are working his chains loose, you slip over and lock them in, and can kill them at your leasure. Do just what I tell you and nothing else, or they will suspicion something and raise whoop-jamboreehoo. I want no reward, only to know I did right.
UNKNOWN FRIEND

chapters.title: Chapter XL — Fishing
paragraphs: After breakfast we were feeling pretty good. We took my canoe across the river to go fishing, packed a lunch, and had a fine time. We looked in on the raft and found her fine, and we got home late for supper. The family was in such a sweat and worry they didn’t know which end was up. The minute we finished eating, they sent us straight to bed, wouldn’t tell us what the trouble was, and never breathed a word about the new letter. They didn’t have to, because we knew as much about it as anybody. We got halfway up the stairs, her back turned, and then slid off to the cellar cupboard, loaded up a good lunch, and carried it to our room. We went to bed and got up around half-past eleven. Tom put on Aunt Sally’s dress that he’d stolen and was about to leave with the lunch, but then he says:
“Where’s the butter?”
“I set a hunk of it out,” I says, “on a piece of corn-pone.”
“Well, you _left_ it there, then. It ain’t here.”
“We can get along without it,” I says.

“We can get along _with_ it, too,” he says. “Run down to the cellar and get it. Then scoot down the lightning-rod and come on. I’m going to stuff straw into Jim’s clothes so it looks like his mother in disguise, and I’ll be set to _ba_ like a sheep and clear out the second you get there.”

So he went out, and I went down to the cellar. The lump of butter, as big as a person’s fist, was right where I’d left it. I picked up the slab of corn-pone with the butter on top, blew out my light, and started back upstairs, real sneaky. I reached the main floor without a hitch, but then here came Aunt Sally with a candle. I shoved the stuff into my hat and jammed the hat on my head, and the very next second she spotted me. She said:
“Have you been down in the cellar?”
“Yes’m.”
“What were you doing down there?”
“Nothing.”
“_Nothing!_”
“No’m.”
“Well, then, what got into you, going down there at this time of night?”
“I don’t know, ma’am.”
“You don’t _know?_ Don’t you answer me like that. Tom, I want to know just what you were _doing_ down there.”
“I haven’t been doing a single thing, Aunt Sally, I hope to goodness I haven’t.”

I figured she’d let me go now, and most times she would have. But I suppose with so many strange goings-on, she was in a lather over every little thing that wasn’t straight as a yardstick. So she said, very firmly:
“You march right into that sitting room and stay there until I come. You’ve been up to something you had no business doing, and I’ll find out what it is before _I’m_ through with you.”

Then she left, and I opened the door and walked into the sitting room. My, what a crowd was in there! Fifteen farmers, and every one of them held a gun. I felt awfully sick. I slunk over to a chair and sat down. They were sitting around, a few of them talking a little in low voices, and all of them fidgety and uneasy and trying not to look it. But I could tell they were, because they kept taking their hats off and putting them back on, and scratching their heads, and moving to different seats, and fiddling with their buttons. I wasn’t easy myself, but I kept my hat on, just the same.

How I wished Aunt Sally would come and be done with me. She could whip me if she wanted, so long as she let me get away and tell Tom how we’d gone too far with this business, and what a terrible hornet’s nest we’d landed in. Then we could quit our foolishness right then and clear out with Jim before these rough fellows ran out of patience and came after us.

At last she came and started asking me questions, but I _couldn’t_ answer them straight. I didn’t know which end of me was up. The men were in such a stew by now that some wanted to go right _now_ and lie in wait for those desperadoes, saying it was only a few minutes to midnight, while others tried to talk them into holding on and waiting for the sheep signal. And there was Aunty, pecking away with her questions, and me shaking all over and ready to sink right through the floor I was so scared. The room kept getting hotter and hotter, and the butter began to melt and run down my neck and behind my ears. Then one of them said, “_I’m_ for going and getting in the cabin _first_, right _now_, and catching them when they come,” and I nearly dropped. A streak of butter came trickling down my forehead, and Aunt Sally saw it, turned white as a sheet, and said:
“For heaven’s sake, what _is_ the matter with the child? He’s got brain fever as sure as you’re born, and they’re oozing out!”
Everybody ran to look, and she snatched off my hat, and out came the bread and what was left of the butter. She grabbed me and hugged me, and said:

“Oh, what a scare you gave me! And how glad and thankful I am that it’s no worse. Luck’s been against us, and it never rains but it pours, and when I saw that stuff I thought we’d lost you, because by the color I knew it was just what your brains would look like if—Dear, dear, why didn’t you _tell_ me that’s what you’d gone down there for? _I_ wouldn’t have cared. Now clear out to bed, and don’t let me see another sight of you till morning!”

I was upstairs in a second, and down the lightning-rod in another, and then I was hurrying through the dark toward the lean-to. I could hardly get my words out, I was so worried, but I told Tom as fast as I could that we had to jump for it right now, with not a minute to lose—the house was full of men over there, with guns!
His eyes just blazed, and he said:
“No! Is that so? _Ain’t_ it grand! Why, Huck, if I could do it over again, I bet I could bring in two hundred! If we could put it off till—”
“Hurry! _Hurry!_” I said. “Where’s Jim?”
“Right beside you. Stretch out your arm and you’ll touch him. He’s dressed, and everything is ready. Now we’ll slip out and give the sheep signal.”
But right then we heard men tramping up to the door. They started fumbling with the padlock, and one of them said:

“I _told_ you we’d be too early. They haven’t come yet—the door is locked. Here, I’ll lock some of you inside the cabin, and you can wait for them in the dark and kill them when they come. The rest of you spread out a little way and listen for them coming.”

So in they came, but they couldn’t see us in the dark, and they nearly stepped on us while we scrambled under the bed. But we got under all right, and out through the hole, quick but quiet—Jim first, me next, and Tom last, which was how Tom had ordered it. Now we were in the lean-to, and we could hear footsteps close by outside. So we crept to the door, and Tom stopped us there and put his eye to the crack, but he couldn’t make out anything, it was so dark. He whispered that he would listen until the footsteps moved farther off, and when he nudged us, Jim was to slip out first and him last. So he put his ear to the crack and listened, and listened, and listened, with the footsteps scraping around out there the whole time. At last he nudged us, and we slid out and crouched down, not breathing and not making the slightest noise, and slipped quietly toward the fence in single file. We reached it all right, and Jim and I got over, but Tom’s pants caught fast on a splinter on the top rail. Then he heard the footsteps coming, so he had to yank himself loose, which snapped the splinter and made a noise. And as he dropped down beside us and we started to run, somebody shouted:
“Who’s that? Answer, or I’ll shoot!”
But we didn’t answer. We just picked up our heels and ran. Then there was a rush, and a _bang, bang, bang!_ and the bullets whizzed all around us! We heard them shout:
“Here they are! They’ve made a break for the river! After them, boys, and let the dogs loose!”

So here they came, running full tilt. We could hear them because they wore boots and yelled, but we wore no boots and didn’t yell. We were on the path to the mill, and when they got pretty close behind us, we ducked into the bushes and let them go by, then fell in behind them. They’d kept all the dogs shut up so they wouldn’t scare off the robbers, but by now somebody had let them loose, and here they came, making enough racket for a million. But they were our own dogs, so we stood still until they caught up. When they saw it was nobody but us, with no excitement to offer them, they just said hello and tore on ahead toward the shouting and clattering. Then we got going again and raced along behind them until we were almost at the mill, and then cut up through the bushes to where my canoe was tied. We hopped in and paddled for dear life toward the middle of the river, making no more noise than we had to. Then we set off, nice and easy, for the island where my raft was, and we could hear them yelling and barking at each other all up and down the bank, until we were so far away that the sounds grew faint and died out. And when we stepped onto the raft, I said:
“_Now_, old Jim, you’re a free man _again_, and I bet you’ll never be a slave anymore.”
“En a mighty fine job it wuz, too, Huck. It wuz planned beautiful, en it wuz _done_ beautiful. Dey ain’t _nobody_ kin come up wid a plan mo’ mixed-up en splendid den dat one wuz.”
Everyone was as happy as could be, but Tom was happiest of all, on account of the bullet sitting in the calf of his leg.

When Jim and I heard that, we didn’t feel so cocky as before. It was hurting him a good deal, and bleeding, so we laid him down in the wigwam and tore up one of the duke’s shirts to bandage him. But he said:

“Give me the rags; I can do it myself. Don’t stop now, don’t fool around here, with the escape going along so handsomely. Man the sweeps and set her loose! Boys, we did it elegantly—indeed we did. I wish _we’d_ been in charge of Louis XVI. There wouldn’t have been any ‘Son of Saint Louis, ascend to heaven!’ written in _his_ biography. No, sir, we’d have whooped him over the _border_—that’s what we’d have done with _him_—and done it as slick as nothing at all, too. Man the sweeps—man the sweeps!”
But Jim and I were talking it over—and thinking. And after we’d thought for a minute, I said:
“Say it, Jim.”
So he said:

“Well, den, here’s how it look to me, Huck. Ef it wuz _him_ dat wuz gittin’ set free, en one er de boys got shot, would he say, ‘Go on en save me, never mind ’bout a doctor fer dis one’? Is dat like Mars Tom Sawyer? Would he say dat? You _bet_ he wouldn’t! _Well_, den, is _Jim_ gwine to say it? No, sah—I ain’t movin’ one step from dis place widout a _doctor;_ not if it’s forty year!”

I knew he was white inside, and I figured he’d say just what he did say. So it was settled, and I told Tom I was going for a doctor. He made a considerable fuss about it, but Jim and I stuck to our decision and wouldn’t budge. So he started to crawl out and set the raft loose himself, but we wouldn’t let him. Then he gave us a piece of his mind, but it did no good.
Then, when he saw me getting the canoe ready, he said:

“Well, then, if you’re set on going, I’ll tell you what to do when you get to the village. Shut the door and blindfold the doctor tight, and make him swear to be silent as the grave, and put a purse full of gold in his hand. Then lead him all around the back alleys and everywhere in the dark, and bring him here in the canoe, by a roundabout way among the islands. Search him and take his chalk away, and don’t give it back until you have him back at the village, or else he’ll chalk this raft so he can find it again. It’s what they all do.”
So I said I would, and left. Jim was to hide in the woods when he saw the doctor coming, and stay there until the doctor was gone again.

chapters.title: Chapter XLI — The Doctor
paragraphs: The doctor was an old man, a very nice, kind-looking old man, when I got him out of bed. I told him my brother and I had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and had camped on a piece of a raft we found. Around midnight he must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go over there and fix it, and not say anything about it or let anybody know, because we wanted to come home this evening and surprise the family.
“Who are your people?” he asked.
“The Phelpses, down yonder.”
“Oh,” he said. And after a minute, he said:
“How did you say he got shot?”
“He had a dream,” I said, “and it shot him.”
“Strange dream,” he said.
So he lit his lantern and got his saddlebags, and we set off. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like the look of her. He said she was big enough for one, but didn’t look very safe for two. I said:
“Oh, you needn’t be afraid, sir. She carried the three of us easily.”
“What three?”
“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and _the guns;_ that’s what I meant.”
“Oh,” he said.

But he put his foot on the edge and rocked her, and shook his head, and said he thought he’d look around for a bigger one. But they were all locked and chained. So he took my canoe and told me to wait until he came back, or I could look around further, or maybe I’d better go home and get everyone ready for the surprise, if I wanted. But I said I didn’t want to. So I told him exactly how to find the raft, and then he set off.

Pretty soon I hit on an idea. I said to myself, suppose he can’t fix that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying goes? Suppose it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do? Just lie around there until he lets the cat out of the bag? No, sir. I know what _I’ll_ do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back, if he says he has to go there again, I’ll go down there too, even if I have to swim. We’ll tie him up and keep him, and shove off down the river. And when Tom is done with him, we’ll pay him what it’s worth, or everything we’ve got, and then let him get ashore.

Then I crept into a lumber pile to get some sleep, and when I woke up next, the sun was high over my head! I shot out and headed for the doctor’s house, but they told me he’d gone off sometime in the night and hadn’t come back yet. Well, I thought, that looks mighty bad for Tom, and I’ll dig out for the island right away. So off I went, turned the corner, and nearly rammed my head into Uncle Silas’s stomach! He said:
“Why, _Tom!_ Where have you been all this time, you rascal?”
“_I_ haven’t been anywhere,” I said, “only out hunting for the runaway nigger—me and Sid.”
“Why, where on earth did you go?” he said. “Your aunt has been terribly worried.”

“She needn’t be,” I said, “because we were fine. We followed the men and the dogs, but they outran us and we lost them. We thought we heard them on the water, though, so we got a canoe and set out after them and crossed over. We couldn’t find any sign of them, so we cruised up the shore until we got kind of tired and worn out. Then we tied up the canoe and went to sleep, and didn’t wake up until about an hour ago. Then we paddled over here to hear the news. Sid’s at the post office to see what he can find out, and I’m off to get us something to eat, and then we’re going home.”

So then we went to the post office to get “Sid,” but just as I suspected, he wasn’t there. The old man picked up a letter at the office, and we waited a while longer, but Sid didn’t come. So the old man said, come along, and let Sid walk home, or canoe it, when he was done fooling around—but we would ride. I couldn’t get him to let me stay and wait for Sid. He said there was no use in it, and I had to come along and let Aunt Sally see that we were all right.

When we got home, Aunt Sally was so glad to see me that she laughed and cried at the same time, and hugged me, and gave me one of those whippings of hers that don’t amount to a thing. She said she’d give Sid the same when he showed up.

The house was packed with farmers and their wives, all there for dinner, and you never heard such a racket in your life. Old Mrs Hotchkiss was the worst of the lot; her tongue never stopped for a second. She says:

“Well, Sister Phelps, I’ve gone through that whole cabin, and I do believe the nigger was crazy. I said so to Sister Damrell—didn’t I, Sister Damrell?—I said, he’s crazy, I said. Those are the very words I said. You all heard me: he’s crazy, I said; everything shows it, I said. Look at that grindstone, I said; are you telling _me_ that anybody in his right mind is going to scratch all those crazy things onto a grindstone, I said? Here’s so-and-so who broke his heart; and here’s such-and-such who pegged along for thirty-seven years, and all that—natural son of Louis somebody, and all that endless rubbish. He’s plumb crazy, I said; that’s what I said in the first place, that’s what I said in the middle, and that’s what I say last and all the time—the nigger’s crazy—crazy as Nebokoodneezer, I said.”
“And look at that ladder made out of rags, Sister Hotchkiss,” says old Mrs Damrell. “What in the name of goodness could he ever want with—”

“Those are the very words I was saying not a minute ago to Sister Utterback, and she’ll tell you so herself. Look at that rag ladder, she said, and I said, yes, _look_ at it, I said—what could he have wanted with it, I said. Sister Hotchkiss, she said, she said—”
“But how in the world did they ever _get_ that grindstone _in_ there, anyway? And who dug that _hole?_ And who—”

“My very _words_, Brother Penrod! I was saying—pass that saucer of molasses, will you?—I was saying to Sister Dunlap just this minute, how _did_ they get that grindstone in there, I said. Without _help_, mind you—without _help! That’s_ the point. Don’t tell _me_, I said; there _was_ help, I said, and a _good deal_ of help, too, I said; there’s been a _dozen_ helping that nigger, and I swear I’d skin every last nigger on this place to find out who did it, I said; and what’s more, I said—”

“A _dozen_, you say!—_forty_ couldn’t have done everything that’s been done. Look at those case-knife saws and the like, and how slow and hard that work must have been; look at that bed-leg sawed through with them, a week’s work for six men; look at that nigger made of straw lying in the bed; and look at—”

“You may _well_ say so, Brother Hightower! It’s just what I was telling Brother Phelps himself. He says to me, what do _you_ think of it, Sister Hotchkiss? Think of what, Brother Phelps, I said. Think of that bed-leg sawed off like that, he says? _Think_ of it, I said? I bet it never sawed _itself_ off, I said—somebody _sawed_ it, I said; that’s my opinion, take it or leave it, it may not count for much, I said, but such as it is, it’s my opinion, I said, and if anybody can come up with a better one, I said, let him _do_ it, I said, that’s all. I said to Sister Dunlap, I said—”

“Why, dog my cats, there must have been a house full of niggers in there every night for four weeks to do all that work, Sister Phelps. Look at that shirt—every last inch of it covered with secret African writing done in blood! There must have been a whole crowd of them at it the entire time. Why, I’d give two dollars to have it read to me; and as for the niggers that wrote it, I reckon I’d take and whip them till—”

“People to _help_ him, Brother Marples! Well, I expect you’d _think_ so if you’d been in this house lately. Why, they’ve stolen everything they could lay their hands on—and us watching the whole time, mind you. They stole that shirt right off the line! And that sheet they made the rag ladder from, there’s no telling how many times they _didn’t_ steal it; and flour, and candles, and candlesticks, and spoons, and the old warming-pan, and about a thousand things I can’t remember now, and my new calico dress; and me and Silas and my Sid and Tom keeping constant watch day _and_ night, as I was telling you, and not one of us could catch hide nor hair nor sight nor sound of them; and then at the last minute, what do you know, they slip right in under our noses and fool us, and not just _us_ but the Injun Territory robbers too, and really do get _away_ with that nigger safe and sound, with sixteen men and twenty-two dogs right on their heels at that very moment! I tell you, it beats anything I ever _heard_ of. Why, _spirits_ couldn’t have done better or been any smarter. And I reckon they must have _been_ spirits—because you know our dogs, and there are none better; well, those dogs never even got on the _trail_ of them once! You explain _that_ to me if you can!—_any_ of you!”
“Well, that does beat—”
“Lord have mercy, I never—”
“So help me, I wouldn’t have—”
“_House_-thieves as well as—”
“Goodness gracious, I’d have been afraid to _live_ in such a—”

“Afraid to _live!_—why, I was so scared I hardly dared go to bed, or get up, or lie down, or _sit_ down, Sister Ridgeway. Why, they’d steal the very—well, goodness, you can guess what kind of a fluster _I_ was in by the time midnight came last night. I declare to gracious, I was afraid they’d steal some of the family! I got to the point where I had no reasoning left in me at all. It looks foolish enough _now_, in the daytime; but I said to myself, there are my two poor boys asleep, way up the stairs in that lonesome room, and I declare to goodness I was so uneasy that I crept up there and locked them in! I _did_. And anybody would. Because, you know, when you get scared like that, and it keeps going on and getting worse and worse, and your wits get all muddled, and you start doing all sorts of wild things, and before long you think to yourself, suppose _I_ was a boy, and was up there, and the door isn’t locked, and you—” She stopped, looking kind of wondering, and then she turned her head around slowly, and when her eye landed on me—I got up and took a walk.

I said to myself, I could explain better how come we weren’t in that room this morning if I went off to one side and thought it over a little. So I did. But I didn’t dare go far, or she’d have sent for me. Late in the day the people all left, and then I came in and told her that the noise and shooting woke up me and “Sid,” and the door was locked, and we wanted to see the fun, so we went down the lightning-rod, and both of us got hurt a little, and we never wanted to try _that_ again. Then I went on and told her everything I’d told Uncle Silas before; and then she said she’d forgive us, and maybe it was all right anyway, and about what you might expect from boys, since all boys were a pretty harum-scarum lot as far as she could see; and so, as long as no harm had come of it, she figured she’d better spend her time being grateful we were alive and well and she still had us, instead of fretting over what was past and done. Then she kissed me, and patted me on the head, and fell into a kind of brown study; and pretty soon she jumps up and says:
“Why, mercy me, it’s nearly night, and Sid not here yet! What _has_ become of that boy?”
I saw my chance, so I hop up and say:
“I’ll run right up to town and get him,” I say.
“Oh no you won’t,” she says. “Stay put, right here. One lost boy at a time is plenty. If he hasn’t turned up by suppertime, your uncle will go looking.”
Well, he wasn’t there by supper; so right after supper Uncle went.

He got back around ten, a little worried; there was no sign of Tom anywhere. Aunt Sally was a good _deal_ worried. Uncle Silas told her there was nothing to fuss about—boys are boys, he said, and this one would come strolling in by morning, safe and sound. She had to make do with that. But she said she would wait up for him a while regardless, and keep a light burning so he could see it.

Later, when I went up to bed, she climbed the stairs with me, candle in hand, and tucked me in, and fussed over me so kindly that I felt low-down and couldn’t look her in the eye. She sat on the edge of the bed and talked to me for a long while, about what a splendid boy Sid was, and she didn’t seem able to stop. Again and again she asked whether I thought he might have gotten lost, or hurt, or maybe drowned, and might be lying out there this very minute, suffering or dead, with her not beside him to help; and the tears would slide down her face without a sound. I would tell her Sid was fine and would be home in the morning, sure, and she would squeeze my hand, or maybe kiss me, and make me say it again and keep saying it, because it comforted her, and she was in such distress. When she was leaving she looked into my eyes, so steady and gentle, and says:
“Tom, I won’t lock your door, and there’s the window and the lightning-rod. But you’ll be good, won’t you? You won’t slip off? Do it for _me_.”
Lord knows I _wanted_ to go, badly enough, to find out about Tom, and was fully planning to; but after that I wouldn’t have gone, not for kingdoms.

But she was on my mind and Tom was on my mind, so I slept very restlessly. Twice in the night I went down the rod and slipped around to the front, and saw her sitting there by her candle in the window, her eyes toward the road and tears in them; and I wished I could do something for her, but I couldn’t, except swear that I’d never do anything to grieve her again. The third time I woke up at dawn and slid down, and she was still there, and her candle was nearly out, and her old gray head was resting on her hand, and she was asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter XLII — Tom Sawyer Wounded
paragraphs: The old man was back in town before breakfast, but he couldn’t get any trace of Tom; and the two of them sat at the table thinking, saying nothing, looking mournful, their coffee going cold, and not eating anything. After a while the old man says:
“Did I give you the letter?”
“What letter?”
“The one I got yesterday at the post office.”
“No, you didn’t give me any letter.”
“Well, I must have forgotten it.”
So he searched his pockets, then went off to wherever he’d laid it down, fetched it, and gave it to her. She says:
“Why, it’s from St. Petersburg—it’s from Sis.”

I thought a second walk might do me good, but my legs wouldn’t move. She had barely started to open the letter when she dropped it and ran, because she had seen something. So had I. There was Tom Sawyer lying on a mattress; and that old doctor; and Jim, wearing _her_ calico dress, hands tied behind his back; and a crowd of people. I stuffed the letter behind the first thing I could reach and ran out. She threw herself down over Tom, sobbing, and says:
“Oh, he’s dead, he’s dead, I know he’s dead!”
And Tom turned his head a little and muttered something, which showed he wasn’t in his right mind; then she flung up her hands and says:

“He’s alive, thank God! That’s all I need!” She snatched a kiss from him and flew off toward the house to ready the bed, shouting orders left and right to the niggers and everyone else, as fast as her tongue could go, with every step she took.

I followed the men to see what they meant to do with Jim, while the old doctor and Uncle Silas went into the house behind Tom. The men were in a foul temper, and some wanted to hang Jim as a lesson to every other nigger in the county, so none of them would try running off as Jim had, causing such a heap of trouble and scaring a whole family half to death for days and nights on end. But others said no, don’t do it, that won’t do at all; he isn’t our nigger, and his owner will show up and make us pay for him, sure. That cooled the hangers down some. The people who are always the most eager to hang a nigger for stepping out of line are the very same ones who are the least eager to pay for him after they’ve had their satisfaction.

They cussed Jim plenty, though, and gave him a cuff or two on the side of the head now and then, but Jim never said anything, and he never let on that he knew me. They took him to the same cabin, put his own clothes back on him, and chained him again—and not to a bed-leg this time, but to a big staple driven into the bottom log—and chained his hands too, and both legs. They said he wasn’t to have anything but bread and water to eat from now on until his owner came, or until he was sold at auction if the owner didn’t come within a certain time. They filled up our hole, and said a couple of farmers with guns must stand watch around the cabin every night, and a bulldog would be tied to the door in the daytime. About this time they were done with the job and were tapering off with a kind of general good-bye cussing, and then the old doctor comes and takes a look, and says:

“Don’t be any rougher on him than you have to be, because he ain’t a bad nigger. When I found the boy, I saw I couldn’t cut the bullet out without help, and he wasn’t in any shape for me to leave him and go fetch some. He got a little worse, then a little worse again, and after a long while he went out of his head. He wouldn’t let me come near him anymore, and said if I chalked his raft he’d kill me, and a whole lot of wild foolishness like that. So I saw I couldn’t do a thing with him, and I said to myself, I’ve got to have _help_ somehow. The minute I said it, this nigger crawls out from somewhere and says he’ll help, and he did, too, and did it very well. Of course I figured he must be a runaway nigger, and there I _was!_ I had to stay put right through the rest of the day and all night. It was a fix, I tell you! I had a couple of patients with the chills, and naturally I’d have liked to run up to town and look in on them, but I didn’t dare, because the nigger might get away, and then I’d be to blame. And yet not one skiff came close enough for me to hail. So I had to stay right there until daylight this morning. And I never saw a nigger who made a better nurse or was more faithful, and all the while he was risking his freedom to do it, and he was worn out, too, and I could plainly see he’d been worked mighty hard lately. I liked the nigger for that. I tell you, gentlemen, a nigger like that is worth a thousand dollars—and kind treatment, too. I had everything I needed, and the boy was doing as well there as he would have at home—better, maybe, because it was so quiet. But there I _was_, with the two of them on my hands, and I had to stay until about dawn this morning. Then some men in a skiff came by, and as luck would have it, the nigger was sitting by the pallet with his head propped on his knees, sound asleep. So I waved them in quietly, and they crept up on him and grabbed him and tied him up before he knew what was happening, and we had no trouble at all. And since the boy was in a sort of feverish sleep too, we muffled the oars, hitched the raft on, and towed her across very nicely and quietly, and the nigger never made the least fuss or said a word from start to finish. He ain’t a bad nigger, gentlemen. That’s what I think of him.”
Somebody says:
“Well, it sounds very good, doctor, I have to say.”

Then the others softened up a little too, and I was mighty grateful to that old doctor for doing Jim such a good turn. I was glad it matched what I’d thought of him, too, because the first time I saw him I figured he had a good heart and was a good man. Then they all agreed that Jim had behaved very well and deserved some notice and a reward. So every one of them promised, right out and heartily, that they wouldn’t curse him anymore.

Then they came out and locked him up. I hoped they were going to say he could have one or two of the chains taken off, because they were awful heavy, or that he could have meat and greens with his bread and water. But they didn’t think of it, and I figured it wasn’t my place to butt in. Still, I judged I’d get the doctor’s story to Aunt Sally somehow, as soon as I’d got through the rough water lying just ahead of me—explanations, I mean, of how I’d forgotten to mention Sid being shot when I was telling how he and I spent that cursed night paddling around hunting the runaway nigger.
But I had plenty of time. Aunt Sally stayed in the sickroom all day and all night, and every time I saw Uncle Silas drifting around moping, I ducked out of his way.

The next morning I heard Tom was a good deal better, and they said Aunt Sally had gone to get some sleep. So I slipped into the sickroom, thinking that if I found him awake we could cook up a story for the family that would hold water. But he was asleep, and sleeping very peacefully, and pale, not red-faced with fever the way he was when he came. So I sat down and waited for him to wake up. In about half an hour Aunt Sally came gliding in, and there I was, in a tight spot again! She motioned for me to keep still, sat down next to me, and started whispering. She said we could all be happy now, because all the signs were first-rate, and he’d been sleeping like that for ever so long, looking better and more peaceful all the time, and ten to one he’d wake up in his right mind.
So we sat there watching, and after a while he stirred a bit, opened his eyes in a natural way, took a look around, and said:
“Hello!—why, I’m at _home!_ How come? Where’s the raft?”
“It’s all right,” I says.
“And _Jim?_”
“The same,” I says, though I couldn’t say it very boldly. But he didn’t notice, and says:
“Great! Wonderful! _Now_ we’re in the clear and out of danger! Have you told Aunty yet?”
I was about to say yes, but she cut in and says: “Tell me what, Sid?”
“Why, about how the whole thing was done.”
“What whole thing?”
“Why, _the_ whole thing. There’s only one: how we set the runaway nigger free—Tom and me.”
“Good land! Set the run— What on earth is the child babbling about! Dear, dear, his mind’s wandering again!”

“_No_, I ain’t out of my HEAD. I know exactly what I’m talking about. We _did_ set him free—Tom and me. We planned to do it, and we _did_ it. And we did it elegantly, too.” He’d got a running start, and she never stopped him. She just sat and stared and stared and let him rattle on, and I saw it was no use for _me_ to put in a word. “Why, Aunty, it cost us a power of work—weeks of it—hours and hours, every night, while you were all asleep. And we had to steal candles, and the sheet, and the shirt, and your dress, and spoons, and tin plates, and case knives, and the warming pan, and the grindstone, and flour, and just no end of things. You can’t imagine what work it was to make the saws, and pens, and inscriptions, and one thing and another, and you can’t imagine even _half_ the fun it was. And we had to make up the pictures of coffins and such, and anonymous letters from the robbers, and climb up and down the lightning rod, and dig the hole into the cabin, and make the rope ladder and send it in baked in a pie, and send in spoons and things to work with in your apron pocket—”
“Mercy sakes!”

“—and stock the cabin with rats and snakes and such, to keep Jim company. And then you held Tom here so long, with the butter in his hat, that you almost ruined the whole business. The men showed up before we were out of the cabin, so we had to dash for it. They heard us and shot at us, and I took my share. We ducked off the path and let them go past, and when the dogs arrived they had no interest in us and ran after the loudest racket. We got to our canoe and paddled for the raft, and everything was safe, and Jim was a free man, and we’d pulled it off all by ourselves, and _wasn’t_ it bully, Aunty!”

“Well, in all my born days I never heard the like! So it was _you_, you little rapscallions, who’ve been causing all this trouble and turning everybody’s wits inside out and scaring us all half to death. I’ve as good a mind as I ever had in my life to take it out of you this very minute. To think of me, night after night, a—_you_ just get well, you young scamp, and I promise I’ll tan the Old Harry out of both of you!”

But Tom was so proud and joyful he just _couldn’t_ hold it in, and his tongue just _went_ at it, with her cutting in and spitting fire the whole time, and the two of them going at once, like a cat convention. And she says:
“_Well_, enjoy yourself all you can _now_, because let me tell you, if I ever catch you messing with him again—”
“Messing with _who?_” Tom says, and his grin drops away and he looks startled.
“With _who?_ Why, the runaway nigger, of course. Who did you think?”
Tom looks at me very gravely and says:
“Tom, you just said he was all right, didn’t you? He didn’t escape?”

“_Him?_” says Aunt Sally. “The runaway nigger? Of course he didn’t! They brought him back, safe and sound, and he’s locked in that cabin again on bread and water, weighed down with chains, until somebody claims him or he’s sold!”
Tom sat straight up in bed, his eyes blazing and his nostrils opening and closing like gills, and sings out to me:
“They’ve got no _right_ to shut him up! _Go!_—and don’t lose a minute. Turn him loose! He ain’t a slave. He’s as free as any creature that walks this earth!”
“What _does_ the child mean?”

“Every word I _say_ is the truth, Aunt Sally, and if nobody goes, then _I’ll_ go myself. I’ve known him my whole life, and Tom there has too. Old Miss Watson died two months back. She felt ashamed that she’d ever thought of selling him down the river, and she _said_ so, and she freed him in her will.”
“Then why in the world did _you_ go setting him free, when he was free already?”
“Well, now _there’s_ a question! And typical of a woman! I wanted the _adventure_ of it, that’s why. I’d have waded up to my neck in blood to—goodness alive, AUNT POLLY!”
There she stood, right inside the door, looking as sweet and satisfied as an angel who’d had a little too much pie. I swear I never saw the like!

Aunt Sally rushed at her and squeezed her half to pieces and wept all over her. I found myself a decent spot under the bed, since things were turning pretty hot for _us_, it seemed to me. I peeked out, and soon Tom’s Aunt Polly pulled free and stood gazing across at Tom over the top of her spectacles—sort of grinding him into the dirt, you know. And then she says:
“Yes, you _had_ better turn your head away—I would if I were you, Tom.”
“Oh, dear me!” says Aunt Sally. “_Is_ he so changed? Why, that ain’t _Tom_, it’s Sid. Tom’s—Tom’s—why, where is Tom? He was here a minute ago.”

“You mean where is Huck _Finn_—that’s who you mean! I haven’t brought up a rascal like my Tom all these years without knowing him on sight. That _would_ be a fine mess. Crawl out from under that bed, Huck Finn.”
So I did. But I didn’t feel bold about it.

Aunt Sally was one of the most mixed-up-looking persons I ever saw—except one, and that was Uncle Silas, when he came in and they told it all to him. It made him sort of drunk, you might say, and he didn’t know a thing for the rest of the day. That night he preached a prayer-meeting sermon that earned him a rattling reputation, because the oldest man in the world couldn’t have understood it. So Tom’s Aunt Polly told all about who I was and what I was. And I had to speak up and tell how I’d been in such a tight place that when Mrs. Phelps took me for Tom Sawyer—she cut in and says, “Oh, go on and call me Aunt Sally, I’m used to it now, and there’s no need to change”—that when Aunt Sally took me for Tom Sawyer, I had to put up with it, there was no other way. And I knew he wouldn’t mind, because it would be nuts for him, being a mystery, and he’d make an adventure out of it and be perfectly satisfied. And so it turned out, and he pretended to be Sid and made things as easy as he could for me.

And his Aunt Polly said Tom was right about old Miss Watson setting Jim free in her will. So, sure enough, Tom Sawyer had gone to all that trouble and bother to set a free nigger free! And until that minute and that talk, I never could understand how he could help a person set a nigger free, with the way he’d been brought up.
Well, Aunt Polly said that when Aunt Sally wrote to her that Tom and _Sid_ had arrived safe and sound, she said to herself:

“Would you look at that! I should have known better than to let him wander off with nobody keeping an eye on him. Now I have to tramp all the way down the river, eleven hundred miles, to find out what that creature’s up to _this_ time, since you never answered a thing I asked.”
“Why, I never heard anything from you,” says Aunt Sally.
“Well, imagine that! Why, I wrote to you twice, wanting to know what you meant by having Sid there.”
“Well, I never got them, Sis.”
Aunt Polly turns around, slow and stern, and says:
“You, Tom!”
“Well—_what?_” he says, kind of crabby.
“Don’t you ‘what’ _me_, you impudent thing—hand over those letters.”
“What letters?”
“_Those_ letters. I’ll be bound, if I have to take hold of you I’ll—”

“They’re in my trunk. There. They’re exactly as they were when I picked them up at the post office. I never opened them or touched them. But I knew they’d cause a fuss, and I figured if you weren’t in a hurry, I’d—”
“You certainly _do_ deserve a skinning, no doubt about it. And I sent one more to say I was on my way, and I suppose he—”
“No, that came yesterday. I haven’t read it yet, but _it’s_ all right, I’ve got that one.”
I wanted to offer to bet two dollars she hadn’t, but I figured it was maybe just as safe not to. So I didn’t say anything.

chapters.title: Chapter the Last
paragraphs: The first time I caught Tom in private, I asked him what his idea was, back at the time of the escape. What had he planned to do if the escape worked all right and he managed to set a nigger free who was already free? And he said what he’d had in his head from the start was this: if we got Jim out safe, we’d run him down the river on the raft and have adventures all the way to the mouth of the river. Then we’d tell him he was free, take him back home on a steamboat in style, pay him for his lost time, write ahead and get all the niggers around to waltz him into town with a torchlight procession and a brass band. Then he would be a hero, and so would we. But I figured it was about as well the way it was.

We had Jim out of the chains in no time. When Aunt Polly and Uncle Silas and Aunt Sally found out how well he’d helped the doctor nurse Tom, they made a big fuss over him, fixed him up fine, gave him all he wanted to eat and a good time, and nothing to do. We had him up to the sickroom and had a grand talk. Tom gave Jim forty dollars for being our prisoner so patiently and doing it so well, and Jim was pleased nearly to death, and burst out and says:

“_See_, now, Huck, what did I tell you? What did I tell you up there on Jackson’s island? I _told_ you I had a hairy chest, and what that’s a sign of. I _told_ you I was rich once, and gwine to be rich _again;_ and now it’s come true, and here it is! _See_, now! Don’t you talk to _me_—signs is _signs_, I’m telling you. And I knowed I was gwine to be rich again just as sure as I’s standin’ here this minute!”

Then Tom kept on talking and talking, and he said let’s all three sneak out of here one of these nights, get an outfit, and go off on some howling adventures among the Indians, over in the Territory, for a couple of weeks or so. I said all right, that suited me fine, but I didn’t have any money to buy the outfit, and I didn’t reckon I could get any from home, since Pap had likely come back by now, taken it all off Judge Thatcher, and drunk it up.
“No, he hasn’t,” Tom says. “It’s all still there—six thousand dollars and more—and your pap hasn’t been back since. He hadn’t when I came away, anyhow.”
Jim says, kind of solemn:
“He ain’t comin’ back no more, Huck.”
I says:
“Why not, Jim?”
“Never mind why, Huck—but he ain’t comin’ back no more.”
But I kept after him, until finally he says:

“Don’t you ’member dat house dat was floatin’ down de river, and dere was a man in dere, covered up, and I went in and uncovered him and wouldn’t let you come in? Well, den, you kin git yo’ money whenever you wants it, ’cause dat was him.”

Tom’s nearly well now. He wears his bullet around his neck on a watch chain, for a watch, and is always checking what time it is. So there ain’t anything more to write about, and I am awful glad of it, because if I’d knowed how much trouble it was to make a book, I wouldn’t have tackled it, and I ain’t gonna do it again. But I reckon I’ve got to light out for the Territory ahead of the others, because Aunt Sally’s fixing to adopt me and sivilize me, and I can’t stand it. I’ve been through that before.
THE END. YOURS TRULY, _HUCK FINN_.
